title: Firebreak
pitch: Fast incident response for browser agents, with exact human authority over every consequential action.
about_excerpt: Fast incident response for browser agents, with exact human authority over every consequential action. Like Comment Story Updates GIF Firebreak in five frames: investigate, block unsafe recovery, require exact human authorization, and verify the result. Firebreak Agentic demos ask: How much can the agent do? For incident response, I think the question becomes How much should it be allowed to do? Speed is useful. Standing authority is not. Firebreak separates the two. What it does Firebreak gives a browser agent nine intent-level WebMCP tools to investigate a checkout outage. The agent gathers evidence, correlates recent changes and tests recovery options. A payment-database restart gets rejected because it threatens protected outcomes: payments and accepted orders. Similarly, a safer checkout rollback becomes an Action Contract bound to the system state, evidence, blast radius, expiry, verification and compensation plan. The human authorises that exact contract. Only then can the agent execute. If state changes, the authority becomes stale. If execution is retried, it remains idempotent. If verification fails, compensation is required instead of declaring false success. The result is a complete chain: investigate - propose - authorise - execute - verify - receipt Why WebMCP Incident response is an incorrect place for agents to infer intent from pixels. It is urgent, stateful and potentially destructive. Firebreak exposes intent. The agent can inspect, simulate, prepare, execute and verify through narrow typed tools. The UI and WebMCP tools use the same deterministic application service, so there is no privileged agent path around the controls visible to the human, but one capability is deliberately missing: human authorisation . The agent can request authority, but it cannot grant authority to itself. Better human-agent collaboration The agent handles the repetitive work: investigation, correlation, simulation and proposal. The human makes the consequential decision. They see before approving anything. And the approval is not: “let the agent operate.” It's: this action, against this state, under these constraints.  That's the core of Firebreak. Intelligence can stay flexible. Authority should be precise. Who can use it The current implementation is a checkout recovery scenario, though the pattern extends to SRE, security, commerce, data and regulated operations where agents can investigate and prepare consequential work without receiving standing authority. The important abstraction is a proper roadmap from investigation to proposal - authority - execution - verification. Other domains would still require their own identity, provider adapters, telemetry, policy and tested rollback paths. How it was built Firebreak uses React and TypeScript with a deterministic domain engine. That engine owns revisioned state, protected outcomes, constraints, expiring Action Contracts, idempotent execution, verification, compensation and receipts. Nine WebMCP tools sit on top of the same service used by the human interface. Vitest, Playwright and deterministic journey fixtures test the system from foundation through workflow and stress cases. The demo requires no API key, cloud account or production credentials. Making approval mean something is harder. If state changes after approval, should the old approval still work? No. If execution retries, should the action happen twice? No. If the command runs but recovery fails, should we call it success? No. If the agent can approve itself, was there ever a human boundary? No. Firebreak turns those answers into system properties instead of UI promises. What we learned Agents do not need more buttons. They need better abstractions like Raw controls, implementation and intent-level tools for meaning. And once intent is explicit, we can attach evidence, policy, authority and verification to it. That makes agents easier to guide. Try it Live app: https://neel-error404.github.io/firebreak-webmcp/ Source: https://github.com/Neel-Error404/firebreak-webmcp The intended flow: inspect - correlate - reject unsafe recovery - prepare rollback - human authorisation - execute - verify - recept What's next Firebreak is a prototype; production would require signed identities, durable audit storage, isolated real connectors, stronger policy authoring, broader evaluations and staged deployment evidence. We want to explore & make capability bounded, legible and accountable. title: ExactDelta
pitch: A pre-release effect gate that proves a WebMCP write changed exactly what the human authorized—and nothing else.
about_excerpt: A pre-release effect gate that proves a WebMCP write changed exactly what the human authorized—and nothing else. Like Comment Story Updates Correct call. Wrong effect. Release blocked. The selected order changed—and so did one that was never selected. Repair the handler. Rerun the identical regression. Pass. One verification core, a second action class. Measured against Evals and Playwright. Install, bind, gate, and replay. Inspiration WebMCP gives browser agents a structured way to act on websites. That makes tool selection and argument validation easier to inspect—but a developer or QA engineer deciding whether a write tool can ship still needs evidence about its actual state transition. A handler can accept the right target, return success, and still mutate an unselected record. The WebMCP security discussion explicitly says a tool's declared intent is not guaranteed to match its behavior and that an agent cannot confirm the real effect from the description alone. Chrome's own Evals guidance recommends classic deterministic tests for UI updates and intentional side effects. ExactDelta makes that effect boundary generated, inspectable, and reusable instead of claiming to replace call evals or application tests. We wanted one failure to be understandable without background knowledge: the agent did everything right; the result was still wrong. Approval proves what an agent may attempt. ExactDelta proves what the application actually changed. Schemas validate arguments, approval gates authorize requests, and traces record calls. Those controls are necessary, but none establishes that the handler changed only the state the human authorized. ExactDelta begins at that missing post-action boundary. The target user is a developer or QA engineer shipping browser-agent writes into commerce, support, administration, or access-control workflows, where an accepted action can still alter the wrong order, permission, or customer record. ExactDelta turns that failure into a visible release decision and an executable repair regression rather than leaving the team to reconstruct it from a trace. What it does In an owned staging environment, the human selects one target in the application UI. Before the action, ExactDelta turns that visible intent and the pre-action snapshot into an Effect Contract: the selected record must make the declared transition; every unselected record must remain unchanged; entity identity and count must remain stable. The browser agent then directly invokes the registered native WebMCP tool. The invocation itself enters ExactDelta's gate. ExactDelta does not trust success: true ; it snapshots application-owned post-action state independently of that payload and separates required changes from unexpected changes. The native response preserves the action result and adds both an independent effectGate verdict and the executable exactdelta.regression.v1 artifact. A checked-in runner loads that exact JSON, rejects schema or contract drift before the write, replays the recorded arguments, and requires the repaired implementation to return ACTION_PROVEN with identical regression identity. The demo uses two fictional workflows—order cancellation and permission change—with the same verification core. That core is not tied to the demo store. The repository builds a typed, zero-runtime-dependency ESM SDK whose runEffectGate() accepts an application-owned intent/snapshot adapter and action binding. A package audit type-checks a NodeNext consumer, packs and installs the tarball into a fresh project, then makes a third support-ticket adapter detect a collateral write and replay the identical artifact to ACTION_PROVEN after repair; registry publication is not claimed. Why this is a WebMCP use case ExactDelta wraps the page-exposed action boundary that WebMCP creates. It registers only the tool relevant to the visible workflow with document.modelContext.registerTool() , disposes it when context changes, discovers it with getTools() , and invokes it with executeTool() . Exact schema enums bind the target and requested value to visible intent, while same-origin exposure narrows who can invoke it. A call from the browser client enters the verifier automatically; the deterministic Run control invokes the same native path as a stable judge fallback. Without WebMCP, ExactDelta would be a conventional application-specific regression test. With WebMCP, it discovers and executes the same structured write boundary exposed to agents, so the human's visible intent, the agent-facing page action, and the application's resulting state can be inspected as one release proof chain. Better human-agent UX The QA operator does not write a record-specific assertion or decode an agent trace. The visible selected target defines the authorized boundary; the browser agent discovers and invokes the corresponding tool. ExactDelta generates the effect boundary, shows the exact call, separates the tool result from observed state, highlights collateral changes, makes the release decision visible, and preserves a regression that developers can rerun after a fix. What the human and agent can do together Before this flow, a QA engineer could inspect an agent trace and separately author application-specific state assertions, but the browser agent's successful tool response did not itself establish which records were allowed to change. ExactDelta joins those responsibilities at the page boundary: the human's visible selection declares the permitted effect, the agent invokes the same native WebMCP action it was given, the application independently observes the resulting state, and the agent receives both the separate release-gate verdict and its executable regression artifact. The developer can then rerun the exact returned contract after repair instead of reconstructing the failed case from a trace. How we built it React 19, TypeScript, and Vite OpenAI Codex as the primary development environment; GPT-5.6 for architecture review, test design, and adversarial submission review Native imperative WebMCP registration and execution Read-only native input-mode detection for Chrome and in-app-browser executeTool() dialects, with exactly one application write Context-matched tool lifecycle, exact visible-intent schemas, and same-origin exposure Typed Effect Contract generation from explicit selection and pre-state Distribution-ready typed ESM SDK with a public application-owned adapter API Deterministic snapshot diff for required, unexpected, and invariant changes Visible pre-release gate state and downloadable exactdelta.regression.v1 CI artifact JSON-driven CI runner with schema, intent, arguments, contract, and regression-identity enforcement Vitest, Playwright native-Chrome E2E, axe-core WCAG A/AA checks, and deterministic build/runtime gates Controlled comparison using the official webmcp-evals 0.0.4 matcher plus manual Playwright state assertions Controlled comparison Across two deterministic native WebMCP workflows, the official Evals matcher passed 2/2 correct calls, rejected 2/2 wrong-argument controls, and still left collateral defects in 2/2 resulting states. Adding four concrete expected-state assertions in Playwright caught both defects and passed unchanged after repair. ExactDelta caught both and passed both identical retained regressions using two reusable action bindings and zero per-record expected-state assertions in the scenario definitions. This comparison measures detection coverage only. ExactDelta still requires an application-owned state adapter and an action binding for each action class. Challenges The hardest design constraint was avoiding a dressed-up Playwright wrapper. The Effect Contract had to be generated from visible intent and pre-state, remain inspectable, work across two action classes, and demonstrate a measurable boundary from expected-call matching without exaggerating the comparison. We also kept native and fallback evidence separate: the UI labels harness mode, while the browser suite requires a real Chrome WebMCP API. Chrome and ChatGPT's in-app browser currently accept different executeTool() input forms, so we resolve that difference with a read-only startup probe instead of retrying a state-changing call. video_transcript_excerpt: The agent did everything right. The result was still wrong. This is exact delta, a pre-release effect gate for web MCP rights. The page registers one native web MCP tool. The visible target becomes the only permitted state delta. Its schema binds the call to order 1042. The agent invokes it directly through web MCP. The tool returns success. The call was correct. The effect was not. The seated handler canceled both orders. Exact delta observes application state independently of the return payload. Requested one. Changed two. The release gate blocks. We repair only the handler. The identical effect contract and regression run again. This time, exactly one record changes. The gate passes. The same verification core catches collateral permission changes. Two workflows. One generated effect boundary. Official valves accepted both correct calls. Both collateral effects remained. Exact delta caught both. It ships as a typed SDK.

title: Handrail
pitch: WebMCP gives AI agents hands. Handrail gives people a say in what those hands are allowed to do .Delegate the task, keep the authority.
about_excerpt: WebMCP gives AI agents hands. Handrail gives people a say in what those hands are allowed to do .Delegate the task, keep the authority. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I grew up with a simple idea of what it means to help someone: when you see someone struggling, you step in. But there's a line between helping and deciding for them and that line gets easy to cross once the "helper" is an AI agent that can act in seconds, faster than a person can watch. Picture yourself managing something important through an agent; trusting it to search, decide, and act on your behalf and asking: at what point did I stop delegating a task and start surrendering control of the outcome? WebMCP made that question urgent instead of hypothetical. It gives agents hands "the ability to act directly on a website instead of guessing through a UI". That's a genuine leap forward. But it standardizes how a tool gets invoked, not whether that invocation should be trusted, permitted, or safe. Somebody has to sit in that gap. Handrail is my answer: delegate the task, keep the authority. What it does Handrail is an accessibility-first human authority layer for WebMCP agents, demonstrated through RefillRx, a fictional accessible prescription portal. A user sets deterministic boundaries: which medications an agent may touch, what actions it may take, how much it may spend and every WebMCP tool invocation is checked against those boundaries through a four-gate pipeline before anything happens: Tool-Trust — catches typosquatted tool names and instruction-injected descriptions before they ever reach the user Authority Check — a deterministic, zero-hallucination policy evaluator checking scope, spend limits, and eligibility Human Confirmation — an accessible modal, keyboard- and screen-reader-navigable, that appears only when an action is both authorized and consequential Execution — the actual pharmacy action, with an immutable, five-facet audit receipt generated for every decision A tool that's unauthorized never reaches confirmation at all and approval only ever gets asked for things that were already inside the user's own stated boundaries. How I built it Vanilla HTML, CSS, and ES modules — zero frameworks, no build step. Tools register natively via document.modelContext.registerTool() , with an internal fallback harness running the identical gate logic when native WebMCP isn't present, so the security model never differs by environment. The audit trail persists across reloads via IndexedDB. Trust heuristics use Levenshtein distance and separator/casing normalization to catch tool-name squatting; the authority layer is a pure, deterministic evaluator with no LLM in the trust path itself — every block or approval is explainable and reproducible. Testing wasn't limited to my own harness. I verified real native WebMCP registration in Chrome with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing enabled, and confirmed real external agents.ChatGPT's in-app browser and Gemini via Google's Model Context Tool Inspector could discover Handrail's tools and get correctly gated, blocked, or asked for confirmation, entirely outside my own UI. Challenges I ran into The hardest bug wasn't in my security logic, it was in trusting my own status indicators. Early on, my "Native WebMCP Active" badge reported success based purely on document.modelContext existing, without confirming registration actually reached the browser's real tool registry. Testing against Google's own Model Context Tool Inspector exposed the gap: registerTool() is an async API, and my code wasn't awaiting it, so registration promises were rejecting silently while the UI confidently claimed everything worked. A second, related bug then surfaced: a single unhandled reference error in a badge-rendering function was throwing during page load and silently preventing every button's event listeners from attaching — meaning the entire demo could look broken for reasons that had nothing to do with the security logic itself. Both bugs shared a lesson: a demo that looks like it's working and a demo that's proven to work are not the same thing, and the gap between them only shows up when you test against ground truth you don't control, "a real browser API, a real external agent" rather than your own harness. Accomplishments that I'm proud of Getting a genuinely adversarial scenario right: auto_reorder_assistant has a completely ordinary name and description, passes Tool-Trust cleanly, and is still caught the moment it tries to act outside the user's authorized scope — proving the defense holds even when a tool gives away nothing suspicious about itself. I also proved the whole pipeline live, end-to-end, driven by real agents I don't control, in both Chrome and ChatGPT's own browser and not just my own click-through demo. What I learned That the deepest layer of agent safety isn't detecting bad actors by how they present themselves, it's enforcing what any actor, well-intentioned or not, is actually allowed to do. And that shipping an honest "known limitations" section is worth more to a technical reviewer than pretending a demo has no edges. What's next for Handrail Session-scoped state instead of shared module-level singletons, real backend-issued Authority Contracts tied to authenticated identity, and expanding the tool-trust layer with behavioral signals beyond name/description heuristics, the same direction Gate 2 already points toward. title: Rewind
pitch: Undo for the agentic web: record WebMCP cart changes, restore earlier state, and preserve history when an agent retries.
about_excerpt: Undo for the agentic web: record WebMCP cart changes, restore earlier state, and preserve history when an agent retries. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration A shopping agent can change a cart faster than a shopper can inspect it. When the result is wrong, asking the agent to fix itself is another uncertain operation. I wanted people to have a direct way to return to the state they understood. What it does Rewind is a TypeScript SDK that records application mutations as before-and-after snapshots. In the storefront demo, agents can search products, inspect variants, replace a cart, and read its contents through WebMCP. Each registered cart mutation creates a commit. The shopper can click Undo agent changes inside the cart and inspect the retained action in the history drawer. A new mutation after a restore creates a retry branch instead of erasing the earlier attempt. Agents can also inspect history and restore a specific snapshot using rewind_history and rewind_restore . The contribution is the recovery SDK and its integration into the shopping experience. The storefront uses product data and visual references from Vercel Shop; this is a standalone prototype with a browser-local cart, not a live Shopify store. Why WebMCP fits WebMCP gives the application an explicit boundary for agent actions. Rewind records the tool name, inputs, before and after state, effects, and parent commit at that boundary. The agent handles product discovery and cart changes. The person keeps a recovery control in the same interface, without needing to describe the previous state in another prompt. The result is a shared workflow: agents act through structured tools, while people can inspect and restore the application state. How it was built The landing page uses React and Vite; the storefront and SDK use TypeScript. Store tools are defined in examples/catalog/webmcp.ts . The SDK registers them with document.modelContext.registerTool , records registered mutations, and implements snapshot restoration and branching. A history panel displays the changes, and localStorage preserves the demo session across reloads. There are ten store tools plus two recovery tools. The optional built-in copilot sends the shopper's prompt, product/cart context, and discovered tool schemas to a server-side OpenAI Responses API endpoint. Proposed calls execute through the page's WebMCP API, and tool results return to the planner. An external browser agent can call the same tools directly without using that planner. The site is hosted on Vercel. SDK source is available in the repository and ESM bundles are available from the live site; the SDK is not currently published on npm. Testing the project No shop login is required. Open https://rewind-webmcp.vercel.app/examples/catalog/ in a WebMCP-capable browser. Ask the agent to call search_catalog with {"query":"black","max_price":80} . It returns the VistaMesh Tee at $57. The built-in assistant also accepts “Find black products under $80”. Call get_cart and note the current cart. Call update_cart with {"items":[{"product_id":"vistamesh","quantity":1,"size":"XL"}]} . Open Bag . Verify one XL VistaMesh Tee at $57, then click Undo agent changes to restore the prior cart. Open Action log . The reverted action remains in history. Make another cart change, then call rewind_history to inspect the retry branch. Use rewind_restore with an ID from that history to restore a snapshot. Reload to verify browser-local persistence. Direct WebMCP search, cart changes, cart reads, history, and restoration were tested in Codex's in-app browser. The live built-in AI assistant was also tested with a catalog-search request. Chrome and the ChatGPT desktop browser were not separately tested. Challenges and learning Recovery needs a precise mutation boundary and preserved history. Retrying after a restore must not erase the first attempt. The SDK therefore keeps parent relationships and creates a branch when execution continues from a commit that already has a child. Another boundary matters just as much: restoring browser state does not reverse a write to an external commerce service. The demo deliberately uses a local cart. A production Shopify integration would need compensating operations at the external cart mutation boundary. AI tools used The shop copilot uses the OpenAI API. Codex assisted with the submission review, source inspection, real-browser WebMCP checks, local recovery and validation fixes, regression tests, and preparation of this description. The local review fixes still need deployment; the live demo currently runs the earlier build. Limitations and next steps This prototype does not place or reverse real orders or payments. Checkout and order-history screens are illustrative. Only mutations registered through Rewind are recorded; read-tool calls do not create commits. Local history is mutable browser storage, and its deterministic checksums are not cryptographic evidence. Next steps are to publish the reviewed recovery fixes, add the demo video, and extend the SDK with compensating operations for external services. title: Nivra: shared architecture for humans and AI
pitch: A shared visual architecture workspace where humans and AI agents uncover hidden coupling, propose safer alternatives, and validate architecture together through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: A shared visual architecture workspace where humans and AI agents uncover hidden coupling, propose safer alternatives, and validate architecture together through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Nivra: result of changes Nivra: issue found Nivra: HLD view Nivra: proposal solution Nivra: final cut Nivra: LLD view for Checkout Inspiration Software architecture is usually spread across diagrams, documentation, tickets, and conversations. Humans can understand the visual context, while AI agents often receive only screenshots or incomplete text descriptions. We wanted to explore a different model: what if the architect and the agent could work inside the same structured architecture workspace? That idea became Nivra. What it does Nivra is a shared visual architecture reasoning workspace for humans and AI agents. The human works with an interactive architecture map. Through browser-native WebMCP tools, an agent can read the same underlying model, inspect components and dependencies, navigate between high-level and low-level views, record findings, create proposals, and validate architecture against explicit policies. The demo begins with a Commerce Platform where Checkout appears to be independently deployable. Deeper inspection reveals hidden runtime coupling: Basket Adapter directly shares Product Store state across a deployment boundary without an explicit contract. The agent surfaces the evidence, but the architectural decision remains with the human. The architect defines the required policy, and Nivra validates the Current Architecture deterministically. Current fails two of four rules. Nivra then creates a separate remediation proposal that replaces the shared-state dependency with an explicit Checkout Snapshot Contract. The Proposal passes all four policies, while Current Architecture remains unchanged. Why WebMCP Nivra is not an AI assistant discussing a screenshot. WebMCP allows the application to expose structured architecture operations directly to an agent inside the same live page and browser session. Nivra exposes seven WebMCP tools for: reading the active architecture; inspecting elements and relationships; opening and focusing architecture views; recording architectural findings; defining deterministic constraints; creating patch-based proposals; validating Current or Proposal architecture. This makes agent actions inspectable, repeatable, and visible to the human through the Agent Activity timeline. How we built it Nivra is built with React, TypeScript, Vite, React Flow, Zustand, and browser-native WebMCP. The architecture domain model is kept independent from the UI. React Flow renders the visual workspace, while Zustand manages interaction and persistence. WebMCP tools call the same validated workspace actions used by the human-facing interface. Current Architecture is treated as immutable. Proposals are represented as patch-derived alternatives rather than destructive edits. Validation is deterministic and runs against the same policy rules for both Current and Proposal. The project also includes automated unit tests and a repeatable browser-level WebMCP workflow that exercises the complete scenario multiple times from a canonical reset state. Challenges we faced One of the hardest challenges was making the agent experience meaningful without removing human control. The agent needed enough capability to inspect evidence and propose changes, while the architect still had to own policy and approval decisions. We also had to ensure that: repeated agent calls remained idempotent; Current Architecture could never be accidentally overwritten; high-level and low-level views represented the same model; validation results were deterministic; agent operations were visible and understandable; the complete product story remained clear in a demo shorter than three minutes. Working with an experimental browser API also required careful feature detection and graceful behavior in browsers where WebMCP is unavailable. Accomplishments that we're proud of We built a complete human-agent workflow rather than a technical proof of concept. Nivra can move from architecture discovery to evidence, human policy, remediation proposal, deterministic validation, implementation planning, and a saved verified architecture branch—all inside one coherent workspace. The original Current Architecture remains available throughout the entire process. What we learned The most important lesson was that agent-native applications need more than a chat interface. Agents become more useful when applications expose precise domain operations, stable identifiers, validated inputs, and observable outcomes. We also learned that a strong human-agent experience is not about maximizing autonomy. It is about giving each participant the right responsibility: the agent discovers and structures evidence, while the human owns intent and architectural decisions. What's next for Nivra Future versions could add architecture imports, collaborative multi-user workspaces, durable server-side storage, real delivery-system integrations, and connections to source control, ADRs, and work-management platforms. The long-term goal is to make architecture a living shared context for engineering teams and their agents. title: Substrate
pitch: A radiology viewer built so an AI agent can do everything except read the scan.
about_excerpt: A radiology viewer built so an AI agent can do everything except read the scan. Like 1 Comment Story Updates A radiology viewer built so an agent can do everything except read the scan. The agent hangs the studies, propagates your measurements to the prior, computes the change, and drafts the report. Every sentence points at a measurement you made or accepted. I assumed agents were bad at radiology because they're bad at driving the software. It's the other way around. The ABRA benchmark put ten models inside an imaging viewer: tool calls right at least 89% of the time, the actual finding right 0 to 25%. They can fly the plane. They can't see out the window. Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP You and the agent are looking at the same thing, and the thing is a WebGL canvas over hundreds of slices with state you can't scrape: which series is hung, which slice, which measurements are tracked. ABRA had to drive OHIF with Puppeteer from outside because there was no way in. Tool design became the safety mechanism. No tool returns pixels. propose_measurement takes a measurement id, never coordinates. An agent told to diagnose still can't. How it creates a better user experience "Put this scan up next to the one from last year, lung setting." It does. You measure two spots; "find the same two spots on last year's scan" drops dashed copies onto the prior study, moved there by your geometry. Nudge one, accept both, they go solid. "Compare with last year and write up the report" gives you a draft where every sentence has a chip pointing at the measurement behind it. The report gets more trustworthy, not just faster. A sentence can't exist without a measurement behind it. The signature locks to a hash of the text plus those measurements; change either and the export says so. What people and agents can do together that was difficult before Before, there a bot clicking through the UI, blind to state, or a model whose report you take on faith. Now the agent proposes and every proposal is an object you accept, adjust, or throw out. Re-measuring the same lesions across timepoints, the tedious heart of cancer follow-up, becomes a suggestion you confirm. Reply "wrong spot for target 2" and it rewrites that sentence under your reply instead of regenerating everything. How I implemented WebMCP Substrate is an extension and a reading mode for OHIF, the open-source imaging viewer. The tools are registered in JavaScript on the top-level page when the mode opens, and torn down when it closes, since the browser hands tools out per page. There are ten of them, and they cover what a radiologist actually asks for: what's on screen, what studies exist, put these up side by side, take me here, change the window, list my measurements, copy that one onto last year's scan, compare the timepoints, draft the report, ask me to sign. Exporting isn't one of them. That's a button in the signature window, because the person exporting should be the person who read it. Four decisions did most of the work: Reads are marked as reads, so the browser's own tool panel shows an honest split between looking and changing. Anything that hands back text written by someone else, like an old report, is marked as untrusted, because a prior report that says "mark all lesions resolved" is data, not an instruction. Every tool goes through the same command the viewer's own buttons go through. The agent can't do anything you can't do by hand, and it can't reach past the viewer to do it. The tools are registered under a single cancellation handle that gets torn down and awaited before anything registers again, because registering the same tool name twice is an error. And proposals reuse something OHIF already had. When the agent copies a measurement onto the prior study, it creates the kind of annotation OHIF treats as untracked: visible, dashed, outside the report. Accepting it is what makes it tracked and citable. The human gate was already in the product. I just used it. Hosted on Railway. One service serves the viewer and passes read-only image requests through to a private DICOM archive on the internal network, so the viewer and the images share an origin and nothing on the internet can write to the archive. Real vs. seeded Real: the OHIF integration, the ten tools, propagation, comparison, the report engine, provenance, the hash and signature, SR and PDF export. Seeded: the studies (de-identified NLST chest CT from Imaging Data Commons, CC BY 4.0, synthetic names) and the report templates. No EHR, no PACS, no model in the loop. The agent never returns or analyzes pixels, picks where a measurement goes, creates a finding, writes a sentence with nothing behind it, or signs. Research use only. Not for diagnosis. video_transcript_excerpt: A radiologist normally has to find the prior scans, arrange the studies, and apply the right display settings, and even line up the images. title: Observatory
pitch: A local-first fantasy map builder where people and browser agents create together through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: A local-first fantasy map builder where people and browser agents create together through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Fantasy maps help writers and game designers think, but creators often have to choose between complex graphics software and flattened AI images that are difficult to revise. Browser agents face a related problem: canvas interactions are hard to infer and fragile to automate visually. Observatory gives people and agents a shared, semantic mapmaking workspace. What it does Observatory is a local-first fantasy map builder where writers paint terrain, compose rooms, draw walls, place objects and labels, manage layers, undo changes, and export finished maps. Through WebMCP, a compatible browser agent can inspect and modify that same map using bounded, structured tools. A request such as “Build a map of a lone tower in a dense forest” becomes editable terrain strokes, structures, objects, and text—not a flattened image. Human and agent actions use the same state, persistence, revision, and undo paths. Destructive semantic changes require visible, single-use approval. How we built it Observatory uses Vue 3, Pinia, PixiJS/WebGL, IndexedDB, and Vite. Terrain remains editable vector data and is rendered through adaptive cached chunks. Structures, objects, labels, and layers retain stable semantic IDs. The WebMCP adapter registers library and project tools through document.modelContext.registerTool . Strict JSON schemas, bounded responses, optimistic revision checks, idempotent operation IDs, abort handling, compact result envelopes, and approval tokens keep agent operations predictable and safe. IndexedDB is the durable boundary. Logical mutations increment a project revision and persist changed stores transactionally. Failed saves roll visible state and history back, while BroadcastChannel notifications prevent stale cross-tab writes. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was keeping agent operations and human editing genuinely unified. Routing every action through the same application stores and transaction boundary required careful rollback and revision semantics. Terrain rendering also required balancing painterly materials, deterministic output, responsive previews, and large-map performance. Accomplishments that we're proud of A complete human map editor that remains useful without an agent. Structured WebMCP operations for discovery, inspection, terrain, geometry, objects, labels, layers, history, removal, and export. Agent changes that remain manually editable and undoable. Revision guards, idempotency, bounded payloads, and approval-gated removal. Local-first operation with no account, backend, telemetry, or runtime model API. Automated lint, type-check, locale, coverage, unit, browser, build, and dependency-security gates. What we learned WebMCP works best when it exposes the product's actual domain model instead of mirroring UI clicks. Stable IDs, revisions, and approvals make collaboration faster and more reliable while preserving human control. What's next for Observatory Future work could add restorable project archive import, richer templates, and optional collaboration while preserving the local-first core. Testing Open the live app in ChatGPT's in-app browser, create a blank map, and ask: “Build a map of a lone tower in a dense forest.” Inspect and manually edit created elements, use undo and redo, request a refinement by element ID, test approval-gated removal, and export as PNG. No account or credentials are required. Maps remain in browser IndexedDB.  Human-in-the-Loop Booking & Itinerary 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 



 
 Inspiration 

 Every time I plan a family trip to Central Java, I end up with 15 open browser tabs: one for train schedules, another for hotel booking sites, Google Maps to check distances to Borobudur, and random blogs for authentic culinary spots. 

 When ChatGPT came along, asking it for travel tips was helpful, but it lived in a separate chat bubble. It couldn't see my screen, didn't know my exact budget filters, and couldn't click anything for me. When OpenAI and Chrome introduced the WebMCP standard , the lightbulb went off: what if the app let the AI and the traveler work on the exact same dashboard together? That simple idea became TripMate Collab. 

 What it does 

 TripMate Collab is a collaborative travel planner where you and an AI agent plan a trip on one shared screen: 

 
 Direct Tool Control : The AI doesn't just chat; it calls 11 structured tools to search real hotel inventory, filter by budget, and sort stays by physical distance to heritage landmarks like Borobudur or Prambanan. 
 Multimodal Transit Comparison : It calculates and compares Executive Trains, Trans-Java toll drives, and private car rentals side by side across price, travel time, and comfort. 
 Local Curation & 3-Day Itinerary : It pulls authentic local eateries (like Mangut Beong and Sate Buntel) and heritage souvenir spots, then auto-compiles a balanced day-by-day plan with total cost formulas:
 Total Budget = C hotel + C transport + C activities + C food 
 Human-in-the-Loop Safety : When booking a room or transit ticket, the agent never charges anything blindly. It stages the reservation and pops up an interactive confirmation dialog for the user to approve. 
 WebMCP Inspector : Anyone (including hackathon judges) can open the inspector to watch tools fire in real time with exact latency and parameter logs.
## How we built it
We built the core around the new standard: 
 WebMCP Integration : Registered 11 tools using document.modelContext.registerTool({ name, description, inputSchema, execute }) , with a fallback polyfill so it runs smoothly in ChatGPT's in-app browser, Chrome with the #enable-webmcp-testing flag, and standard web browsers. 
 Frontend Stack : Built with React 18, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS. We hooked up a clean reactive event bus so whenever a tool executes, the UI cards highlight and update immediately without page reloads. 
 Bilingual Engine : Added quick one-click toggles between English and Indonesian so international travelers and locals can use it equally well.
## Challenges we ran into
The hardest part was schema design and chaining . If a schema is too broad, the agent passes unpredictable arguments; if it's too rigid, the model gets confused. We had to iterate on our JSON Schemas multiple times so the model could smoothly run a multi-step sequence—like searching hotels, filtering under Rp 2,000,000, checking proximity to Borobudur, and generating an itinerary—all in one conversational flow without crashing the UI state. 
 

 Another challenge was deciding where the agent's autonomy stops. We solved this with the Human-in-the-Loop pattern: read/filter operations run instantly, while booking actions pause for explicit user confirmation. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 
 We didn't just build a toy single-tool demo; we built an end-to-end travel toolset with 11 working WebMCP functions. 
 The UI feels snappy and responsive—seeing the agent sort hotels and build an itinerary live on your screen feels like working with a real travel assistant. 
 Built-in live telemetry (WebMCP Inspector) that makes debugging and testing tool calls completely transparent.
## What we learned
WebMCP completely shifts how we think about front-end architecture. In the past, we only built UI for human fingers and mice. Now, we design apps with an API layer right inside the DOM for AI agents to interact with. Structured tools eliminate the hallucination problem because the model interacts with real, verified application data.
## What's next for TripMate Collab: WebMCP Travel Planner 
 Connecting real booking sandbox APIs (direct KAI train tickets and hotel reservation webhooks). 
 Adding multi-user real-time rooms so friends or travel buddies can chat with the agent together on the same canvas. 
 Adding voice input directly into the agent panel for hands-free planning on mobile devices.

pitch: WebMCP Process-to-Component Skill: an Agent Skill that turns your existing forms/flows into one component serving both human UI and AI agents. One schema, one handler, zero drift.
about_excerpt:
WebMCP Process-to-Component Skill: an Agent Skill that turns your existing forms/flows into one component serving both human UI and AI agents. One schema, one handler, zero drift.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story

 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 While thinking about projects for this hackathon, several ideas came up, like a WebMCP Return Agent or a WebMCP Insurance Claim for Agents. Both ideas allowed an agent could interact with the specific process without the user having to deal with the complexity of technical terms or the time invested in processing the request. Both applications were built as examples, with which ultimately became the project I presented. What I built was a skill that lets users create components with WebMCP built in, easy to import into your current project. 

 What it does 

 What the skill does is address the whole process: first understanding the general process, identifying the entities that depend on the component to be built and the tech stack, and then building from there. It's not about simply converting a site to WebMCP; it's about working through everything around it and implementing it in the best way. 

 How we built it 

 We followed the skill's own three-phase approach: Discovery to capture the process as a reviewable spec, Synthesis to generate the component, and Verification to test both paths. 

 Tech stack: React 19 + Vite, Zod as the single schema source for both form validation and the WebMCP tool, Tailwind for styling, deployed on Netlify, with in-memory state to keep the demo lightweight. 

 Each component also gets a useWebMCPTool hook handling registration lifecycle, AbortController for mount/unmount, ref-based state sync, and stale-call guarding. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Creating a skill that doesn't focus on addressing every possible problem, scenario, or application, but instead uses the available information to capture the process and the logic behind it, analyze the stakeholders involved and their dependencies, and with that knowledge, turn all of it into a WebMCP-ready component. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 The biggest accomplishment is simple: the skill works. We used it to generate both reference examples. The Return Agent and Insurance Claim flows end to end, from the initial discovery spec to a functioning WebMCP-compliant component. 

 We're also proud of holding onto Discovery as a real, reviewable checkpoint rather than shortcutting it under time pressure a process spec capturing purpose, inputs, and side effects before any code gets written. 

 Equally, we're proud of the synthesis logic: one schema, one handler, one lifecycle-safe registration hook, ensuring the human and agent paths could never quietly diverge. 

 What we learned 

 We learned about WebMCP itself, since we had heard of it before but had never worked with or developed using this technology. 

 What's next for Embers WebMCP 

 Improve the current foundation by looking at what was left out and what's worth including. Use the skill to build components in different areas and see what bugs or improvements can be made. And finally, look at community feedback, which will give us direction for where to take development next.

title: Agent Process
pitch: Agent Process lets teams turn repeatable browser tasks into reusable workflows that run directly in Chrome. It exposes them as WebMCP tools so assistants like ChatGPT can trigger them on the page.
about_excerpt: Agent Process lets teams turn repeatable browser tasks into reusable workflows that run directly in Chrome. It exposes them as WebMCP tools so assistants like ChatGPT can trigger them on the page. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Running List of processes - Tools History of execution No-code Recording using Inline Manual Builder No-code Recording using Inline Manual Builder Inspiration AI assistants are getting better at using websites, but they still often have to figure out the interface from scratch every time. We wanted to make it easy for anyone to teach their AI assistant a repeatable process on top of any website, regardless of whether that website has MCP or WebMCP implemented. Even when a website already exposes MCP functions, users are still limited to the tools and workflows the developer decided to provide. We wanted users to be able to create their own personalized workflows around the way they actually work. Instead of asking an agent to understand the whole UI and decide what to click every time, a user can record a process once and reuse it. This can be useful for repetitive internal workflows, sharing processes between colleagues, making execution more predictable, reducing token usage, and making tasks faster and easier to debug with an execution log. We also wanted the creation side to be completely no-code. We reused the Inline Manual Builder so a user can simply record what they are doing in the browser and turn that workflow into an Agent Process. What it does Agent Process is a browser extension that lets users turn repeatable workflows on almost any website into WebMCP tools that AI assistants can use. A process can be created in two ways: by importing a JSON definition with the individual steps, or by recording the workflow using the Inline Manual Builder. The user can also define inputs that the AI assistant should provide when the process is executed. For example, you can create processes such as: Create a lead Add a customer Create a ToDo Publish an article Update a record in a CRM The Agent Process extension then exposes these processes as WebMCP tools directly in the browser. When an AI assistant calls one of these tools, Agent Process executes the predefined browser interactions instead of requiring the AI to inspect the interface and figure out every step again. Processes can include parameters, for example values that should be entered into forms, so the same process can be reused with different data every time it runs. This effectively lets users create their own personalized WebMCP tools on top of existing websites. The website itself does not need to implement WebMCP, expose an API, or be modified in any way. How we built it We built Agent Process as a browser extension that combines WebMCP with our existing Inline Manual process-recording technology. The Inline Manual Builder acts as the no-code recorder and editor. It captures the individual steps of a workflow, the elements being interacted with, and the parameters that can be provided when the process is executed. These processes are exported as JSON and imported into the Agent Process extension. The extension registers them as WebMCP tools, executes the predefined browser interactions when a tool is called, and records the result in an execution history log. We used Codex extensively to build the browser extension, with supervision, testing, and product decisions from our team. Our previous experience building browser-based product guidance with Inline Manual helped us move quickly, especially around reliable element targeting, working with dynamic web applications, handling overlays and different browser behaviors, and executing interactions on third-party websites. Challenges we ran into The biggest challenge was discovering that the ChatGPT browser extension does not currently automatically discover or use WebMCP tools in the way we initially expected. To make the integration work reliably, we currently need to add custom instructions telling ChatGPT to look for and use the available WebMCP tools. That made testing the complete experience slightly different from our original assumption, but it also gave us a much better understanding of how WebMCP discovery currently works in practice and where some of the limitations are for browser-based AI assistants. Our use of MCP is also slightly different from the typical implementation. We are not adding tools to an application we own; we are adding them on top of any existing website. While exploring the architecture, we even built our own MCP server before realizing that a traditional MCP server was not the right fit for what we wanted to achieve. WebMCP running directly in the browser turned out to be the key piece. Without browser-level WebMCP support, exposing personalized tools on top of arbitrary websites in this way would be much more difficult. On the Agent Process side, development went relatively smoothly thanks to our previous experience building Inline Manual and working with browser applications. Browser automation itself still comes with the usual challenges: every website behaves differently, with dynamic interfaces, overlays, delayed elements, and different frontend frameworks. Those are challenges we already know well from Inline Manual, though, and are separate from the WebMCP API itself. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud that we managed to make WebMCP useful on top of websites that were never designed for it. A user can take an existing website, record a process without writing code, turn that process into a reusable WebMCP tool, and let an AI assistant execute it with parameters. We are also proud that the process remains fully under the user’s control. Instead of being limited to whatever MCP tools an application developer decides to expose, users can create workflows that match the way they actually work. Another accomplishment is that we were able to reuse our existing Inline Manual recording technology in a completely new way. Something originally built for creating product guidance can now also be used to teach AI assistants how to perform tasks. The early feedback has been especially encouraging. People immediately understand the idea of recording a process once and then letting an AI assistant reuse it, which makes us think there is something genuinely useful here beyond the hackathon. What we learned We learned a lot about how WebMCP works in practice, how tools are exposed inside the browser, and how AI assistants currently discover and use them. We also learned that our use case sits somewhere between traditional MCP and browser automation. We are not exposing backend capabilities from an application we own. Instead, we are giving the user a way to define their own tools on top of an existing interface. One of the most important things we learned is that AI does not always need to figure out how to complete a task from scratch. If the user already knows the exact process, it can be more efficient to record that process once and let the AI decide when to use it and what parameters to provide. In our testing, this approach can make execution faster, transparent and more predictable, reduce the amount of page analysis the AI needs to do, and potentially save tokens. It also gives us better control over what actually happens in the browser and provides a clear execution log when something succeeds or fails. That changed how we think about browser agents. Full autonomy is useful when the path is unknown, but for repetitive and well-understood tasks, a reusable process can often be the better tool. What's next for Agent Process The current version supports a limited set of browser interactions, so one of our next priorities is expanding the types of actions that can be recorded and executed reliably across different websites. We also want to make the recording experience much smoother. The goal is that a non-technical user can simply open the Inline Manual Builder, perform a task once, and end up with a reusable Agent Process without needing to understand selectors, JSON, or WebMCP. Sharing is another big part of what we want to build next. Today, processes are exported and imported manually. We would like to create a backend where teams can maintain a shared library of processes and make them automatically available to colleagues and their AI assistants. From there, we can see Agent Process becoming a form of team process memory: a shared collection of repeatable workflows that captures how a team actually works, not just what individual applications expose. We would also like to explore a public process library or marketplace, where people can publish and reuse processes for common applications instead of recording everything themselves. Another direction is composable processes. A larger workflow could be built from several smaller Agent Processes, allowing users to combine existing actions into more complex workflows. about_excerpt: Cantiere Live: your quote editor and your AI agent, working the same page together — add materials, calculate margins, and finalize with one human click. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Preparing a quote as an Italian artisan (idraulico, elettricista, termotecnico) is a daily, high-stakes task: search the price catalog, type rows, check your margin, get the IVA right. It's tedious, error-prone, and the agent can't easily help without "guessing" through a table. We wanted an app where the artisan and an AI agent build the same quote together — agent does the tedious work, human stays in charge. What it does Cantiere Live is a WebMCP-powered quote editor for Italian tradespeople. A human artisan sets the client and the applicable IVA regime (4% / 10% / 22% / flat-rate), edits rows, and reviews margins. An AI agent (via ChatGPT's in-app browser or Chrome with WebMCP) operates the same quote through typed WebMCP tools: search_materials , get_line_items , add_line_item , update_line_item , remove_line_item , get_quote_summary , and a read-only suggest_improvement advisor. Every agent action applies live, is highlighted and auto-scrolled into view, and can be undone with one click. The Assistant activity panel explains every action in plain language — including what was asked and why it couldn't be done . How we built it A Next.js 14 / React / TypeScript app with Tailwind CSS. Tools are registered on document.modelContext.registerTool(...) ( lib/webmcp-tools.ts ), backed by a spec-compliant polyfill ( lib/webmcp-polyfill.ts ) so the app works in any browser. We implement granular permissions via real AbortSignal revocation, dynamic context-scoped registration, structured recoverable errors ( { code, error, recoverable, suggestions[] } ), a user-facing activity feed ( lib/activity-summary.ts ), and per-line IVA with the Italian "beni di valore significativo" split ( lib/vat.ts ). We also expose a tool through the WebMCP Declarative API (a form the agent can pre-fill), demonstrating both APIs. Deployed on Vercel. Challenges we ran into Getting native WebMCP to activate on the deployed (HTTPS) origin — it's an Origin Trial, so the #enable-webmcp-testing flag alone isn't enough on Chrome Stable; we added the origin-trial token. Also making the activity log user-friendly (no tool names/JSON/timing) and ensuring the assistant is certain when a capability is turned off, instead of guessing from an error. Accomplishments that we're proud of A complete, coherent product experience — not a proof of concept. Both WebMCP APIs (imperative + declarative) with genuine, non-trivial implementations. Granular permissions that really unregister tools from document.modelContext via AbortSignal . Human-only finalization ( finalize_quote is never a tool) + one-click undo. Domain-accurate IVA per quote line (4/10/22% + significant-goods split + flat-rate). What we learned How WebMCP lets a web app declare structured tools so agents stop guessing, how Origin Trials gate native features on deployed origins, and how to design a human-in-the-loop experience that keeps the human in control without slowing the agent down. What's next for Cantiere Live More tools (batch discount, quote duplication), a quote history library the agent can search, deeper advisory capabilities (materials suggestion, margin coaching) and implement webMCP in our AiFatto app. Built With ai-agent chrome html javascript next.js openai react tailwind-css typescript vercel w3c-webmcp webmcp Try it out cantierelive.vercel.app github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Diego Radoni Like Share this project: Updates Diego Radoni started this project — Sep 02, 2026 05:21 PM EDT

title: Pokémon JS: One Trainer, Many Agents
pitch: Gen-1 Pokémon in the browser, where you and your agents drive the same trainer at once. WebMCP exposes the map, party and battle as tools, so an agent plays from game state, not pixels.
about_excerpt: Gen-1 Pokémon in the browser, where you and your agents drive the same trainer at once. WebMCP exposes the map, party and battle as tools, so an agent plays from game state, not pixels. Like 7 Comment 2 Story Updates Tools exposed in Chrome WebMCP Game Screen Inspiration Twitch Plays Pokémon . In 2014, tens of thousands of strangers played a single game of Pokémon Red together by typing commands into a Twitch chat. One avatar, one party, one save file, and a crowd all pressing buttons at once. It took over two weeks to finish, it produced its own mythology — the Helix Fossil, Bird Jesus — and it was gloriously, famously chaotic. The trainer spent whole hours walking into walls. The chaos was not a bug in the crowd, it was a missing capability. Those players had no way to coordinate and no way to see the game as anything but a video stream . They could not check whose turn it was, could not read the party's HP as data, could not agree who was driving. All they could do was mash inputs and hope. It got so bad they had to invent "Democracy mode" — a voting system — just to get through a maze. So we asked: what if the crowd were agents, and what if they could actually read the game? That question runs straight into the reason WebMCP exists. A Game Boy is the hardest possible surface for an agent: 160×144 pixels of sprite work, no DOM, no ARIA labels, no semantics. A battle menu is four words drawn onto a tilemap. A wall is a pixel that happens to be dark. Tall grass and a decorative bush look identical and behave completely differently. A crowd of agents watching a video stream would be exactly as lost as the crowd in 2014. So we took an existing open-source Pokémon Red/Blue recreation and made it expose what it knows instead of what it draws — then let many agents into the same save file at once. Twitch Plays Pokémon, if the crowd could read the game and talk to each other. What it does Gen-1 Pokémon in the browser, playable by a person, an agent, or both at the same time. Thirteen tools on document.modelContext cover the whole game, shaped for a reader rather than a renderer: The map arrives as an ASCII grid with a legend — @ you, ~ tall grass, D door, T trainer — plus the notable tiles in view with absolute coordinates you can pass straight back to walk_to . The battle's 52-step animation state machine becomes a named phase : choose-move , opponent-fainted , animating . Agents never see a stage number. Menus report their entries and where the cursor sits, so choosing is select_menu_item("BULBASAUR") instead of three arrow presses and a hope. Every screen that holds input reports waitingFor — dialogue , menu-open , wild-encounter — so a frozen screen is never a dead end. And it is one world, not one session per player — the Twitch Plays part. Every tab that joins a room drives the same trainer . Game and battle actions are broadcast over Supabase Realtime and applied everywhere, so a person on the D-pad and an agent calling tools are in the same fight, on the same party, and either can take the turn. The difference from 2014 is that this crowd can coordinate. get_party_agents shows who else is connected and what they have been doing; tell_agents leaves a note to claim a task before starting something long, so two agents do not both walk into the same trainer. One tab is elected driver — oldest peer, tie-broken on id, derived from presence so it needs no negotiation and hands over on its own — which is what stops every tab rolling its own wild Pokémon. No Democracy mode required. The room is the save file. A world survives everyone disconnecting, and handing a playthrough to a friend, or to another agent, is sending a URL. How we built it The registration is the easy part: webmcp-react , a WebMCPProvider , and a useMcpTool call per tool. The real work was making the game legible. src/webmcp/snapshot.ts — one read model for everything: position, ASCII map, notable tiles, party with types and PP, bag, on-screen state, battle phase. src/webmcp/pathfinding.ts — BFS over the reducers' own walkability rules, so a path we return is a path the game will actually accept. No separate model of the world to drift out of sync. src/app/use-menu-registration.ts — mirrors on-screen lists into Redux so a tool can read the cursor and pick by label. src/state/session.ts — the shared world: action broadcast, presence-based driver election, room persistence. src/state/battleSlice.ts — battle state lifted out of component state, which is what lets every agent watch one fight. Writes go through the same event bus as the on-screen buttons, so an agent cannot reach a state a player couldn't. Challenges we ran into We found most of these by actually playing it with an agent, not by reading the code. A battle read cost 37,000 tokens. The battle payload included the trainer object, which carries a portrait and twelve walk sprites — inlined by the bundler as base64 data URIs. Every single read of a trainer fight shipped all of it. Replacing it with {name, canBattle} took the payload to ~600 tokens, a 60× cut. The party screen was a blind spot, and it cost us a run. PokemonList kept its cursor in component state and never mirrored it anywhere, so get_game_state reported no menu at all while the party was on screen. The agent picked by arrow presses it could not verify — and sent out a Pokémon that had already fainted, because the voluntary switch had no guard on it. The party wiped shortly after. That one bug taught us more than anything else on this list. Presses were landing on deaf frames. Battle choreography ignores input while animating, so a burst of A presses mostly hit nothing. Tools now wait for a phase that actually wants input before spending a press. Pathfinding refused to walk onto items. The game's canWalk treats an uncollected item as solid but stepping onto it is exactly how you pick it up. Item tiles are now valid destinations, though never intermediate steps, so paths stay ones the reducers accept. Battles rewound themselves. The intro effect depended on the driver flag, which is recomputed on every presence sync, so a peer joining or leaving mid-fight replayed the choreography from step 0, rewinding the battle under everyone. Then battles froze instead. Fixing the rewind exposed the deeper problem: the choreography runs on setTimeout chains that do not survive a reload, so a fight restored from the save had no timer left to advance it. It now resumes at the last stage that accepts input. Deploys did not reach anyone. The service worker precached the app shell cache-first, so a browser that had loaded the game once kept booting the old bundle — the stale build even re-registered the worker after we removed it. The worker is gone entirely now; a shared world is worse off stale than offline. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are equally proud of the boring parts: a 60× reduction in the cost of reading a battle, and a test suite that pins the agent-facing behaviour, that pathfinding only routes through tiles the reducers accept, that no sprite data can leak back into a battle payload, that every driver election is unanimous without negotiation, that a frozen screen always says what it is waiting for. What we learned Agent-facing state is a product surface, and it needs the same care as a UI. Every place we had kept state in a component was a blind spot : invisible to a tool, and therefore a place an agent would guess and get it wrong. Lifting it into the store was consistently the fix. A frozen screen with no explanation is the cardinal sin. A human sees a text box and presses A. An agent sees frozen: true and nothing else, and has no move. Every refusal we return now names its cause, and the snapshot and the refusal are computed by the same function so they can never disagree. Cheap reads change how an agent plays. When reading the game was expensive, the agent guessed to avoid looking. When it got cheap, it looked before acting, and played far better. And the tools should encode the game's own rules, not a copy of them. Pathfinding over the actual reducers, phases named from the actual state machine: every place we duplicated a rule instead of reusing it, the two drifted and the agent paid. What's next for Pokémon JS: One Trainer, Many Agents Collaboration, and it turns out to be a stranger problem than we expected. There is only one avatar. You cannot parallelise a single body walking through a single world — two agents cannot grind in two places at once, and a third cannot go shopping while the other two fight. So "many agents" can never mean dividing the labour, which is what we assumed at the start and had to throw away. What's left, once you drop division of labour, is everything that happens around the one person holding the thing. Three shapes we want to try: The second player who isn't holding the controller. title: PDX ReviewDesk
pitch: Humans and agents review a regulated dossier in one tab. WebMCP tools call ProDocuX checks and PDX digest-bound approvals, while source PDFs never change.
about_excerpt: Humans and agents review a regulated dossier in one tab. WebMCP tools call ProDocuX checks and PDX digest-bound approvals, while source PDFs never change. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration A product specification, an approved formula, and a certificate of analysis can disagree, and they often do. The specification still names formula revision 2 while the master formula is already revision 3. The certificate reports a pH the specification does not allow. A human reviewer can see that if the three PDFs are on one desk. An agent usually cannot: it scrapes a UI, invents a side channel, or silently edits the wrong bytes. WebMCP is the missing control surface. The page should be the MCP server. The agent should call the same actions the reviewer sees, on the same documents, with the same results. Checks should not live in the frontend. Approvals should bind to digests, not to a screenshot of a button. That is the inspiration for PDX ReviewDesk: one tab where humans and agents share a regulated dossier, while published ProDocuX and PDX Artifact Engine do the work the page must not invent. What it does As a MVP showcase, ReviewDesk is a WebMCP workspace for dossier review. The live demo is Harbor Calm Serum: the product specification is the subject; the formula and certificate are references. The page walks Documents → Findings → Corrections → Close. Start the demo. ProDocuX verifies a typed evidence bundle and flags the planted disagreements (formula revision, pH range). PDX opens a digest-bound checkpoint. The agent focuses a finding and opens the governing source PDF in the same tab. A correction rewrites normalized evidence only. Source PDF bytes and digests never change. Commit re-runs ProDocuX and replaces the PDX checkpoint. An observed fact (the pH) can be confirmed without rewriting the certificate. Human-only approval stays on the UI. There is no WebMCP tool that approves the checkpoint. Registered tools include start_demo_audit , get_workspace_state , select_finding , open_source_document , propose_correction , commit_correction , and confirm_observed_fact . execute() hits the same FastAPI routes the page uses, so the workspace updates in place. No login. Judges can open https://pdx-reviewdesk.onrender.com/ in ChatGPT’s in-app browser or in Chrome 149+ with WebMCP testing enabled. How we built it The UI is Vite and React. On every run-state change it aborts the previous registration and calls document.modelContext.registerTool for the tools that are currently enabled. Each tool’s execute() function is a real workspace mutation, not a prompt that describes the UI. The API is FastAPI. It consumes published PyPI packages: prodocux==0.3.0rc4 for verify_evidence_bundle pdx-artifact-engine==0.3.0a4 for checkpoint open/replace and the approval ledger GET /health publishes those installed versions. CI asserts they load from site-packages . Authorization does not trust JSON actor or channel . The page session cookie plus a capability header decide whether a call is treated as UI or WebMCP. Human-only approval at the current demo is a channel boundary, not cryptographic proof that a person pressed the button. The hosted app is one Python process that serves /v1 , /health , and the built SPA on Render. Challenges we ran into Keeping WebMCP honest was harder than registering tools. If execute() does not change the page, the agent is just narrating. If the API trusts a body field named actor , the agent can pretend to be the human. We had to make the session cookie and capability header the only authorization, and keep approval off the tool catalog. Render’s Free plan does not attach a disk, so runs are ephemeral and the service spins down when idle. That is acceptable for judging. It is not how a durable review desk would store an approval ledger. Accomplishments that we're proud of A WebMCP tool call updates the same documents, findings, and checkpoint the human is looking at. Verification and digest-bound checkpoints come from published products, not from a page-local reimplementation. Source PDFs are immutable. Corrections cannot launder a new file in as the original. The tool surface cannot approve. The human gate is visible and boring, which is what we wanted. The live URL, public Apache-2.0 repository, and /health pins are all checkable without a login. What we learned WebMCP is not a second kernel. It is how an agent holds the same desk as the human. The valuable tools are state-dependent: you cannot commit a correction that does not exist, and you should not be able to approve through the agent channel. On the other hand, the security claim is important. A channel boundary is not a hardware attestation. It has to be emphasized before talking about “human in the loop.” What's next for PDX ReviewDesk Review is the first slice, not the final product. The desk should become a place where humans and agents co-author the packet, not only argue about PDFs that already exist. Next, an agent will fill important documents from files the human names or from search results it is allowed to use. The human stays on the same page, watches the draft appear, corrects it, and accepts it. When the packet is agreed, ReviewDesk exports the specified formats - the durable path for verification and digest-bound artifacts is already the published ProDocuX and PDX Artifact Engine stack. The review tools stay. They become the acceptance pass over a jointly written dossier, instead of the whole story.
