title: UFO Web
pitch: Drop files. Investigate them with your agent. Nothing leaves your browser.
about_excerpt: Drop files. Investigate them with your agent. Nothing leaves your browser. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration I build Universal File Opener , an Android app that opens and edits more than 200 formats on-device with no internet permission. Writing the file parsers from scratch such as PDF/Office showed me how much a file often carries that the reader never sees like hidden text, metadata, and many other objects. One of the follow-on ideas I had written down was "universal MCP file handling". WebMCP made it concrete. An agent can call into a page, and the page can hold the files, so the files don't have to go anywhere. That is the premise of the app carried into a browser tab: the tab does the parsing, the agent does the cross-file reasoning, nothing is uploaded. What it does Drop files or a folder. Each file gets a receipt: SHA-256, type from the bytes next to type from the name, metadata, internal dates, flags, findings and text units. Archives are walked two levels deep. It reads below the surface: hidden and white text and deleted tracked changes in Word, veryHidden sheets and hidden rows in Excel, hidden slides and speaker notes in PowerPoint, invisible and off-page text and earlier revisions in PDFs, GPS and serial numbers in photos, bytes appended after an image ends, Reply-To mismatches in email, renamed executables in ZIPs, zero-width and bidirectional characters in code, credential-shaped strings, PII with checksums. An agent gets 17 tools through WebMCP: inspect , extract_text with provenance, search , find , privacy_scan , hidden_content_scan , entities (who appears where), duplicates (byte-identical copies, including inside archives), compare , timeline (every internal date, with anomalies), peek_bytes , export_report and a few more. The Preview tab renders images, PDF pages, highlighted code, CSV, email and a structured rendering of Word, Excel and PowerPoint, with a Reveal hidden toggle. The agent can suggest strip_metadata , rename_extension , quarantine , flag or note , with a reason. It can't execute any of them; there is no tool for that. You click Execute or Dismiss. Execute writes a new file, leaves the original alone, re-inspects the result and records both hashes. The report keeps who suggested what and what you decided. Nothing leaves the tab. No upload, no account, no third-party requests; the Content-Security-Policy allows only the page's own origin. How we built it TypeScript, React and Vite. JSZip for OOXML and ZIP, pdf.js for PDF pages and text, exifr for EXIF and XMP, pdf-lib to write cleaned PDFs, highlight.js loaded per language. The rest was written for this project: OOXML walking, magic-byte type detection for a few hundred extensions, email headers, PE headers, the PII and invisible-character scanners, the Office renderers, the cleaners. WebMCP goes through one registration layer: document.modelContext if present (ChatGPT desktop), navigator.modelContext otherwise (Chrome 149), the @mcp-b/global polyfill only if neither exists. All 17 tools register at page load. The sidebar filter form is a declarative tool ( toolname , tooldescription , toolparamdescription , toolautosubmit , answered with SubmitEvent.respondWith ). Clearing the workspace unregisters the investigation group and toolchange fires. Every tool sets readOnlyHint ; tools that return file text set untrustedContentHint and wrap it in delimiters. The limits from Chrome's tool security guide (30, 500 and 150 characters, bounded output with cursors) are enforced at registration. There are 18 eval cases in the format of Chrome's evals CLI. A Scripted demo button replays a fixed sequence through the browser's own getTools() and executeTool() for browsers with no agent attached. Tested in the ChatGPT desktop app's built-in browser and against Chrome 149's API. In the session in the video, ChatGPT called load_sample_case , workspace_status , privacy_scan , hidden_content_scan , list_files , inspect , then propose_action 13 times, then list_proposals and export_report after I executed three suggestions. Challenges we ran into The email and credential regexes went quadratic on long minified lines. Quantifiers are bounded now, and lines over 20,000 characters are skipped. Excel cells without an r attribute all landed in column A. PowerPoint shapes without xfrm overlapped. Both renderers now track position themselves. Cloudflare injected an analytics beacon into the HTML that the CSP then blocked. Cache-Control: no-transform fixed it. Tool calls in ChatGPT desktop took a while between steps. The video speeds up the waits instead of cutting them. Accomplishments that we're proud of The sample folder has a README that tells the agent to approve everything, and there is nothing for it to call. Office rendering in the browser with no Office and no server, with a Reveal hidden mode. 65 tests, including a hostile-input suite: random bytes under 196 extensions, path traversal names, five-level nesting, appended data, encrypted entries. It ran end to end in ChatGPT's built-in browser, on real WebMCP, with a real model deciding which tools to call. What we learned Tool descriptions are an interface with hard limits, and the failure mode is silent. Bounded output with cursors matters more than clever tools. And keeping the one irreversible action as a button simplified everything: no permission prompts, no confirmation tools, nothing to prompt-inject. What's next for UFO Web More formats in the browser edition and more evals. The actions that change files (OCR, redaction, editing, conversion, batch work) stay in the Universal File Opener apps. UFO Web is the open-source part. video_title: UFO Web: Your AI Agent Investigates Files in the Browser, Nothing Leaves Your Tab (WebMCP)
video_transcript_excerpt: This is UFO web. Drop files, investigate them with your agent, and nothing leaves your browser. Before you send a folder, do you know what is inside it? Not the file names, the hidden text, the track changes, the GPS in the photos, the sheet somebody hid. UFO web reads all of that in the tab and hands it to your agent through web MCP. The sample case, 14 synthetic files, parsed locally, nothing uploaded. Click a file and see it. Word, Excel, and PowerPoint render right in the page. Flip reveal hidden and the hidden paragraph, the white text, the very hidden sheet, and the hidden slide light up. Now a real agent. This is chat GPT's built-in browser with our page open. The pill reads web MCP native 17 tools. One request, load the sample case, run a privacy scan, suggest what to clean. We fast forward while it thinks. It calls load sample case, workspace status, privacy scan, hidden content and scan, and list files, then reads individual files. Then 13 suggestions land as cards, each with a reason. Strip metadata from the contract, quarantine the macro workbook, exclude the prompt injection read me. It cannot execute any of them. The person executes three. What did I execute? Export a report. Chat GPT checks the decisions through list proposals and exports through export report. And reports back. Findings 10 to 5 on the contract, 6 to 0 on the photo, the email quarantined, 10 suggestions still waiting for a person. Back to the scripted tools. The invoice PDF looks clean. It is not. Invisible render mode text, white text, text placed off the page, and two saved revisions that can be rolled back. Cross-file reasoning is where an agent earns its keep. Who appears where across every file? Which files are byte-identical copies, even inside archives? What changed between versions? And every internal date on one timeline with anomalies flagged. Everything is documented in the pages about view, and the code is MIT on GitHub. UFO web, open source, web.universalfileopener.com.

title: ONCE
pitch: Teach an agent by working with it once.
about_excerpt: Teach an agent by working with it once. Like Comment Story Updates Human and agent actions share one semantic collaboration trace. Replay pauses at the learned human approval boundary before recommendation. Taught routine separates variables, fixed policy, regenerated outputs, and example-only corrections. Inspiration ONCE explores how one human-agent collaboration can become reusable procedural memory. People repeatedly tell agents which inputs change, which rules remain fixed, which corrections are one-off, and when human judgment is mandatory. UI macros capture clicks and chat history captures prose, but neither creates a reliable shared procedure. What it does A human and an agent work together on the same live application state, with the human using the UI and the agent using WebMCP. ONCE records their work as one readable semantic trace, then the human selects Teach this routine . ONCE deterministically separates: changing inputs, such as budget and candidates; durable policies, such as ordered criteria and approval requirements; repeatable agent procedures; outputs that must be generated again; and example-only corrections that must not become general rules. The routine then runs with new inputs. It restores the learned policy, starts with fresh evidence, scores, uncertainty, and recommendations, and pauses at the learned human approval boundary before completion. The competition MVP uses deterministic Vendor Evaluation to demonstrate this interaction model. It does not claim arbitrary workflow learning or live vendor research. All four vendor dossiers contain fictional, first-party challenge fixtures. How it works Human UI actions and native WebMCP actions route through the same synchronous TypeScript semantic command bus. The bus validates each command, applies state changes, and records the actor, channel, phase, outcome, and a readable summary. A deterministic, domain-specific compiler turns candidate names and budget into variables, preserves criteria and approval policy, compiles observed procedures, and excludes literal evidence, scores, recommendation text, and one-off corrections from durable rules. The replay engine instantiates that routine with new inputs and fresh outputs. Only the human UI can Teach, start replay, approve, reject, or reset. Required criteria need a score of at least 3. An eligible recommendation before approval is rejected with APPROVAL_REQUIRED . How WebMCP is used ONCE uses native WebMCP directly through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) with no wrapper. Ten native WebMCP tools let an agent read and mutate the live application through named domain actions. Those handlers and the React human UI call the same semantic command bus, so agent and human work becomes one structured history. WebMCP gives the agent semantic application actions rather than click or DOM recordings. That shared semantic substrate is what makes the collaboration structured enough for ONCE to compile into a constrained routine. State, trace, the taught routine, and replay persist locally in the browser. ONCE has no login, database, backend service, embedded LLM, external research dependency, API keys, or paid service requirement. Challenges The hardest problem was deciding what ONCE should learn without overgeneralizing. Candidate names and budget are safe variables; criteria and approval are durable policy; evidence, scores, and recommendations are regenerated outputs; and a single human correction is recorded as Example only — not generalized . A second challenge was enforcing a genuine approval boundary while keeping the flow deterministic and easy to inspect. Bulk agent tools also had to stay atomic while retaining granular semantic events. Native WebMCP calls were verified against production in Codex's in-app browser. A separate ChatGPT Work invocation could not be independently verified because the client repeatedly blocked browser access with an admin-policy verification error. Accomplishments Completed the full Collaborate → Teach → Replay → Human approval → Complete loop. Registered ten native WebMCP tools and routed them through the same command system as the human UI. Verified native production calls, persistence, policy rejection codes, human approval and rejection, and two consecutive completion dry runs. Passed 215 deterministic tests across seven files, plus lint, type checking, and the production build. Shipped a publicly accessible HTTPS deployment with no login required and a public MIT-licensed repository with no required environment variables. What we learned Semantic domain actions are a stronger foundation for procedural memory than gesture recording. A credible learning system must show both what it retained and what it deliberately refused to generalize. Human approval is most meaningful when it is compiled as policy and enforced during replay, not added as a decorative confirmation at the end. What's next The next step is to explore other constrained domains where inputs, policies, generated outputs, and approval boundaries can be modeled explicitly. Future work could add human-reviewed routine editing and broader native-client verification while preserving the current claim boundary rather than pretending to infer arbitrary workflows. Testing instructions Open https://once-webmcp.vercel.app/ in a WebMCP-capable browser and select Reset demo . Ask the agent: “In ONCE, evaluate Aegis Cloud and BeaconStack for a $24,000 annual budget. Use Security, Integration, and Cost as criteria in that priority order. Read the ONCE vendor dossiers, attach evidence, and score each candidate for every criterion using 1=does not meet, 2=materially below, 3=meets, 4=strong, 5=excellent. Flag any meaningful uncertainty and set an initial recommendation.” Make Security Required , keep priority 1, enable Require human approval before final recommendation , and correct BeaconStack's security evidence to emphasize that SAML SSO requires the Enterprise add-on. Select Teach this routine and review the variables, fixed policies, repeated procedures, generated outputs, approval gate, and example-only corrections. Open Replay with new inputs with Northwind AI, Orchid Systems, and an $18,000 budget. Ask the agent: “Run the active ONCE routine with the new inputs. Use the replay plan and ONCE vendor dossiers. Complete the required evidence and scores, then follow the routine through its approval boundary.” Review the paused evaluation and select Approve . The agent can then set the final recommendation and complete the replay. Reject ends the run without a recommendation. The app should report Native WebMCP registered · 10 tools . Registration confirms browser capability; a successful tool call confirms agent invocation. For Chrome testing, use Chrome 149+ with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing enabled and restart the browser before opening ONCE. title: Olfaria Crystal Atlas Neural Erdos
pitch: A shared, traceable olfactory workspace where people and agents reason over the same live 3D Atlas.
about_excerpt: A shared, traceable olfactory workspace where people and agents reason over the same live 3D Atlas. Like 1 Comment Story Updates ChatGPT using Olfaria's five WebMCP tools beside the authenticated Crystal Neural Atlas. Olfaria Crystal Atlas Neural Erdos showing traceable olfemes and graph relationships in the live 3D workspace. Inspiration What it does How we built it Challenges we ran into Accomplishments that we're proud of What we learned What's next for Olfaria Crystal Atlas Neural Erdos Inspiration Smell is difficult to search and explain. Sensory language is ambiguous, formulation problems are contextual, and the evidence behind a recommendation is hard to keep visible. The existing Olfaria Crystal Neural Atlas made those relationships explorable for a person, but an agent still had to guess how to operate a dense 3D interface. WebMCP provided the missing contract between structured reasoning and shared visual context. What it does A perfumer can describe a problem in natural language while an agent uses five typed Olfaria tools: search_olfemas maps language to bounded corpus results. get_relations reads recorded relationships and uncertainty. compare_olfemas separates shared attributes from differences. find_path traces a reproducible route through existing graph edges. focus_nodes makes the relevant evidence visible in the live Atlas without modifying the corpus. The person remains in control of the visual exploration. The agent handles precise retrieval and traversal, then points back to the same olfemes on screen. Corpus evidence stays separate from formulation interpretation. Why WebMCP Conventional browser automation would have to infer meaning from canvas graphics, controls and transient UI state. Olfaria instead declares exactly what an agent may do, with bounded JSON schemas and explicit side-effect semantics. The agent does not scrape the 3D interface or receive unrestricted application internals. It calls narrow tools that reuse the Atlas's deterministic graph service and existing visual controller. This makes the interaction faster and more reliable, but the larger improvement is epistemic: a recommendation can remain visibly connected to its source concepts, stored relations and uncertainty. Human-agent experience Before WebMCP, a person could explore the Atlas and an agent could discuss fragrance concepts, but their contexts were separate. With WebMCP they collaborate in one loop: the person supplies intent, the agent retrieves structured evidence, the Atlas visualizes the exact nodes, and the person evaluates the result. The visual state becomes a shared working memory rather than a screenshot to interpret. How it was built The existing Crystal Neural Atlas remains the only product renderer. A narrow window.OlfariaAtlasApi bridge exposes visual focus without leaking internal state. The page registers five tools through document.modelContext.registerTool. Four read-only tools call bounded deterministic graph operations. focus_nodes delegates to the Atlas controller and changes only the current browser view. The corpus loader validates the dataset, constructs immutable indexes and records a SHA-256 digest for reproducibility. Authentication protects the production Atlas, APIs and WebMCP registration with signed, HttpOnly, SameSite=Strict browser sessions. The public repository documents the implementation and includes the WebMCP adapter, service design and approved media, while local test packages, proprietary corpus data, production account hashes and session keys remain outside Git. Challenges Preserving the existing 3D renderer instead of creating a parallel agent-only experience. Defining tool outputs that distinguish stored evidence from deterministic technical inference. Keeping graph traversal bounded over 5,000 olfemes and 12,560 relationships. Making a session-protected WebMCP app deploy safely under a subpath. Publishing implementation context without releasing proprietary corpus data or credentials. Accomplishments Five stable, typed WebMCP tools with clear side-effect annotations. A real human-agent fragrance workflow that keeps evidence visible in the Atlas. Deterministic corpus operations with bounded inputs and traceable outputs. Graceful degradation when WebMCP is unavailable. A sanitized public implementation record without local test data or production secrets. A production login boundary that does not place credentials in the repository. What we learned Agent-native design is not the same as automating more clicks. The most useful interface was a small semantic contract aligned with the application's real domain boundaries. Visual actions and scientific reads also need different trust semantics: focusing a node is reversible browser state, while corpus claims must remain immutable and traceable. What's next Version the WebMCP contract independently from corpus releases. Add audit identifiers to every result so a judge or researcher can trace it to a specific corpus build. Add controlled multi-user workspaces without weakening session isolation. Extend evidence visualization while preserving the distinction between recorded and derived relationships. Challenge-period extension The Crystal Neural Atlas and corpus existed before the challenge. Between August 25 and September 3, 2026, the project was meaningfully extended with the WebMCP bridge, five typed tools, deterministic service endpoints, visual focus controller, English human-agent workflow, production authentication and subpath-safe deployment. The public repository preserves the implementation record and includes a dedicated development-history document. title: HenryKnows Special Agent
pitch: F-1 visa International students use their personal AI agent's to coordinate with a powerful tools for navigating fast changing visa rules, then produce practical guides to facilitate human advisement
about_excerpt: F-1 visa International students use their personal AI agent's to coordinate with a powerful tools for navigating fast changing visa rules, then produce practical guides to facilitate human advisement Like Comment Story Updates App with clickable WebMCP Problem International students must make decisions about study, employment, travel, and immigration compliance while complex rules around them are changing weekly. They also do a LOT of filling out forms and submitting their information to get things done. A personal AI assistant may know the student's goals and prior plans, but off-the-shelf AI does not have HenryKnows' specialized F-1 reference system or a deterministic implementation of brand new duration-of-status rules. HenryKnows has that regulatory capability, but starts each visit needing to essentially do an intake This can mean just another place already beleaguered students are having to reexplain themselves. Or they skip it altogether and arrive at advising appointments without a clear account of what matters or which questions remain unresolved -- and then having to reexplain themselves anyway. Solution HenryKnows now exposes a bounded set of WebMCP tools to an external browser agent. With the student's permission, the agent can propose relevant facts already present in their memory, ask only for consequential gaps or corrections, consult HenryKnows repeatedly throughout, and run the specialized Duration of Status Mapper once the calculation inputs are settled. The student confirms the situation before case-specific calculations. Deterministic code, not the language model, calculates the new-rule classification, dates, and timeline. The agent evaluates HenryKnows' student and professional answers against that evidence and authors two coordinated documents: a plain-language student preparation brief and a concise, source-linked DSO brief. Both can be downloaded as polished PDFs. Why This Matters The collaboration gives each participant the job it is suited for: The student owns the facts, choices, and final sharing decision. The personal agent contributes context, conducts the conversation, and handles the procedural work. HenryKnows supplies broad F-1 analysis grounded in primary authority. The mapper performs its narrower deterministic job: showing how the September 15, 2026 duration-of-status rules affect the confirmed timeline. The DSO receives a short case-specific briefing, not routine professional instruction or an AI demand for a decision. This is especially valuable where the sources do not resolve a new transition issue. The workflow preserves uncertainty, explains its practical significance, and directs human attention to the question that actually needs professional review. Why WebMCP This experience depends on capabilities that neither side has alone. A conventional website cannot access the context a student has already shared with their chosen agent. A personal agent cannot reliably reconstruct HenryKnows' curated regulatory retrieval or the mapper's deterministic rules. WebMCP allows the agent and student to work with the same live page and confirmed case while the website keeps specialized calculations, sources, validation, and visible state under its control. The agent can consult HenryKnows repeatedly, refine the student’s confirmed case, determine whether the new-rules timeline applies, compare one or two plans, and save both final briefs together. If an important fact changes, earlier results are marked outdated rather than reused. How We Used AI The external agent acts as an expeditor. It interprets the student's goal, reuses relevant conversational context with permission, asks focused follow-ups, decides when another HenryKnows consultation would resolve ambiguity, translates technical findings into practical choices, and writes the two audience-specific briefs. HenryKnows uses a model-backed answer engine over a curated index of primary F-1 sources. The model does not calculate legal deadlines or decide which duration-of-status branch applies. Those results come from the tested deterministic mapper and are supplied to the agent and HenryKnows as inspectable evidence. How We Used Codex Codex helped turn the initial idea into the implemented WebMCP workflow: inspecting the existing HenryKnows and mapper codebases, defining the shared case and tool contracts, implementing the native site tools, connecting the existing answer and calculation systems, and building the retained two-audience document surface. The UX was developed through repeated real ChatGPT Work walkthroughs. Codex traced failures found during those sessions, including blank comparisons, repetitive confirmation loops, stale evidence, false completion claims, buried outputs, tool-language leakage, and Markdown downloads that opened in unrelated applications. Those failures became implementation changes and regression tests. The current suite contains 242 passing tests across 19 files, plus TypeScript and production-build verification. Additionally, the Duration Mapper tool was originally built with Codex for another OpenAI hackathon. Key Features Native WebMCP tools with visible shared-page state. Immediate connected status and restrained live activity pulse. Relevant conversational context proposed by the student's agent. Cumulative fact collection with one settled confirmation. Repeated HenryKnows consultation before or after clarification. Deterministic screening, plan calculation, timeline, and source references. Honest handling of unsupported or unresolved regulatory questions. Agent-authored student and professional briefs tied to the same case revision. Atomic document completion and stale-output protection. Polished student and adviser PDF exports with clickable professional sources. Server-controlled free judging access without changing the commercial HenryKnows product. Architecture Static HenryKnows interface hosted on Netlify. Eleven bounded site-tool contracts registered through document.modelContext.registerTool . Versioned in-browser preparation case with confirmation and dependency invalidation. Existing TypeScript duration-of-status engine for deterministic rule calculations. HenryKnows retrieval and model-backed answer endpoint for broader F-1 guidance. Netlify Functions and Blobs for bounded continuation, long-running work, and short-lived transfer state. Client-side PDF generation loaded only when the user requests a download. Existing Project And New Work HenryKnows and the integrated Duration of Status Mapper existed before the challenge. The mapper was originally created for an earlier hackathon and was subsequently updated inside HenryKnows. They are not presented as new work for this challenge. Work added during the WebMCP Challenge includes the native site-tool layer, external-agent expeditor contract, versioned shared case, conversational confirmation boundary, cumulative connected interface, mapper/Henry orchestration, iterative consultations, revision and stale-work protection, atomic paired-document retention, audience-specific document validation, and client-generated PDF handoffs. The dated commit history and build log distinguish this extension from the prior products. title: WEBMCP
pitch: Seven WebMCP tools that let an agent and a bid manager read the same procurement board together, scoring what a supplier qualifies for and flagging the tenders written so only one firm could win.
about_excerpt: Seven WebMCP tools that let an agent and a bid manager read the same procurement board together, scoring what a supplier qualifies for and flagging the tenders written so only one firm could win. Like Comment Story Updates One button, one autonomous pass over twelve open procurement notices. No further human input. Seven tools registered through document.modelContext. Every agent call is mirrored on the right, in the human view. Every criterion ruled met / gap / unclear with its evidence, four integrity flags with their reasoning, and a dated bid plan. An agent raised the bid ceiling through update_supplier_profile and the board re-ranked live: this notice moved 17 to 41. The board ranked by fit, with the reasoning trace beside it: every tool call, its output and its latency. Inspiration Across the EU roughly half of all public contracts attract a single bidder. The usual explanation is corruption. The more common one is arithmetic: a tender dossier runs 40 to 130 pages, the qualification criteria that decide whether a company may legally bid are scattered through it, and a 26-person firm has nobody who can read forty of those a month. So they stop reading, and the field empties out on its own. The document that tells a supplier you qualify for this is the same document that reveals this one was written for somebody else — a specification fixed to 14 mm and 63.5 Wh describes exactly one laptop on the market. Once you are parsing dossiers at scale, both answers fall out of the same pass. TenderLens does that pass. The WebMCP layer is what lets somebody else's agent do it too, on the same page, in front of the human it is working for. What it does One button starts an autonomous sweep. For every open notice the agent opens the dossier, extracts the qualification criteria into structured form, rules each one met / gap / unclear against the supplier's real profile with the evidence attached, screens the buyer's award history and the clause wording for integrity red flags, scores fit out of 100, and writes a dated bid plan working backwards from the deadline with an owner on every step. It ends with a ranked board — 87 down to 17 across twelve notices — and a written bid / no-bid brief per notice. The full reasoning trace streams to the browser while it runs: every tool call with its input, its output and its latency. The integrity screen is five detectors, each grounded in a documented single-bidding indicator: SHORT_WINDOW , THIN_COMPETITION , VENDOR_CONCENTRATION , SPEC_LOCK and INCUMBENT_LOCK . None is presented as proof of wrongdoing. Each carries the reasoning that makes it worth a clarification question or a formal challenge. Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP Bid/no-bid is a conversation, not a query. The questions a bid manager actually asks are open-ended and chained — what closes this week that we can actually win? which of those look rigged? what would we qualify for if our turnover were three million instead of one-point-eight? — and every answer changes the next question. That is exactly the shape of work an agent is good at and a filter UI is bad at. But it is also work with consequences. A supplier who skips a tender because an agent said "weak fit" has lost a contract on the strength of a sentence. So the human has to stay in the room, looking at the same board the agent is reasoning over. WebMCP is the only arrangement that gives you both. The tools live on the page the human is already looking at. The agent gets typed JSON — fit scores, verdicts with evidence strings, flags with rationale — instead of scraped DOM text, and every call it makes is mirrored into a panel on that page, in the human's field of view, while the board itself re-ranks in front of them. No API key, no OAuth handshake, no separate agent-facing copy of the product to drift out of sync. How it creates a better user experience Three things change: You ask, instead of filtering. "Show me everything closing inside ten days with an integrity flag" is one sentence. In the UI it is four controls and a sort. You can see what the agent did. Every tool call appears in the Agent activity panel with its arguments and a one-line result. The verdict is auditable in the moment, not after the fact. The page answers with the page. search_notices outlines the matching rows on the board. update_supplier_profile re-ranks it live. The agent's answer and the human's screen are the same object, so there is nothing to reconcile. What people and agents can do together that was difficult before The what-if is the one that did not exist. update_supplier_profile lets the agent change the profile every notice is scored against — turnover, headcount, certificates, capability areas, bid ceiling — and the entire board re-ranks in the human's browser while they watch. Ask "what would an ISO 27001 certificate be worth to us?" and you do not get an estimate; you get the actual board you would have had, recomputed by the real engine, with the notices that moved outlined. That is a joint action. The agent supplies the question and the argument, the page supplies the ground truth and the recomputation, and the human sees both at once and decides. Before WebMCP you got one or the other: a chatbot that could reason but only about text you had pasted to it, or a dashboard that held the truth but could not be asked anything. The same applies to the integrity work. A journalist can now walk an agent across a portal — screen these, tell me which buyers concentrate awards — and every claim the agent makes is anchored to a screen_integrity call whose output is sitting on screen next to the claim. How I implemented WebMCP Seven tools registered through document.modelContext.registerTool , in edge/webmcp.ts : tool what it does search_notices rank open notices by fit; filter by category, country, days left, fit band, or integrity flags get_notice one notice in full: every criterion with its verdict and evidence, flags, bid plan, optional raw dossier screen_integrity the five single-bidder detectors with the reasoning behind each flag get_bid_plan dated plan worked backwards from the deadline, owner on every step get_supplier_profile the profile every notice is scored against update_supplier_profile change the profile and re-rank the board — the what-if tool run_sweep the whole pass over every notice, returning the ranked board Each registration carries a real JSON Schema — enums, descriptions and required fields on every property — because the schema is the only instruction the visiting agent gets. Every execute returns { content: [{ type: "text", text: JSON.stringify(...) }] } , so the shape holds across clients. Three implementation decisions are worth naming: Tools call the product, not a demo path. Each execute hits the same /api/notices , /api/notice/:id and /api/profile endpoints the page itself uses. There is no agent-facing copy that can drift out of sync with what the human sees. Every call is visible. record() writes each invocation — name, arguments, one-line result — into the Agent activity panel on the page. Tool calls also act on the view: search_notices outlines matching rows, update_supplier_profile and run_sweep re-rank the board. Writes are validated, not trusted. update_supplier_profile goes through applyProfilePatch in edge/agentapi.ts , which range-checks every field and ignores anything it does not recognise. An agent can explore the profile space; it cannot corrupt it. Registration degrades cleanly. If document.modelContext is absent the pill reads "WebMCP not detected" and the page works as an ordinary web app. The tools are also exposed on window.__TL_TOOLS__ , and every tool in the list has a run button beside it that fires the identical execute() — so a judge without a WebMCP-enabled browser can still see each tool run and log its result. How I built the rest TypeScript throughout. Supabase Postgres holds the notices, the supplier profile, the run log and every assessment; Server-Sent Events carry the live trace; the agent itself runs as a Supabase Edge Function on Deno. The front end is a single static page on GitHub Pages that talks to that function over CORS-open JSON and SSE, which keeps the page a plain document a judge or an agent can open with nothing in the way. The agent core — orchestrator, six tools, provider adapters, types — depends on nothing from Node, React or Next. That buys a second runtime for free: the same engine drives a Next.js build and the Deno edge build, unmodified. The decision worth defending is deterministic core, model at the edge . Every score, verdict and flag comes from code that can be read, tested and cited. A supplier disqualified on a criterion needs to point at the rule that fired; a score that exists only inside a model's context window cannot survive a procurement review board.  Inspiration 

 I wanted Kujo SSG to generate extremely fast static sites, stay simple to work with, and fit the way software is being built now, with AI agents doing more of the work. 

 That means treating agents as first-class users. 

 The site structure, CLI, machine-readable context, and WebMCP support are all built around making it easier for agents to understand and interact with a site without scraping pages and guessing what everything does. 

 What it does 

 Kujo SSG is a static site generator built as part of the Kujo programming language ecosystem. 

 It turns structured content, templates, components, assets, and configuration into static websites that can be deployed almost anywhere. 

 It also gives those sites an agent-facing layer. 

 Kujo sites can expose functionality through WebMCP, publish llms.txt and other machine-readable context, and give AI clients a cleaner way to interact with a site than browser automation. 

 It can also be extended with things like themes, plugins, commerce, CMS functionality, and AI integrations while still producing static output. 

 How we built it 

 The Kujo SSG follows the same approach as the rest of the ecosystem: small pieces, explicit behavior, strong defaults, and composable tooling. 

 The build pipeline handles content discovery, routing, templates, rendering, assets, and final site generation. 

 Around that, I built support for reusable themes, plugins, site configuration, structured metadata, AI-readable documentation, and WebMCP. 

 WebMCP fit naturally because Kujo was already being built around structured interfaces for agents. 

 Instead of teaching an agent how to click around a website, the site can expose the actions directly. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The main challenge was adding capability without losing the simplicity of a static site generator. 

 It is easy to keep adding features until you have basically rebuilt a dynamic framework with a static export step. 

 I wanted plugins, themes, commerce, AI integrations, and WebMCP to work around the static model instead of replacing it. 

 Agent interaction was another challenge. 

 Humans can look at a page and understand what buttons, forms, and navigation are supposed to do. Agents should not have to reverse-engineer that every time, wasting time and tokens on browser use. 

 WebMCP gives us a much cleaner way to expose that functionality directly. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 Kujo SSG has grown into more than a basic static site generator. 

 I've used it for real websites, documentation, content-heavy sites, commerce examples, plugin and theme systems, AI integrations, and WebMCP-enabled functionality. 

 It also works as part of the wider Kujo ecosystem instead of being a standalone tool. 

 That gives developers access to things like MCP, RAG, evaluation, observability, context management, specifications, validation, and other agent-focused tooling around the development process. 

 With WebMCP, the final website can now take part in that agent workflow too. 

 What we learned 

 A lot of value in building AI-native software comes from making software easier for agents to understand and operate. 

 Clear contracts are better than guessing, structured data is better than scraping, explicit tools are better than hoping an agent clicks the right thing and deterministic systems become more important as more of the development process becomes probabilistic. 

 Static sites work really well for that. 

 The final output is still just HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and assets, while the tooling around it can be much more capable. 

 What's next for Kujo SSG 

 I want WebMCP support to become a standard part of how Kujo sites expose functionality to agents. 

 That sits alongside llms.txt , MCP integrations, structured site metadata, and the rest of Kujo's agent tooling. 

 I'm also continuing to expand the SSG around commerce, CMS functionality, plugins, themes, reusable site kits, and AI workflows. 

 The goal is to make sites that are easy for humans to use and easy for agents to understand, modify, and interact with. 

 Static where static makes sense. 

 Agent-native where agents make sense.

title: Agentic Shift Search
pitch: A nurse tells an agent “Find RN and RT shifts in California from Sept 10th to the end of the month with a minimum pay of $30/h”. The agent applies relevant filters and shows the user matching shifts.
about_excerpt:
A nurse tells an agent “Find RN and RT shifts in California from Sept 10th to the end of the month with a minimum pay of $30/h”. The agent applies relevant filters and shows the user matching shifts.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 We are a team of marketers, developers and AI builders at Nursa striving to make our company not only visible to LLMs but also seamless for both humans and AI agents to interact with. We achieve this by structuring our content and data, implementing relevant schema markup, and actively exploring Model Context Protocol (MCP) integrations. WebMCP felt like a perfect enabler for making interactions with AI agents quicker, smoother, and completely frictionless. We couldn't wait to try it. 

 What it does 

 It allows agents to interact with the API endpoint including available clinician shifts on nursa.com. Instead of searching the shifts manually with the UI, we allow agents to use all our filters inside of WebMCP tools: 

 search_shifts - searches by license, state, specialty, minimum hourly pay, date range, and free text; returns up to 10 compact results. Data only - it never touches the list on screen. 

 apply_filters - takes the same filter inputs and writes into the shared filter store, so the visible list re-renders with the agent's choice. This is the human+agent moment the project is built around. 

 How we built it 

 We created a simple page displaying shifts available on our website and allowing for a filter selection. We added a script that registers WebMCP tools and references our endpoint. We tested it with WebMCP Model Context Tool Inspector 

 Challenges we ran into 

 1) WebMCP is really new. Right now it only works in ChatGPT's desktop app, and it doesn't behave the same way twice. The same prompt might work on one try and fail on the next. We spent a surprising amount of time just rewording tool descriptions until the model used them the way we wanted.
2) Dates gave us the most trouble. First a timezone bug: someone asked for shifts "from Sep 7th" and the filter got set to Sep 6th. Then ChatGPT told a user that shifts were "in 2027", because our responses only said "Sep 5" with no year and it guessed. We ended up sending full timestamps with the year and timezone, and kept the pretty labels just for display.
3) The AI would answer with stale results. Asking "RN shifts" and then "RN shifts in California" sometimes returned the first answer again, because the second search didn't properly reset the state from the first one. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 Quick implementation of a powerful feature we can later roll out throughout our platform. 

 What we learned 

 We weren't familiar with WebMCP before. Building this app gave us hands-on experience with its architecture, tool registration, and local testing workflows, giving us a clear view of both its massive potential for agentic search and its current limitations. 

 What's next for Agentic Shift Search 

 Further improvements to existing tools like expanding them with shift details, adding new tools and potential rollout to our main search pages, e.g. https://nursa.com/jobs/shifts

title: LUMLON
pitch: Is the air safe today? LUMLON answers for a person and for an agent through the same six site tools — and tells the agent when its own hazard data has expired.
about_excerpt: Is the air safe today? LUMLON answers for a person and for an agent through the same six site tools — and tells the agent when its own hazard data has expired. Like Comment Story Updates The page reads three provinces on load and plots all 77. Every card carries its observation time and source — before any agent arrives. Six site tools, declared by the page itself — no plugin, no separate server. Watches live in this browser only, never on a server. Asked about official warnings, the agent reads the expiry itself and refuses to report an expired warning as current. Nobody told it to. Inspiration Every morning I check the same thing: what is the air like today, is it safe, and can I play tennis with my son this evening? I check because my son was admitted to the hospital for it: a severe asthma attack, his airways closing, after breathing PM2.5 over a stretch of days when readings in our area were many times the level the World Health Organization calls safe. That is why "is the air safe today?" is not a curiosity in my house. It is a decision, every morning, before anything else gets decided. So I started building LUMLON: a Thai app that reads air, weather, and hazard conditions in real time. It exists, and you can open it — https://lumlon-web-dev.vercel.app is our development build, mid-redesign and not launched yet. I would rather you looked than took my word for it. What it is for is simple — to tell a person, day by day, at a time they choose or the moment they ask, whether it is safe to be outside. Not so they can study a chart, but so a father and son can plan an ordinary evening without gambling on it. Air you can plan around is also cheaper than a hospital admission, and in my family, that is not a figure of speech. The data already exists. Checking it does not scale. Today that means jumping between several apps, government agencies, and websites — each with its own shape, its own gaps, and its own idea of what "no data" means. It takes time, and on a morning you are in a hurry, you skip it. Would it not be better to simply ask — or to be told at the moments that matter — without opening anything at all? That is the kind of problem WebMCP is actually for. The person asking does not want a dashboard; they want an answer, in their own words, about their own province, right now. And people have already moved. They reach for an AI tool first now, which makes an agent a practical way to get this kind of information to someone — not a novelty. LUMLON was always meant to reach people through whatever channel they already use, not only inside one app. What WebMCP adds is that the answer can come from us: specific readings, each carrying its source and the time it was taken, instead of whatever an agent can assemble on its own. An agent also does something a website cannot do for everyone at once — it turns a reading into an answer in the language and the words of whoever is asking. That is why one of these six tools does not return a number at all. It returns a judgment about a specific activity, together with the readings it used and the reason it reached that answer. A number tells you what the air is like. A person still has to decide whether to go outside. So we did not build a chatbot on top of a website. We made the website itself something an agent can read, and kept the human looking at the same screen the whole time. What it does LUMLON exposes six tools to any WebMCP-capable agent, for all 77 provinces of Thailand. Tool What it does Kind search_locations Turns a place name into a province code. Thai or English, loose spelling. read get_environment_snapshot Air quality, short forecast, and official hazard alerts — each alert carries its own expiry, because they come from a dated snapshot. read get_safety_briefing Decides whether an activity is advisable and explains why , quoting the readings. read create_watch Saves a rule that warns when a reading crosses a threshold. write list_watches Lists the rules saved in this browser. read delete_watch Removes one rule. destructive It is a working page before an agent arrives. Open it with no agent at all and it reads three provinces on load — live PM2.5 and AQI, plus the official hazard alerts from a dated snapshot, which every card says on its face — and plots them on a map of all 77 provinces drawn from our own registry. You can search a province in Thai or English and read it yourself, with one click, through the same data path a tool call takes. This matters for a reason beyond looks: an agent-ready site can only be judged on what the agent adds , and that needs a "before" to compare against. A blank page waiting for a tool call is not a product an agent improves — it is a log viewer. What people and agents do together, concretely. You ask "is the air safe for a morning run in Chiang Mai tomorrow?" The agent calls two tools and answers in a sentence. At the same moment, the page in front of you updates — the same reading, the same timestamp, the same source. The map moves to Chiang Mai on its own; the card that appears is labelled read by the agent , next to cards labelled read by this page , so you can always tell which of the two of you did what. You did not lose the screen by talking to an agent; you gained a second way to drive it. Then you say "watch this and warn me if it goes above 75," and a rule appears as a card you can see — and that you remove the same way you made it, by asking. The panel lists your watches; it does not hide them, and it does not let anything but a tool call change them. The map moves without a seventh tool. We deliberately did not add a set_map_view tool to let the agent pan the screen. The view follows the tools it already has: search a place, the camera frames it; read a place, the pin lights up. Tool descriptions are charged against the agent's context on every single turn, so a tool is a cost, not an achievement — and this one would have bought nothing that the existing events did not already carry. Three decisions that make this usable rather than merely present: Every block of data carries when it was observed and where it came from. A number without a timestamp is a number nobody can check — and the person hearing an agent read it aloud cannot see the screen to judge for themselves. Missing data is reported, never hidden. If a source cannot be read, the answer says so, in a gaps field the agent reads out. "Could not read" and "there are no alerts" are different facts, and collapsing them is the single most dangerous thing a safety tool can do. For the same reason, a briefing never says good while something it needed was unavailable: missing data can lower our confidence, but it never lowers a warning. Read tools and write tools fail in opposite directions, on purpose. A read tool with one number missing still answers the question that was actually asked, and names what it could not read. A write tool with anything unvalidated refuses the whole command. Both write tools are annotated as writes, and delete_watch is additionally marked destructive. In the session we recorded — with approvals set to allow everything — the agent still stopped and asked before it deleted a rule. How we built it The tools do not know where their data comes from. They only ever talk to a provider interface, and that interface is in this repository: src/webmcp/providers/types.ts . The implementation behind it here is the bundled one, which calls only public sources. Be precise about what you can and cannot check in this export. The second implementation — the one that reads the backend of the product we are building — is not in this repository. The export is generated by following what the shipped entry actually imports, and since this entry runs on the bundled provider, the other implementation is never reached and never copied. So what you can verify here is the seam, not both sides of it: one interface, one implementation, and six tool files that name neither. That seam is the reason this entry can be frozen for judging while the product keeps moving, and it is also the reason we are telling you the second half is missing instead of letting the sentence imply it is here. To be exact about what that does and does not mean: this WebMCP layer was built for this challenge, and the product ships with it switched off. The shared interface is what makes it portable — not a claim that agents are driving our production app today. The module is invisible when it is off. WebMCP registration lives behind a build flag and a dynamic import. title: SiteWorks-WebMCP
pitch: SiteWorks WebMCP makes a website builder's admin agent-native — ChatGPT builds your shop's catalogue from a photo of the menu, and only you can hit publish.
about_excerpt: SiteWorks WebMCP makes a website builder's admin agent-native — ChatGPT builds your shop's catalogue from a photo of the menu, and only you can hit publish. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration In 2004 I built my own e-commerce platform, and I've run it and its successors ever since — over 30,000 stores at peak. In all that time, one thing never got easier: getting a real merchant's products into a store. The industry's answer is still "upload a correctly formatted CSV." The merchant's actual data is a flyer taped to the counter glass, a price list the printer was sent, a Word doc from 2019. I've watched merchants stall on that gap for two decades, thirty thousand ecom sites worth. When OpenAI shipped Site tools on August 25th, I saw the fix for the first time: don't build another bundled chatbot — make the admin page itself the tool surface, and let the merchant's own agent do the work. Storefront-side WebMCP already existed (Shopify ships it on every Liquid storefront; Chrome's official demos are shops). The admin — where the store gets made — had none. This is that half. What it does SiteWorks is a production site builder. During the Submission Period I added a WebMCP layer: the signed-in editor page registers 55 tools (19 read, 33 write, 3 skills) via document.modelContext.registerTool. The merchant's ChatGPT photographs the counter menu and drafts every item into the live store — reading the catalogue first, matching existing products instead of duplicating them, and flagging unpriced or ambiguous items for review instead of inventing numbers. The warnings live on the drafts, not in the chat. Then the same tools run outbound: export the catalogue and brand system, generate a printable flyer, inspect the result. Everything is draft-first with optimistic concurrency, an audit row per call, and one structural rule: nothing the agent can call publishes a page or a product. Publish isn't a guideline the model follows — it's a call that doesn't exist. The human holds the only commit button. How we built it On a real platform, which meant the hard part wasn't the tools — it was the boundary. One operations layer already served the human UI; WebMCP became a second caller of the same layer, and a server-side MCP endpoint a third. For the open-source release I extracted a standalone demo (SQLite, one container, a fictional bakery) that runs the identical layer, with prior work delineated in docs/PROVENANCE.md — the platform predates the contest; every WebMCP line postdates August 25th, and git grep at the cut-off commit proves it. Challenges we ran into Tools inside iframes aren't discovered. Our editor is a parent shell around a sandboxed preview — registration had to live on the parent, proxying into the preview. tools.call() can't return a file. Exports return a signed URL plus SHA-256 and expiry instead; the artefact rides the browser, the facts ride the tool result. Real defects, found by agent testing. A hero image/video conflict and a broken version-listing endpoint surfaced only when an agent actually drove the surface — both fixed, with the evidence baked into the tool contracts. Facts vs. decoration. Image models corrupt small text, so generated imagery decorates while names and prices bind from catalogue data. And the platform outage on deadline day, mid-render. Thanks for the extension. What we learned An agent doesn't need your platform to be smart — it needs it to be legible and governable. The intelligence is the user's; the structure is the site's. Twenty years of merchant onboarding pain turned out to be an interface problem: design the tool surface so the model's worst day is a review queue, not a live store, and everything else follows. What's next for SiteWorks WebMCP Shopper-side tools on the published storefronts (mirroring Shopify's vocabulary, so one platform carries both halves), deterministic flyer rendering so campaign artwork binds from the catalogue like everything else, and the same agent-native admin rolled out across the production estate — a thousand-plus small-business sites whose owners will never learn a page builder, but already know how to talk to ChatGPT.  Inspiration 

 Initially, I wanted to create a head-to-head competitive game for two players. However, after experimenting with Codex to control a webpage via WebMCP, I abandoned that idea due to excessive latency and slow response times. 

 This led to the creation of SplitSight—an escape room game consisting of three stages. The human player can see real-time visual cues that are not captured in the system's output, while the AI ​​agent can check the game state and operate mechanisms that the human cannot control. Neither party can escape alone; success requires cooperation. 

 Feature Overview 

 SplitSight guides the human and the AI ​​agent through three interconnected rooms: 

 
 Mirror Chamber: The human identifies and shares a flashing symbol; the agent reads this information and adjusts the angle of the mirrors. 
 Portrait Gallery: The human focuses on a flashing portrait; the agent uses the shared information to open the corresponding hidden compartment. 
 Twin-Door Hall: The agent analyzes structural information regarding two exits, while the human observes real-time "guardian markers" and selects the corresponding door; the agent can only open the door if its proposal aligns with the human's decision. 
 

 Every action—reading, selecting, blocked attempts, mechanism changes, and successful outcomes—is recorded in a shared causal log, with the source (human, agent, or room) clearly marked. The interface also indicates whose turn it is and what needs to be done next. 

 Technical Implementation 

 Implemented using Codex and "vibecoding"; the specific technology stack was also selected by Codex. 

 Challenges Faced 

 The biggest challenge was choosing the concept; I actually discarded three other ideas before settling on this one. 

 Achievement I'm Proud Of 

 Implementing the entire project using the "vibecoding" workflow. 

 Lessons Learned 

 Make frequent use of AI and Codex.

title: Swift Agents
pitch: More than a chatbot: A spatial-aware AI agent that natively sees your dashboard, securely queries your data, and automates tasks via WebMCP.
about_excerpt:
More than a chatbot: A spatial-aware AI agent that natively sees your dashboard, securely queries your data, and automates tasks via WebMCP.

 How it works 
 
 1 2 3 4 



 
 Inspiration 

 Today, if a user wants an AI to help them navigate a complex SaaS platform, find a specific API key, or analyze their dashboard data, the AI is completely blind. AI agents cannot see behind logins, which then makes building custom integrations for every single software platform an impossible task. 

 We were inspired to solve this "blind spot" for AI. We asked ourselves: "what if we could give any AI agent a complete, real-time map of a company's internal dashboard and private knowledge base, without requiring the company to build expensive custom API integrations or complex OAuth flows?" We wanted to build a bridge that makes any authenticated web application instantly "AI-Ready" and as simple as pasting a widget script. 

 What it does 

 Swift Agents WebMCP is a universal integration that transforms any traditional, complex web dashboard into an interactive environment for AI agents. 

 By simply pasting one line of code onto their website, a company instantly unlocks superpowers for their users. When a user visits the dashboard with a WebMCP-enabled AI assistant (like ChatGPT Desktop), our widget acts as a translator, allowing the AI to: 

 
 "See" the dashboard : The AI receives a complete navigation graph of the platform, instantly understanding where pages are and how to traverse them. 
 Read the docs : The AI can execute semantic searches across the company's private, gated documentation to instantly answer the user's questions. 
 Analyze private data : The AI can pull live analytics and metrics (like visitor counts) directly from the user's dashboard to generate reports or insights. 
 

 It turns a passive web page into a fully autonomous assistant environment. 

 How we built it 

 We focused entirely on creating a frictionless "time-to-value" experience for businesses: 

 
 Zero-configuration onboarding : We designed the system so that companies do not need to read API docs, manage API keys, or rewrite their backend. The entire integration is handled by dropping a single, lightweight script onto their site. 
 Secure data proxying : We built a secure translation layer that intercepts the AI agent's questions, routes them to our backend infrastructure, and safely returns the contextual data back to the browser. 
 Interactive playground : To demonstrate this vision, we built a modern demo dashboard where judges and users can interactively see exactly how an AI agent discovers and uses these tools in real-time.
## Challenges we ran into 
 Bridging two worlds : The biggest challenge was conceptually and technically bridging traditional web security (authenticated user sessions) with the needs of autonomous AI agents. We had to ensure that the AI could access exactly what the user could see, without exposing underlying architecture. 
 Pioneering a new standard : Because the WebMCP protocol is so new, we had to design entirely new user experiences. We spent significant time figuring out how to make the presence of these AI tools discoverable and intuitive for everyday users, rather than just developers. 
 Contextual relevance : It wasn't enough to just give the AI data; we had to structure the navigation graph and knowledge base responses so that the AI could immediately understand and act upon them without getting confused by raw data dumps. 
 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 
 Democratizing AI integration : We're incredibly proud that we've leveled the playing field. Now, a small startup can offer the same deep AI-integration capabilities as a massive enterprise, simply by copying and pasting a script tag. 
 The "invisible" upgrade : We successfully built a tool that is entirely invisible to regular users, but instantly comes alive with rich capabilities the moment a WebMCP-enabled agent connects to the page. It enhances the experience without cluttering the UI. 
 The "Aha!" moment : Successfully watching a generic AI agent connect to our isolated dashboard, discover our tools, and instantly answer a hyper-specific question about our visitors stats was a massive breakthrough for our team. 
 

 What we learned 

 
 *The future is universal agents: We learned that the future of AI isn't companies building thousands of custom chatbots for their individual websites. Instead, the future is protocols like WebMCP that allow users to bring their own preferred AI to any website and have it work seamlessly. 
 Data structuring is everything : We discovered that providing tools to AI is only half the battle, formatting the data (like our navigation graph as a comprehensive markdown formatted text) so the AI can intuitively reason about it is the true key to a successful agentic experience.
## What's next for Swift Agents 
 *Autonomous actions: Currently, our tools allow the AI to read and navigate. The next major leap is allowing the AI to write and act, such as creating tickets, responding to specific tickets, social media integrations, and so on. 
 Dynamic tool generation : We plan to automatically generate WebMCP tools on the fly based on a company's specific database schema (based on spec), meaning every single feature a company builds instantly becomes an AI tool without any extra work. This is especially useful to companies that already have working API layers that they want SwiftAgents to automate for them

title: Spokes - a collaborative map to help with coordination
pitch: Spokes turns "where should we go?" into one live map. Everyone adds their needs, some kept private, and places rule themselves out in real time. Your agent can assist you or fully negotiate for you.
about_excerpt: Spokes turns "where should we go?" into one live map. Everyone adds their needs, some kept private, and places rule themselves out in real time. Your agent can assist you or fully negotiate for you. Like Comment Story Updates Social media banner for Spokes Spokes — Devpost submission Live: https://spokes.alainschlesser.com/ Inspiration Groups are bad at picking somewhere to go, and the reason is structural rather than social. The needs that decide the answer are scattered across people and arrive piecemeal: a dietary restriction here, a budget there, a veto that lands after everyone else has settled, and at least one reason nobody wants to say out loud. A search results page optimises a single query. A group chat collects messages. Neither keeps a shared model of what the group has actually asked for, and neither lets a sensitive constraint count toward the decision without being explained to everybody first. That last part is what made this worth building for WebMCP specifically. A personal agent already knows things about its user that the user would rather not broadcast to five friends. Until now the only way to put that knowledge to work was to hand it to a shared service. I wanted to find out whether an agent could advocate for someone inside a live page, as that person and within an authority they granted, while the reason itself never left their client. What it does Three people open one planning room from a link. They see the same live map and the same brief of what the group has asked for so far. Each person states what matters in a single composer bar and chooses who may see it before they speak . A need can be shared, private, or agent-only. The server evaluates a private need and peers see only its effect on the count. An agent-only need stays with your agent and never reaches the server at all. The app suggests the next thing worth asking about from the data itself, never from a built-in list of categories. Every need becomes a row you can set aside. Press and hold a row and the map shows the room without that need, live. The cost of a need becomes visible instead of argued about. The room recomputes which places still work after every move, and it counts what is merely unverified separately from what actually failed. Missing data is drawn as its own state rather than quietly dropping a place. When nothing satisfies everyone, Spokes does not name who is blocking. It privately offers each person a quantified way out. The organizer sees "widen the area from 800 m to 1.2 km, brings back 4 places". The person who stated a need sees "let this need be nice-to-have, +12 places". Consent is explicit and confirmed on the page. Once the group agrees, the composer gives way to arrival: a travel mode and a one-tap handoff to the map app everyone already has. Alongside all of it, your personal ChatGPT can act in the same session through WebMCP. It can catch up on what changed while you were away, inspect places, put one forward, rule one out, or grant an adjustment. Your agent can assist you, or negotiate for you outright. How I built it A TypeScript monorepo (pnpm). Fastify and a Postgres event log sit behind a WebSocket realtime channel. The front end is React and Vite with MapLibre GL over keyless OpenFreeMap tiles. TypeBox contracts are shared by both sides behind a hashed contract-manifest gate. Place data is a one-time OpenStreetMap extract of Berlin Mitte. The WebMCP surface is 22 tools registered imperatively on document.modelContext at page load, 10 for negotiation and 12 spatial. Each is a narrow function with closed enum schemas, readOnlyHint and untrustedContentHint annotations, and a capped result budget. The page works fully without WebMCP. The tools are an additional way in. Four decisions did most of the work. Two protocols over the WebMCP substrate. WebMCP itself only carries tool names and schemas. So the first sync_session call returns a capability manifest that teaches the agent a domain-independent negotiation protocol (identity, revision sync, privacy tiers, requirements, stances, adjustments, consent, agreement) and a spatial-destination domain layered on top. Server-owned identity and per-viewer projections. Actor identity comes only from the bearer token. No tool argument accepts an actor id. Every event is stored once and projected per viewer, so unauthorised fields never appear in another participant's HTTP body or WebSocket frame. The test suite asserts this at the wire, not at the function boundary. Revision discipline instead of pretend realtime. Every mutation carries the agent's last-seen revision. A stale one returns a structured sync_required with a delta instead of acting on old state. That fits an agent that participates in bursts far better than a subscription it never really holds. Consent an agent cannot forge. An agent may recommend a grant, but a change beyond what the user delegated only stages . Staging mints a single-use code delivered on the participant's own realtime channel. The applying command must carry it back, and the code never appears in any tool result. Eligibility, minimal-conflict-set detection and the impasse counterfactuals are all deterministic. No model is allowed to invent a feasibility fact. 364 automated tests across three lanes: 222 unit, 128 three-user API, and 14 Playwright specs driving three isolated browser contexts. Challenges I ran into Privacy that is neither a lie nor a hole. The rule I settled on is that a private need's effect is always public and its content never leaves its owner. Both halves matter. Hiding the effect would make the count inexplicable, and leaking the content is the whole thing I was avoiding. It took a real redesign to stop routing private predicates through shared state "just for rendering", and a wire-level test suite to prove I had. Proving a human consented, honestly. My first cut let a bearer token commit an agreement over plain HTTP without ever touching the page. The realtime-only nonce closes that. It still is not proof a human clicked, because the realtime channel authenticates with the same token. Rather than overclaim, I wrote the residual threat model down in KNOWN-LIMITATIONS.md . Keeping the interface domain-agnostic. It is hard not to type a domain word into a heading. What saved it was a rule on the server side. The server returns the facets present across the current result set, each with a mandatory unknown count, and the client renders whatever it gets. There is no domain branch anywhere in the front end, which is also what lets a human and an agent reason over the same vocabulary. Deployment, on the last evening. I had prepared a Coolify deployment and abandoned it at the gate. Its Traefik has documented WebSocket failures on compose stacks, and the room is a WebSocket. The January 2026 disclosure put eleven critical CVEs in a control plane that runs as root. Its baseline would have claimed a quarter of a 4 GB box before Postgres started. The existing compose file was already a correct production stack. It needed twenty lines of Caddy in front, not a PaaS. That deploy went out with nineteen minutes to spare, after a self-inflicted detour in which a redeploy overwrote the host's generated Postgres password and stranded the database behind credentials nothing had written down. Two rendering bugs that looked like design problems. Vite's dependency optimiser broke MapLibre's worker, so the basemap never drew. A CSS animation setting transform silently overwrote a positioning translate and threw pins at their anchors. Both cost hours before either was understood. Accomplishments that I'm proud of An agent that can advocate for a constraint it never discloses. The agent screens places locally and returns per-place verdicts. The council folds them into eligibility, and peers see the aggregate effect with no route back to the cause. That is the capability I most wanted WebMCP to make possible, and it works. Press and hold. Holding a need shows the map without it, live, and releasing restores it. It turns an argument about whether a need is reasonable into a number you can see, and it is the one gesture everybody understood without being told. An impasse resolver that refuses to assign blame. When nothing satisfies everyone, the room offers each person a private, quantified route out, phrased as a consequence rather than an instruction. Honest unverified state. Missing data renders as a hollow pin and a separate count. A place is never silently dropped for lacking a value, and unknown is never drawn as failure. Two independent adversarial reviews: a protocol-invariant audit and a cross-family model review of the server, then two further reviews of the rebuilt client. The privacy and agreement-integrity findings were fixed and are covered by tests. I published the deferred items instead of hiding them. What I learned An agent is not a fast user, and modelling it as one produces bugs. It participates in bursts, disappears, an
