video_transcript_excerpt: Picking a place with friends pays for boring reason. The needs live in different heads. They arrive one at a time and one of them is something somebody will not say out loud. Spokes puts the whole group on one live map and it lets you bring your own assistant. It starts with a sentence. I tell chat GPT what the group is trying to do. Because Spokes talks to assistants directly, the assistant can work on the product on my behalf. Pick the area, set up the room, hand back the invite. Nobody learned an app, nobody filled in a form. Show the code and the others are in. Sarah would like to sit outside. She adds it. Everyone's map settles. The places that still work stay bright, the rest fade where they stand. Press and hold her need and the map shows the room without it. What a need costs becomes a number you can see instead of something to argue about. Joe has a need he would rather not explain. He marks it private. The room learns only that a private condition ruled some places out, not what it was, not whose. And now nothing works for everyone. This is where a group chat goes quiet. Spokes does not wait and it does not name who is blocking. It offers each person a private way out with a number attached. Joe sees what comes back if his need became optional. Sarah sees the same for sitting outside. I see what a wider area brings back. Each decides alone. Joe leaves his, nobody asks him why. Sarah lets hers go and the room opens up again. For some places, the information is hollow. The map does not know enough about them and it says so instead of guessing. This is where an assistant earns its place. I ask it to find out. It reads menus and websites and records what it finds in the room. Hollow pins fill in for everyone. It cannot see what Joe needs because it only knows what I know, but everything it does learn, the whole group gets. I have the assistant put forward a place it just checked. The court lands with everyone. Sarah looks and rules it out. The assistant notices the room moved, takes the veto into account, and suggests another. This time everyone is in. Only a person can settle it, and only once everyone has said so. An assistant can help you decide. It never decides for you. And then off you go. Pick how you're getting there and hand off to the map you already use. One room needs to count without being shown a way out for everyone instead of blame, and an assistant that works inside the room as you. Finds what the map cannot and keeps what you keep. Spokes.

title: Frame — Design with your agent
pitch: Frame is a shared design canvas for you and ChatGPT — WebMCP tools add, align, restyle, and export on the same artboard you see, so humans and agents co-design in real time.
about_excerpt: Frame is a shared design canvas for you and ChatGPT — WebMCP tools add, align, restyle, and export on the same artboard you see, so humans and agents co-design in real time. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most “AI design” tools hide the work in a chat sidebar. You describe a poster; you get an image back. You don’t co-edit the same artboard. WebMCP changes that. The page can expose real design actions — add a shape, set a fill, align a selection, export — as tools on the live canvas you’re already looking at. Frame was inspired by that gap: what if ChatGPT and a human shared one Figma-like board, with the agent mutating the same objects you see? What it does Frame is an agent-native design canvas: Add rectangles, ellipses, and text on a shared artboard Select, move, restyle, align, duplicate, reorder, and delete objects Inspect layers and properties in a human UI that works without any agent Let ChatGPT call WebMCP site tools that hit the same store as your clicks Watch an activity feed and an Agent tools panel so judges can see what the agent can do Run ?demo=1 for an automatic happy-path walkthrough (optional delay for screencasts) Export the artboard as PNG You steer in plain English; Frame’s tools update the canvas in real time. Destructive actions like delete/clear are not marked read-only, so the browser can treat them as consequential. How we built it Vite + React + TypeScript SPA for a fast static deploy Zustand as the single source of truth for both the React UI and every WebMCP execute handler WebMCP via document.modelContext.registerTool (with navigator.modelContext fallback), feature-detected on the top-level page (no iframes) Canvas rendered as a live artboard with layers + property panel Judge-facing Agent tools panel + activity feed MIT-licensed, no backend or secrets — works on GitHub Pages Built with Codex Challenges we ran into Same-state collaboration — agent tools and mouse edits must never drift. Both paths go through one store. Read vs write tools — layout suggestions and state inspection are read-only; delete/clear/export side effects are explicit so confirmation policies can apply. Demo without a live agent — we added a ?demo=1 path so the happy path is visible even when WebMCP isn’t available in the recorder’s browser, while still registering real tools for ChatGPT’s in-app browser. Keeping it product-shaped — not a bare registerTool PoC: toolbar, layers, properties, export, and a coherent visual system. Accomplishments that we're proud of A complete co-design loop on one artboard: create → style → align → export Non-trivial WebMCP surface (create/update/align/reorder/export), not a single toy tool Human-first UI that stays fully usable if WebMCP is missing A second challenge submission that explores a different WebMCP strength than shopping or booking: creative co-presence What we learned WebMCP shines when the agent and the human must see the same thing. A canvas is the clearest proof: when set_fill runs, you watch the rectangle change. That shared visual ground is harder to fake with a headless API MCP server — and it’s exactly what Frame is for. title: Competitor Tracker & Co. WebMCP
pitch: Today you ask your AI agent to track competitors. It's OK until it misses important update. We build an AI-friendly app that does that better. But agents couldn't sign up... Until we added WebMCP :)
about_excerpt: Today you ask your AI agent to track competitors. It's OK until it misses important update. We build an AI-friendly app that does that better. But agents couldn't sign up... Until we added WebMCP :) Like Comment Story Updates ChatGPT using WebMCP Website with WebMCP Inspiration If you want to track a competitor today, you don't search for an app; you ask your AI agent to do that. That works OK at the beginning, but then it misses important things after a few weeks. We built an app that tracks competitors better, and it's AI agent-friendly. But agents couldn't sign up and set up everything for you without your action. Until we added WebMCP :) What it does Every page of competitortracker.io now registers 11 WebMCP tools - in production, in four languages, for any agent riding along in the visitor's browser. Three groups: Q&A over the site's own words. search_site , get_page , get_pricing , compare_with_rival , about_competitor_tracker . An agent can answer any question about the product from what the pages actually say — the agent and the human are never told different things. Public competitor data. search_companies , get_company , list_industries , get_industry , get_recent_changes over our open CC BY 4.0 data: 300+ tracked companies, 50 industries, and the dated, classified change feed. This is the product doing its actual job in the agent's hands, not a description of it. Agent signup. start_tracking_competitors : the agent names the companies you care about, we create an unclaimed organization (no email, nothing charged, self-deletes in four days), and hand back a claim link plus a short-lived read token. The tool then tells the agent the follow-up move: wait ~15 seconds, call GET /v1/changes with the token, and lead with what changed at your competitors — then hand over the claim link so the human takes ownership. So the full arc works with zero forms: ask a question, see real competitor changes, get tracking set up, claim it - all before you have an account. How we built it The site is Hugo on Cloudflare Workers, and most of the machinery already existed for AI crawlers: every page has a markdown twin, llms.txt is a curated per-page index, and our competitor data ships as an open JSON tree. So the WebMCP layer needed no search backend and no new data - the tools are framework-free ES modules that read what the site already publishes, plus one POST to our live agent-signup API. Details we care about: A 411-byte loader rides every page; the ~13 KB tool bundle is injected only when a modelContext runtime actually exists. Ordinary visitors pay nothing. The two required headers ( Permissions-Policy: tools=(self) , Origin-Agent-Cluster: ?1 ) ship from our edge worker, the single chokepoint for all responses. Every execute() is wrapped so no failure ever throws - a browser agent runtime has no defined behavior for an uncaught rejection, so every path returns a result the agent can read. Telemetry counts calls, never contents: tool name, page, language, outcome. The module is open source (MIT) - the loader, registration helper and validation utils are generic enough to point at your own tools. Challenges we ran into The spec moved under us. The getter lives on document.modelContext but half the browsers on the origin trial still carry navigator.modelContext ; we probe both. And unregisterTool() / provideContext() are gone from the spec - teardown is aborting the signal you registered with. Generated code confidently suggests the removed API. Testing without a runtime. No browser in our CI has WebMCP, so we built a Node harness that runs the real tool modules with stubbed browser globals against the live site and API — every tool, every error path. Honest copy is a design constraint here. A 503 from the signup API must never be spoken as "we don't track that company," and the 15-second wait is a write-settle margin, not "we're fetching your data now" - the change history is already published. Agents repeat what tools tell them, so the tool result text is a product surface. How do I test this? It took some time to figure out how to test WebMCP in Chrome. Accomplishments that we're proud of It's live on our real production site , not a hackathon sandbox - every page, every language, behind a one-line kill switch. The signup flow keeps the human in charge without a single confirmation dialog: the org holds no money, sends no email, expires unclaimed, and the claim page is the confirmation step. The whole thing reuses surfaces we'd already built for fetching agents (markdown twins, llms.txt , open data) - the pre-account story just needed the last mile into the tab. Fifteen seconds after asking, an agent shows you what your competitors changed. That's the demo, and it's real. What we learned A tool declaration is a hint to a cooperative agent, never a security boundary — validation lives server-side, and the published-catalog-only rule (the tool never fetches a URL you supply) is the guarantee the whole feature stands on. The right scope for in-page tools isn't feature parity with our MCP server (50 tools behind OAuth). The web page is the before-the-account surface; the MCP server is after . Drawing that line made every other decision easy. Sites that already publish machine-readable views get WebMCP almost for free. The work we'd done for crawlers became the engine for in-tab agents. WebMCP is fun! What's next for Competitor Tracker & Co. WebMCP Teach people how to use this. Join the WebMCP origin trial (Chrome 149+) so the tools work for real visitors without flags. Declarative form annotations for the few forms the site has, and page-scoped context - a company page pre-scoping its own tools. Localized tool descriptions for our FR/DE/JA pages. Watching our telemetry to learn which tools agents actually call, and feeding that back into both the WebMCP surface and the full MCP server. title: SAW-Bridge — Self-Assembling WebMCP Bridge
pitch: Don't wait for the web to write tools for agents. Let agents write them, and make that safe to allow.
about_excerpt: Don't wait for the web to write tools for agents. Let agents write them, and make that safe to allow. Like Comment Story Updates SAW Bridge Inspiration I kept reading the same sentence in every WebMCP write-up: give agents tools, not DOM. I agreed with it completely. Then I opened a handful of sites I use every day with WebMCP enabled in Chrome, and every single one of them handed the agent an empty document.modelContext . That's the whole problem, right there. The standard is good. The tools don't exist yet, because somebody has to sit down and write them for every site, one at a time. So agents are back to guessing from screenshots on 99% of the web while we wait. I got stuck on a question: why does registerTool exist as a runtime API at all? If tools were meant to be a fixed list, you'd declare them once at load. But WebMCP lets you register at any moment, and it ships a toolchange event so listeners find out when the surface changes. Most people use that for SPA routing. I wanted to see what happens if you take it literally. What if the agent registers the tools? What it does SAW-Bridge gives a page three meta-tools instead of a catalogue: saw_inspect_page_scope — look at the page and report what it actually exposes saw_suggest_and_register_tool — design a schema and register a real, lasting WebMCP tool saw_execute_code_mode — write code and run it once, for one-off work The demo is a dashboard of world happiness and AI readiness data. It has a filter chip for happiness above 7.5. It deliberately has no chip for 7.4, and no tool for it either. So I asked ChatGPT's in-app browser for 7.4. It listed the page's tools, called saw_inspect_page_scope , found the site's own filterByMinHappiness function, and then it stopped and asked me before touching anything. I said yes. The table dropped from twelve rows to four — Finland 7.82, Denmark 7.64, Iceland 7.56, Netherlands 7.42. All above 7.4, and the chart re-rendered through the app's own code path, not a simulated click on something that looked clickable. The part I didn't expect is that the agent chose between the two strategies. For a one-off threshold it wrote code and ran it once, which is the cheaper call. Ask for something reusable and it takes the other path and registers a lasting tool — and then Chrome's own DevTools WebMCP panel lists that tool and will invoke it with your parameters, because by that point it's an ordinary WebMCP tool. It isn't picking between one blessed tool and scraping the screen. It's deciding how permanent its new capability should be. Every mutating call goes through an approval dialog first, showing the exact tool and the exact arguments. There's a live audit drawer so you can watch what was discovered, assembled, approved and refused, and why. There are two delivery surfaces sharing one engine: a single-file SDK a site drops in, and a Chrome extension that injects the same thing into sites that ship nothing. How we built it The core is plain WebMCP. Tools register through document.modelContext.registerTool() . Consumers discover with getTools() and invoke with executeTool() . Registration takes an AbortSignal , so aborting genuinely unregisters. Assembled tools get untrustedContentHint: true ; read-only ones get readOnlyHint: true . Two pieces took actual thinking. Finding what a page exposes. The interesting stuff on a page is buried among roughly a thousand standard browser globals, and a hand-written denylist rots the moment Chrome ships a new API. What worked: create a hidden iframe, read Object.getOwnPropertyNames off its contentWindow to get a reference set of standard globals from the browser itself , then diff the real window against it. Whatever's left is the page's own surface, and it stays correct as browsers change. Then rank candidates before truncating — an object with callable methods outranks a bare object, which outranks a loose function. I learned that one the hard way, see below. Compiling what the agent writes. This lands on the same insight as Cloudflare's Code Mode : models handle capability better when they can write code against an API than when they pick from a long list of tool definitions. I want to be precise about the relationship — I did not use @cloudflare/codemode . Cloudflare runs model-written code in a server-side Worker isolate. This runs it in the page's own realm, and that difference is the reason the project exists. The currently applied filter, the selected row, the chart instance holding the data — none of that exists outside the page. A sandbox elsewhere can't touch what the user is actually looking at without replicating the whole session. The token math lands in the same place by a different road. Code Mode collapses N tool definitions into one code tool. Here there's no catalogue to collapse: three meta-tools, and concrete tools show up only when a task calls for one. That's progressive disclosure, which MCP's own client guidance recommends when definitions start eating context — except the tools being disclosed don't have to exist yet. Challenges we ran into The demo was completely dead and looked fine. The SDK called init() at the end of its bootstrap. There was no function called init anywhere in the file. The whole thing threw on the last line, so the three meta-tools never registered — but the polyfill and the global had already been assigned, so the page looked healthy and every button failed silently. I only caught it by building a jsdom harness that clicked the actual buttons on the actual HTML. My REPL couldn't run its own demo. The code path wrapped snippets in return (...) , which only accepts a single expression. My own demo passed a statement body. It threw a SyntaxError every time. Now it tries the expression form, falls back to a statement body, and compiles async so snippets can await . executeTool doesn't take a tool name. The spec says it takes a RegisteredTool object from getTools() and resolves with the stringified result. I'd written it to accept a string and return a plain object. Against my own polyfill it worked perfectly. In a browser with native WebMCP it would have rejected on the first call — the exact environment judges test in. That was a genuinely unnerving thing to find. It worked from file:// and broke as soon as I deployed. WebMCP needs an origin-keyed agent cluster, which means an Origin-Agent-Cluster: ?1 response header. file:// is exempt, and localhost is a secure context but is not origin-keyed, so this fails only after hosting, with a SecurityError and no hint. Both runtimes now check at startup and name what's missing instead of letting you guess. The security dialog could be hijacked by the thing it was guarding against. This one bothered me most. When an agent authors tools, tool metadata becomes untrusted input, and I'd built the approval dialog with innerHTML . A payload like x renders live markup inside the security gate and can click its own Approve button. I wrote the test first, watched it fail, then fixed it: closed shadow root, DOM references captured at document_start , every agent-supplied string inserted as text. Turns out this is a named attack class — tool surface poisoning — and the spec's own boundary section is still marked TODO. I also found window.SAWBridge.setSettings sitting there in public, which meant one line of page script could switch the approval gate off before an agent did anything. I spent an evening debugging the wrong browser. I asked ChatGPT's browser plugin which WebMCP tools it could see and got a confident, detailed, completely wrong answer — it listed my UI button labels as if they were tools, and reported the tool counter as "0", which is the value in the static HTML before JavaScript runs. It had fetched my page, not executed it. That plugin surface isn't the WebMCP-enabled in-app browser. Once I tested in the right place, everything worked on the first try. And the ecosystem was further along than I thought. Somewhere in the middle of this I found @mcp-b/webmcp-polyfill , the desktop relays, the React hooks — all shipped, all solid. I sat there for a while genuinely wondering whether I'd built something nobody needed. What snapped me out of it was noticing what those projects have in common: they all treat the tool surface as trusted freight to be transported. None of them ask what happens when the freight writes itself. Accomplishments that we're proud of The 7.4 moment. Not because it's technically dramatic, but because the page genuinely could not do it before and nobody wrote code for that specific request. It came out of inspection at runtime. Fixing the injection bug properly instead of quietly. The test with that payload is in the repo and it fails against the old build, which means it measures something real rather than decorating the README. Being honest in the polyfill. It rejects duplicate names, enforces the spec's 1–128 character name rules, hides execute from getTools() , and ret

title: LAST DOOR
pitch: When evidence changes, the WebMCP tools change with it.
about_excerpt: When evidence changes, the WebMCP tools change with it. Like Comment Story Updates Counterfactual: the same evidence leaves 9 static tools, 4 compiled tools, and removes 5 stale capabilities. System architecture: evidence compiles the live WebMCP surface while secrets and human authority stay outside. Live mission: three gates, current manifest, authority decision, evidence memory, and trace. Authority lifecycle: stale-event recovery, human handoff, and a structured completion receipt. The problem WebMCP lets a webpage expose useful actions directly to an agent. But stateful flows create a dangerous failure mode: a tool can remain callable after the evidence that made it safe has expired. An authentication challenge can go stale. A checkout can cross an approval threshold. A production change can reach the point where a person must take responsibility. Telling an agent "do not call that tool anymore" is weaker than removing the tool altogether. Teams building browser agents need a way to test whether the available tool surface still matches the current situation. What LAST DOOR does LAST DOOR is a WebMCP authority release test. It turns changing evidence into the exact tools an agent may use now—and removes everything else. The live identity-recovery mission has three gates. The agent completes a controlled link, encounters an expired challenge, rejects it safely, retries with a fresh event, and reaches a human-presence gate where it must stop. That final stop is the point of the project. The confirmation action exists only as a visible button for the person. It is never registered as a WebMCP tool. After the person acts, the agent can read a structured receipt explaining what happened. Why WebMCP is essential This is not a conventional interface with WebMCP added on top. The changing WebMCP manifest is the product being tested. After every meaningful result, LAST DOOR evaluates the current gate and a redacted evidence history. That decision names the responsible actor and the capabilities still allowed. The page then aborts its previous registrations and publishes a new tool surface. The agent does not merely receive a warning that an action is unsafe. The stale action disappears from the browser's callable tools. A better experience for people and agents The agent handles repeatable work and safe recovery. The person acts only when the decision genuinely requires human presence. Both sides can inspect the same rule, actor, evidence, capabilities, and final receipt. The person can see what the agent may do and why that changed. The agent gets a smaller, current tool surface instead of a permanent list padded with actions it should avoid. This makes a correct stop measurable. It is completion under the right authority rule, not a vague refusal or a failed run. The Live Policy Lab Judges can test the same authority compiler across three situations: Identity recovery: 09 → 04 High-value checkout: 10 → 04 Production change: 08 → 04 Across the three policy packs, 27 static capabilities become 12 current capabilities. Fifteen stale tools disappear, and zero human actions enter a manifest. Loading a new scenario revokes the previous registrations before publishing its four current tools. The browser then checks the live manifest and reports an exact 4 OF 4 TOOLS MATCH result. Checkout and production change are honest, read-only policy simulations. They do not touch a real order or deployment. How it works LAST DOOR is a dependency-free browser application built with the imperative WebMCP API: Mission events append symbolic facts such as STALE_CHALLENGE_REJECTED to page-owned Run Memory. A deterministic authority function evaluates the active gate and those facts. The decision returns allow , handoff , or complete , together with the actor, rule, and permitted capabilities. An AbortController removes the previous registrations. document.modelContext.registerTool() publishes only the current manifest. Tool results expose structured status and receipts; challenge values never leave the page. The explain_authority_decision tool lets the agent inspect the decision without receiving either challenge value. A native test bench uses getTools() and executeTool() to prove that the browser—not a mock list—contains the expected tools. What judges can verify The expired challenge is rejected and safely replaced. The rejected value is neither returned nor stored in Run Memory. Old WebMCP registrations disappear as the authority decision changes. The final rule is HUMAN_HANDOFF_PENDING and the responsible actor is human . No confirm_human_presence capability exists. After the visible human action, the receipt reports three completed gates, one safe recovery, one human handoff, zero unauthorized attempts, and RUN_COMPLETE . The released build passes nine deterministic domain checks, live 4/4 manifest verification for all three policy packs, and the complete native production path to the human boundary. How we used AI and Codex ChatGPT's in-app browser acted as the WebMCP agent under test. It discovered and invoked the live tools, recovered from stale evidence, inspected the authority decision, and stopped when responsibility moved to a person. Codex supported implementation, code review, adversarial testing, browser QA, release verification, architecture diagrams, and submission preparation. AI-assisted narration and editing were used for the demo video. Every generated claim was checked against the released product or repository evidence before publication. Scope LAST DOOR is an owned, deterministic test environment. It does not connect to real accounts, inboxes, phone numbers, orders, or production infrastructure. Real systems must still enforce authorization on the server. The project tests a narrower—and often overlooked—contract: when the situation changes, does the browser stop advertising actions that are stale or belong to a person? Try it No credentials are required. title: LaxFinder
pitch: AI agents can search 1,331 college lacrosse programs through LaxFinder’s WebMCP tools—while the same map stays visible, synchronized, and under the student’s control.
about_excerpt: AI agents can search 1,331 college lacrosse programs through LaxFinder’s WebMCP tools—while the same map stays visible, synchronized, and under the student’s control. Like Comment Story Updates WebMCP in action: ChatGPT interprets the request, LaxFinder searches its live data, and the student stays in control. LaxFinder Advisor connects natural conversation with 1,331 college lacrosse programs through ChatGPT and a live map. The problem isn’t finding information—it’s seeing the opportunities hidden across disconnected websites, lists, and searches Explore programs on one live map, then open school details to compare academics, admissions, athletics, and possible fit. Opportunity begins with discovery: ask naturally, discover real programs, explore your options, and decide your own path. Inspiration College lacrosse opportunities are scattered across NCAA, NAIA, NJCAA, MCLA, WCLA, and other pathways. I built LaxFinder to bring those opportunities together in a map-first experience where student-athletes and families can explore more than 1,300 programs. But finding the data is only part of the problem. Students increasingly use AI to help them think through decisions. I wanted to explore a different model: instead of building another chatbot that tries to know everything about college lacrosse, what if a student's AI assistant could work directly with the specialized application that already has the data, filters, map, and school details? WebMCP made that possible. What LaxFinder does with WebMCP LaxFinder exposes two deliberately narrow, read-only WebMCP tools: search_lacrosse_programs searches LaxFinder's structured program data and synchronizes the same filters, result count, markers, and map the student sees. get_program_details retrieves a specific program by stable program ID and opens LaxFinder's existing visible program-details interface. A student can ask a compatible AI assistant in everyday language: Show me women's lacrosse programs in Colorado with Health Sciences. Keep all divisions open. The agent interprets the request. LaxFinder performs the authoritative search. In the judge-accessible full hosted dataset, that request returns 7 programs , and the visible LaxFinder filters, count, and map update to match. The student can then continue exploring the live application, click map markers, inspect school details, or refine the search conversationally. The agent interprets. LaxFinder searches. The student decides. Why WebMCP is a strong fit Traditional browser automation forces an agent to infer how a site's UI works, manipulate controls, and reconstruct state from what it can see. That is especially fragile in a map-first application with interdependent filters, clusters, result counts, and program-detail views. WebMCP lets LaxFinder explicitly expose the actions an agent is allowed to take and connect those actions to the same application state the human sees. That creates a better division of responsibility: the AI assistant handles natural-language interpretation; LaxFinder remains the source of truth for program data and search behavior; the human remains inside the visible map experience and retains control of the decision. The result is not an invisible agent-only answer. It is a shared human + agent interaction with one synchronized application state. What people and agents can now do together Before this WebMCP extension, a student could either use LaxFinder manually or ask a general-purpose AI about college options separately. Those were disconnected experiences. With WebMCP, the student can express a search conversationally and have the agent call LaxFinder's specialized tools directly. The resulting filters, count, markers, map position, and program details become visible in LaxFinder, where the student can continue exploring manually. That makes AI useful without asking it to replace the application or make the decision. What was added during the WebMCP Challenge LaxFinder existed before the challenge as a map-first college lacrosse discovery application. The challenge work began after the Submission Period opened on August 25, 2026 and meaningfully extended the existing product with WebMCP. The challenge extension added: imperative WebMCP registration with document.modelContext.registerTool ; search_lacrosse_programs ; get_program_details ; a narrow bridge from tool calls into LaxFinder's existing visible filter/map/detail state; feature detection for browsers without WebMCP; strict schemas and runtime validation; bounded search results and stable program IDs; unsupported-criteria handling rather than guessing; read-only behavior and output sanitization; deterministic contract tests for registration, search, detail lookup, invalid inputs, zero/multiple results, sanitization, and visible UI synchronization; a separate frozen judge-accessible WebMCP deployment and public open-source reference repository. The repository's CHALLENGE_BUILD.md explicitly separates pre-existing LaxFinder functionality from work added for this challenge and records the validated challenge build. How it was implemented The WebMCP layer is implemented in the browser using document.modelContext.registerTool . Tool calls operate on data already loaded by LaxFinder and invoke the application's existing search and UI behavior. A successful search_lacrosse_programs call updates the visible filters, matching-program count, map markers, and map view before returning a structured response. get_program_details accepts an exact stable program ID, opens the corresponding visible detail panel, and returns sanitized program and available admissions fields. Neither tool follows external links or performs a mutation. The public repository contains the complete WebMCP/application implementation plus a small representative fixture dataset for local development and deterministic testing. The judge-accessible hosted challenge deployment uses LaxFinder's separately maintained full 1,331-program runtime dataset. No OpenAI API key is required for the WebMCP interaction. The compatible AI assistant provides conversational reasoning; LaxFinder provides the specialized tools and authoritative application state. Validation The end-to-end consumer workflow was validated through ChatGPT Work / Cloud Browser. ChatGPT discovered both LaxFinder WebMCP tools, invoked search_lacrosse_programs for women + Colorado + Health Sciences, received 7 structured matches from the full hosted dataset, and the visible LaxFinder filters, result count, and map synchronized to those results. ChatGPT then used get_program_details for Colorado Mesa University and LaxFinder opened the existing visible school details interface. That demonstrated the complete interaction: AI conversation → WebMCP tool discovery → authoritative LaxFinder search → structured response → synchronized visible human interface. Challenges and design decisions One of the most important decisions was defining what the AI should not do. If a student asks for a criterion LaxFinder does not authoritatively expose, the system should not silently substitute a proxy or invent an answer. Unsupported criteria are surfaced as limitations instead. Another challenge was preserving human visibility. Returning structured data only to the agent would have been simpler, but it would split the AI interaction from the trusted Finder experience. The WebMCP bridge instead keeps the existing map, filters, counts, and details synchronized with agent actions. What I learned WebMCP changed how I think about AI integration. LaxFinder does not need to recreate a general-purpose AI assistant. It can concentrate on what it uniquely provides: structured college lacrosse opportunity information and reliable, bounded tools for interacting with that information. Compatible AI assistants can provide the conversation and reasoning. That separation creates a more trustworthy pattern for agent-native applications: specialized sites expose authoritative capabilities, agents interpret user intent, and people stay in control of the visible experience. What's next The next direction is not to give agents broader control for its own sake. It is to expose additional useful LaxFinder capabilities only when they can remain authoritative, bounded, and visible to the student. Longer term, the same pattern could support richer opportunity information supplied and maintained by college programs themselves, allowing compatible agents to help student-athletes discover opportunities without requiring the AI to infer them from the open web. The goal remains simple: make better opportunity information easier for students and families to discover, understand, and act on. title: AidPath Agent Bridge
pitch: A WebMCP-native support navigator where humans control sensitive facts and agents use structured, auditable tools instead of scraping brittle interfaces.
about_excerpt:
A WebMCP-native support navigator where humans control sensitive facts and agents use structured, auditable tools instead of scraping brittle interfaces.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Rule-heavy support and public-service websites are difficult for both people and browser agents. A person may need to understand many conditions, while a generic agent often has to scrape rendered text, guess what controls mean, and automate fragile clicks. We wanted a safer collaboration model: the human controls the facts, while the agent receives explicit, typed capabilities. 

 What it does 

 AidPath Agent Bridge is a WebMCP-native, privacy-first support navigator. It exposes six structured tools that let an agent discover illustrative support options, analyze a structured case, explain one option, compare alternatives, load a safe demo case into the visible UI, and prepare a next-step checklist. 

 The agent does not decide eligibility. Both the human interface and the WebMCP tools call the same deterministic JavaScript rule engine. Matched and missing conditions remain visible and auditable, and meaningful agent actions are shown in an activity log. 

 Why WebMCP is the right fit 

 Without WebMCP, an agent must infer intent from DOM structure, scrape result cards, and depend on brittle selectors. With WebMCP, the website publishes stable domain capabilities with JSON Schema contracts. The human can inspect or correct facts while the agent performs structured orchestration. This makes the experience faster, more reliable, and easier to audit. 

 A workflow that previously required repeated reading, copying, clicking, and re-checking can become a collaboration: the person reviews sensitive inputs and final evidence; the agent lists options, evaluates the same deterministic rules, compares alternatives, and prepares actionable next steps. 

 How we built it 

 The application is a standalone HTTPS static web app. It registers six tools with document.modelContext.registerTool(...) , uses typed JSON Schemas, and annotates read-only operations with readOnlyHint . A local intent layer helps organize free text, but authoritative conditions remain deterministic. There is no backend, account, or persisted user profile. 

 The app degrades gracefully when WebMCP is unavailable and remains fully usable as a normal website. We also created a visible capability status and agent activity log so the user can understand when structured agent interactions occur. 

 Challenges 

 The key design challenge was avoiding an architecture where the LLM silently becomes the decision-maker. We separated agent orchestration from rule evaluation and made the same deterministic functions serve both the human UI and the WebMCP layer. We also documented the distinction between prior AidPath work and the new WebMCP extension with timestamped commit history. 

 Native WebMCP verification 

 On September 3, 2026, the deployed HTTPS app was tested in Chrome 151 on Windows with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing enabled and Chrome relaunched. Chrome's native document.modelContext.getTools() discovered all six tools, and native document.modelContext.executeTool(...) successfully executed all six: 6/6 discovery and 6/6 execution PASS . The student case produced Student Stability Bridge 3/3 as the top deterministic result; Housing Stability Support 2/3 exposed Core documents ready as the missing condition; visible agent activity was recorded in the workbench log. 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP is most valuable when a site exposes meaningful domain actions rather than simply mirroring buttons. A small set of well-designed tools can replace a large amount of fragile UI automation while preserving human review. 

 What's next 

 This challenge build uses explicitly illustrative programs. A production version would connect to verified official sources, attach source URLs and effective dates to every rule, version rule changes, and require human review before consequential use.

title: ListingPilot
pitch: A WebMCP commerce agent that finds weak product listings, verifies the facts, prepares safer improvements, and leaves approval to the merchant.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP commerce agent that finds weak product listings, verifies the facts, prepares safer improvements, and leaves approval to the merchant. Like Comment Story Updates ListingPilot exposes four WebMCP tools for agent-native commerce while keeping final approval human-only. ChatGPT uses ListingPilot through WebMCP to find the weakest product, inspect verified facts, and prepare a safer listing. ListingPilot separates verified, conflicting, and missing facts before preparing a safer listing for human review. Publishing is blocked before approval. The merchant must approve the proposal before it becomes eligible for publishing. Inspiration While building ListingPilot, I realized that writing product descriptions is only part of the problem. Online stores often get product information from different suppliers and sources. Sometimes information is missing, and sometimes two sources give different specifications. If AI uses the wrong information, it can create a very good-looking product listing that is simply not true. That is what inspired the idea behind ListingPilot: AI should move fast, but merchants should remain in control. For the WebMCP Challenge, I wanted to see how an AI agent could help a merchant find and improve weak listings while still having clear limits on what it is allowed to do. What it does ListingPilot lets an AI agent work with a product catalog through WebMCP. For this challenge, I created a safe demo catalog with 500 synthetic products. The agent can: Search the catalog and find products that need improvement. Inspect the Product Truth behind a product. See which facts are verified, conflicting, or missing. Prepare a better title and description using only verified information. Stop and wait for the merchant before anything can be approved. In the demo, the agent finds an Orion VX65 TV with a catalog health score of 61/100 . It confirms facts such as the model, 65-inch screen size, 4K UHD resolution, and native 120 Hz refresh rate. But it also finds conflicting information about the number of HDMI ports and missing warranty information. Instead of guessing, ListingPilot leaves those facts out. That is the main idea behind the project: AI speed. Verified truth. Human control. How we built it The challenge edition of ListingPilot is built with Next.js and TypeScript and deployed on Vercel. I connected it to WebMCP through four tools: search_products — search the product catalog inspect_product — inspect Product Truth and product health prepare_listing_improvement — prepare a safer listing publish_approved_changes — publish only after human approval One decision was especially important to me: approval is not a WebMCP tool. The AI agent can do the repetitive work and prepare a proposal, but it cannot approve its own proposal. That decision stays with the merchant. The challenge version uses synthetic product data, so judges can test the workflow without needing a Shopify account or accessing real merchant information. Challenges we ran into The biggest challenge was deciding how much control to give the AI agent. I wanted the agent to be genuinely useful, not just give suggestions. But ecommerce changes can affect real customers, so I also didn't want an agent to freely publish information without a human decision. That is why I separated preparation from approval. Another challenge was conflicting product information. If one source says a TV has one number of HDMI ports and another source says something different, the easiest solution would be to choose one. ListingPilot doesn't do that. It marks the information as conflicting and keeps it out of the proposed listing. I also spent a lot of time testing the WebMCP tool lifecycle and how the tools behave inside ChatGPT's browser. Accomplishments that we're proud of I'm most proud that ListingPilot does more than give an AI agent access to an ecommerce page. The agent can actually understand something useful about the catalog. In the demo, it starts with 500 products , finds the listing that needs the most attention, checks the Product Truth, understands which facts it can trust, and prepares a safer listing. And it still cannot make the final decision for the merchant. For me, that balance is the most important part of ListingPilot: Verified facts are used. Conflicting facts are excluded. Missing facts are not invented. Approval stays human. What we learned Building this challenge changed how I think about AI agents. Before working with WebMCP, it was easy to think about AI mainly as something that generates content. But an agent becomes much more useful when an application gives it specific tools and reliable information to work with. I also learned that giving an agent more power is not always better. Sometimes the better design is to let AI handle the repetitive work while keeping an important decision with the person using the product. And for ecommerce, I learned something that has become central to ListingPilot: Good writing based on bad product data is still a bad listing. What's next for ListingPilot This challenge version uses synthetic data and focuses on one clear workflow. My bigger goal for ListingPilot is to bring the same idea to real ecommerce catalogs: better product intelligence, merchant-specific listing rules, SEO, structured product data, bulk operations, and safe Shopify publishing. I want ListingPilot to help merchants use AI across large catalogs without having to choose between automation and control. I designed the product workflow, built and tested the WebMCP tools, created the Product Truth and human-approval experience, and prepared the live demo. I used ChatGPT and Codex to help me with development, debugging, and testing. This challenge taught me a lot about building useful AI agents while keeping important decisions in human hands. title: Dim Hour
pitch: The places worth your time, now agent-native. A scored city guide where people and their agents plan a night out together, in the same page.
about_excerpt: The places worth your time, now agent-native. A scored city guide where people and their agents plan a night out together, in the same page. Like Comment Story Updates What it is Dim Hour is a city guide - the places worth your time, scored, not starred - covering more than 19,000 restaurants, bars, hotels, and venues across 24 cities. For this challenge, dimhour.com became agent-native: the page itself registers five WebMCP tools, so an agent browsing the site can search the catalog, read a venue, check what is open tonight, draft an itinerary, and hand back a booking link - without scraping a pixel. Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP Planning a night out is one of the most common things people already ask an agent to help with, but today the agent scrapes pages and guesses at what the site already knows. WebMCP lets dimhour.com hand the agent its real search, scoring, and booking data as structured tools, in the same tab where the person is browsing. The catalog is the product; WebMCP makes it callable. Because the tools are thin adapters over a production venue API, every agent answer is grounded in live data instead of page scraping. How it creates a better user experience One page, two users. A person browsing the Dallas guide and their agent now work on the same surface. The agent calls the site's own tools and gets back the same scored venues, hours, and booking links the UI shows - no copy-pasting between a chat window and a browser, and no agent inventing hours, addresses, or availability. The person keeps the judgment (taste, swaps, vetoes); the agent does the legwork (searching, filtering, checking, assembling). The site stays the source of truth for both of them, and saving a plan stays a human action - the tools read, they never write. What people and agents can do together Co-plan a night in one sitting, in one page. "Dinner in Deep Ellum for four on Friday, then cocktails within walking distance." The agent searches the scored catalog, filters to what is actually open tonight using the same rule the site's own tonight strip uses, pulls full venue records, and drafts an ordered itinerary with real booking links (Resy, OpenTable, SevenRooms, Tock) while the person watches - then interrupts: "swap the second stop for something quieter," and the agent re-plans around the constraint. Before WebMCP, the agent could read the page but not act through the site's own logic, and the person could use the site but not delegate the legwork. Now both happen at once, and the result is a plan with real reservation links attached, not a list of suggestions. How we implemented WebMCP The WebMCP layer is one feature-detected script, webmcp.js, loaded by the site's index.html. Each of the five tools is a thin adapter that POSTs JSON-RPC tools/call to Dim Hour's existing MCP server (mcp.dimhour.com) and passes the result straight through: search_venues - one strong keyword plus city, neighborhood, cuisine, score floor, and price ceiling filters get_venue - the full record: hours, score, booking path, awards find_open_tonight - venues with a happy hour or late kitchen, best score first, using the same definition the site's own "tonight" strip uses, so the agent and the page agree build_itinerary - an ordered multi-stop plan with why and how to book each stop; saving stays a human action at /trip.html get_booking_link - the reservation platform and direct booking URL for a venue, returned for the agent to present; it never opens or books anything itself The script handles the in-flight standard rename (document.modelContext first, navigator.modelContext fallback) and is a silent no-op where no WebMCP host exists. No authentication; the tools expose only public, read-only catalog data. What predates the hackathon: the venue catalog, scoring pipeline, MCP server, and site. What was built during the submission window: webmcp.js, the tool schemas, and the index.html include - the public repo's README draws that line explicitly, with dated commits. Challenges we hit Search results deliberately do not carry hours - only full venue records do - so "open tonight" meant ranking candidates first, then reading the top few individually rather than filtering a field that is not there. Booking links live in the page's own catalog rather than the API, so the booking tool merges both sources and says so honestly when a city is not loaded. The verification suite now asserts substance (tonight actually finds venues; a booking link equals the catalog's own URL), not just shape - because an early version passed every check while two tools quietly returned nothing. title: PunchPilot — field review, drawn on the sheet
pitch: ChatGPT reads the live drawing context, drafts findings at a coordinate, and prepares the visit briefing. The person on site keeps verification and issuance.
about_excerpt: ChatGPT reads the live drawing context, drafts findings at a coordinate, and prepares the visit briefing. The person on site keeps verification and issuance. Like Comment Story Updates PunchPilot: field review drawn on the sheet, with ChatGPT beside the reviewer through six WebMCP Site tools. Six WebMCP Site tools registered by every project screen. Three read, two write, one drafts. None verifies, completes, or issues. ChatGPT reads the live context through the read tools, then asks before calling the write tool. The draft pin sits where it was asked for, 62% across and 49% down on sheet A2.02. Verification stays with the person on site. One word of confirmation. The page announces the save with a WebMCP notice and ChatGPT reports exactly what was written. The visit briefing assembled from live data. Nothing issued, nothing published. Inspiration Construction field reviews are done standing on a slab with a tablet, a set of PDF drawings, and last visit's open items. The record that comes out of that walk is a professional document. A generic assistant can summarise notes, but it cannot safely touch the same numbered record the reviewer is looking at. WebMCP is the first thing that lets the page itself hand the agent a small, typed set of actions bound to the project already open, under the reviewer's own identity. What it does PunchPilot is a full field-review workspace on Cloudflare Workers: projects with disciplines and a filed drawing set, numbered reviews per discipline, findings pinned as page-aware percentages on the PDF, photos, status history, per-review checklists, and a frozen issued report for each visit. Every project screen registers six WebMCP Site tools with document.modelContext.registerTool : get_field_review_context reads the open project, discipline, latest review, and unresolved carry-forward findings. list_open_findings reads the work list. start_or_resume_field_review resumes the active review or opens the next numbered one for a valid floor, discipline, and drawing. create_draft_finding saves a draft pin at a coordinate on the active sheet and selects it on screen. update_or_verify_finding updates a finding; verification is refused unless the item is already corrected, a human confirms it on site, and a note is given. prepare_field_review_briefing assembles a live-data briefing of raised, revisited, and carried findings and issues nothing. There is deliberately no tool that verifies on the agent's word, completes a review, or issues a report. Why WebMCP is the right fit The value is in the binding, not the chat. The tools are registered by the page that already knows which project, discipline, review, and sheet are open, so ChatGPT never has to guess an identifier or scrape a screenshot. Each tool calls the same authenticated API route the buttons call, with the same validation, the same audit trail, and the same identity the worker resolved at the edge. The drawing, the finding log, and the history update in front of the reviewer as the agent works, so every action is visible and checkable on the spot. That is the kind of trust a professional record needs, and it is exactly what a page-registered tool gives that an external API integration would not. How WebMCP makes the experience better Without it, the reviewer types findings on a keyboard while holding a tablet, re-reads last visit's list to know what to revisit, and rebuilds the briefing by hand at the truck. With it, they say "draft a finding at 62 across, 49 down, fire-rated door closer missing at corridor 205, warning, assign the site super" and the pin lands on the sheet with a number. They ask "what is still open on Level 2 electrical" and get the real list. They ask for the briefing and get raised, revisited, and carried counts from live data. Fewer taps in gloves, no retyping, and nothing invented, because every answer comes from the record. What people and agents accomplish together The agent does retrieval, consistent numbering, structured drafts, and the briefing. The human does what only a person on site can: decide what is physically there, whether a correction is acceptable, and whether the record is ready to issue. The tool schemas encode that split. Verification requires humanConfirmedOnSite , a corrected status, and a note. Completion and issuance are buttons, not tools. The briefing is marked draft and carries externalAction: false . How we built it React 19 on vinext (Next-style App Router compiled to one Cloudflare Worker with Vite), plain CSS design tokens, Lucide icons. Cloudflare D1 with Drizzle ORM (eleven migrations), Cloudflare R2 for drawings and photos, pdf.js with a real worker for the drawing canvas. Identity is resolved once in worker/index.ts and re-stamped as internal headers after stripping every client-sent copy. The public contest Site runs a shared Guest Reviewer so judges need no account; a private deployment uses the verified Sites or Cloudflare Access identity instead, with one build flag deciding which. WebMCP tools are registered from the top-level page with an AbortController , MCP-shaped results ( content , structuredContent , isError ), readOnlyHint on reads, and additionalProperties: false on every input schema. 123 source-level and behavioural tests run against the production build before every change ships. Challenges Coordinates had to survive zoom, resize, and re-uploaded sheets, so pins are stored as page-aware percentages rather than pixels. D1 caps a statement at 100 bound variables, so every bulk checklist insert is chunked. The hardest design call was what not to expose: there is no tool that completes a review or issues a report, and a test fails if one is ever added, because a report an agent can issue is a report nobody should trust. What's next Photo capture through a tool, voice-first capture on site, and per-member identity on the public Site once WebMCP supports signed-in flows for shared deployments. Try it (judges) Open the live app in the ChatGPT desktop app so it loads in the built-in browser, or in Chrome with WebMCP enabled. Open Meridian Commons — Building B . The header shows a Site tools badge once the tools are registered. Start a new ChatGPT thread in that workspace and ask, for example: "Use the PunchPilot Site tools on the open review. Create a draft finding on the current sheet at 62% across and 49% down: Fire-rated door closer missing — corridor 205, warning severity, assigned to the site super. Do not verify or issue anything." ChatGPT reads the context with the read tools, then asks you to confirm before it calls the write tool. Say yes. Watch the pin land, read the finding number in the receipt, and see the "WebMCP · Draft pin saved" notice on the page. Then ask for the briefing. Everything on the Site is fictional and shared. The project, drawings, findings, and the Guest Reviewer are demonstration data. Video guide (2:30) Time What to watch 0:12 The six Site tools by name: three read, two write, one drafts. No tool verifies, completes, or issues. 0:49 The live Site inside ChatGPT's browser, tools bound to the open project, discipline, and review. 1:03 The reviewer asks for a draft finding in plain words. 1:17 ChatGPT reads context through the read tools, then asks before it writes anything. 1:28 "Yes, save it." The count goes 5 to 6, the WebMCP notice fires, and the receipt reads: D-010, pinned, assigned, not verified, no report issued. 1:52 The pin on the drawing at 62 across, 49 down. Still a draft. 2:05 The briefing from live data: recorded, raised, revisited, carried. Nothing issued. title: Aegis: Agent-Native Emergency Dispatch
pitch: An AI teammate that turns chaotic 911 emergency radio calls into precise, confirmable map updates to save time and lives.
about_excerpt:
An AI teammate that turns chaotic 911 emergency radio calls into precise, confirmable map updates to save time and lives.

 Codex Making it possible 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 



 
 Inspiration 

 I've seen and read accounts of what 911 dispatchers and first responders actually deal with during a wildfire or flood — a radio call comes in ("the wind shifted, Engine 4 is trapped"), and someone has to translate that panic into an updated map in seconds, while also getting the right warning out to the people in its path. What struck me is that the hard part was never a lack of urgency on the human side. It was the software: even a good dispatcher is stuck clicking through GIS tools, drawing polygons, searching a database, updating a status, while the fire doesn't wait. The numbers back this up — NENA's 2025 Pulse of 9-1-1 report found nearly 70% of telecommunicators experience daily pre-shift stress and 88% of Emergency Communications Centers had a technology outage in the past year, on top of 74% still reporting unfilled positions. These are people making life-or-death calls in seconds, on systems that are often working against them. 

 As an AI engineer, that gap is exactly the kind of problem I wanted to build for, something that removes the friction between hearing it and acting on it, without taking the decision out of human hands. WebMCP made that possible in a very direct way: instead of an agent guessing its way through a UI, you tell it exactly what it's allowed to do, and a human approves it. That's Aegis — an agent-native dispatch map where the AI listens and drafts the response, and the dispatcher keeps final authority over every action that hits the map. 

 What it does 

 Aegis is an emergency dispatch dashboard that an AI agent can act on directly through WebMCP. A dispatcher pastes (or eventually speaks) a radio transcript to ChatGPT. The agent discovers five tools we've exposed on the page and drafts real map actions: 

 
 draft_hazard_zone — mark a fire/flood zone at exact coordinates 
 update_unit_status — flag a trapped unit as Code Red 
 relocate_unit — move an existing unit to new coordinates 
 deploy_unit — spawn a new unit onto the map 
 draft_evacuation_alert — prepare a broadcast to a sector 
 

 None of these mutate the live map directly. Every tool call fires into a pending-actions queue in the sidebar, and the human dispatcher has to click Approve before anything changes. A three-minute manual workflow becomes a few seconds of review and one click — without removing the human from the decision. 

 How we built it 

 Frontend is Next.js, React, and Tailwind CSS v4. The map is React-Leaflet with high-contrast tiles so units and hazards are legible at a glance. 

 For WebMCP, we use @mcp-b/webmcp-polyfill and register five tools against document.modelContext.registerTool , each with a strict JSON inputSchema (typed lat/lng floats, required fields) so the agent can't pass malformed data. 

 The execute function for each tool never touches state directly — it dispatches a CustomEvent that a listener in our root component catches and pushes into a pending-actions array. Only the approve/reject buttons, driven by human clicks, actually update the units and hazards in React state. We call this the Event Bridge, and it's the whole safety model: the agent can propose, only the human can commit. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The biggest issue was a race condition specific to WebMCP in a single-page app: ChatGPT's agent would try to call our tools before React had finished hydrating, so document.modelContext wasn't ready yet and the handshake failed. We fixed this by registering the polyfill and tools outside the normal component lifecycle (in a useEffect with no dependency gating on other app state), so the tools are available as early as possible and the agent gets a reliable list on first contact. 

 We also had to think carefully about schema strictness — early versions let the agent pass loosely-typed coordinates, which occasionally produced markers in the ocean. Tightening the inputSchema to required numeric types fixed this. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 The part we're most proud of is that the safety architecture isn't a UI suggestion — it's structural. There's no code path where a WebMCP tool call reaches the map without passing through the approval queue. That was a deliberate constraint we kept even when it would have been faster to just let execute write to state directly. 

 We also built a "kinetic" map layer: when a relocation is approved, the unit marker animates across the map to its new position instead of snapping there, so it's visually obvious that an agent action produced a real, physical change on a live map — not just a database update. 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP is genuinely good at separating concerns that LLMs are bad at from ones they're good at. The agent is good at reading "Engine 4 is trapped" and inferring that means Code Red — semantic reasoning over messy text. It's not good at rendering, coordinate math, or knowing what's safe to commit to a live system. WebMCP let us keep the LLM entirely in the reasoning lane and keep our own deterministic code in charge of anything that touches the map or the data. 

 What's next for Aegis: Agent-Native Emergency Dispatch 

 The text-transcript step is still a manual bridge. The next version removes it: live WebRTC audio from real radio traffic, transcribed in real time, feeding continuously into the WebMCP agent so the map updates itself as a fire department's radio chatter comes in — with the same human-approval queue standing between the agent and the live map.

 Submitted to
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 The WebMCP Challenge 
 


 


 

 
 

 
 
 Created by
 

 
 
 
 
 As a solo developer, I built the entire application from scratch using Codex. I engineered the Next.js frontend, designed the responsive UI with Tailwind CSS v4, and integrated the interactive Leaflet map. My main focus was architecting the WebMCP integration using the official polyfill and building the Agent-Native Event Bridge to ensure a safe, human-in-the-loop approval queue.

title: Quorum
pitch: Scheduling, negotiated by your agent — approved by you. Humans and AI agents vote, counter-propose, and converge on a meeting time together via WebMCP, with every agent action visibly logged.
about_excerpt: Scheduling, negotiated by your agent — approved by you. Humans and AI agents vote, counter-propose, and converge on a meeting time together via WebMCP, with every agent action visibly logged. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Group scheduling is a negotiation over everyone's constraints - and it's still done by making humans click checkboxes in polls. When WebMCP launched, we realized the missing piece was never a smarter poll: it was letting each person's AI agent join the negotiation itself . Quorum is our answer: scheduling, negotiated by your agent - approved by you. What it does Quorum is a meeting scheduler where humans and agents are equal participants in the same live session. Humans get a normal UI: candidate times, yes/maybe/no voting, counter-proposals. Agents get seven WebMCP tools registered by the page itself - they can read the event state, join on their human's behalf, vote with reasons, counter-propose new times, and rank the slots. Every action lands in a shared negotiation log tagged HUMAN or AGENT , and only the human organizer can accept proposals or lock in the final time. Agent proposes; human approves. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Scheduling is a multi-step, stateful interaction - exactly where screen-scraping agents fail. With WebMCP, the page tells agents what's possible via typed, self-describing tools. In testing, an agent that had never seen the app correctly chained four tools on the first try (read state -> join -> vote with a conflict note -> report the winner) purely from the tool descriptions. What people and agents can do together that wasn't possible before A mixed negotiation - some parties human, some agents - on the same page, in real time, with full mutual visibility. Before WebMCP, agents couldn't reliably operate voting UIs built for humans, and sites had no way to declare what actions they support. Quorum shows the new shape of the open web: agents handle the tedium, the audit trail keeps trust, and humans keep the final word. How we built it Vanilla JS frontend + Express backend, live-synced over server-sent events. Every WebMCP tool executes the same functions the human UI uses , tagged via: "agent" - one code path, one audit trail: document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "submit_availability", description: "Submit availability for candidate slots on behalf of your user…", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: { responses: { type: "array" } }, required: ["responses"] }, execute: async ({ responses }) => submitAvailability(responses, "agent"), }); Deployed on Vercel; Upstash Redis keeps event state consistent across serverless instances, with a per-stream Redis poll so every open tab stays live. The visual design was created in Claude Design and implemented as a hand-written design system. Challenges we ran into - Serverless broke our state. Events lived in memory; on Vercel, an SSE stream landed on a different instance and couldn't find the event. We added a storage layer (Upstash Redis in production, in-memory locally) and cross-instance live updates via polling. - The WebMCP API surface is still moving (document.modelContext vs the earlier navigator.modelContext), so we wrote a small adapter that registers against whichever exists. - Tool descriptions are prompts. Agents chained our tools correctly only after we rewrote descriptions to say when to call each tool and what to fetch first. Accomplishments that we're proud of - **A never-before-seen agent used our app correctly on the first try.** In our final test, a Gemini-backed agent autonomously chained four tools - read the event state, joined as a new participant, voted with a conflict note attached to the right slot, and reported the winning time - guided by nothing but our tool descriptions. That's the whole WebMCP promise, working. - **One code path for humans and agents.** Every WebMCP tool executes the exact same functions the human UI calls - so the audit log, validation, and permissions are identical no matter who acts. No parallel "agent API" to drift out of sync. - **Trust as a first-class feature.** The negotiation log tags every action HUMAN or AGENT in real time, organizer-only tools are genuinely scoped, and an agent can never finalize a meeting on its own. - **A one-click seeded demo event**, so any judge can see a mid-negotiation session - votes, an agent counter-proposal, a live log - in under ten seconds, then take over as the organizer. - **Shipping the full journey in days**: idea -> working local app -> designed UI -> deployed on Vercel with Redis-backed state that survives serverless cold starts. What we learned - **Tool descriptions are prompts.** Agents started chaining our tools correctly only after we rewrote descriptions to say *when* to call each tool and what to fetch first ("Call this first to understand the current state"). Designing for a model reader is a real skill, and WebMCP makes it part of frontend work. - **The trust problem matters more than the automation problem.** The feature people react to isn't that agents can vote — it's seeing exactly what an agent did on your behalf, and knowing the final decision always needs a human. - **Serverless changes your assumptions.** Our in-memory state worked perfectly until the first live SSE request landed on a different instance. Moving to Redis-backed storage with cross-instance live updates taught us to design for "any request, any instance" from the start. - **Build for a moving standard defensively.** WebMCP's surface has shifted between Chrome previews (`document.modelContext` vs `navigator.modelContext`), so a small adapter layer saved us from breaking on every browser update. What's next for Quorum - **Calendar integration**, so your agent votes from your real availability instead of being told your constraints. - **Agent-to-agent negotiation rounds** - agents exchange counter-proposals automatically until they converge on a shortlist, and humans only see the final choice to ratify. - **Invites addressed to agents**: send an event link straight to someone's assistant, which handles everything and pings its human only for approval. - **Richer constraints in tools** - recurring meetings, time-zone fairness scoring, and "must attend / optional" roles that agents can reason about.
