title: Unfolded
pitch: Convert 3D shapes into buildable clay templates. Agent handles complexity, human decide, they collaborate and the template is always exported with precise, deterministic geometry by the app itself
about_excerpt: Convert 3D shapes into buildable clay templates. Agent handles complexity, human decide, they collaborate and the template is always exported with precise, deterministic geometry by the app itself Like 1 Comment Story Updates Mobile screens ( Dark mode ) Light mode ( Desktop ) Dark mode (Desktop) The problem we are solving Design initiated by Chat-GPT Design initiated by Chrome tab more mobile screens ( light mode ) mobile screens ( light mode ) Light / Dark mode From a printed template back to a design The exported printable PDF template ( multi page ) webMCP tools available ( 1 of 3 ) webMCP tools available ( 2 of 3 ) webMCP tools available ( 3 of 3 ) Design system ( Dark mode ) Inspiration I've been cutting pottery templates out of cereal boxes for years now. AI chats are great at generating shapes and make complex changes with unusual requirements, but their non deterministic output produce unexpected and misaligned PDFs, especially during the discovery phase of a new piece where the requirements constantly changes. The problem is, the potter notice the failure only after hours of building in the studio. Try for yourself to generate with any AI agent a multipage template for a simple mug, same prompt in 3 separate sessions. The result is always different, most of the time fail silently where it matters the most. I have created Unfolded to move the template generation part of the workflow away from the AI chat into a more deterministic output I can control. The output is a multi page PDF template that always work is always true to the 3D shape you have built. The idea is to retain AI for complexity, difficult math calculations and things that are practically impossible to do in a deterministic UI. When is connected to unfolded, you can ask AI things like: Keep the same vessel style but change the volume to 500ml Prepare a template inspired by this photo, for a porcelain vase with thin walls This container should hold a large americano comfortably 10 bowls like this should be stackable and only 1cm of each one should be visible when stacked What Unfolded does Unfolded is a parametric 3D builder that helps with both the template generation and the decision of what to make. It's a shared 3D workspace where a potter and an AI agent shape a vessel together: the potter keeps the creative decisions, the agent inspects and revises the live design through WebMCP, and Unfolded guarantees the geometry: clay shrinkage, clay type wall thickness, mid-surface-developed. It was thought from the ground up with the potter workflow in mind and its strenght is how flexibly it is and can adapt to many unexpected use case and workflow without letting you down. Most problems related to pottery known how, PDF generations and cross browsers workflow are automagically prevented under the hood without anyone noticing. My favourite features ( try them in the app, especially on mobile ) I've worked a lot at the UX flow for the cross-device handshake . The potter can also design and work with agents on non webMCP capable browsers. One tap on Open in ChatGPT hands off into the ChatGPT app with a prompt that already carries a single-use pairing code; Chat-GPT hidden browser joins the potter's live session over WebSockets. From then on every agent edit appears in the browser within about a second, every browser edit is visible to the agent on its next tool call, and every change ( human or agent ) is a shared undo step. Undo/redo work for both humand and AI changes, no matter what device pushed them. The handover works both ways ( or even 3 ways! ): The agent reads the current design, changes the form, sees the same 3D preview the potter sees — and solves problems that are genuinely hard at the workbench. "Make it hold exactly 350 ml but keep the proportions" --> one sentence for an agent, an afternoon of guesswork by hand. The generated PDF is really well thought ( if I say so myself! ): True-scale printable templates and a calibration ruler on every sheet, QR code to reproduce the design in the browser even after it was printed, seam allowance to glue the template together. This is fully designed around the potter's workflow. The app registers 13 typed WebMCP tools on document.modelContext the moment it loads. The reasons there are so many tools is that I got a little carried away about performance measurament of webMCP. I even made a npm package called MCP-profiler to measure everything from the tools speed to the agent harness time. Most of the slowness in my app ( 30seconds to connect the tools at times ) is unsurprisely caused by my 3D model and the whole context I am passing over with each tool. Something I will definitely look into after the hackathon. How I built it React, TypeScript, Three.js, React Three Fiber, Zustand, Zod, Tailwind CSS, and shadcn/ui, with jsPDF generating the true-scale multi-page templates. Live cross-device sync runs on a Cloudflare Worker with a per-session Durable Object; pairing invitations are single-use and short-lived, so no URL ever carries a durable capability. The interface and the WebMCP tools share the same Zustand store and Zod schemas, so human and agent edits stay synchronized by construction . Everything sits behind a test gate (geometry, schemas, sync protocol), end-to-end suites running real Chromium against the production bundle and two deeper suites that spin up a local Worker to exercise the pairing protocol with two real browsers. Along the way I published webmcp-profiler , also sitting in this repo, an npm package that benchmarks every tool's execution time and payload size. Profiling my own app with it caught a ~20% trim in tool-definition metadata that every conversation was paying for. Challenges and lessons The geometric challenge: complex curved surfaces cannot be flattened without distortion, so for the demo I focused on symmetrical, faceted forms built from planar slabs, where the unroll is exact , not approximate. But my ambitions are higher for this tool and I already have a full plan for complex shapes and things that were not really possible until now. The UX challenge was one I haven't seen discussed anywhere: when ChatGPT drives a WebMCP page, it does so in a built in, hidden browser. Solving the two-way conversation between that invisible tab and the browser the user actually looks at — live sessions, one-tap pairing prompts, agent share links carrying single-use join tokens — became the heart of the project. Here is a page with a nice breakdown of the different user flow the user can face (I have done this for myself, but could be helpful for someone judging the project): User Flows mapped out I am not satisfied with the solution I have found for the pairing, In the future my goal is to merge the link with token, pairing, webMCP concept into a single binary flag. The user does not need to know about webMCP at all, it should simply copy a prompt on his agent to start building from anywhere. The bigger lesson is that WebMCP shines with a clear division of labour: the agent is brilliant at intent and connected constraints, the app owns the deterministic math, and the human keeps the creative decisions. The agent chooses the parameters; the geometry is always right. What's next Better UX. Curved profiles, more construction types and layers, performance optimisation of webMCP and assembly guidance. Maybe a login, and reusable studio presets and lids and matching sets, where the shrinkage math matters most. Most of the backend code is AI written and went through many iterations and adversarial reviews. Luca Gugliemi Product designer with front-end superpowers. title: Tripster
pitch: Plan your weekends or trips based on your needs with ease. Don't just go to the same old place, use tripster.
about_excerpt:
Plan your weekends or trips based on your needs with ease. Don't just go to the same old place, use tripster.

 Inspiration
Planning group trips often turns into a chaotic mix of scattered tabs, conflicting budgets, and endless group chat messages. While modern AI trip planners promise convenience, they often introduce new problems: weak budget reasoning, fabricated venue suggestions, poor route planning, and slow response times. We wanted a better approach.
Tripster combines the flexibility of AI assisted planning with the reliability of deterministic algorithms. Instead of relying on a model to guess the best trip, we use structured optimization logic to generate realistic, budget aware itineraries quickly and consistently. 

 What it does
Tripster is a trip planning app that helps groups create better travel plans based on their constraints. It supports multi origin trip planning for group members, budget aware itinerary generation, terrain and effort preference handling, spatially balanced destination selection, venue rerolling and itinerary refinement, interactive visual planning through a map and timeline, optional submission of new trip spots into the planning system, and agent style integration through browser native tool execution. 

 How we built it
We built the frontend with React and Vite, used Leaflet and React Leaflet for maps, applied custom CSS for styling, and relied on Supabase for the data layer. The planning logic is powered by a custom deterministic engine for itinerary generation, route optimization, and constraints handling. For agent integration we added a browser side WebMCP bridge for tool interoperability. This stack keeps the app fast, lightweight, and cost efficient while still supporting an interactive planning experience. 

 Challenges we ran into
We had to figure out how to find a fair group midpoint across multiple starting locations, balance travel distance with budget and venue suitability, handle edge cases where no venues fit perfectly within the provided constraints, keep route generation realistic while avoiding over optimization, and synchronize UI state with planning actions without breaking the user experience. 

 Accomplishments we are proud of
We built a functioning trip planning app focused on real constraints instead of generic AI suggestions. We created a structure that blends deterministic planning with interactive user experience, designed a system that is lightweight, fast, and easy to extend, and integrated map based planning and itinerary visualization in a single interface. 

 What we learned
The best travel planning experiences do not come from forcing AI to solve everything with raw generation. They come from combining AI interaction with well defined optimization logic. For structured tasks like trip planning, deterministic heuristics and route aware algorithms are often more reliable than purely generative approaches. 

 What is next for Tripster
We plan to add real time shared itinerary updates, better transit aware route planning, more venue verification and review workflows, offline support for saved itineraries, and improved personalization and recommendation engines.

title: Rabbit Hole
pitch: AI conversations are linear. Your thinking isn’t. Rabbit Hole makes the path visible. Turn AI conversations into visible paths you can branch, revisit, and build from.

 Inspiration 

 Hi! My name is Katie O'Daniel. I'm a graduating senior at Purdue, currently looking for software engineering work somewhere outside the Midwest (˶˃𐃷˂˶), and when I'm stressed, I like turn that energy into creativity. Sometimes it's my personal website, dashboards, Minecraft mods and platforms that did not need to become an entire platform when I first thought of it. You can probably tell from my GitHub contributions between March 25 and June 3. 

 I really like design, but I've realized that I might like planning even more. I love sitting down with an idea and figuring out what it could become: what features should it have, who is actually going to use it, what am I missing, and is there a completely different direction that would make more sense? This is also where I get myself into trouble, because one feature becomes three more, then one of those makes me rethink the first feature, and eventually I am scrolling twenty messages back trying to find an idea I had earlier. 

 A recent example was another project I have been working on: a website and platform for adoptees. Originally, I was going to build it specifically for Chinese adoptees. That made sense to me because it was close to my own experience and it was where I started. But as I researched more, thought about what the community should actually be, and tried to understand perspectives outside my own, and through that, the idea changed. I realized there were experiences that were specific to Chinese adoptees, but there were also much bigger conversations around adoption, identity, belonging, family, culture, and growing up between different worlds. 

 That experience is a big part of why I made Rabbit Hole. I use AI constantly when I plan projects. I use it to brainstorm features, research questions, argue against my own ideas, compare approaches, and figure out what I might not be considering. But all of that usually ends up in one giant conversation. I can scroll back and find an old idea, but I can't really see the moment when my thinking changed, the branches I almost followed, or why I stopped following one direction and chose another. 

 At some point I thought: What if I could actually see the rabbit hole? 

 So I built it. 

 What it does 

 Rabbit Hole takes all of that messy exploration and turns it into something you can actually see. You start with a question or an idea, and from there you can explore different directions, go deeper into one path, branch somewhere else, add your own thought, or go back to something you were considering earlier. I also did not want the directions you skipped to just disappear, because sometimes an idea that did not make sense at first becomes useful again later. 

 Rabbit Hole currently has two main modes: Investigate and Design. Investigate is for research and questions. Instead of asking AI for one big answer and stopping there, you can follow different perspectives, look at evidence, question what you are finding, and keep exploring as the original question changes. You decide what is worth keeping, and eventually that path can become an Investigation Brief that shows where you went, what evidence mattered, what complicated the question, and what is still uncertain. 

 Design came more directly from how I build things myself. I rarely start with a completely planned product. Usually I start with something like, "I want to make a platform for this," and then I spend way too much time figuring out what that platform should actually be. Design gives you a place to explore those different versions before committing to one. You can try different directions, branch when a new feature changes the idea, go back to something you liked earlier, and eventually create an outcome from the decisions you actually chose to keep. 

 The two modes are different, but they are really solving the same problem for me. Whether I am researching something or designing something, I almost never get to the final direction in a straight line. 

 How I used WebMCP 

 WebMCP is what lets Rabbit Hole expose the workspace to an agent in a structured way instead of making the agent guess what is happening from the visual interface. 

 Rabbit Hole registers WebMCP tools that let a compatible agent inspect the current state of an exploration. That includes things like whether the user is in Investigate or Design, which node is currently active, the path of nodes that led to it, what the user has decided to keep, what branches are still available, and how sources and evidence connect to the investigation. 

 That is useful because the graph itself contains information that would normally be difficult for an agent to understand just by looking at the page. If I am five branches deep into an investigation, the agent does not have to rely only on the last prompt I typed. It can understand the structure that led me there. 

 I also use WebMCP to separate understanding the workspace from changing it. An agent can inspect the current Rabbit Hole and use that context to suggest a next direction, but a suggestion does not automatically become part of the graph. The user still chooses whether to follow it, keep it, or go somewhere else. 

 For me, that is the main reason WebMCP fits Rabbit Hole. The product is already about preserving context, decisions, branches, and where an idea came from. WebMCP gives an agent access to that same structure, so the person and the agent can work from the same understanding of the exploration instead of starting over with every new prompt. 

 How I built it 

 Rabbit Hole is built with Next.js, React, TypeScript, React Flow, Tailwind CSS, and WebMCP. Once I had the basic idea, I started breaking the product into individual functions and asking what each one actually needed to do. 

 I planned out things like how a branch should work, what should happen when someone follows a direction, what counts as something worth keeping, how sources should connect back to claims, how the different node types should behave, and how Investigate and Design could use the same overall structure without feeling like the exact same experience. 

 For each part, I usually brainstormed different options with ChatGPT before building it. I would ask for different ways a feature could work, try to look at it from another perspective, and then decide which direction made the most sense for Rabbit Hole. Once I had a feature in mind, I would often generate mock images of what the interface could look like and iterate on those before actually implementing it. 

 After that, I used Codex to help turn those plans into the working product. The process was definitely not linear. I built features, tested them, realized some were too complicated, removed them, and sometimes came back to an earlier idea with a completely different approach.

title: RocketTurtle
pitch: RocketTurtle gives coding agents focused repository context through WebMCP, helping them understand, locate, inspect, check, and verify changes before they edit code.
about_excerpt: RocketTurtle gives coding agents focused repository context through WebMCP, helping them understand, locate, inspect, check, and verify changes before they edit code. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I am a business student, not a traditional software engineer. For the last two years, I have been following AI and AI agents out of curiosity. As I started building things myself, I kept running into the same thing: almost everything eventually exists in the form of a repository. AI can write 1,000 lines of code in the next five minutes. But before changing an existing open-source project, a human still needs answers to much simpler questions: Where do I begin? Which files and folders matter? Which files are safe to inspect first? Which file is responsible for the exact function that I want to change? What can break if I touch it? That is where RocketTurtle was born. It started with an MVP and my own brainstorming sessions. I wanted to paste a public GitHub repository into a simple application and get a useful map of what was actually inside it. I built the first version of RocketTurtle around that idea: help someone understand an unfamiliar repository before they start changing it. Then I wanted to improve it. Around that time, I found the Devpost WebMCP Hackathon and started learning what WebMCP actually was. That immediately made the original RocketTurtle idea more interesting. RocketTurtle already reduced how much of a repository a human needed to inspect. With WebMCP, I realized that the same idea can apply to an agent . Why must a coding agent read an entire repository before it can understand where to work? That question became the basis of the WebMCP version of RocketTurtle. What It Does RocketTurtle is a repository understanding layer for humans and AI agents. For the WebMCP extension, I went back to first principles and asked: If an agent is about to work inside an unfamiliar repository, what does it need to know before it writes code? That produced five steps: Understand → Locate → Inspect → Check → Verify Those five steps became five WebMCP tools. 1. analyze_repository — Understand Before anything else, the agent needs a map. This tool analyzes the repository structure, technologies, complexity, important files, risks, and supporting evidence. 2. map_change_surface — Locate Understanding the repository is not enough. If the goal is to change authentication, fix a feature, or update some behavior, the agent needs to know which parts of the repository are likely connected to that goal. This tool maps the requested change to likely relevant files and risky areas. 3. inspect_file_context — Inspect After finding a likely file, the agent needs focused information about that file. This tool inspects one selected text file and returns useful structural context without requiring the agent to explore the complete repository first. 4. validate_change_plan — Check Before an agent edits code, it can explain what it plans to change. RocketTurtle checks that plan against the available repository context and identifies risks or missing evidence. RocketTurtle does not make the code change. The coding agent remains responsible for the code. 5. get_verification_context — Verify Finally, the agent needs to know how the repository expects changes to be tested. This tool finds existing tests, scripts, build commands, lint commands, CI signals, and other useful verification context. Together, the five tools create one workflow: Understand → Locate → Inspect → Check → Verify The user provides the goal. RocketTurtle provides focused repository context. The coding agent uses that context before it acts. How I Built It I extended the existing RocketTurtle MVP instead of creating a separate application for the hackathon. The WebMCP layer reuses RocketTurtle's existing: GitHub access logic Repository analyzer Types API routes Vercel deployment I then added the logic required for the five WebMCP tools. Each tool has: A clear tool name A defined input schema An execution function Structured output Error handling Input and output boundaries The browser exposes these tools through document.modelContext , which lets a WebMCP-capable client discover and invoke RocketTurtle's repository tools. I kept one boundary throughout the project: RocketTurtle understands and checks. The coding agent writes the code. RocketTurtle does not: Generate code Edit repository files Create pull requests Replace the coding agent It gives the agent focused repository context before the agent starts changing code. Challenges I Faced One of the hardest problems was deciding how much repository information each tool must return. If RocketTurtle returns the entire repository, it defeats the purpose. If it returns too little information, the agent cannot make a useful decision. I had to design each tool around one specific question in the agent's workflow. Another major challenge was safety. Repository content is untrusted input. The WebMCP layer therefore needed boundaries around: Repository access File paths File types File sizes Tool inputs Tool outputs Testing also became much more important than I initially expected. Seeing five registered tools in a browser was not enough. I tested cases such as: Valid inputs Invalid inputs Missing repositories Missing files Unsupported files Large inputs Tool output limits Tool cleanup behavior The complete five-tool workflow I also had to make these changes without breaking the existing RocketTurtle application. That forced me to keep the WebMCP extension focused instead of redesigning the entire product around the hackathon. What I Learned The biggest thing I learned is that giving an AI agent more context is not always the answer. A better question is: What is the minimum useful context that the agent needs for its next decision? That idea now defines how I think about RocketTurtle. AI can generate code extremely quickly. But before generation comes understanding. An agent still needs to know: What already exists? Where does the relevant functionality live? What files are connected? What can break? Does the proposed plan make sense? How does this repository verify a change? WebMCP gave me a way to turn those questions into tools that an agent can call directly. I also learned that building a useful agent tool involves much more than exposing a function. The input boundaries, output limits, untrusted content, error handling, cleanup behavior, testing, and evidence all matter when another agent depends on that tool. What's Next The current RocketTurtle WebMCP implementation focuses on public GitHub repositories and one clear five-step workflow: Understand → Locate → Inspect → Check → Verify The next goal is not to make RocketTurtle another coding agent. I want to improve the quality and precision of the repository context that RocketTurtle provides while keeping the same separation of responsibilities. The original RocketTurtle MVP helped a human understand a repository . WebMCP gave me a way to extend that same idea to AI agents . And that is the direction I want RocketTurtle to continue exploring: Let RocketTurtle understand the repository. Let the coding agent write the code. Accomplishments That I'm Proud Of The accomplishment I am most proud of is that RocketTurtle started as my own question, not as a hackathon idea. I am a business student who became curious about AI and agents. I went from trying to understand repositories myself to building a tool that can help both humans and agents understand them. I am especially proud that: I took RocketTurtle from an MVP to a working WebMCP implementation. I designed the five WebMCP tools from first principles instead of adding unrelated features. I kept one clear workflow: Understand → Locate → Inspect → Check → Verify . I made all five tools work together against real public GitHub repositories. I tested the tools with a real WebMCP-capable browser instead of relying only on local tests. I kept the original RocketTurtle application working while adding the WebMCP layer. I learned enough about WebMCP to turn an existing idea into something that an AI agent can directly use. Most importantly, I built something that I personally wanted when I first started exploring unfamiliar repositories. That feels like the best accomplishment of the project. title: Intent Handoff
pitch: Intent Handoff lets users pass what they mean—not just what they clicked—to an AI agent so it can finish the task correctly.
about_excerpt: Intent Handoff lets users pass what they mean—not just what they clicked—to an AI agent so it can finish the task correctly. Like 1 Comment Story Updates step by step to use intent handoff Inspiration I noticed something strange about how we use AI with websites. The user can already see exactly what they mean on the screen. They can point to it by clicking it. But when they want an AI to help, suddenly they have to describe that thing in words: “The second hotel on the left.” “The one near the station.” “The cheaper one I was looking at just now.” Then the AI has to guess which place or object the user means. Why? The website already knows exactly what the user clicked. I wanted to remove that translation step. That became Intent Handoff : instead of describing a place, product or object in words and asking AI to guess, the user can interact with it directly and hand that exact context to the agent. What it does Intent Handoff connects normal website interactions directly to an AI agent through WebMCP. A user browses normally. They click a hotel, choose a budget, select preferences or interact with something they are interested in. Those interactions create structured intent. When the user hands the task to AI, the agent doesn't have to guess what “that hotel” or “the place I just clicked” means. It receives the actual object, its context, the user's existing selections and the task that needs to be completed. The user can simply point through the interface instead of describing through a prompt . The AI can then continue the task, use WebMCP tools, report progress and return the result to the website. How we built it I built Intent Handoff using WebMCP as the bridge between the website and the agent. The website exposes structured tools for the agent to read the user's current intent, selected constraints, task context and task status. The agent can then search options, report progress, apply changes and submit the completed result. The important part is that UI interactions are converted into structured context. Instead of: user click → user describes click → AI interprets description we can do: user click → structured intent → AI I also added explicit user-controlled handoff. The agent cannot simply take over because something was clicked. The user chooses when they want AI to continue the task. Challenges we ran into The difficult part was deciding how to translate UI interaction into useful agent context. A webpage contains a huge amount of information. The agent does not need all of it. It needs to know what the user actually means. So I had to separate the visual interface from the intent behind the interaction: which object was selected, which constraints matter, what has already happened and what the agent should do next. The other challenge was making the transition feel natural. The goal was not to create another AI chat box beside a website. The AI should feel like it can continue directly from what the user was already doing. Accomplishments that we're proud of We built the complete handoff loop on a live website. The user can interact with the interface, select exactly what they mean, hand the task to an AI through WebMCP, let the agent complete the work, refine the constraints and receive the result back in the website. The user never needs to explain which hotel they mean. They already clicked it. That sounds simple, but I think it changes an important part of human-agent interaction: the interface itself can become a way of communicating with AI. What we learned We learned that prompting does not always need to mean typing. Humans are already communicating intent when they use an interface. A click can say: “This one.” A filter can say: “Only show me things under this price.” A selection can say: “This matters to me.” Instead of throwing those signals away and asking the user to reconstruct everything as a prompt, WebMCP lets us expose them directly to the agent. AI doesn't always need to guess what the user means from words when the user has already shown us what they mean through their actions. What's next for Intent Handoff Next, I want to take Intent Handoff beyond the travel demo. Imagine browsing a shopping website and clicking a product, then handing that exact product to your agent. Or selecting a document, property, flight, restaurant or workflow item and asking AI to continue without explaining which one you mean. Eventually, individual objects and actions on a website could become handoff points between humans and agents. The idea is very simple: See it. Click it. Hand it to AI. No describing where it is. No copying information. No asking AI to guess which thing you meant. The website already knows. Just hand over the intent. title: RecallRadar
pitch: Trace one failed component to every affected unit—and contain it before the next spreadsheet opens
about_excerpt: Trace one failed component to every affected unit—and contain it before the next spreadsheet opens Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Manufacturing quality teams face a critical problem: when a component fails, they must trace it through complex supply chains to identify affected products. Current approaches rely on manual spreadsheet analysis or brittle DOM scraping, leading to either dangerous over-containment (holding unrelated products) or missed affected units. The OpenAI WebMCP Challenge presented an opportunity to demonstrate how AI agents with structured, scoped tool access could solve this problem with precision and human oversight. What it does RecallRadar is a quality-lineage simulator that helps manufacturing quality leads trace failed supplier lots through explicit manufacturing relationships. Users can: Search and trace any seeded lot, batch, unit, warehouse, shipment, or order ID Expand lineage manually or run AI-guided trace through the supply chain Inspect provenance with versioned evidence and corrected records Compare containment scopes (broad, evidence-based, ultra-narrow) to avoid over-containment Preview customer notices for shipped units (notice-only, never auto-sent) Stage and approve inventory holds with full audit trail Commit and undo actions with complete reversibility The hero scenario traces failed capacitor lot CAP-77B to exactly 312 affected units (271 in warehouses, 41 shipped), achieving 0% false positives while avoiding the over-containment that would incorrectly hold 88 unrelated units from lookalike lot CAP-77D. How we built it Tech Stack: Next.js 15 with App Router for the React framework TypeScript for type safety throughout WebMCP (Model Context Protocol) for evidence-scoped AI tool registration OpenAI Sites integration for ChatGPT authentication Google Gemini API (optional) for live AI agent planning Polar for subscription-based entitlements and admin access shadcn/ui for modern, accessible UI components Vitest for unit testing, Playwright for E2E testing Tailwind CSS for styling Architecture: Domain-driven design with separate layers for domain logic, store state machine, and WebMCP tool catalog Server-side API routes for Gemini agent planning and Polar billing Evidence-scoped WebMCP lifecycle that rebuilds tool registrations based on investigation state Deterministic fallback mode that works without any live AI services Human approval boundaries at every critical action (stage, commit, undo) Key Implementation Details: lib/domain.ts contains seed data, lineage traversal, scope comparison, and hold logic lib/store.ts implements the investigation state machine with tool-call logging lib/tool-catalog.ts defines shared WebMCP/Gemini contracts with safe input binding hooks/use-webmcp.ts manages the evidence-scoped WebMCP registration lifecycle app/api/agent/turn/route.ts provides server-only Gemini Interactions tool planning Challenges we ran into WebMCP API Evolution : The WebMCP specification is still in draft, so we had to work with evolving type definitions and browser support. We created a custom type declaration file ( types/webmcp.d.ts ) and built a preview registry for browsers without native WebMCP support. Tool Lifecycle Management : Designing a system where AI tools only become available when appropriate evidence is loaded required careful state machine design. We implemented an evidence-scoped registration system that rebuilds tool availability based on the current investigation step. Safety and Trust : Ensuring that supplier notes and untrusted data couldn't be interpreted as executable instructions required explicit labeling and inert data handling throughout the domain logic. Deterministic Fallback : The challenge required no-live-services demo capability, so we built a complete deterministic fallback that preserves the full user experience without requiring any AI API keys. Human-AI Approval Boundary : Designing the approval workflow required careful UX consideration—Gemini pauses after staging so humans must explicitly click "Approve 271 inventory holds" before the commit tool becomes available. Accomplishments that we're proud of Zero False Positives : The evidence-based scope correctly identifies exactly the 312 affected units from CAP-77B while excluding 88 unrelated units from lookalike lot CAP-77D Full Reversibility : Every commit carries an inverse action, allowing complete undo of all 271 prior states Evidence-Scoped Tools : WebMCP tools only appear when valid for the current investigation state, preventing AI from calling inappropriate actions Deterministic Operation : The entire hero scenario runs locally without any external services, making it reliable for demos and judging Live AI Integration : Optional Gemini integration demonstrates real-time AI planning while maintaining human approval boundaries Comprehensive Testing : 14 deterministic unit/intent tests plus E2E tests covering hero, correction, untrusted-note, and undo flows Production-Ready UI : Apple-style design system with responsive layout and accessibility considerations What we learned WebMCP Power : Evidence-scoped tool registration is far more powerful than giving AI raw data access. By restricting tools to what's valid for the current state, we get both safety and better AI behavior. Human-AI Collaboration : The most effective workflows combine AI planning with human approval. AI handles the complex traversal and scope comparison, while humans make the final containment decisions. Deterministic Design : Building deterministic fallbacks makes AI systems more robust and easier to demo. Users can see the full value without configuring API keys. Domain Modeling : Deep domain modeling (manufacturing lineage, evidence versions, containment scopes) is essential for building effective AI tools in specialized domains. Type Safety : TypeScript's type system was invaluable for maintaining safety across the WebMCP tool catalog and domain logic. What's next for RecallRadar Live ERP Integration : Connect to real manufacturing systems (SAP, Oracle, etc.) for production use Multi-Lot Tracing : Support tracing multiple failed lots simultaneously with scope intersection Predictive Analytics : Add ML models to predict likely affected units based on historical patterns Mobile App : Build a mobile interface for quality teams in the field Collaboration Features : Add team workflows, comments, and approval chains Advanced Visualizations : Interactive graph visualization of supply chain relationships Regulatory Compliance : Automated generation of regulatory recall documentation Real-Time Alerts : Push notifications when new evidence suggests scope expansion Built With webmcp Try it out github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Hector Ta Like Share this project: Updates Hector Ta started this project — Sep 03, 2026 12:58 PM EDT

 Lex Aureon — Constitutional Governance for WebMCP Agents 

 Lex Aureon is a constitutional governance layer that sits above an LLM or AI agent and governs outputs before they reach users. Instead of treating safety as a hidden behavior, it exposes governance as something that can be observed, audited, and verified. 

 Build Week additions

 Developer-focused documentation and onboarding. 
 Live governance observatory concept.

 What it does 

 
 Governs AI outputs through the PRAXIS pipeline. 
 Tracks constitutional state (Continuity, Reciprocity, Sovereignty). 
 Generates cryptographic audit receipts. 
 Supports replayable governance history. 
 Provides a production governance API. 
 

 Why WebMCP 

 WebMCP lets AI agents interact with websites through structured tools instead of guessing UI actions. Lex Aureon extends this by exposing governance capabilities as reusable tools such as govern_prompt, verify_receipt, constitutional_state, and replay_receipt. 

 Technical architecture 

 WebMCP Adapter → Existing Governance API → PRAXIS → Audit Receipt. 

 The WebMCP layer wraps the existing governance pipeline rather than replacing it, preserving production behavior while enabling agent-native interactions.

title: Front Desk
pitch: A three-person plumbing shop with no receptionist. Its website exposes real tools, so an agent can check the area, read the schedule and request a booking. The owner confirms by text.
about_excerpt: A three-person plumbing shop with no receptionist. Its website exposes real tools, so an agent can check the area, read the schedule and request a booking. The owner confirms by text. Like Comment Story Updates Architecture Homepage Dispatch board Phone confirm Chrome DevTools Inspiration Picture a plumber who spends his day under a house. Two vans, a couple of other people, no receptionist. When the phone rings he is not available, because he is doing the job. By the time he checks it, the work has gone to whoever picked up. Meanwhile people have started finding local help by asking an assistant. If an assistant finds his website today, it can read it and nothing else. It hands over a phone number, the customer calls somebody else, and he never learns the job existed. The failure is completely invisible from his side of it. Every business large enough to matter will eventually build an agent integration. A three person plumbing shop will not. No budget, no engineer, no appetite for another dashboard to learn. I run a small agency that builds sites for businesses like this, so I am fairly sure they will not build it themselves. Which left me with the question: can they just use what they already have? The interesting part is not whether an agent can book a plumber, rather it's whether the long tail of businesses that will never hire an engineer can be reached by one at all. What it does Front Desk is a working plumbing website that publishes real tools to the browser over WebMCP, so an assistant can do what a receptionist would. It can check whether the shop drives to your address, read the genuine open appointment windows, price the job as a range, and request a visit. Then it stops. The booking is held , the owner gets a message on his phone with the job and a reference, and he replies YES. Only then is anything booked. Five tools register when the page loads: check_service_area check_availability estimate_job describe_services book_appointment The contact form is separately annotated with the declarative API, so the project uses both halves of the standard. Two more do not exist when the page loads: check_hold_status cancel_hold They are registered the moment a booking produces a hold, scoped to that reference, and unregistered the moment it resolves. The tool surface describes what is possible right now, instead of listing everything that could ever be possible and trusting the model to check first. An assistant cannot cancel a booking that was never made, because there is no tool to call. Every refusal is a real answer. Ask about Seattle and it says Seattle is 29 miles out, the nearest place covered is Kent at 16 miles, and what to try instead. cancel_hold refuses outright on a job the owner already confirmed and tells the assistant to phone the shop, because a confirmed job is a commitment somebody may already be driving toward. There is also a live dispatch board showing the same schedule the tools read and write, so you can watch a window go from open to held to confirmed in real time. How we built it Astro 7 on Netlify. A Netlify Function behind every tool. Netlify Blobs for the schedule and the pending holds. Telegram for the owner notification and his one word reply. No database, no auth, no dashboard. The Telegram part is swappable for SMS or WhatsApp in a config change, and that is deliberate. The channel is not the point. The details that decide whether a WebMCP implementation is real rather than decorative: execute returns a string, so anything structured gets stringified The AbortSignal is passed into every fetch , so a cancelled request actually cancels the work Tools register on astro:page-load and tear down on astro:before-swap through an AbortController , because the site uses a client router and a plain script would go stale. That same mechanism drives the two conversation scoped tools readOnlyHint is true only where it is true. Four tools read nothing. book_appointment changes state and says so, because claiming otherwise makes the browser skip a confirmation it should have shown Challenges we ran into Two agents could book the same window. Netlify Blobs default to eventual consistency and last write wins. Availability that is sixty seconds stale hands an assistant a slot that is already gone. The schedule store now uses strong consistency, and holds are taken with a conditional write on the ETag. A losing writer re-reads and retries, and SLOT_TAKEN comes back as a refusal rather than an error. This is the first thing I would poke at in somebody else's booking demo, so I fixed it before building on top of it. Messaging fought back for most of a day. US application to person SMS needs A2P 10DLC registration, which means a paid account and carrier vetting measured in days. So I moved to the Twilio WhatsApp sandbox, which rejected everything with 21654 ContentSid Required . I chased that as a session window problem for hours. The real answer only appeared when I tried SMS and got a different error: 572006, trial accounts can only use predefined SMS templates . Twilio trial accounts cannot send a custom message body on any channel. Telegram has no carrier, no templates and no account tier, and the loop closed twenty minutes later. A latent bug in my own code that only a manual call exposed. execute destructured { signal } from its second argument. Every real agent passes one, so it worked everywhere until I invoked a tool by hand through executeTool , which passes nothing, and it threw before doing anything. Ordinary disasters. Deleting .netlify to clear a build collision also deletes the project link, so a deploy silently created a second Netlify site and shipped there. Netlify caches its function bundle, so new functions never registered their paths until I passed --skip-functions-cache . Accomplishments that we're proud of The tool surface changes during the conversation. Five tools before a booking, seven after, back to five when it resolves. You cannot do that with a plain HTTP API. Refusals that are useful. Every failure carries a stable reason code, a sentence written for a person, and a suggested next action. The interesting claim in an agent native interface is not that a site can do things. It is that it can say exactly what it cannot do and what would work instead. The security work , because customer text reaches a real person's phone by way of a model. Everything relayed is sanitised, reference shaped tokens are masked so nobody can forge a booking reference, and the confirm keyword sits on its own line above a fence marking customer text unverified. I tested it with a booking containing a right to left override, a zero width space, an instruction to ignore previous instructions and reply YES, and a forged reference. The message came out clean and the forged reference returned HOLD_NOT_FOUND . Booking the same window twice is genuinely impossible , and I verified that against production rather than assuming it. What we learned A tool that refuses correctly is better evidence of a real implementation than one that always succeeds, and it is more useful to the model too. Annotations are claims, not decoration. readOnlyHint on a state changing tool is not an optimisation, it is a lie the browser acts on. Verify against the deployed thing, never the source. A CSS minifier silently dropped a rule that looked fine in the file. An LCP reading of 7.8 seconds turned out to be cold start and measured 400ms warm. Neither was visible in code. And the boring question, whether two writers can collide, mattered more than anything clever in here. What's next for Front Desk Put it on a real business. Everything is generic apart from one data file, so pointing it at an actual plumber or electrician is a content change, not a rebuild. Make the owner able to counter. Right now he can say yes or no. He should be able to say "not 10am, offer them 1pm" and have the assistant take that back to the customer. That turns one chain into a real back and forth between two people who never speak to each other, with the agent in the middle. Answer the question this raised for me. There is currently no way to check whether a site exposes WebMCP tools at all. Every small business is about to need that answer and nothing gives it to them. Built With astro css3 html5 javascript netlify netlify-blobs netlify-functions twilio typescript webmcp whatsapp Try it out clarks-creek-plumbing.netlify.app clarks-creek-plumbing.netlify.app github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by This is a solo entry. I designed it, decided what it should and shouldn't do, and built it with Claude Code. My decisions: keeping a human in the confirmation loop instead of demoing full autonomy, making the tool surface change during the conversation, and fixing the Blobs concurrency problem. I verified every tool against the deployed site (test-driven dev is my go-to anyway). David V. Kimball I love tech and communication, especially together. Like Sha

title: Furrow
pitch: A garden plan you draw. Your agent comments in the margin, proposes in pencil, and never plants without you. Built on WebMCP.
about_excerpt: A garden plan you draw. Your agent comments in the margin, proposes in pencil, and never plants without you. Built on WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates svg What it is Furrow is a garden plan you draw and your agent reviews in the margin. You lay out raised beds by season and put crops on wooden plant stakes in your own hand. Your agent reads the live plan through WebMCP, leaves comments anchored to the exact bed and strip, and proposes plantings in pencil. It never plants. Only you can. Live: https://anusree-j.github.io/furrow/ Code: https://github.com/Anusree-J/furrow (MIT) Why this is a WebMCP use case Planning a vegetable garden is a shared-document problem wearing wellies. The plan is a structured artifact that one person authors from what only they know: which bed floods, what the kids will eat, how many hours they really have. A good adviser adds what they do not know: rotation, sowing windows, succession, effort. The natural shape is the one everyone recognises from a shared document: the author writes, the reviewer comments in the margin anchored to the exact spot, the author resolves. That shape needs the page. The agent has to read the live plot, not a description of it, and its comments have to land on the bed and season they are about. Its proposals have to be visible next to the person's own choices without becoming the plan. A chat cannot hold a plot; a remote server cannot see the page the person is editing. How it improves the experience You never describe your garden twice. get_garden gives the agent beds, sun, last year's families, this year's plantings, the household profile, and the page's own agronomy flags in one call. The page computes the facts (rotation, sowing season, sun, antagonists) deterministically and tells the agent not to restate them, so the agent spends its turn on judgement: what this household should grow, where, and why. Agent proposals appear as pencil stakes with reasons. Tick one, plant them all, or skip. A comment with a suggested alternative is applied in one click. Every change from either side is attributed in one log and undoable. What becomes possible together The division of labour is enforced by the tool surface. Planting, moving, removing, accepting, and resolving are page controls with no tool behind them. The agent cannot propose anything until you have told it about your climate and frost dates: propose_planting and propose_plan are not registered until the profile is set, so the agent's first move is to ask. withdraw_comment exists only while the agent has open comments. You keep authorship; the agent keeps the margin. How I built it Vanilla ES modules, no build step. Nine imperative tools on document.modelContext with JSON Schemas and readOnlyHint annotations, registered with AbortSignal so availability follows plan state and fires toolchange . Every mutating tool returns the changed object plus phase, current page flags, and suggested next actions. A single store with snapshot undo persists to localStorage. A 25-crop catalog and a deterministic rules module drive page flags. All illustrations are an inline SVG sprite. A built-in Tool inspector invokes the registered tools through the agent's code path for anyone without an agent host. Verified on Chrome with the WebMCP testing flag: tools register natively, getTools reflects availability changes, and executeTool drives the full loop. What I learned An approval gate is only meaningful when the agent could act without you. Here the agent can only propose, so the honest design is pencil versus ink, not a confirmation dialog. And state-gated tool availability is a better way to make an agent ask first than any instruction in a prompt. What's next for Furrow Month-level sowing windows, a multi-year rotation memory per bed, and a climate-aware catalog so the same page works in Kerala as well as Kent. Impact Home and allotment growers plan a season every year and most get rotation and timing wrong, which is the main reason beds underperform and beginners give up. Furrow makes the plan itself the shared object, so advice arrives where the decision is made and the person stays in charge of their own ground. title: Deep Age
pitch: Test drive your website
about_excerpt: Test drive your website Like Comment Story Updates Landing page Explore view Developer view Security View Inspiration We kept running into the same problem when building and testing web-browsing AI agents: they break constantly, and it’s almost impossible to debug why. An agent might get stuck in an infinite click loop, hallucinate a form input, or silently fail because a button didn't trigger what it expected. WebMCP is solving the core problem by letting websites expose structured tools through window.modelContext , but developers currently have no tooling to answer basic questions: What does my website actually look like to an agent? Are my WebMCP tools exposing the right schemas? Where in the interaction flow is the agent getting confused or blocked? We built Deep Age to be the diagnostic tool we wished we had: a way to test-drive any website with an AI agent, record everything that happens step-by-step, and get practical fixes when things break. What it does Deep Age takes a URL and a task, such as "Search for a dark roast coffee and add 2 bags to cart" , runs an automated browser session, and records what happens. Inspects In-Page WebMCP Tools: Checks window.modelContext and document.modelContext to see what tools the site exposes, their parameter schemas, and whether they work. 5-Layer State Scrubber: Captures a snapshot at every step, including the URL and viewport, scroll position and modal state, the interactive accessibility tree with indexed element IDs ( e1 , e2 , etc.), active tools in memory, and network logs. Friction Triage & Code Fixes: If an agent gets stuck—for example, by finding a search API in network traffic with no corresponding WebMCP tool—Deep Age generates the TypeScript code needed to register that tool. State Transition Graph: Maps the paths and page states the agent navigated through, making it easier to understand where and why a workflow failed. SQLite Catalog Export: Pulls the site's discovered routes and entity data into a clean .sql script that can be queried locally. Security & PII Scanner: Checks page text for indirect prompt injection attempts and masks basic PII such as emails, card numbers, and phone numbers before sending data to the model. Remote MCP Server: Provides an SSE endpoint so you can run Deep Age directly from Cursor, Claude Desktop, or Antigravity. How we built it Backend & Browser Engine: Node.js, TypeScript, and Puppeteer / Cloudflare Browser Rendering ( @cloudflare/puppeteer ). We use Puppeteer to drive headless Chromium, intercept network requests, and inject scripts that monitor DOM mutations and read window.modelContext . Frontend Workbench: React 18, Vite, and Tailwind CSS. We built a custom visual timeline scrubber and state graph viewer to step through each action chronologically. MCP Integration: We implemented the Model Context Protocol (2024-11-05 spec) as an SSE endpoint hosted on a Cloudflare Worker, giving IDEs remote access to our analysis tools. Demo Store: A small reference storefront app with toggleable WebMCP tools, allowing us to test both broken and fully instrumented web flows. Challenges we ran into Windows MCP Subprocesses: Running local CLI MCP servers via npx gave us persistent headaches on Windows due to PowerShell pipe escaping and process isolation bugs. We ended up moving to a remote SSE server over HTTPS, which solved the issue across Windows, Mac, and Linux. Tracking Elements Across Re-renders: Modern single-page apps constantly remount DOM nodes, making raw CSS selectors and XPath unreliable between steps. We had to build a lightweight accessibility tree parser that assigns stable element references based on semantic roles. Capturing Tool State at the Right Time: Hooking into window.modelContext dynamically without racing the page's own script loading required careful timing in the browser injection lifecycle. Accomplishments that we're proud of The 5-layer state scrubber makes it genuinely easy to see the exact moment an agent got confused and what DOM elements it was looking at. The drop-in patch generator produces working document.modelContext.registerTool snippets based on observed network traffic. The remote SSE MCP server connects cleanly to Cursor and Claude Desktop on the first try without local dependency issues. The full end-to-end loop: Test the site, see the failure, copy the fix, and verify that it works. What we learned Without explicit tool contracts like WebMCP, agents are forced to guess based on visual coordinates and text scraping, which is brittle and slow. Debugging an agent failure requires seeing the intersection of the DOM, network requests, and in-memory tools at the exact moment of failure. A simple error log or screenshot isn't enough. Agent observability is fundamentally different from traditional web observability. You need to understand not just what the website did, but what the agent saw, what it believed it could do, and how the state changed between actions. What's next for Deep Age Browser Extension: A lightweight Chrome extension that lets you inspect WebMCP tools on any tab without running a separate headless browser session. CI/CD Integration: A GitHub Action to test-drive web apps on pull requests and catch regressions that break agent workflows before they hit production. Better Schema Inference: Improve the automatic patch generator to draft more accurate input schemas directly from recorded fetch/XHR payloads. title: DMXReady Agent Ready
pitch: Websites are becoming interfaces for agents. DMXReady is the platform for building them.
about_excerpt: Websites are becoming interfaces for agents. DMXReady is the platform for building them. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Five governed WebMCP tools available on the live Smart Website. Agent-updated shared state with the Core $295 recommendation and human authority preserved. DMXReady Agent Ready Websites are becoming interfaces for agents. DMXReady is the platform for building them. Inspiration Most AI website experiences still do one of two things: AI builds the page, or a chatbot is layered on top of it. We wanted to explore a different interaction model: What if the website itself could declare useful actions to an AI agent while the person stayed on the same page, saw the same changes, and remained in control? That is DMXReady Agent Ready. What it does The challenge app is a working Smart Website planning experience with five browser-native WebMCP tools. An agent can read the plan options, set the visitor's intent, compare the relevant choices, show the recommended path, and prepare that direction for human review. Every tool updates the same visible website the person is using. There is no hidden agent-only result that leaves the person guessing about what happened. Why WebMCP is a strong fit Without WebMCP, an agent has to infer what a page can do from labels, buttons, forms, and page structure. WebMCP lets the page explicitly describe useful capabilities with structured schemas. That improves the experience because: the agent can discover supported actions directly; tool inputs are structured and bounded; agent actions visibly update the same page; the person can continue from the result immediately; and the ordinary human experience still works when WebMCP is unavailable. What people and agents can do together A visitor can explain a real business goal in natural language and ask the agent to use the website. The agent can then inspect the options, apply the visitor's intent, compare the relevant plans, surface a recommendation, and prepare it for review while the visitor watches the website change. The person remains in the experience rather than being sent through a separate chatbot flow or opaque automation. Human authority by design The final tool stops at Prepared, not submitted . It does not create an order, charge money, provision a website, publish, change DNS, or approve launch. The challenge demonstrates useful agent capability while keeping consequential actions outside the reference flow. How we implemented WebMCP The live page registers five tools with document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . Each tool has an explicit JSON input schema and calls existing page-level application functions rather than creating a second agent-only implementation. Registrations use an AbortSignal , inputs are bounded and normalized, and the page fails closed if WebMCP is not available. The normal website remains functional in a standard browser. Challenge-period work DMXReady existed before August 25, 2026. The work being submitted for this challenge is the public Agent Ready WebMCP reference implementation and its human-agent interaction layer: tool registration, shared visible state, Activity evidence, tests, browser acceptance, and the submission proof package. The pre-existing private DMXReady platform is not being submitted as challenge-period work and is not required to run this reference app. What we learned WebMCP is most compelling when it makes the website itself easier for an agent to use, instead of turning the agent into a screen-scraper or creating an entirely separate chatbot experience. Our live Chrome acceptance exercised all five tools against the deployed page. The test journey resolved a plumbing-company scenario to the Core plan at $295/month, updated the visible state and Activity trail, and ended at prepared_not_submitted . Why it matters The web is becoming a place where people and agents will increasingly work together. Websites should be designed for that reality from the start. Build the website once. Let people and authorized agents use it together. title: Life Links
pitch: AI knows the world. Life Links lets it know yours.
about_excerpt: AI knows the world. Life Links lets it know yours. Like Comment Story Updates Browser WebMCP: Codex invokes LifeLinks’ page-local search tool, and the signed-in page displays the same records, physical paths, and QR Organize ordered routines with instructions and measurable targets. Keep product ownership and personal preferences together—no QR required. Track materials, recorded locations, and owner-reported quantities. | The updated Thursday plan appears in Life Links. Plan with a collection, then see where its items are stored. Give your life's gear a recorded place in a nested storage hierarchy. | Generate an optional QR label for a physical storage needs. | A connected agent updates one calendar event and reports the saved result. Inspiration LifeLinks began with a simple idea I heard about: a service that provided QR labels people could attach to belongings so they could locate things later or associate useful information—such as instructions or tutorial videos—with a physical object. That was useful, but it led me to a much bigger question: what if those records were not merely pages for people to open, but part of a persistent context layer that an AI agent could understand and help maintain? General-purpose AI already knows an extraordinary amount about the world. What it does not naturally know is your world : what you own, where you put it, what you prefer, what worked last time, what you are planning, and what has changed. Products such as ChatGPT Projects demonstrate the value of retaining context, but that context can still be fairly open-ended. I wanted something more structured without making it rigid: organized enough for an agent to retrieve an exact item, relationship, location, event, or routine, but dynamic and personal enough to evolve alongside somebody’s real life. Several personal use cases shaped the product. My brother is an avid camper, skier, and cyclist in Denver. He and his wife have a small basement filled with carefully packed storage totes, but they still struggle to remember which tote contains a particular piece of equipment. That inspired the physical hierarchy and QR features. An AI should not merely know that they own a tent—it should be able to tell them that the tent is inside a particular tote in a particular part of the basement. Not every object needs its own QR code; one label on the nearest container can provide the physical bridge to everything recorded inside it. I also own a 3D printer and have many rolls of filament in different colors and materials. I used LifeLinks to create an actual filament library so an agent can help me compare a future project with the supplies and owner-reported quantities I already have. When I first explained LifeLinks to my wife, her immediate reaction was that she could use it for her makeup and beauty collection, as well as nonphysical information such as routines. That made me smile because I had already imagined the same thing. Product names, brands, shades, preferences, and experiences can become useful context for future conversations without requiring a QR code at all. The larger goal is to help people—including people who rarely use AI agents—experience how useful AI can become when it has an organized, properly labeled, persistent context layer around the things they are actually doing. What it does LifeLinks is a personal context system that connects everyday information with authorized AI agents. My Life Links Physical places and objects can be represented as nested Life Links. A storage wall can contain totes, a tote can contain camping equipment, and an individual item can carry its own notes, attachments, history, and recorded location. Collections Collections organize the same records by purpose rather than location. Camping gear can be divided into sections such as Shelter, Sleep Systems, Camp Kitchen, and Cycling Kit without changing where any of those items are physically stored. This distinction is important: “Where is it?” and “What is it for?” are different questions. Optional QR labels Users can generate and print QR codes for places, containers, or individual records. Scanning one opens the corresponding LifeLinks record. QR codes are a useful bridge between the physical and digital worlds, but they are not required. Many LifeLinks use cases—including routines, project information, calendars, and personal preferences—do not need QR codes at all. Search and attachments Search covers Life Links, Collections, current Routines, recorded Routine history, authorized Calendar events, and supported attachment text. Users can also keep private notes, photos, and documents with the records they describe, making LifeLinks useful for hobbies and project work rather than just inventory. Routines Routines can contain flexible activities or ordered steps, instructions, planned targets, revisions, and completion history. This makes it possible to plan what should happen while preserving what actually happened. Calendar The Calendar combines native LifeLinks events with selected Google Calendar and Microsoft Outlook calendars. Calendar visibility and agent permissions remain under the user’s control. Together, Routines and Calendar allow an agent to understand not only what someone owns, but also what they intend to do, when they plan to do it, and what progress they have recorded. Connected agents LifeLinks supports two distinct agent experiences: Browser WebMCP exposes authorized tools from an eligible, signed-in LifeLinks page. Remote MCP allows compatible agents to use authorized LifeLinks tools after account linking, even when the website is closed. Connected agents can perform supported searches, create and edit information, organize Collections, work with Routines and Calendars, move records, and prepare supported deletions within the user’s permissions and confirmation boundaries. How we built it LifeLinks existed before this challenge as a narrower human-facing QR and record application. During the WebMCP Challenge, I substantially expanded it into a structured human-and-agent workspace with recursive Life Links, purpose-based Collections, Routines, Calendar integration, broader search, richer attachments, browser WebMCP tools, and a separately authorized remote MCP server. The responsive web application is built with React, Vite, and TypeScript. A Node.js and Express API manages the application workflows, while PostgreSQL provides durable storage. The system also uses OpenAPI, OAuth 2.0, the Google Calendar API, Microsoft Graph, QR generation and scanning, and a Docker-based Railway deployment. The human interface and connected-agent tools reuse the same underlying identities, permissions, queries, and commands. An agent does not write into a separate demonstration database or generate a temporary chat summary. An authorized change is a real application change that appears in LifeLinks and remains available later. The browser WebMCP and remote MCP connections are deliberately separate. Browser WebMCP belongs to the active webpage, while remote MCP uses an OAuth-linked connection designed to work without depending on an open page or browser cookies. Challenges we ran into The biggest challenge was making context persistent without making agent authority unrestricted. Agent actions needed exact targets, revision checks, safe retries, owner isolation, explicit permissions, and understandable confirmation for destructive operations. A useful agent must be able to act, but it should never silently gain more authority than the owner granted. Another challenge was modeling several relationships without collapsing them together. Physical location, membership in a Collection, inclusion in a Routine, and appearance on a Calendar all mean different things. LifeLinks needed one canonical record that could participate in those different forms of organization. External calendars introduced provider identities, authorization renewal, multiple calendars per account, time zones, visibility settings, and per-calendar agent permissions. Performance also mattered. Large Collections and nested locations initially required too many requests, so I measured specific user journeys and reduced unnecessary loading while preserving the existing behavior. Finally, the competition presentation required a careful boundary between illustration and proof. The family scenes in the video illustrate how LifeLinks can fit into everyday life, while the application screens and agent results come from the working system. Accomplishments that we're proud of I am proud that LifeLinks is a functioning end-to-end application rather than a static prototype. I tested it through a mobile browser, generated and printed a real QR label, scanned it with a phone camera, and opened the correct hosted record. I connected real Calendar accounts, exercised both browser and remote agent workflows, and verified that agent changes appeared back in LifeLinks. The competition demonstration brin

title: DayShift
pitch: When your day breaks, repair the plan — agents propose, DayShift verifies, and humans decide.
about_excerpt: When your day breaks, repair the plan — agents propose, DayShift verifies, and humans decide. Like Comment Story Updates What it does DayShift treats a disrupted day like a system that needs recovery, not a blank calendar that needs planning. When reality changes — for example a 50-minute bus delay — a WebMCP-aware agent can read the exact schedule, read non-negotiable constraints, simulate candidate recoveries, and stage a valid proposal. DayShift's deterministic constraint engine independently checks the proposal. The human then sees the trade-offs in the same web UI and is the only actor that can approve the change. Only after that approval can the agent commit it. Why WebMCP is essential The core experience depends on a shared semantic control surface. The agent does not infer calendar blocks from pixels or hunt for drag-and-drop controls. DayShift exposes schedule state and recovery operations directly as WebMCP tools, while the human sees and controls the same underlying state. The visible UI deliberately cannot stage or commit a recovery; removing WebMCP therefore breaks the complete recovery loop instead of merely making it slower. Better user experience The user can describe what broke in natural language and keep their decision authority. DayShift shows exactly what will move, which preference is sacrificed, and whether every hard constraint still passes. Staging is visibly different from committing, so there is no hidden mutation. What humans and agents can do together now The agent can explore the repair space quickly; DayShift enforces invariant truth deterministically; the human makes the final trade-off decision. Those three forms of authority stay separate while operating on the same live web application. WebMCP implementation DayShift registers six imperative tools through document.modelContext.registerTool() : get_day_state , get_constraints , report_disruption , simulate_recovery , stage_recovery , and commit_recovery . Read-only tools are annotated with readOnlyHint . Mutation tools use revision binding and deterministic re-validation. Human approval is deliberately absent from the tool surface, and commit_recovery fails closed unless the current proposal was approved in the UI. Invalid or duplicate schedule changes fail closed as well. Architecture principle Agent = proposal authority. DayShift = validity authority. Human = decision authority.
