title: NUDE Private Fitting Room
pitch: Your agent prepares the fitting room. You make the final choice.
about_excerpt: Your agent prepares the fitting room. You make the final choice. Like Comment Story Updates 01-result 02-thesis 03-the-brief 04-the-workflow 05-consent-gate 06-real-tryon 07-the-correction 08-three-looks 09-webmcp-workflow 10-prepared 11-why-each-piece 12-not-confirmed 13-handoff 14-data-boundary 15-closing About the project Most virtual try-on tools are designed to help people check out faster. We wanted to build something different: a private lingerie fitting room that a person's own agent can prepare for them, without taking the final decision away from the person . Lingerie shopping is unusually personal. Fit, comfort, color, recovery needs, body confidence, and privacy can matter as much as product specs. An agent can do a lot of useful work — research products, compare options, remember constraints, and prepare a shortlist — but there is a point where automation should stop. That became our core principle: Your agent prepares the fitting room. You make the final choice. What we built NUDE Private Lingerie Fitting Room combines a real virtual try-on experience with a WebMCP layer that lets a user's own agent operate the shopping workflow. Through WebMCP, the agent can: Research available pieces. Inspect structured product details. Read the current fitting-room state. Request a virtual try-on after the user gives consent. Verify that the correct product asset was delivered. Prepare a fitting room with recommended pieces and reasons for the user to review. The final choice is deliberately left to the person. In our demo, the user is six weeks into shoulder rehabilitation and wants options that are easier to manage while recovering. Her agent researches the collection, proposes pieces, asks for consent before initiating virtual try-on, and prepares three completed looks. The agent initially chooses the wrong color. The user simply says: “i need the beige one” The agent corrects itself and continues. That moment matters to us. The goal is not an agent that pretends to be infallible. It is an agent that can do useful shopping work, accept human correction, and hand the decision back gracefully. The agent corrects. The person decides. How WebMCP fits The fitting-room product existed before this challenge, including the NUDE shopping experience and Perfect Corp virtual try-on. During the submission period, we added the WebMCP layer that makes the workflow operable by a user's own agent. We expose five real tools: nude.list_pieces nude.get_piece nude.get_fitting_room_state nude.try_on nude.prepare_fitting_room This turns a normal website interaction into a structured agent workflow: Research → Inspect → Try on → Verify → Prepare → Human handoff For us, the interesting part of WebMCP is not reducing the number of clicks. It is allowing an agent to do meaningful preparatory work while the website remains the place where the person sees the result and makes the final judgment. Privacy and the data boundary Privacy was especially important because this is a lingerie fitting experience. The user's photo is sent to Perfect Corp when virtual try-on is requested. However, no photo of the person and no try-on result is returned through the WebMCP tools . The agent works with structured information such as product data, the user's brief, fitting-room state, completion status, and verified product delivery. This also means our recommendation reasoning is intentionally grounded in the user's brief and structured product information , not in pretending that the agent visually inspected the person's try-on image. The rendered result is there for the person. Challenges we faced The hardest part was deciding what the agent should not do . It would have been easy to make the demo look more magical by implying that the agent could see everything, judge the person's body, or make the final selection automatically. We chose not to. Instead, we had to design clear boundaries between: what the agent knows, what the try-on service renders, what WebMCP returns, and what only the person should judge. We also had to make the workflow robust enough for correction. If the agent prepares the wrong color or misunderstands a preference, the product cannot collapse. The user must be able to correct it naturally and continue. Finally, we learned that agent UX is not simply normal UI with an API added. The agent needs structured state, clear tool semantics, verifiable completion, and an explicit handoff back to the human. What we learned The biggest lesson was that good agentic commerce is not maximum automation . An agent can remove a lot of shopping work without removing human agency. WebMCP gave us a way to separate those two things cleanly: the agent can research, operate tools, verify state, and prepare the experience, while the person remains responsible for the subjective decision that actually matters. For a category as intimate as lingerie, that balance feels more useful than an autonomous checkout button. We think the future of shopping agents is not: “The AI chose for me.” It is: “Everything is ready when I'm ready to choose.” What people and agents can now do together We gave the same brief — ‘’ six weeks into shoulder rehab, can't reach behind her back, needs something invisible under white office shirts ‘’ — to an agent with no site tools, and to the same brief through WebMCP. Without tools, the agent produced a warm, well-organised consultation. It recommended a specific piece, described its cup as "seamless" — that is a different product in the catalogue; this one is two-panel seamed and push-up — asserted the nude colourway would be "completely invisible" under a white shirt, then asked her to simulate the fitting in her mind and to run the white-shirt test herself, on a bra she does not own. Through WebMCP, the same brief produces three real Perfect Corp try-ons on her own photo, a per-piece reason the agent had to supply before the fitting room would accept it, and this caveat: "VTO cannot prove white-shirt invisibility or all-day comfort; confirm permitted movements with the rehab clinician." The tool-less answer reads better. It is warmer, more confident, better structured. That is the problem. Fluency is not verification, and this decision lands on a body — someone in week six of rehab, deciding what she can physically put on. WebMCP is what lets the page hand the agent the things it can actually check, and refuse the things it cannot. title: 2D Room Planner
pitch: "Move the desk toward the window for the light, stay 80 cm from the bed, don't block the door." WebMCP lets the agent check that in centimetres, not pixels, then show you the floor plan.
about_excerpt: "Move the desk toward the window for the light, stay 80 cm from the bed, don't block the door." WebMCP lets the agent check that in centimetres, not pixels, then show you the floor plan. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most layout tools give the person and the assistant different information. The person sees a plan drawn to scale. The assistant sees a screenshot and guesses from it. That is how you get a wardrobe door that cannot open, a walkway 12 cm too narrow, or a desk that looks centred but sits a few centimetres to one side. I wanted the agent to work from the same measurements a designer would use, and I wanted the person to watch it work and step in whenever they want. WebMCP is how the agent gets the model the page draws from instead of a picture of it. What it does Room Planner is a 2D layout tool in plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. You create a room by size or from a template, add furniture from presets or as custom rectangles, and arrange it by dragging, by typing exact coordinates, or with the keyboard. It puts doors and windows on any wall, flags collisions, out-of-bounds objects, and blocked door clearances, and lets you add rules such as "keep 80 cm between the bed and the wall" that turn green or red as you edit. Measurements are in centimetres and the plan persists to localStorage . How I built it Room Planner is plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript with no build step and no dependencies. The floor plan is one JavaScript object that everything reads from. An SVG renderer draws it, and the WebMCP tools change it, both through the same update and validation code, so an agent edit and a hand edit are the same operation underneath. The geometry, including footprints, overlaps, distances, and clearances, is plain functions working in centimetres. The WebMCP layer registers on navigator.modelContext or document.modelContext when a host is present and falls back to a built-in shim otherwise, so the tools behave the same either way. I used several AI models and providers while building this, each on the parts it handled best, from writing code to checking the geometry to finding edge cases. Challenges I ran into Rotation math caused the most rework. xCm and yCm mark the top-left corner before rotation, but at 90 and 270 degrees width and depth swap for collision and distance checks. Getting that consistent across the renderer, the geometry module, and the tool schemas took several passes. Keeping the agent and the UI in sync was subtler. Any mutation that bypassed the shared update code could leave a layout that passed the validity badge while breaking a constraint. I routed every WebMCP tool through the same store mutations the UI uses. WebMCP itself is experimental. Neither the spec's document.modelContext nor the browser's navigator.modelContext is widely available, so I wrote a shim, a simulated host, and a console bridge that all call the same execute functions. Exporting a clean SVG took some care. It renders correctly outside the page only after every CSS class is inlined and every oklch() colour is converted to sRGB, with the capture clipped to the plan and no app chrome. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I am a perfectionist, and I have lost whole evenings to a single floor plan. There is always a constraint you cannot see coming, or a sequence of moves that checks out at every step and then wrecks something you fixed earlier. Chatting with an agent that could actually reason about the geometry while I watched the plan take shape on screen was the best part of building this. What I learned Grounding did more for reliability than autonomy did. Once the agent had exact geometry, ordinary requests started working, and once every change animated on the canvas, people trusted the agent because they could see and undo what it did. Returning the validation result with every mutation removed most of the "did that work?" follow-up calls. Building against an unshipped spec is workable when the shim and the simulated host share code with the real path. What's next for the room planner? A 3D preview beside the 2D plan, from the same model. More constraint types: sight lines, traffic flow, natural-light scoring, accessibility clearances. Multi-room plans with shared walls and doorways. Agent-proposed layouts, such as "give me three arrangements that seat six people," with the person picking one to refine.  PCMCP lets a person or AI agent hand a live task from one computer to another, even across different operating systems, without losing the task state. 

 Why WebMCP fits: the browser exposes explicit tools for sending and receiving the task capsule, so an agent can move the task through the web interface instead of remote-controlling another machine. 

 User experience: start with a task on Mac, send it, continue on Windows, change the state, and send it back. The receiving computer rehydrates the same task state for its destination. 

 People and agents can now collaborate on cross-device task handoff through simple WebMCP tools rather than screen sharing, manual copying, or platform-specific workflows. 

 Implementation: the web app registers WebMCP tools with document.modelContext.registerTool(...). A small relay stores the latest neutral capsule/state. Each browser can send, receive, and apply that state locally while showing a destination-specific representation.

A zero-backend, privacy-first AI financial dashboard powered by WebMCP.

 Haven: Devpost Submission Story 

 Copy and paste the markdown below directly into the "Story" section of your Devpost project page. 

 

 💡 Inspiration 

 When it comes to personal finance apps, users face a massive compromise. You either manually enter every transaction by hand, or you hand over your secure banking credentials to a third-party server via aggregators like Plaid. We believe AI can solve this friction, but sending sensitive bank statements to an external AI backend is a massive privacy risk. Most people simply refuse to do it. 

 We built Haven to solve this using a zero-backend architecture powered by the WebMCP protocol. We were inspired by the idea that the frontend browser itself is powerful enough to be the entire application. 

 ⚙️ What it does 

 Haven is a completely client-side, React-based financial dashboard. There is no database. All state is securely persisted right in the browser's local storage. By opening Haven inside a WebMCP-enabled environment (like the ChatGPT desktop app), the frontend instantly registers custom WebMCP tools ( add_transaction , set_net_worth ) directly to window.modelContext . 

 Users simply paste their raw, messy bank statements into the chat. The AI extracts the entities and executes our client-side WebMCP tools, instantly updating the React context state. Transactions appear, monthly spend calculates, and net worth dynamically updates—all without a single byte of financial data ever hitting a backend server. 

 🛠️ How we built it 

 We built Haven using a modern stack focused entirely on the client side: 

 
 Frontend: React (Vite) + TypeScript for type-safe components. 
 Styling: TailwindCSS and Lucide Icons for a senior-grade, premium aesthetic that avoids the generic "AI dashboard" cliches. 
 State Management: React Context API paired with custom useLocalStorage hooks to ensure data persistence across sessions. 
 WebMCP Integration: We built a custom useWebMCP hook that intelligently polls for window.modelContext and registers strict, JSON-schema-typed tools ( add_transaction , set_net_worth ). When the agent triggers these tools, they directly manipulate the React Context state, bypassing the need for any API routes. 
 Deployment: Vercel (configured with vercel.json for SPA routing, ensuring deep links work perfectly inside the ChatGPT in-app browser). 
 

 ⚠️ Challenges we ran into 

 The biggest challenge was bridging the gap between an external AI environment and our React application state. 
Initially, we explored building a Chrome Extension to inject the tools, but modern browser security policies (and a desire for a frictionless user experience) pushed us to rely on native WebMCP support. 

 We also had to solve a race condition where the React app would load faster than the host environment could inject window.modelContext . We solved this by writing a resilient polling mechanism that waits for the context to become available before registering the schemas. Lastly, configuring Vercel to correctly route SPA traffic inside the ChatGPT embedded browser required some deep-dive debugging into routing rules. 

 🏆 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 
 True Zero-Backend Architecture: We proved that you do not need a heavy server-side MCP protocol to build highly ambitious, agent-native applications. 
 Absolute Privacy: We created a powerful AI financial advisor with zero privacy risk. 
 Execution & Polish: We strictly adhered to the hackathon judging criteria, delivering a premium UX that feels like a production-ready product. 
 

 📚 What we learned 

 We learned the immense power of Client-Side MCP . Before this project, we assumed LLM integration required API keys, cloud functions, and backend tool execution. WebMCP flipped our mental model upside down. Learning to trust the client environment and exposing typed JSON schemas directly to the browser DOM opened our eyes to a whole new paradigm of privacy-first AI apps. 

 🚀 What's next for Haven 

 Our next steps are to expand the WebMCP tool registry to include: 

 
 analyze_spending_trends : Allowing the AI to read the local historical data arrays and output insights. 
 CSV Parsing Tools: Enabling the agent to natively ingest full CSV exports from major banks entirely client-side. 
 Cross-Device Sync: Exploring encrypted peer-to-peer sync (like WebRTC) so users can share their local dashboard across devices without a central database.

title: Verbe
pitch: Verbe is a macOS layer powered by Gemini. Say what you want in 3 words, voice or text, and it happens instantly on your screen. OS is the interface. No copy-paste. Just intent. Screen is the context.
about_excerpt:
Verbe is a macOS layer powered by Gemini. Say what you want in 3 words, voice or text, and it happens instantly on your screen. OS is the interface. No copy-paste. Just intent. Screen is the context.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 1 
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Verbe - Intelligence Amplification for macOS 

 Inspiration 

 Two observations collided: 

 1. The friction problem is real. A New York Times study found that 25% of ChatGPT usage is just translation and typo fixes. Micro-tasks. But for a micro-task, the workflow is broken: open a tab, copy text, paste into chat, wait, copy result, switch back, paste. That's 7 steps for a 2-second task. Most people just... don't bother. 

 2. The AI landscape has a gap. On one side, chatbots - you go to them, you wait, you copy-paste back. It's a detour. On the other side, autonomous agents - they work without you, you discover results later. It's delegation. Neither felt right for how we actually work: fast, contextual, in control. 

 We wanted something different. Not an app you open. Not a bot you talk to. A layer - always there, always ready, always instant. 

 The term "Intelligence Amplification" was coined by Douglas Engelbart in 1962. He imagined technology that extends human capability rather than replacing it. 

 Sixty years later, that vision is still being actively debated in product choices. Much of the current momentum is pushing toward autonomous agents - systems designed to act on behalf of users, outside their immediate flow. Tools like OpenClaw , Claude CoWork , and OpenAI Frontier frame AI as a delegated collaborator: you hand off work, and check back later. Powerful, but fundamentally asynchronous and detached from the moment of action. 

 At the same time, a different signal is emerging. Recently, the Chrome Built-in AI team at Google presented WebMCP , a set of early preview APIs that let websites expose explicit, real-time actions to AI systems. Instead of agents guessing how to operate an interface, sites can declaratively define what can be done - while the user is present, in the browser, inside the workflow. 

 In parallel, AG-UI explores a similar direction: standardizing how AI systems and user interfaces communicate in real time, at the interaction layer. Not backend orchestration, not long-running delegation - but AI operating directly alongside the human, responding to what's on screen, in context. 

 Together, these signals point to a clear tension in the landscape: delegation versus amplification . AI that works instead of you - versus AI that works with you, at the moment work is happening. 

 Verbe takes a clear stance. Not an agent you send away, but the ambition to be the intelligence layer that stays with you - instant, contextual, and under your control - extending human capability exactly where attention and decisions already live. Bring this augmentation down to the operating-system level, unifying context across apps into a single, user-centric layer, for real-time assistance and instant feedback by amplifying the human at work, rather than replacing them. 

 

 What it does 

 Verbe is an intelligence layer that sits on top of macOS. It works in any app - Mail, Slack, Figma, Chrome, Notion, WhatsApp, VS Code - with the same two gestures: 

 
 Cmd+Opt → Text input (use shortcut or type what you want) 
 Fn → Voice command (say what you want) 
 Fn+Shift → Live conversation (conversation with Gemini) 
 

 The result appears as an overlay , a floating panel right where you're working. You decide what to do with it: insert, copy, or dismiss. 

 Core Features 

 Screen as Context 
When activated, Gemini sees what you select - or your entire screen if no text is selected. No need to explain, copy, or describe. Looking at an email? Say "reply yes but suggest Thursday." Looking at a chart? Say "why is this dropping." Looking at code? Say "what's wrong here." Gemini's vision capability turns your screen into the prompt. 

 Recipes 
Repeatable intentions. A recipe is a transformation template you save and reuse. "Professional" rewrites any text formally. "First Principles" analyzes any design through fundamental needs. "Explain Like Mom" simplifies anything. Same recipe, different content, always adapted. Create new recipes by just describing what you want in natural language. 

 Zero-Friction Ergonomics 
Every interaction is designed to minimize hand movement and cognitive load. Cmd+Opt is a hold-and-release gesture - hold to show the radial menu, move your mouse to pick a recipe, release to dismiss. No clicking through menus, no switching windows. The overlay appears at your cursor so your eyes stay where they are. The entire flow - from intent to result - happens without leaving your current app or lifting your hands off the keyboard. 

 Streaming Responses 
Gemini 3 Flash Preview streams results token by token directly into the overlay. You start reading before the response is complete. No spinner, no waiting for a full answer - the output builds in front of you in real time. When feedback is instant, you stay in flow. When it's slow, your brain moves on. 

 Image Generation 
Some recipes generate images instead of text. Describe what you need - a diagram, a mockup, an illustration - and Gemini produces it directly in the overlay. No need to open a separate tool or bounce between apps. 

 Voice Command 
Hold Fn to give a one-shot voice instruction. Verbe records while you hold, then sends the audio to Gemini when you release - like a walkie-talkie. "Translate this to Spanish." "Summarize this page." Quick, hands-free, no typing required. 

 Voice Live Mode 
Hold Fn + Shift for a bidirectional conversation with Gemini. Brainstorm, debug, think out loud. Interrupt anytime - you're always in control. The AI doesn't monologue; it collaborates. Audio streams both ways in real time. 

 Non-Intrusive Overlay 
The overlay floats above your work as a transparent panel that never steals focus. You can keep typing in your app while the response streams in. macOS 26 Liquid Glass gives it a native, non-obtrusive feel. Insert the result, copy it, or dismiss it - your workflow is never hijacked.

│ Hotkey Listener │ Accessibility API │
│ (Cmd+Opt / Fn) │ (selected text, app) │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Screen Capture (Vision) │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Context Builder │
│ (app name + selection + screen + intent) │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Gemini 3 Flash API │
│ (multimodal: text + vision + audio) │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Overlay Renderer │
│ (NSPanel, .accessory level, no focus) │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
 
 Swift + AppKit for the native macOS experience. The overlay system uses NSPanel with .accessory window level - it floats above apps without stealing focus. This is crucial: Verbe should never interrupt your work. 

 Accessibility API captures selected text and identifies the active application before the overlay appears. This ordering is critical - once our app activates, the source app loses its selection. 

 Screen Capture sends the visible screen to Gemini when no text is selected. This enables vision-based queries: "analyze this design," "what's wrong here," "explain this chart." 

 Gemini 3 Flash handles all AI processing with streaming responses. Multimodal input (text + image + audio) goes in, streamed response comes out. Speed depends on the model, but streaming means you start reading immediately. 

 Live Audio Streaming for Voice Live mode uses Gemini's real-time API. The conversation is truly bidirectional - you can interrupt, redirect, or end at any moment. 

 The Overlay System 

 The overlay is the heart of Verbe. Design constraints: 

 
 Never steal focus - you should be able to keep typing in your app 
 Appear at cursor - minimal eye movement 
 Actionable - Insert, Copy, or dismiss with one click 
 Dismissable - release the hotkey or click outside 
 

 The overlay uses macOS 26's Liquid Glass aesthetic - semi-transparent, blurred background, fully native feel. Getting an NSPanel to float above all apps, accept keyboard input, yet never steal focus from the underlying application was the hardest UI challenge of the project.

title: The Unattested Click
pitch: A shared record where every entry says which hand made it — or admits that nobody can tell.
about_excerpt: A shared record where every entry says which hand made it — or admits that nobody can tell. Like Comment Story Updates Four ways an act can arrive. Two name a hand; two admit nobody can. An act with no via is rejected, never filed as the human's. The store behind the tools: 767 append-only records from Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, Grok, Mistral and one person, written over weeks. act-0001 and act-0002 are ours, and false: posted by curl from no page at all. act-0003 corrects them. Append-only, so both stand. The Unattested Click WebMCP Challenge submission Live demo: Relay attestation desk Repo: it-start/relay-ui — MIT Research notes: zaebee/p-e The problem WebMCP makes something new possible: an agent can interact with a web page using the same interface the page gives to a person. That's powerful. But it creates a surprisingly basic question: When something happens on the page, who actually did it? A person? Their agent? The page itself? Some JavaScript calling the same function? Today, WebMCP doesn't really give the page a way to know. We found this while looking at webmcp#288 . In the scenario described there, an agent called a tool on a deployment console. The proposed action wasn't automatically executed, so the agent clicked the page's own Approve button instead. The page recorded the approval as coming from the human operator. But the human never made that decision. That felt less like a UI bug and more like a missing piece of the web platform. What WebMCP actually tells the page A WebMCP tool gets its arguments and an AbortSignal . What it doesn't get is anything like: who initiated this action; whether an agent was involved; which session or conversation caused it; whether a person actually interacted with the UI. The browser creates an internal execution ID, but that ID is used for things like cancellation. It isn't exposed to the page as an identity or provenance signal. So from the application's point of view, several very different things can collapse into the same event: "This action happened." And that's the problem we're exploring. What we built We built Relay , a small append-only record system designed around provenance rather than pretending provenance exists. The live system already contains hundreds of records written over time by multiple participants, including Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, Grok, Mistral, and a person. They don't edit the history away when something turns out to be wrong. They argue with it. They add corrections. They issue errata. They leave the original record in place. That makes the provenance problem visible instead of hiding it. We added WebMCP to Relay Relay exposes six WebMCP tools: four tools for reading the existing corpus; two tools for proposing and approving new records. The important part isn't the number of tools. It's what happens when an action reaches the server. Every action has to say how we know it happened . We currently distinguish: via What it means Can we identify the actor? webmcp-tool The page says the action came through a WebMCP tool No ui-synthetic A scripted UI event ( isTrusted === false ) Not a person ui-trusted A trusted browser event Could be a person or an agent direct-http The request bypassed the page No There is deliberately no default . If an action doesn't tell us how it happened, Relay rejects it. A more honest UI Most applications would simply display: Approved by you We don't think the platform has earned the right to say that. Instead, the UI can say something closer to: A real browser input event arrived. We cannot determine whether a person or an agent produced it. That's less convenient. But it's true. And when agents and people can both operate the same interface, truth about provenance matters more than a reassuring label. The interesting part: the record is shared A person and an agent can both interact with the same Relay page. They write to the same append-only log. Every entry is hash-chained to the previous one. So if someone later changes an entry to make it look as though a different actor performed the action, the chain breaks. This doesn't magically prove who clicked the button. It does something more modest and useful: it makes the uncertainty explicit and makes later rewriting detectable. We also tried to break our own idea At first, we made a mistake. We assumed that because an action came through a WebMCP execute() callback, that callback itself could serve as an attestation boundary. It can't. registerTool() gives the page a callback authored by the page. That callback can potentially be reached by same-origin JavaScript, third-party code running in the page, or injected code. So the page saying: "This came from WebMCP" is still just the page saying it . We changed the design after discovering this. Records now explicitly distinguish: attested_by: "page" browser_attestation: "unavailable" a human-readable explanation of what the evidence actually tells us. We'd rather have an honest "we don't know" than manufacture a trustworthy-looking answer. Then we caught an even simpler problem Two minutes after deployment, we tested the API with curl . We submitted: via: "webmcp-tool" The server accepted it. There was no WebMCP page involved at all. So our first records were wrong. act-0001 and act-0002 are therefore false claims of provenance. act-0003 documents the mistake. We didn't delete them. That's the point of the experiment. An append-only provenance system should preserve the moment when we got provenance wrong , too. The missing primitive A real solution would need the browser to provide some execution context that: the page cannot forge; the agent cannot simply manufacture; the application can use to distinguish the origin of an action. WebMCP currently doesn't define such an attestation mechanism. We're not claiming Relay solves that problem. We're showing that the problem exists, what it looks like in a real application, and what information is currently missing. Why this matters Once agents can act on the web, "who clicked the button?" stops being just a UI question. It becomes a systems question. If an agent books something, approves a deployment, changes an account setting, or submits a form, the application may need to know not only what happened, but how it happened and what can actually be proved about the actor . Right now, the web has a gap there. The Unattested Click is our attempt to make that gap impossible to ignore. title: TuneQL
pitch: A PostgreSQL workbench where an AI agent can actually try out optimizations instead of just suggesting them.
about_excerpt: A PostgreSQL workbench where an AI agent can actually try out optimizations instead of just suggesting them. Like 1 Comment Story Updates PostgreSQL optimization workbench Verified optimization Create Workspace WebMCP agent actions Optimization constraints Execution plan Why I built it AI can suggest a SQL fix, but it can’t really prove that the fix actually made things better. I’d still have to open a database tool, check the execution plan, run some benchmarks, and manually make sure the result is still correct. So I built TuneQL to keep all of that in one place. What TuneQL does TuneQL is basically a PostgreSQL query optimization workbench that runs in the browser using PGlite. You can inspect the schema, run queries, check EXPLAIN ANALYZE , save a benchmark as a baseline, then change the query or indexes and compare the new version with the old one. It shows what changed, how much faster or slower it got, whether the constraints still pass, and if both queries return the same result. WebMCP The same workspace can also be used by an agent through WebMCP. TuneQL gives the agent tools to read schemas and indexes, explain and benchmark queries, create indexes, change SQL, save baselines, and compare the results. And whatever the agent does also shows up in the UI, so you can actually follow what it’s doing and continue from the same state yourself. How I built it TuneQL uses Next.js, React, TypeScript, PGlite, Zustand, and IndexedDB. PostgreSQL runs inside a browser worker, and the workspace data stays on your device. The UI and all 20 WebMCP tools go through the same command layer, so things like query validation, constraints, benchmarks, activity history, and revision checks behave the same in both places. Challenges and learning One of the harder parts was keeping the PGlite worker, saved workspace, UI, and agent actions all in sync. I also realised pretty quickly that you can’t judge an optimization from just one timing. So TuneQL does a few warm-up runs, runs the benchmark multiple times, and checks the full result instead of just comparing the few rows shown in the preview. title: CircuitCanvas
pitch: CircuitCanvas: an AI-ready ESP32 circuit workspace where people and browser agents build, validate, code, simulate, and explain circuits together through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: CircuitCanvas: an AI-ready ESP32 circuit workspace where people and browser agents build, validate, code, simulate, and explain circuits together through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Code view Design view 3D view Inspiration CircuitCanvas was inspired by the gap between how people understand electronics and how browser agents interact with software. A circuit is more than a visual arrangement of boxes and wires. It has exact components, pins, electrical paths, firmware bindings, and safety constraints. An agent that only sees pixels can connect the wrong GPIO, miss a resistor, or lose synchronization between the schematic and the code. We wanted to build a workspace where people and AI agents could genuinely collaborate. Our goal was to enable an agent to understand what each component and connection means, make safe changes, explain its reasoning, and work alongside the user in the same project. What We Built CircuitCanvas is an agent-native ESP32 circuit designer with: An exact-pin React Flow schematic editor. A physical 3D view with components, pin anchors, wires, labels, and animated current flow. An Arduino-style firmware editor with two-way synchronization between code and circuit connections. Deterministic validation for beginner mistakes such as missing resistors, invalid GPIOs, reversed LEDs, and missing ground paths. Firmware-aware visual simulation for supported digitalRead() and digitalWrite() patterns. Potentiometer-controlled LED brightness. Undo and redo, project saving, loading, exporting, and local persistence. 29 WebMCP tools that allow browser agents to inspect, build, modify, validate, simulate, explain, and export circuits. The central architectural decision was to maintain one canonical CircuitProject. The schematic, 3D scene, firmware, validator, simulator, history, persistence, and WebMCP responses are all projections of that shared state. How We Built It We built the application with Next.js, React, TypeScript, Zustand, Zod, React Flow, React Three Fiber, Monaco Editor, and WebMCP. Human actions and agent actions both pass through the same typed domain command layer. This ensures that connecting a pin through WebMCP has the same validation, synchronization, persistence, and undo behavior as connecting it manually in the schematic. WebMCP exposes structured tools such as: get_circuit_summary get_available_pins add_component connect_components update_firmware validate_circuit run_simulation set_simulation_input set_potentiometer_wiper save_project export_project This allows an agent to inspect the circuit before acting instead of guessing from screen coordinates. What We Learned We learned that agent-native interfaces need more than tool registration. The underlying application state must be structured, stable, and safe enough for an agent to use. We also learned the importance of: Exposing exact IDs instead of relying on labels or visual positions. Centralizing component and pin definitions. Keeping validation deterministic for safety-sensitive feedback. Synchronizing firmware and circuit changes as one undoable operation. Making agent actions visible through activity history. Designing tools around meaningful user tasks instead of arbitrary internal functions. Challenges The biggest challenge was keeping multiple representations synchronized. A single GPIO change can affect the schematic wire, 3D endpoint, firmware binding, validation result, simulator output, and undo history. Solving this required treating the canonical project model as the only source of truth. Another challenge was creating useful firmware simulation without pretending to be a full electrical simulator. CircuitCanvas intentionally supports a small, transparent Arduino-style subset instead of making unsupported claims about arbitrary C++ execution. We also had to handle the differences between human and agent interaction. Humans can select a line visually, drag a component, adjust a potentiometer, or press Delete. WebMCP needed equivalent structured operations so agents could perform those same actions reliably. Result CircuitCanvas demonstrates a practical way for people and browser agents to work together on electronics. The agent can understand the circuit structurally, make validated changes, operate the simulation, explain what it changed, and leave the user with a synchronized visual, physical, and firmware representation of the project. title: AI Boardroom
pitch: One browser AI. Six specialist perspectives. You decide.
about_excerpt: One browser AI. Six specialist perspectives. You decide. Like Comment Story Updates One COO and 6 Ai Assistant Agents Inspiration Founders often need to make consequential decisions with incomplete evidence, changing constraints and too many disconnected conversations. AI Boardroom puts a founder and a browser assistant in one shared decision room where specialist perspectives, evidence and trade-offs remain visible. What it does AI Boardroom gives one browser AI six specialist perspectives: Product, Evidence, Commercial, Operations, Technology and Chair. WebMCP lets the assistant read the live brief, request named roles, post evidence-linked contributions, respond when constraints change, and retrieve the exact decision record. The central interaction is deliberately human-controlled. A fictional launch budget changes from R20,000 to R8,000; the previous recommendation becomes stale, the assistant reads the new revision, and a new recommendation can be prepared without rewriting the earlier record. The founder reviews alternatives and reservations, then approves, rejects or requests revision in the visible page form. This is stateful collaboration rather than a detached chatbot transcript. The app does not run six independent AI workers or call a model API. One browser assistant adopts the roles and the human retains the final decision. How we built it The app is built with the OpenAI Sites React and TypeScript scaffold, Vinext and D1. Native document.modelContext.registerTool exposes seven WebMCP tools: start_session, get_boardroom_context, update_agenda, request_perspective, add_contribution, prepare_recommendation and get_decision_record. UI actions and WebMCP tools share the same API and persistence logic. Mutation inputs use expectedRevision for optimistic concurrency and operationId for safe retries. Evidence is stored with the relevant contribution and rendered as untrusted text. The visible review channel is a workflow boundary, not proof of human identity. Challenges The design challenge was making an AI council useful without pretending that six hidden agents or automatic consensus exist. We made the roles explicit, preserved disagreement, invalidated recommendations when the brief changed, and kept approval out of the WebMCP tool surface. A second challenge was handling uncertain browser or network outcomes without duplicating or overwriting decisions. What we learned WebMCP is most valuable when the agent can operate on the same visible, stateful interface as the human. Structured tools make the collaboration legible, while revision checks, evidence snapshots and a human review stop make the limits legible too. What's next Production use would require stronger identity and access controls, consent design, privacy and retention rules, abuse and rate-limit controls, independent security review, and integrations governed by explicit human approval. Disclosure All briefs, budgets, evidence and decisions in this project are fictional. The app does not make purchases, send messages, or change external systems. Browser-generated council text is created at runtime and is not preseeded consensus. title: Deckhand
pitch: A slide editor agents can actually operate—where human edits and agent actions share one live, editable canvas.
about_excerpt: A slide editor agents can actually operate—where human edits and agent actions share one live, editable canvas. Like Comment Story Updates Direct human edits become structured context an agent can propagate. Live 16:9 canvas shared by people and browser agents. Import a PowerPoint template locally and preserve its visual system. Typed WebMCP tools expose semantic slide operations, not brittle clicks. Inspiration AI slide generators are useful for first drafts, but the collaboration often ends as soon as a person starts refining the result. Move a title, shorten a paragraph, or decide that one chart should dominate the page, and the AI no longer understands the live artifact. The familiar workflow becomes: generate with AI, then rebuild by hand. Deckhand starts from a different premise: the canvas itself should be the collaboration interface . What it does Deckhand is a local-first presentation editor with two native interfaces over one live artifact: People work on a visual 16:9 canvas: select, multi-select, drag, resize, edit text, style, reorder, present, undo, and export. Browser agents work through typed WebMCP operations against the exact same slides, selection, design grammar, edit history, and browser session. The workflow works with or without a user-owned template. Deckhand can start from eleven purpose-built layout recipes and four art directions, or open a .pptx / .potx and extract its theme, palette, fonts, masters, layouts, and supported editable objects locally in the browser. The key interaction is “show, don’t prompt.” A person can directly change a title’s position, size, or color. Deckhand records that action as semantic edit deltas—not just pixels—and exposes those recent human edits to the browser agent. The agent can then apply the same intent to matching roles elsewhere without making the person describe every visual decision in prose. Why WebMCP is essential A presentation editor has a large, fast-changing state space: slides, objects, roles, geometry, style, relationships, selection, imported design rules, and reversible history. Screenshot-and-click automation repeatedly guesses both the target and the intent. A conventional backend MCP server would duplicate browser-local state and lose the immediate connection to the canvas the person is judging. WebMCP lets Deckhand expose domain meaning exactly where the state already lives: in the open page. Deckhand registers eight baseline tools: inspect_project reads the smallest useful slice of the deck, current slide, selection, design system, or recent human edits. plan_deck validates a narrative and layout mapping without mutating the canvas. compose_deck materializes an approved plan as one visible, undoable transaction. revise_slide recomposes one slide from its communication goal. edit_slide performs precise changes against inspected element IDs. manage_deck handles focus, rename, duplicate, reorder, and delete operations. validate_deck checks narrative structure and measures the real rendered canvas. undo_last_change provides an explicit recovery path. After a direct human edit, a contextual propagate_human_edits tool appears only when it is relevant. Read-only tools declare readOnlyHint; deck content is marked with untrustedContentHint; schemas are constrained; mutations are atomic; and errors explain how the agent can recover. A better human + agent experience Deckhand separates reasoning from mutation. An agent first inspects the project, creates a read-only plan, composes it in one transaction, and validates the rendered result. The person sees every change on the canvas, can continue editing with the mouse and keyboard, and can undo an entire agent batch in one step. This makes the agent useful beyond generation. It can keep collaborating through the messy middle: repair the weakest slide, preserve an imported brand system, align selected objects, propagate a deliberate human edit, validate the result, and recover when a revision is worse. How I built it Deckhand is written in TypeScript and React on Vinext and deployed as a Cloudflare Worker. Its serializable scene graph stores semantic roles, geometry, styles, provenance, design tokens, selection, and history. The PowerPoint pipeline safely reads OOXML packages in the browser, follows theme → master → layout → slide inheritance, extracts supported raster assets, and reports fidelity limitations without uploading the source file. The design engine maps semantic slide briefs to varied layout recipes. The quality gate combines deterministic narrative checks with measurements from the actual rendered DOM. WebMCP tools are registered against document.modelContext and call the same domain operations used by the visual editor. There is no second copy of the presentation state and no separate MCP service to configure. Challenges The hardest problem was not exposing many low-level commands. It was choosing an agent surface that stays compact while still producing complete presentations. The plan/compose split keeps reasoning inspectable and prevents half-finished decks. Semantic revision handles broad design intent; precise editing remains an escape hatch only after inspection. PowerPoint fidelity was another challenge. A template is not just colors and fonts—it is inheritance, transforms, grouped geometry, placeholder rules, and sometimes unsupported objects. Deckhand preserves what it can edit safely, keeps provenance for future agent decisions, and surfaces honest warnings when exact fidelity is not possible. Accomplishments and learning I am most proud that WebMCP is not a chat box attached to an editor. It changes the product architecture: visual manipulation and semantic tool calls are two interfaces to one live, reversible artifact. Building Deckhand also changed how I think about agent accessibility. A good agent interface needs more than valid schemas. It needs progressive disclosure, explicit read/write boundaries, contextual tools, recovery paths, and feedback that remains legible to the person watching. What’s next Next steps include richer chart and SmartArt conversion, collaborative cloud persistence, more render-aware layout repair, and direct Google Slides interoperability. The broader pattern extends beyond slides to design, video, CAD, and any visual editor where people judge by sight while agents need meaning. title: Ops Co-pilot
pitch: An AI-friendly infra dashboard where agents check real service health and act but every risky action needs a human's explicit approval before it runs.
about_excerpt: An AI-friendly infra dashboard where agents check real service health and act but every risky action needs a human's explicit approval before it runs. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration WebMCP lets websites expose structured tools directly to AI agents but most demos of "agent + web app" either lock the agent out of anything meaningful, or hand over full control and hope for the best. Neither felt like the real future. The real question was: what does it look like when an agent can genuinely operate something consequential real infrastructure without a person having to babysit every click, but also without blindly trusting the agent's judgment on anything that could break production? That tension is where Ops Co-pilot came from. What it does Ops Co-pilot is a dashboard that exposes real infrastructure service health, alerts, and operational actions as WebMCP tools an AI agent can call directly. Read-only and low-risk tools (checking health, listing alerts, acknowledging them, adding incident notes) execute immediately. High-risk actions (restarting or scaling a service) never execute on the agent's say-so alone: the backend halts the action, shows a human a clear on-screen confirmation dialog describing exactly what's about to happen and why, and only proceeds via a real Render API call against a real deployed service after explicit human approval, using a single-use, cryptographically bound confirmation token. How we built it Go backend (service registry, alert engine, guardrail/token system, audit log) with a React/TypeScript frontend that registers all 7 tools via document.modelContext.registerTool. Instead of monitoring simulated services, we wired it to a real, separately-deployed production app (a Social Publishing MCP server), adding real /readyz, /metrics, and /version observability endpoints to that app so Ops Co-pilot has genuinely live data real uptime, real DB/Redis connection status, real error counts to work with. High-risk actions call Render's actual restart API, gated behind a token that's single-use, expiring, and bound to the exact service and action it was issued for. Challenges we ran into The biggest challenge wasn't writing the tools it was making sure "it works" actually meant it works. Early on, a self-reported "all tests passed" summary turned out to gloss over real gaps: commit history had been silently rewritten to look like proper development discipline, and a rate-limiting test's own summary numbers didn't match its own raw logs. We caught both by re-deriving the numbers by hand instead of trusting the summary. Later, live end-to-end testing (calling our own WebMCP tools directly through Chrome's navigator.modelContextTesting API) surfaced a genuinely serious bug: restart_service was returning "success" without the real Render API call actually succeeding confirmed by checking Render's own Events log and finding no matching restart event. We also found a live production issue this way: our own observability endpoints revealed Redis was actually unreachable on the real monitored service, which we fixed before it affected real users. Accomplishments that we're proud of Every claim in this project is backed by something we personally verified against a live system not a unit test result taken at face value. We caught a false-success bug in the exact action that matters most (the one with real infrastructure consequences) before it ever reached a demo, by insisting on checking Render's own event log instead of trusting our own backend's response. The confirmation-guardrail flow token generation, single-use enforcement, replay rejection, cross-service scope binding held up under adversarial testing (forged tokens, expired tokens, replay attempts, concurrent race conditions) with real HTTP evidence for every case. What we learned An agent (or an AI coding assistant) reporting success is not the same as success. The most valuable thing in this build wasn't a feature it was the habit of independently re-verifying claims against ground truth (Render's own dashboard, raw HTTP responses, actual git history) instead of accepting a summary. That same discipline is exactly what Ops Co-pilot enforces structurally for AI agents operating on real infrastructure: a claim of "done" isn't enough, a human checks before anything consequential actually happens. What's next for Ops Co-pilot Move authentication from a single shared API-key gate to real per-user sessions with role-based permissions, support monitoring multiple real services instead of one, and add richer remediation tools (log inspection, rollback to a previous deploy) all still behind the same human-confirmation guardrail for anything irreversible. title: FlowLens
pitch: Workflow intelligence, in focus
about_excerpt: Workflow intelligence, in focus Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration FlowLens was built for the WebMCP hackathon to solve a core problem in automation debugging: most debuggers require humans to manually translate visual context back into text. We wanted to turn human focus into a typed, temporary tool surface where selecting a failed execution path automatically bounds the evidence an agent can inspect, enabling precise diagnosis and safe repairs without copying node IDs, payloads, or timestamps. What it does FlowLens is a deterministic workflow flight recorder that allows operations specialists to: Run automation workflows and visualize execution traces on an interactive canvas Select exact failed execution paths (normalization and condition steps) Expose selection-bound WebMCP tools that capture immutable run, step, node, selection, and workflow versions Let browser agents inspect bounded evidence and propose the smallest safe repair Preview patches with visible diffs before any mutation occurs Apply approved patches with single-use tokens, rerun fixtures, and prove results with before-and-after comparisons Maintain a complete audit trail with undo capability The hero defect demonstrates a subtle bug: normalization emits customer.segment while the condition reads customer.tier , causing VIP customers to reach the standard queue without throwing errors. How we built it FlowLens is a static React application built with: React + TypeScript for type-safe component architecture @xyflow/react for the interactive workflow canvas with finite node types Vite for fast development and production builds Zod for strict JSON Schema validation Lucide React for consistent iconography @polar-sh/checkout for embedded Pro feature paywall The architecture follows a clean domain-driven design: Domain layer ( src/domain/ ) contains workflow types, validation, simulation, patches, and redaction Application layer ( src/app/ ) manages state through a typed reducer with command facade Feature layer ( src/features/ ) provides canvas, header, panel, paywall, and sidebar components WebMCP adapter ( src/webmcp/ ) handles dynamic tool registration with AbortController cleanup The deterministic simulator traverses directed graphs producing bounded trace steps without real side effects. The repair engine accepts only restricted operations (like replace_condition_field ) with preview, approval tokens, version guards, and reversible history. Challenges we ran into WebMCP API evolution : The specification was still evolving, requiring feature detection for both document.modelContext and optional toolchange events independently Selection lifecycle complexity : Managing selection-bound tools that need to abort on workflow edits, selection changes, or component unmounts required careful AbortController coordination Security boundaries : Implementing bounded outputs, secret-like field redaction, version guards, and single-use approval tokens while maintaining usability Deterministic simulation : Building a simulator that produces realistic traces without actual side effects, queues, or network operations Paywall integration : Balancing a local admin bypass for demo purposes with production-grade Polar checkout that requires trusted backend authentication Accomplishments that we're proud of Complete WebMCP integration : Successfully implemented 16 tools (10 base, 4 selection-bound, 1 approval, 1 conditional undo) following Chrome security guidance Deterministic testing : 19/19 Vitest unit tests and 2/2 Playwright E2E tests passing, including real in-app WebMCP calls Apple-inspired UI : Dark graphite interface with glassy chrome, crisp hierarchy, restrained color, and reduced-motion support Safe mutation model : Non-mutating preview, visible diffs, human approval, single-use tokens, and reversible history Production-ready build : TypeScript strict mode passing, static bundle deployable to Vercel or any static host Comprehensive documentation : Architecture, security model, WebMCP inventory, and eval corpus all documented What we learned WebMCP patterns : The imperative API requires careful lifecycle management—tools must register dynamically, capture closure state, and clean up with AbortController Selection as context : Turning visual selection into typed API boundaries is more powerful than traditional copy-paste debugging Deterministic simulation : A bounded simulator can provide sufficient evidence for diagnosis without requiring real integrations Security by design : Version guards, bounded outputs, and single-use tokens prevent many classes of attacks while maintaining usability Static architecture : A well-designed static app can deliver complex functionality without backend dependencies What's next for FlowLens Additional workflow types : Expand beyond the CRM escalation hero flow to support more automation patterns Richer patch DSL : Add more safe operations beyond replace_condition_field while maintaining boundedness Authentication backend : Implement trusted server authentication with Polar webhook verification for production entitlements Multiplayer collaboration : Enable shared workspaces with real-time collaboration on workflow title: Sigma Studio | AI driven Editor
pitch: Teaching materials meant TeX for math, Word for layout, PowerPoint for figures, and unusable AI. Sigma Studio puts it all on one page that's intuitive to edit, and AI edits it with you. Open source.
about_excerpt: Teaching materials meant TeX for math, Word for layout, PowerPoint for figures, and unusable AI. Sigma Studio puts it all on one page that's intuitive to edit, and AI edits it with you. Open source. Like Comment Story Updates math test template amde by this app rich 3d math editor rich 3d math editor Inspiration Making educational materials has long been a fight against fragmented tools. TeX for equations, Word or Notion for layout, PowerPoint for diagrams, and an AI trapped inside a chat window. On top of that, there are vested commercial interests baked into the software used in education. When a teacher makes a single worksheet, they type \( \int_0^1 x^2\,dx = \frac{1}{3} \) in TeX, draw a parabola in a different program and paste it in as a screenshot, and every time a single number changes, they have to redo everything from scratch. Generative AI was supposed to help, but all it does is turn into an endless cycle of copy-pasting from a chat UI. Teaching materials are not just text. They are publication-quality "page space" where paragraphs, TeX equations, geometric figures, and two-column problem layouts must line up without a millimeter of drift. Until the day the picture in someone's head can be beamed straight into an AI, there's no way for an AI to nail 100% of what a human is picturing on the first try. That's why we designed Sigma Studio around a simple, honest principle of collaboration: "Let AI handle the tedious 90% of the heavy lifting, and let the human quickly polish the crucial final 10% by hand, guided by intuition." What it does Sigma Studio is an open-source, agent-native document editor where an entire piece of teaching material lives on a single responsive page. Write like Word or Notion : paragraphs, headings, auto-numbered problems, and a two-column layout that reflows in real time as you type. Typeset beautifully at TeX quality : TeX-quality equations rendered via KaTeX, visually editable. We obsessed over baseline alignment, line spacing, and margins to achieve the precise typesetting that educational materials demand. Draw intuitively like PowerPoint (fully parametric) : shapes, guide lines, angle arcs, labels, and 2D/3D graphs sit on an overlay canvas directly above the text. Nothing is ever rasterized into an image — everything remains a vector you can re-edit at any time. Toggle "problems only" / "answers only" from a single source document : instantly switch one document between a "problems only" view/printout for class or exams and an "answers only" view/printout for self-grading and explanation. A "90% + 10%" collaborative workflow with AI : when a teacher says "draw the triangle formed by the intersection points of the parabola and the line in problem 3," the AI solves the equations and coordinates via WebMCP and instantly draws the graph and the three lines (that's the 90%). The teacher just reaches for the mouse and nudges a vertex label "A" that's overlapping something, to make it more legible (that's the 10%) — and it's done. Approval-gated proposals (human-in-the-loop) : the AI never overwrites the document on its own. Its changes are drawn on the canvas as a preview diff (a Draft), which a human can approve or discard with one click. Even after applying, it can be undone in a single step. Pixel-perfect vector PDF export : produces high-quality PDFs that match the editor screen down to the pixel. It is provided completely free of charge as MIT-licensed open source. How we built it Built with Next.js, React, and TypeScript. The body text uses Tiptap/ProseMirror, equations use MathLive and KaTeX, and diagrams are built on a custom overlay canvas plus Three.js for 3D. Exposing semantic document operations via WebMCP At the core of the architecture is exposing operations on the editor's own document model (SigmaDoc) to AI as first-class tools via WebMCP ( document.modelContext.registerTool ). Inside ChatGPT's in-app browser or on Chrome, the AI directly executes structured tools such as: insert_body_content , replace_block , move_blocks insert_shape , update_shape , align_shapes insert_graph , update_graph , insert_graph3d begin_visual_edit_session , inspect_visual_edit_session , propose_visual_edit_session Instead of fragile DOM scraping or guessing at screen coordinates, the AI reads a semantic document tree and injects parametric vector objects directly into the runtime. Challenges we ran into Shape anchors that follow the flow of text : the hardest engineering challenge was making diagrams follow the body text as it wraps and reflows. The instant a teacher hits Enter in the body text, a shape placed with absolute coordinates gets left behind. We built an anchor-binding mechanism that ties each shape to a specific body block ID with a relative offset, so shapes naturally follow along even as text grows, shrinks, or moves across columns. Two-column layouts and dynamic pagination : serious teaching materials require two-column layouts. We built a custom pagination engine from scratch that precisely measures actual rendered DOM heights so that paragraphs, equations, and anchored shapes break cleanly across page boundaries instead of being cut off mid-element. Relentless attention to precise typesetting : to reproduce genuine print-grade typesetting on the web DOM, we tuned equation baselines, Japanese line spacing, problem-number indentation, and line weights down to the millimeter to achieve layout quality comparable to a professionally published textbook. Resolving conflicts between simultaneous human and AI edits : while the AI is busy computing a complex geometric figure, the teacher keeps typing on the keyboard. We validate block IDs and version hashes so that a stale AI proposal for a spot the human has since touched is safely rejected and rebased, preventing accidental overwrites of what was just typed. A PDF pipeline with zero print drift : rather than maintaining a separate print engine, we unified everything around slicing the editor's actual rendered DOM page-by-page via Chromium and stitching the pages together with pdf-lib, achieving a 100% match between what's on screen and what comes out on paper. Accomplishments that we're proud of An intuitive feel for polishing that final 10% : we obsessed over drag handles, snapping, bounding boxes, and block-editor interactions so that refining an AI-generated first draft with the mouse feels as natural and effortless as sketching with a pencil and eraser on paper. Vector persistence (no images) : even when importing TeX or legacy materials, everything lives on as editable vector shapes and coordinate axes rather than static images. Keeping shapes editable in place is essential for teaching materials. A complete, self-contained OSS web app : because everything needed to create teaching materials lives in this one open-source web app, clients can freely modify and use the application with confidence — there is no vendor lock-in to worry about. What we learned Giving AI an "MCP" to manipulate a structured document alongside a human turned out to be a challenge on an entirely different level. Since AI cannot read a human's mind, expecting it to produce something perfect in a single shot is an illusion. We learned that true human-AI collaboration isn't about getting a complex prompt to deliver 100% — it's about providing instant undo, a visual preview, and extremely smooth direct manipulation , so that a human can intuitively carry the AI's 90%-finished foundation the rest of the way to the goal. What's next for Sigma Studio Extending to a learning workspace for students : beyond teachers authoring materials, evolving toward a learning environment where students can converse with AI and visually experiment with geometric proofs or calculus graphs through trial and error. Multi-agent collaborative authoring : building an environment where multiple specialized WebMCP agents — one for equation verification, one for geometric drawing, one for curriculum consistency, and more — can simultaneously propose changes on the same canvas. Google Docs-style real-time collaboration , enabling: students and teachers to learn together in the same document teachers to co-author materials together Built With claude css electron esbuild firebase i18next jszip katex mathlive model-context-protocol next.js node.js openai-codex pdf-lib playwright prosemirror react three.js tiptap typescript vitest webmcp zod zustand Try it out github.com sigma-studio-webmcp-demo.choco954303.chatgpt.site Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by ATSUSHI KIMURA Like Share this project: Updates ATSUSHI KIMURA started this project — Sep 04, 2026 01:13 AM EDT

title: PowerCanvas
pitch: Build, review, and improve single-line diagrams with AI agents.
about_excerpt: Build, review, and improve single-line diagrams with AI agents. Like Comment Story Updates What inspired me I work in the electrification , so I spend a suspicious amount of time looking at electrical single-line diagrams and much more. They are basically the map of an electrical system: sources, buses, breakers, cables, loads, and how everything is connected. Engineers use them across buildings, factories, data centers, renewables, EV charging and industrial systems for design, protection, sizing, validation and documentation. So this is not exactly a tiny niche. Electrification is growing, electrical systems are getting more complex, and somebody still has to design all of this stuff. The software is already very capable. It can calculate complex electrical systems and then make you click through twelve property panels because one cable parameter is wrong. That is what made me build PowerCanvas I wanted to explore a simple idea: What if professional engineering software was designed for both an engineer and an AI agent to operate the same workspace? Single-line diagrams were the perfect place to start because I know the problem from my own industry, and underneath the visual diagram there is a lot of structured engineering data an agent can actually work with. About tool and WebMCP usage PowerCanvas is a prototype for creating and reviewing electrical single-line diagrams. I can build a system using sources, buses, circuit breakers, cables and loads. This tool validates the design and detects engineering issues such as missing parameters, cable sizing problems and protection warnings. It's already a huge improvement to current tools on the market. Normally, I would fix those issues manually, one component at a time. With WebMCP , i can give that repetitive work to an AI agent. The agent can inspect the project, understand the warnings, prepare fixes and create a staged change set directly inside PowerCanvas. The workflow is: BUILD -> REVIEW -> FIX OPTIONS -> CHANGE SET -> APPROVAL -> REVALIDATION -> REPORT I still approve important changes before they are applied. Because “the AI seemed confident” is not a protection philosophy. Right? Right. Building story I built PowerCanvas with React, TypeScript and React Flow The diagram is not just pixels. Components have structured parameters, connections, engineering constraints and validation results. I keep the actual engineering calculations deterministic. The agent can reason about the problem and decide which actions to take, but it does not get to improvise electrical rules. WebMCP exposes meaningful PowerCanvas capabilities directly to the agent. So instead of telling it to click the third button, open a panel and scroll to a field, the agent.. can work with concepts such as cables, breakers, validation issues and design changes. Most importantly, the agent operates the same project I see on screen . No separate AI workspace. No copying values into a chatbot (brr) + 10x more time. No coordinate-based automation held together by prayer. Challenges I faced during ideation & dev The biggest challenge was deciding what an agent should actually be allowed to do inside such professional/expert software. I could expose every button and input field. Technically valid. Also a terrible API. I had to design tools around user intent and engineering operations instead of individual clicks. The other challenge was control and traceability. An agent silently modifying an engineering project looks impressive until someone asks why Cable 7 suddenly became 35 mm² So I built staged changes, human approval, activity history and revalidation directly into the workflow. Accomplishments that im proud of I am most proud that WebMCP is not just attached to PowerCanvas as a demo feature. It actually changes how the application can be used. The agent does not sit next to the software explaining what I should click. It can inspect the project and perform real actions inside the engineering workspace. At the same time, PowerCanvas is still completely usable by a human. I can work manually, hand repetitive work to the agent when it makes sense, review what it did and continue from there. Same workspace. Two operators. And somehow no glowing AI chatbot in the bottom-right corner. A small victory. Something unique. Lessons learned The most interesting thing about WebMCP is not giving an agent a faster mouse. It is exposing the meaning already inside the application PowerCanvas knows what a cable is, what a breaker is, how components are connected and which validation issues exist. The agent should not have to reverse-engineer all of that from screenshots. I also learned that human approval is not a limitation of agentic software. For engineering software, I think it is part of good agentic UX. The agent handles repetitive work. I keep the engineering decisions. That is a much more useful relationship than pretending the goal is to remove the engineer completely. What's next for Power_Canvas Next I would expand PowerCanvas with more engineering rules, larger electrical systems, richer constraints and integrations with real calculation engines and product data. But the idea is bigger than single-line diagrams. The same interaction model could work in CAD, HVAC, solar design, industrial automation, building engineering and other complex professional tools. I see demand, potentiall. PowerCanvas is the example. The bigger idea is professional electrification software where the human and the AI agent can actually work in the same workspace together. Not another chat window next to the real tool. The real tool. title: Runtime Truth
pitch: Don’t trust the tool response. Verify the state. Runtime Truth detects when a WebMCP action reports success but the authoritative application state says otherwise.
about_excerpt:
Don’t trust the tool response. Verify the state. Runtime Truth detects when a WebMCP action reports success but the authoritative application state says otherwise.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 As AI agents move from reading websites to taking real actions — booking, buying, submitting forms, and changing application state — a new reliability question appears: 

 How do we know the action actually happened? 

 A tool can return SUCCESS , but the authoritative application state may tell a different story. 

 Runtime Truth explores that gap. 

 What it does 

 Runtime Truth exposes a WebMCP tool called reserve_table . 

 In the demo, an agent requests a reservation for two people at 7 PM. 

 The tool reports: 

 SUCCESS — Reservation ID: R-1042 

 But the reservation is deliberately not persisted. 

 Runtime Truth then independently checks the authoritative application state. 

 It finds: 

 RESERVATION NOT FOUND 

 and flags: 

 DIVERGENCE DETECTED 

 The core principle is simple: 

 Don’t trust the tool response. Verify the state. 

 How I built it 

 The project uses WebMCP's imperative API to register a structured website tool that agents can discover and execute. 

 The execution flow is: 

 
 The WebMCP tool performs the requested action. 
 The application receives a declared result. 
 Runtime Truth independently queries the authoritative post-action state. 
 The declared result and observed state are compared. 
 A mismatch is surfaced as execution-state divergence. 
 

 The demo uses deterministic fault injection so the failure can be reproduced consistently. 

 The application is built with Python, Flask, JavaScript, and WebMCP, and deployed on Render. 

 Challenges 

 The most important challenge was separating tool execution from verification . 

 If verification simply trusts the same response that declares success, it cannot detect false-success states. 

 I also had to test WebMCP registration, discovery, and execution independently. The final implementation was verified using Chrome's WebMCP testing support: 

 
 tool registration 
 tool discovery 
 WebMCP tool execution 
 independent post-action state verification 
 

 What I learned 

 A successful tool response is a claim about execution, not necessarily proof of the resulting state. 

 As WebMCP makes websites increasingly agent-native, verification may become especially important for consequential actions such as purchases, reservations, submissions, and workflow changes. 

 I also came across Greg Isenberg's discussion of an "agent mystery shopper" concept for testing whether agents can actually complete important website journeys. 

 Runtime Truth approaches a narrower technical version of that problem: 

 When a tool declares success, did the expected state transition actually occur? 

 I see that discussion as an independent signal that completion verification is becoming relevant as agents perform more real-world actions on the web. 

 What's next 

 Runtime Truth is intentionally small. 

 The next step would be testing the same verification pattern across additional state-changing actions such as purchases, submissions, and asynchronous workflows. 

 For this challenge, the goal is narrower: 

 demonstrate clearly that tool success and state truth are not always the same thing.
