title: DentalSculptor WebMCP
pitch: An app that enables dental educators to generate 3D of tooth and share them, from library of images or web images by chatting inside ChatGPT
about_excerpt: An app that enables dental educators to generate 3D of tooth and share them, from library of images or web images by chatting inside ChatGPT Like 1 Comment Story Updates DentalSculptor — WebMCP Challenge project story Inspiration Dental educators often need custom 3D examples: a fractured cusp for one seminar, an occlusal lesion for another, or a preparation that matches a particular learning objective. Creating those assets usually means learning specialist modelling software, waiting for technical support, or settling for a generic model that does not fit the lesson. DentalSculptor began as doctoral research into educator agency and human–AI co-creation in dental education. The central question was not simply, “Can AI generate a tooth?” It was, “Can an educator remain the author while AI handles the technical complexity?” WebMCP made a new answer possible. Instead of asking an agent to guess its way through buttons, loading states, and a spatial 3D editor, DentalSculptor gives the agent a precise vocabulary for the real workflow. The agent can coordinate; the educator can keep ownership of anatomy, pedagogy, approval, and release. What it does DentalSculptor turns a dental image into an editable 3D teaching case in one visible browser workspace. An educator and an agent can work together to: inspect the current app, authentication, generation, and viewer state; choose a curated tooth image or attach an educator-provided image; start 3D generation and wait until the model is actually visible; continue into a guided clinical case or the Free Editor; synchronize the correct edit preset and mark the intended anatomy; generate a 2D review preview and a reversible 3D variant; accept or reject the revision; export for supported teaching/simulation targets or publish with explicit privacy approval. The result is not an agent-only back channel. Every tool acts on the same project, React state, 3D scene, revision history, and approval controls the educator sees. Why WebMCP is essential Without WebMCP, an agent has to infer whether generation finished, whether a model is visible, which clinical preset is compatible, whether a mask exists, or whether the educator approved the result. Coordinate-based browser automation is especially fragile in a resizable 3D viewport. With WebMCP: tool schemas replace screen-coordinate guessing; live readiness state prevents premature actions; page-scoped discovery reveals only actions relevant to the current workspace; structured results tell the agent what happened and what remains; human approval boundaries are encoded into the workflow rather than left to prompting. This improves speed and reliability without making the clinical workflow less accountable. The human–agent partnership The agent is good at orchestration: inspecting state, explaining prerequisites, selecting a compatible workflow, keeping a multi-stage process on track, and preparing reuse. The educator is responsible for judgment: selecting source material, defining clinical intent, marking the exact anatomy, approving previews, accepting revisions, confirming privacy, and authorizing publication or download. That division is the project’s core contribution. WebMCP does not remove the person from the creative loop; it gives them a more capable collaborator. How we built it The production application uses Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, Three.js, React Three Fiber, Supabase Auth/PostgreSQL/Storage, Prisma, Modal GPU services, and Vercel. The WebMCP adapter is isolated in dentalsculptor-app/src/components/webmcp/ . Google Chrome Labs' lifecycle hook registers tools through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) and unregisters them when their React surface disappears. The tools are organized by page: global app/authentication/navigation tools; image-to-3D generation tools; clinical case and editor tools; confirmed publishing tools in the visible share dialog; public community inspection and reuse tools. Every mutating tool has a constrained JSON Schema. Read-only tools advertise readOnlyHint . Model-dependent tools wait for the viewer—not merely a model URL—to report that geometry is visible. Publishing requires both explicit release approval and confirmation that the model contains no identifiable patient information. Challenges we faced Making 3D readiness truthful A generation API can return a URL before an embedded browser has downloaded, parsed, framed, and rendered the model. We added viewer-level readiness, bounded same-origin asset loading, actionable proxy errors, and a load watchdog. WebMCP reports modelReady only after the viewer confirms the model is visible. Keeping tools synchronized with a changing interface The landing page, editor, share dialog, and community page expose different capabilities. Page-scoped React registration lets the available tool set follow the visible UI and unregister cleanly during navigation. Preserving educator authority The fastest implementation would have let the agent mark anatomy, approve an edit, and publish in one opaque step. We deliberately separated those moments. The agent can prepare the next action, but spatial targeting, revision decisions, privacy confirmation, and release remain visible and reversible. Working with an emerging standard WebMCP is still evolving. We kept the browser adapter isolated, documented the imperative API, added a live diagnostics page, and retained a complete non-WebMCP interface as a fallback. Accomplishments 29 non-duplicated, page-scoped WebMCP tools spanning a real 3D authoring workflow. A model-readiness contract based on rendered geometry rather than optimistic API completion. Structured clinical case authoring with reversible human approval. Secure authentication handoff without exposing credentials, cookies, or tokens. Explicit confirmation gates for export, publishing, and patient privacy. A public diagnostic route that reads the browser’s real tool registry. What we learned The most valuable agent tools are not one-to-one copies of buttons. They expose the state transitions and safety boundaries that make a complex application understandable. We also learned that “human in the loop” is strongest when the loop is visible in the product architecture: the educator and agent should share one workspace and one source of truth. What is next We plan to evaluate how educators divide work with agents across different levels of experience, add richer model-semantic targeting, and contribute practical feedback from spatial authoring to the emerging WebMCP standard. title: jsonloupe
pitch: The JSON surface humans and agents share: via WebMCP, an agent loads, queries, and points at the exact document you're looking at — one lossless viewer, two interfaces, no copy-paste loop.
about_excerpt: The JSON surface humans and agents share: via WebMCP, an agent loads, queries, and points at the exact document you're looking at — one lossless viewer, two interfaces, no copy-paste loop. Like Comment Story Updates GIF The whole loop, live: load_doc -> reveal_path flashes the failure -> highlight_matches lights the chip -> clear_highlights hands it back. reveal_path: the agent scrolled the tree to the failing delivery and flashed the row - pointing, not describing. highlight_matches: the tree filtered to the 9 FAILED deliveries via the toolbar's own filter chip - reversible by the user's button. load_doc: this document was opened by an agent, straight into the viewer the human is watching. No download, no paste. Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP jsonloupe is local-first: the entire lossless JSON engine — worker-parsed, int64-exact, comfortable with five-million-element arrays — already runs inside the page. WebMCP tools execute in page context, so the bridge hands agents the real engine, not a proxy to a backend that doesn't exist. There is no server anywhere: the tools, the data, and the human's view live in the same tab. The tool vocabulary was already proven — jsonloupe ships a stdio MCP server with the same bounded verbs (schema → query → refine, capped responses, the document itself never leaves). WebMCP is the transport that puts those verbs where the human is actually looking, and it enables three tools no headless server could ever offer: pushing a document into the human's open viewer, scrolling their tree to a row and flashing it, and filtering their view through the toolbar's own state. How it creates a better user experience It kills the loop every AI-and-JSON workflow lives in: agent produces JSON → human downloads it → opens a separate viewer → finds the problem → pastes back → repeat. With WebMCP, agent output lands directly in the viewer the human already has open ( load_doc ), questions are answered against the on-screen document with exact int64/decimal arithmetic ( run_query , profile , sample , get_schema ), and instead of describing where something is, the agent points — reveal_path scrolls the tree and flashes the row; highlight_matches filters the view to the evidence. The agent's answers stay small and bounded (counts, groups, capped previews), so conversations stay fast and cheap — the document never round-trips through the model. And the human keeps authority over their own view: highlights use the toolbar's real filter state with the count visible in the chip, reversible by the human's own button at any moment. What people and agents can do together that was difficult or impossible before Look at the same document at the same time. Before, "human + agent + JSON" meant two disconnected copies — one in the chat context, one in a viewer — synced by hand. Now the agent's load_doc , reveal_path , and highlight_matches operate on the very pixels the human is watching: the agent investigates and points, the human sees and steers, and every agent action is visible, bounded, and reversible in the human's own UI. It turns "the agent said the problem is in tasks[1847]" into the row flashing on screen. It also makes the collaboration safe to trust: every tool that returns document content is annotated untrustedContentHint , so the calling agent is told — at the protocol level — that a value like "IGNORE ALL PREVIOUS INSTRUCTIONS" inside the data is data. This carries forward jsonloupe's existing prompt-injection hardening work into the WebMCP era. How WebMCP was implemented A feature-detected, lazily-imported bridge ( src/webmcp/ , ~790 lines + 950 test lines) registers eight tools on document.modelContext : run_query , get_schema , profile , sample , load_doc , reveal_path , highlight_matches , clear_highlights . Tools dispatch over the same UI↔worker message protocol the human's own clicks use, so agent and human literally share one engine and one document. Responses are capped, staleness-checked against a document token (a doc swapped mid-tool aborts cleanly), and annotated with readOnlyHint / untrustedContentHint . Query errors return a caret under the fault plus the grammar, so agents self-correct. Where the API is absent the bridge chunk is never fetched and the app is byte-for-byte unchanged (asserted by e2e). Verified by 70 unit tests plus a Playwright end-to-end suite that drives a real WebMCP-enabled Chromium through every tool, and live on jsonloupe.dev under the Chrome origin trial. Prior work vs. new work The viewer, engine, and stdio MCP server predate the submission window. Everything WebMCP — src/webmcp/ , its tests, the wiring, the e2e suite — is new work within the window; see WEBMCP.md and the timestamped commit history (PRs #50, #51). I built jsonloupe itself over the past months — the lossless viewer, the worker engine, and its stdio MCP server. For this challenge I designed and shipped the WebMCP bridge: eight tools on document.modelContext that share one engine and one document with the human, including the three view-moving verbs (load_doc, reveal_path, highlight_matches) that are the heart of the idea. I worked with ChatGPT desktop app as my development agent throughout — implementation, tests, and automated browser verification — while owning the architecture, the product thesis, and every design decision. title: RecipeBridge for CyberChef
pitch: Turn CyberChef into a shared live workspace for building, testing, and refining recipes through WebMCP, while raw data stays private
about_excerpt: Turn CyberChef into a shared live workspace for building, testing, and refining recipes through WebMCP, while raw data stays private Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration CyberChef provides security analysts, developers, and students with 503 browser-based Operations covering encoding, compression, cryptography, parsing, and data analysis. Even when users know the intended result, they may not know which Operations provide it, which arguments those Operations require, or how to arrange multiple Operations. The author of CyberChef issue #2691 reported working with unreadable data whose algorithms and processing order were unknown. Magic returned no useful Recipe, and manually testing dozens of likely algorithms in different orders did not recover the expected result. The author reported that a locally run AI model later identified the algorithms, arguments, and execution order. The issue discussion explained that sending processed data to an external AI service would conflict with CyberChef’s browser-local processing model. The issue was then closed as not planned. With CyberChef continuing to process the data in the browser, RecipeBridge focuses on two cases: locating and configuring relevant Operations among 503 choices when the intended result is known, and determining a possible Operation sequence when the processing chain is unknown. What it does The Agent can search CyberChef’s 503 Operations, inspect argument definitions, read a redacted view of the Recipe state, submit revision-checked Recipe changes, request a Bake, and use bounded Magic analysis to select subsequent actions. WebMCP provides the Agent with Operation metadata, Recipe structure, execution state, and limited analysis signals. Raw Input, raw Output, current Recipe argument values, Register captures, Magic previews, and candidate arguments remain inside the browser page and are excluded from WebMCP results. Every Agent change appears in the existing CyberChef interface. The user can inspect and edit the Recipe, stop WebMCP access, and restore the Recipe state that preceded the Agent’s latest change while that snapshot remains valid. The access audit classifies each Operation according to its behavior and side effects: direct (447): Operations that use CyberChef’s standard in-page processing flow. approval (51): Operations involving network access, signing and key generation, OTPs, rich-content presentation, nondeterministic results, Recipe flow control, or Input-derived arguments. These require one-use user approval. blocked (5): Magic uses a dedicated analysis flow. The other four still involve direct Input changes, remote resources, or SVG rendering risks. excluded (1): An internal validation Operation that is omitted from the product catalog. How I built it RecipeBridge registers six fixed workflow tools through WebMCP: search_operations get_operation_details get_recipe_state apply_recipe_patch bake_recipe inspect_output The fixed tool set controls the amount of context loaded during discovery. Search and detail tools provide CyberChef’s generated Operation metadata on demand, allowing the Agent to load only the names, options, defaults, and argument definitions required for the current task. Recipe arguments continue to use CyberChef’s existing metadata and validation rules. User and Agent changes pass through the same Recipe transaction. Each step has a stable ID, and each Recipe has a revision number. The Agent must provide the expected revision when submitting a change. CyberChef prepares and validates the complete change before updating the Recipe model and visible interface. A stale request fails and leaves the workspace unchanged. Each Bake records the Recipe revision, Input version, execution-options version, Output tab, and bakeId . These identifiers prevent delayed Web Worker or Magic results from replacing Output produced by a newer run. The page stores complete Magic candidate Recipes and their arguments in memory. inspect_output analyzes up to the first 1,000 bytes of the current Output and returns filtered analysis signals, candidate IDs, ranks, and Operation names. When the Agent applies a candidate ID, the page sends the stored Recipe through the standard access checks, validation, approval, and transaction flow. Magic ranking guides subsequent analysis, while the user verifies the result through the visible Output. Tool results are generated through a fixed field allowlist. Magic-derived results are also bound to the current Output tab and bakeId , preventing stale analysis results from being returned. The browser or Agent host can still observe the page and URL, so the project recommends disabling CyberChef’s URL updates before processing sensitive data. Challenges I ran into Exposing a large application through a small tool surface Registering a separate tool for each of hundreds of Operations would increase discovery context and make the interface harder to use. Six workflow tools provide a stable interface, while catalog search and pagination expose CyberChef Operations on demand. Coordinating a workspace shared by a user and an Agent CyberChef already supports manual editing, Auto Bake, multiple tabs, background Magic analysis, and Web Workers. Agent changes also require handling stale revisions, overlapping runs, and delayed results. Stable step IDs, atomic Recipe transactions, fixed Bake target information, and provenance checks give each state change clear ownership. Providing useful information while protecting user data The Agent needs feedback to refine a Recipe. Limited analysis signals and candidate references stored inside the page support further analysis while keeping raw data, key material, and decoded Output outside WebMCP results. Adapting to an evolving WebMCP implementation WebMCP remained a draft during the challenge, and available WebMCP hosts did not forward invocation cancellation signals consistently. RecipeBridge accesses the browser API through an isolated adapter with feature detection. Page lifecycle checks, session shutdown, timeouts, and stale-result checks protect Recipe and Output state when a host cannot cancel an active invocation. Reusing upstream behavior accurately An early design duplicated Operation rules through separate profiles, which could diverge as CyberChef changed. The revised design reads CyberChef’s defaults, argument structures, fixed options, and validation rules directly. A separate access audit handles only WebMCP permission classification. Accomplishments The deployed fork supports the complete visible workflow, including Operation discovery, Recipe editing, user approval, Bake execution, Output inspection, and Magic candidate application. Browsers without WebMCP support continue to load the existing CyberChef interface normally. The implementation reviews every generated Operation and defines explicit behavior for the direct , approval , blocked , and excluded classifications. It also handles stale Recipe revisions, rejected or expired approval requests, Operation runtime failures, interrupted or superseded runs, and page-scoped collaboration session shutdown. Current automated validation includes 507 passing Node API tests and 12 passing Chrome WebMCP browser scenarios. Independent testing of the deployed site covers 35 representative workflows across encoding, compression, cryptography, parsing, analysis, Recipe control, approvals, failure handling, and privacy checks. What I learned Shared-workspace development should begin by mapping each state owner, revision, authorization, and completion transition. This prevents user actions, Agent requests, and asynchronous Worker results from overwriting one another A large capability catalog should use a small, stable workflow API with on-demand metadata. This limits the Agent’s discovery context without maintaining hundreds of separate tool contracts. Accurate implementation begins with understanding the business meaning of each data value. That meaning must remain consistent across WebMCP tool descriptions, input arguments, result fields, validation, and tests. This reduces ambiguity when the Agent selects Operations, configures arguments, and interprets results. What’s next Future work will improve resource-intensive Intensive Magic analysis, expand interoperability checks as browser implementations evolve, and provide clearer candidate explanations while protecting candidate arguments and raw Output. User feedback can also guide adjustments to Operation access classifications and approval wording. RecipeBridge is currently an experimental fork. Manual review of the added and modified code remains limited, so further review and practical testing are required before using it in security-sensitive production environments. title: memory-canvas
pitch: A bilingual family memory canvas where people and AI reconstruct history from stories, photos, and documents—keeping sources, uncertainty, and contradictions visible
about_excerpt: A bilingual family memory canvas where people and AI reconstruct history from stories, photos, and documents—keeping sources, uncertainty, and contradictions visible Like Comment Story Updates ## Inspiration Family history is often built from incomplete memories: one person remembers a year, another remembers a place, and an old photograph suggests something different. Most software tries to resolve these differences into one clean answer. Memoir Canvas takes the opposite approach. It makes uncertainty visible and gives the final decision back to the family. Every memory appears as a firefly in a moonlit meadow. Green means the story has been told, orange means sources conflict, and white means there is an empty place waiting for someone to contribute. Opening a memory reveals a book-like page where recollections and evidence remain visible together. The project was inspired by a simple principle: An AI must not turn a guess into a fact. ## What I learned The most important lesson was that trustworthy AI behavior cannot depend only on instructions or prompts. If the system truly must not invent certainty, that rule needs to exist below the model. Memoir Canvas uses database constraints, PostgreSQL roles, deferred constraint triggers, and a shared command layer to enforce this boundary. An agent can add memories, cite sources, detect conflicts, and propose follow-up questions. It cannot resolve a contradiction by itself. I also learned that uncertainty can be part of the user experience rather than something hidden in metadata. The open conflict becomes a physical tear in the page, and the book refuses to close until a person resolves it. The interface makes the epistemic state understandable without requiring the user to inspect a database. ## How I built it Memoir Canvas is a local-first Vite and React application. A real PostgreSQL-compatible database runs inside the browser through PGlite and is persisted in IndexedDB. No application server, account, or runtime API is required. The architecture has one write door: Human controls and agent tools both call src/domain/commands.ts . Only the command layer writes to the database. Every write and audit event happens in the same transaction. The view renders a read-only projection from the store. WebMCP tools are generated as a pure function of the current UI state. The app exposes eight WebMCP tools: read_memory_graph , add_person , add_memory_claim , link_claim_to_source , flag_conflict , propose_followup_question , resolve_claim , and generate_story_card . The tool list changes depending on what the person is viewing. In particular, resolve_claim only becomes available when a human has opened a specific conflict. Even then, an agent calling it is refused by the database because only a human can provide the confirmation. The central demonstration follows one family story: An oral account says Grandma moved to Đà Nẵng around 1972. A photograph is dated 1974. The sources are linked as contradictory. The page tears and cannot turn. The agent proposes a follow-up question. A family member opens the conflict and confirms the correct year. The tear heals and the story card carries the weakest certainty of the claims it contains. Story cards are bilingual, with Vietnamese and English content, so the archive remains useful to the family while still being understandable to English-speaking judges. ## Challenges The hardest challenge was preserving the same safety guarantees across both human and agent interaction. It would have been easy to give the agent a separate shortcut, but that would make the human-facing safeguards meaningless. Both paths now use the same command functions and database constraints. Another challenge was representing conflict visually without making the interface feel like a dashboard. The project moved from a conventional panel layout to a book and meadow metaphor: pages turn by gesture, conflicts split the book, and memories appear as lights in the landscape. Browser portability was also important. The app must work in embedded webviews where WebGL or WebMCP may be unavailable. The forest has a CSS fallback, the photographs are processed locally through EXIF metadata, and the core interactions remain accessible through keyboard navigation. The final result is an archive that helps an AI participate in family history without allowing it to decide what the family remembers Built With community css i18next indexeddb learning machine pglite postgresql react typescript vite vitest w3c web webgl webmcp zustand Try it out memoir-canvas.vercel.app Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Ngọc Quý Trần Like Share this project: Updates Ngọc Quý Trần started this project — Sep 04, 2026 12:07 AM EDT

pitch: A live asset analysis tool that shows how current and potential macro conditions affect U.S. stocks, cash, gold, and crypto, then identifies the tailwinds and headwinds facing your portfolio

 Inspiration 

 I worked as a VC analyst, and this is the kind of work I did every day, including tracking growth, inflation, interest rates, and volatility, then asking what changes in the macro environment could mean for different assets and portfolios. 

 The problem 

 
 AI agents can help with this work, but their answers may vary depending on how a question is phrased or which tools and instructions are available. 
 A dashboard provides a more consistent and visual way to present the analysis, but traditional dashboards can be difficult to customize for every scenario and portfolio. 
 

 WebMCP is a good solution. The agent translates a user’s question into structured inputs, while the dashboard applies the same analysis framework and displays the result in a consistent, visual format. 

 What it does 

 Asset Analysis helps users: 

 
 Understand how current macro conditions and hypothetical events may affect U.S. stocks, cash, gold, and crypto. 
 Analyze how a portfolio may be affected by current or potential macro scenarios. 
 

 How we built it 

 I built the website with Codex. 

 I started with the core product experience: a market overview showing how current macro conditions affect four asset classes. I then added detailed analysis for each asset and a portfolio view that combines those signals based on the user's allocation. 

 I created the first working version with Codex, tested it, and iterated on the design and interactions until the experience felt clear. I then asked Codex to add WebMCP tools for the two main workflows: analyzing a specific macro scenario and evaluating a specific portfolio. These tools allow AI agents to interact directly with the website. The finished application was deployed with Vercel. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The biggest challenge was accuracy and trust. How can a user know whether the agent and the website reached a reasonable conclusion? 

 To address this, I made the underlying factors visible. Users can see how changes in growth, inflation, interest rates, credit spreads, oil, and volatility contribute to each result. They can inspect the reasoning and decide whether they agree with the assumptions. 

 The analysis also uses a fixed framework. This limits the agent's freedom, but that constraint is intentional. It makes the results more consistent, comparable, and easier to verify. 

 Accomplishments that I am proud of 

 
 The visualization makes the analysis much easier to understand than a text-only response from an agent. I am especially proud of the interactive scenario compass, which lets users explore different macro events by clicking the circles. 
 The website can analyze a custom portfolio and display its potential tailwinds and headwinds within seconds. This makes personalized scenario analysis fast and convenient. 
 

 What we learned 

 The main question I kept thinking is: What is the best way for humans and agents to work together? 

 I learned two things: 

 
 Agents need a framework. If an agent receives an open-ended request without tools or constraints, its answer may vary from one conversation to another. 
 Humans need visualization (So important!!) This was especially important to me. A long text response is difficult to scan, even when it contains the same information as a well-designed dashboard. 
 

 In this project, the dashboard gives the user a clear and consistent interface. The agent acts as the analyst and point of contact, translating natural-language requests into structured WebMCP tool calls that update the page. 

 I believe this is a useful model for agentic products: the agent provides flexibility, while the website provides structure, context, and results that people can easily inspect. 

 What's next for Asset Analysis 

 
 Add more data sources and use MCP integrations to improve the depth and accuracy of the analysis. 
 Build more advanced asset analysis, including valuation models and other methods for producing quantified valuations. 
 Support more asset classes and potentially add price changes and historical performance to the dashboard.

title: TrustFill
pitch: This is TrustFill. It's a grant application form that an AI agent can fill out for you — but it's built so the agent can never submit anything sensitive without you confirming it first.
about_excerpt: This is TrustFill. It's a grant application form that an AI agent can fill out for you — but it's built so the agent can never submit anything sensitive without you confirming it first. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration WebMCP's whole premise is that agents shouldn't have to guess their way through a page — a site can just declare what an agent is allowed to do. Reading Chrome's WebMCP tool security guidance, one line stuck with us: agents are powerful precisely because they act with the user's session already open, which is also exactly why that power needs a boundary. Most of the WebMCP demos we saw were about letting agents do more — search faster, check out faster. We wanted to explore the opposite question: could WebMCP be the thing that lets an agent do less, on purpose, in exactly the right places? High-stakes forms — grant applications, insurance claims, legal filings — are where people are least willing to hand an agent full control. That felt like the right place to test whether "trust" could be a structural property of a tool, not just a line in a system prompt. What it does TrustFill is a grant application — the Riverbend Micro-Grant form — that a WebMCP-aware agent can fill out on your behalf, with a hard boundary baked into the tools themselves. For low-risk fields (business name, address, EIN, founding date), the agent fills them in directly. For anything with real consequences — annual revenue, requested amount, legal certifications — the agent cannot fill them at all; the tool it would need rejects the call outright and requires it to flag the field with a reason instead. The application cannot be submitted while any flagged field is unresolved. A live audit trail records every action, agent or human, in order, so nothing happens invisibly. The result: an agent that's genuinely useful for the boring 80% of a form, and structurally incapable of guessing on the 20% that matters. How we built it The frontend is React + Vite with Tailwind for styling, and all state lives in a single reducer-driven form model — no backend needed for the demo. Six tools are registered through the real WebMCP API, document.modelContext.registerTool , each with an AbortController for clean unregistration on unmount: get_form_state , fill_field , flag_uncertain , request_human_review , submit_form , and get_audit_trail . The two read-only tools carry readOnlyHint annotations so an agent knows they're always safe to call. The critical piece is inside fill_field itself: it checks each field's risk tier and rejects the call for high-risk fields before it ever touches state — the boundary lives in the tool's own code, not in a prompt telling the agent to behave. We registered the deployed Netlify domain for Chrome's WebMCP origin trial so the API is genuinely available to any visiting browser or agent in production, added /.well-known/webmcp and llms.txt so the site is discoverable before an agent even loads the page, and built an explicit demo-mode fallback (with console diagnostics reporting mode=real-webmcp vs mode=demo ) so the concept is visible even in browsers without WebMCP support yet. Challenges we ran into Getting from "works locally with a Chrome flag" to "works for a real visiting agent in production" surfaced problems we didn't expect. The WebMCP API surface itself has been shifting ( navigator.modelContext moved to document.modelContext ), so we had to make sure we were building against the current spec rather than a stale example. Production availability required registering for Chrome's origin trial, and our first token was scoped as third-party by mistake — a mismatch that silently kept the site in demo mode until we re-registered with the correct scope. We also had to learn the hard way that not every "browser agent" actually uses WebMCP tool discovery — some general-purpose browsing tools simulate a human clicking through the UI instead, which looked like a WebMCP failure at first but was really a different agent entirely. Most importantly, testing surfaced a real bug where the Submit button's enabled state wasn't reading from the same blocker logic as the submit_form tool — meaning the UI could have let someone submit with unresolved high-risk fields, which would have quietly undermined the entire premise of the project if we hadn't caught it. Accomplishments that we're proud of The core guarantee isn't a claim, it's enforced in code: fill_field structurally cannot touch a high-risk field, and submit_form and the Submit button now share one blocker calculation, so there's no path to submitting with something unresolved. We verified the full six-tool integration independently with a WebMCP tool inspector showing real, callable schemas — not just our own word for it. And the live audit trail means every decision, whether made by the agent or by the human reviewing it, is visible and traceable rather than happening behind the scenes. What we learned The biggest shift in thinking: safety for agentic web apps doesn't have to live in a prompt at all — it can live in the shape of the tool contract itself, which is a guarantee no amount of clever prompting can quietly break. We also learned that the gap between local, flag-enabled WebMCP testing and real production behavior is bigger than the docs make it sound, and that "an agent used my site" can mean two very different things depending on whether it discovered structured tools or just simulated a human — a distinction worth designing and testing for explicitly, not assuming. What's next for TrustFill We'd like to make the risk tiers (low/medium/high) configurable per organization instead of hardcoded per field, so the same pattern could be dropped onto any long form — insurance claims, rental applications, government paperwork — without rebuilding the gating logic each time. We're also interested in extending request_human_review to support multiple humans on one application (co-applicants, cosigners) negotiating shared fields, and in exploring WebMCP's declarative HTML-attribute tools alongside our imperative ones to see whether the same trust boundary can be expressed even more simply. Longer term, we'd like to publish the gating pattern itself — reject-by-default on high-risk tool calls, shared blocker logic between tools and UI — as a small reusable library other WebMCP-based forms could adopt directly. title: Precidra Viewer
pitch: Let AI agents reason about precise drawing geometry, not screenshots.
about_excerpt: Let AI agents reason about precise drawing geometry, not screenshots. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Technical drawings contain precise geometrical information, but AI agents usually encounter them as screenshots or opaque user interfaces. From pixels alone, an agent cannot reliably determine exact distances, intersections, containment, adjacency, or object geometry. Building a fully semantic model from the ground up for every drawing is expensive and often unnecessary. Precidra Viewer explores a different approach: expose the drawing's existing geometry directly through WebMCP and let an agent derive useful spatial understanding from it. What it does Precidra Viewer is an open-source, read-only companion for .prec technical drawings created with Precidra . Humans can view a drawing, pan and zoom, inspect objects, and toggle layers. At the same time, an AI agent can query the same document through seven focused WebMCP tools. The agent can: summarize the document and its layers; list and inspect individual objects, using nearby annotations and layer names as semantic hints; retrieve exact contour and vertex geometry; measure minimum distances; test intersections; discover containment, adjacency, overlap, proximity, and disjoint relationships; evaluate hypothetical geometry without modifying the drawing. This enables questions such as: Which rooms share a real wall edge rather than only a corner? How far is an object from the nearest obstacle? What objects are contained inside this area? Would a proposed shape intersect existing geometry? Why WebMCP WebMCP lets Precidra expose domain-level capabilities instead of asking an agent to interpret pixels or automate toolbar controls. The tools return deterministic geometric results from the same model rendered for humans. This creates a clear division of work: a human selects and visually verifies the drawing, while the agent searches, measures, compares, and explains its spatial structure. The interface is intentionally read-only, so agents can investigate freely without accidentally changing the document. What changed for the challenge Precidra existed as a drawing application before the challenge. During the submission period, I created the standalone open-source viewer and added the WebMCP interface for querying document structure, exact geometry, measurements, intersections, and spatial relationships. How it was built The viewer is implemented in dependency-free HTML5 and JavaScript and runs as a static site on GitHub Pages. It reuses a small set of Precidra's geometry, model, parsing, and rendering modules inside a new standalone viewer shell. WebMCP tools are registered through document.modelContext.registerTool() . The tool layer provides document orientation, compact object summaries, detailed geometry on demand, exact distance and intersection operations, and spatial predicates including contains , within , touches , overlapping , close , and disjoint . Tool descriptions guide the agent to begin with compact document metadata, inspect only the necessary objects, account for document-specific coordinate units, and distinguish meaningful shared edges from incidental point contact. Challenges The main challenge was turning raw geometry into useful agent semantics without requiring drawings to contain a complete semantic model. Spatial relationships also need to remain reliable across open and closed shapes, modeling tolerances, different coordinate scales, and drawings in which a shared corner has a very different meaning from a shared wall. Another challenge was designing responses that provide enough precision for reasoning without overwhelming the agent with every coordinate in the document. The tools therefore use progressive disclosure: summaries first, exact geometry only when requested. What I learned WebMCP is most valuable when it exposes the underlying domain model rather than reproducing visible UI actions. A relatively small set of carefully designed geometric tools allows an agent to answer questions that would be unreliable or impossible through screenshot interpretation alone. Open source and full editor The submitted project is the open-source Precidra Viewer, licensed under AGPL-3.0. It includes all code, assets, instructions, and a sample drawing required to run and test the submission. The full Precidra editor, including DXF and SVG import, can be used freely without an account. It remains separate from this open-source submission. pitch: An agent-native PC configurator where people and AI build the same PC together without sacrificing compatibility or trust.
about_excerpt: An agent-native PC configurator where people and AI build the same PC together without sacrificing compatibility or trust. Like 1 Comment Story Updates HowToPC logo High-End Gaming PC RTX 4060 starter build Inspiration Building a PC looks like shopping. In reality, it is a constraint problem. A CPU determines which motherboard sockets are valid. A motherboard determines memory type, expansion capacity, and storage resources. A GPU needs enough power, the right connections, and enough physical clearance. A cooler needs the correct socket and enough room inside the case. One component can quietly invalidate several others. Our starting question was simple: What if an AI could help build a PC without becoming the authority on whether the hardware actually works together? Most AI assistants sit outside the configurator. They can recommend parts, describe what buttons to click, or attempt to understand a page through browser automation. That creates an awkward divide: Traditional AI assistant HowToPC with WebMCP Reads or scrapes the interface Reads structured application state Guesses what actions are possible Uses explicitly registered tools Maintains its own idea of the build Shares the real builder session Can suggest incompatible changes Mutations pass deterministic checks Needs UI automation Calls semantic application capabilities WebMCP gave us a different model. Instead of teaching the agent how to operate HowToPC, we made HowToPC itself explain what it can do . The result is a configurator where the human and the agent can alternate control of the same build while deterministic application logic remains the final authority. The AI proposes. HowToPC verifies. The person stays in control. What it does HowToPC is an agent-native PC configurator that combines a traditional hardware builder with structured WebMCP capabilities. A person can browse a large sourced component catalog, assemble a computer, inspect compatibility, monitor motherboard resources, and visualize the configuration through a parametric Digital Twin. At the same time, an AI agent can work with that exact same configuration. For people HowToPC provides: 26,415 sourced hardware products CPU, motherboard, memory, GPU, storage, PSU, case, cooler, fan, and networking categories searchable catalog filters and compatibility-aware discovery RTX 4060 Gaming PC and High-End Gaming PC starter templates deterministic compatibility checks DIMM, M.2, SATA, PCIe, and other resource accounting GPU length and CPU cooler clearance checks modeled component collision detection a real-scale parametric Digital Twin explicit UNKNOWN states when reliable geometry or topology is unavailable For agents The same page exposes 10 structured WebMCP tools : WebMCP tool Capability builder_get_state Read the current PC configuration catalog_search Search the sourced hardware catalog catalog_inspect_product Inspect structured component specifications builder_add_product Add a component builder_remove_product Remove a component builder_replace_product Replace an installed component builder_compatibility_report Request deterministic compatibility diagnostics builder_resource_usage Inspect consumed and available hardware resources builder_geometry_diagnostics Inspect physical clearances and modeled collisions builder_find_compatible Search for hardware compatible with the current build The important part is not simply the number of tools. It is that they operate on the same canonical builder session used by the visible interface . If a person changes a component, the agent immediately sees it. If the agent replaces a component, the person immediately sees it. There is no hidden "AI version" of the PC configuration and no synchronization layer trying to keep two builds aligned. Compatibility remains deterministic The language model does not decide whether two components are compatible. For example, if an agent attempts to install an Intel LGA1700 motherboard into a build containing an AMD AM5 CPU, the mutation is rejected by HowToPC's transaction and compatibility logic. CPU socket does not match motherboard. That same protection applies whether the requested change came from a person or an agent. Unknown is not compatible. When HowToPC does not have enough evidence to verify something, it reports that limitation rather than fabricating confidence. How we built it HowToPC is a TypeScript monorepo built around a separation between product data, engineering rules, application state, geometry, and agent capabilities. Architecture ┌───────────────────────┐ │ Human UI │ │ Parts / Build / Twin │ └──────────┬────────────┘ │ ▼ ┌───────────────────────┐ │ Canonical Builder │ │ Session │ └──────────┬────────────┘ │ ┌────────────┼─────────────┐ ▼ ▼ ▼ Compatibility Resources Geometry Engine Accounting Engine ▲ ▲ ▲ └────────────┼─────────────┘ │ ┌──────────┴────────────┐ │ WebMCP Tools │ │ AI agent actions │ └───────────────────────┘ Both interfaces converge on the same state and the same validation logic. Sourced hardware catalog We normalize a pinned snapshot of BuildCores OpenDB into deterministic product records. The public catalog contains: Source Products Normalized BuildCores products 26,408 Curated sourced references 7 Total public catalog 26,415 Catalog searching, facets, compatibility filtering, and pagination happen against the full data set rather than a small demo fixture. Deterministic compatibility Compatibility is handled outside the language model. The rules cover areas including: CPU and motherboard sockets memory generation motherboard and case form factors CPU cooler socket support GPU and case clearance motherboard resource consumption installed quantities PSU and component requirements compatibility-aware builder transactions An agent can request a change, but it cannot bypass these rules. Parametric Digital Twin We also built a geometry layer that converts known hardware dimensions into a real-scale parametric preview. The system can reason about values such as: GPU length CPU cooler height Case internal limits Modeled component volumes Component collisions Mount topology We deliberately avoid presenting the Twin as manufacturer CAD. If exact mounting geometry is not sourced, the application says so. That makes the model less visually magical, but much more trustworthy. WebMCP bridge The WebMCP implementation registers tools through the browser's native model context surface. Conceptually: document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "builder_find_compatible", description: "Find products compatible with the current PC build", // structured input schema // deterministic application handler }); The important architectural decision was to reuse existing application services . We did not create separate AI-only compatibility rules, a separate agent catalog, or a parallel builder state. Engineering confidence The project currently has: 53 test files / 182 automated tests Coverage includes: catalog ingestion normalization catalog searching compatibility rules quantity transactions resource accounting geometry collision detection starter templates API routes canonical builder sessions WebMCP registration WebMCP tool behavior The starter templates also have regression gates requiring them to remain both deterministically compatible and free from modeled component collisions . Challenges we ran into 1. Deciding where AI reasoning should stop The easiest implementation would have been a tool like: change_my_pc_build(prompt) That would also have been the least interesting architecture. It would make the language model responsible for interpreting hardware constraints and deciding whether its own proposed changes were valid. We wanted a stronger boundary. The model can decide what it wants to try . HowToPC decides whether the requested transaction is allowed . That separation became one of the most important design principles in the project. 2. Working with incomplete real-world hardware data Real hardware catalogs are messy. Some components have detailed measurements. Others omit dimensions, connector topology, mounting coordinates, or other fields required for exact mechanical reasoning. We had a choice: invent reasonable-looking values make uncertainty visible We chose the second option. For example, if exact PCIe slot topology is unavailable, the Digital Twin can use a standardized parametric position for visualization while separately reporting that the exact topology is unknown. Similarly, if an AIO cooler has known radiator dimensions but no reliable case mounting coordinates, we do not invent a radiator location. Missing data is treated as information, not an invitation to hallucinate. 3. Making the Digital Twin honest and useful A visually convincing 3D scene can create false confidence very quickly. title: Future Doors
pitch: Future Doors turns a saved opportunity screenshot into an official-source-backed, human-approved career path that people and agents build together for one or more career futures.
about_excerpt: Future Doors turns a saved opportunity screenshot into an official-source-backed, human-approved career path that people and agents build together for one or more career futures. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Future Doors Your camera roll is full of possible futures. Future Doors turns a saved opportunity into a source-checked career path that a person and an agent can build together. The problem People who are exploring more than one career direction constantly save internships, fellowships, challenges, research calls, and communities from Instagram, LinkedIn, and group chats. Those posts disappear into a camera roll. Even when someone returns to one, they still have to find the official page, interpret eligibility and dates, check whether it fits their schedule, and understand what the experience would actually add to their longer-term direction. Most job products optimize for one role and one application. Future Doors is designed for people whose experience does not fit one label: a builder may also be a technical storyteller, researcher, or future education founder. What it does Future Doors turns scattered opportunity clues into a small, explainable plan: A person shares a saved screenshot or link. The agent finds the original official HTTPS source and stages the deadline, relevant rules, schedule, format, concrete outputs, and one unresolved fact for review. The same profile can hold several possible futures. AI product, hardware storytelling, and learning, for example, produce genuinely different recommended work. Source-checked cards are grouped as activities, projects, research, or credentials. Fit hearts represent verifiable alignment with the person's facts and preferences—not acceptance or hiring odds. The person chooses up to three near-term moves. The plan shows timing, prerequisite relationships, schedule conflicts, and which goal-specific evidence each move can create. Ineligible or unresolved opportunities remain visibly blocked. The agent can stage a separate source-backed path, but it cannot pretend that the original eligibility was restored. The result is not another ranked list. It is a visual evidence deck: what to do, when it fits, what it can produce, and what is still missing. Why WebMCP is essential Future Doors is a shared stateful surface, not a chatbot wrapper. Through WebMCP, an agent can read the same profile, futures, saved opportunities, constraints, timing, and proof gaps that the person sees. It can then focus a route, compare constrained paths, check a saved post, surface one missing fact, or stage a source-backed change directly on the page instead of guessing through visual controls. The live app registers 15 structured tools with document.modelContext.registerTool . Tool inputs are schema-validated, read-only operations are identified, externally sourced text is treated as untrusted, outputs are bounded, and invalid dates or IDs return explicit errors. Most importantly, there is no WebMCP approval tool. An agent may prepare profile facts, an opportunity, a priority plan, an alternative route, or a work link, but the person must approve every consequential change in the interface. Source facts, agent inference, planned work, saved links, and verified proof are never presented as the same state. That boundary is the product: the agent prepares; the person decides. What is new Future Doors combines three ideas that are normally separated: a scrapbook for opportunities discovered outside job platforms; official-source and eligibility checking by an agent; a multi-future portfolio planner that shows how selected work can create reusable evidence. It does not force a premature career choice and does not manufacture a success score. It helps someone make a bounded decision across several plausible futures while keeping every important claim inspectable. How we built it Next.js 16, React 19, and TypeScript Browser-native WebMCP via document.modelContext.registerTool 15 scoped tools for reading, staging, comparing, simulating, and explaining paths Vercel deployment with no account required for the judge demo Vitest regression tests covering tool registration, route-aware recommendations, invalid inputs, source requirements, bounded outputs, rule mismatches, and human-only approval boundaries Motion-based transitions that explain source checking, future-specific recommendations, card selection, and proof coverage The current automated suite contains 38 passing tests . The production site has also been verified to expose all 15 tools and return a successful live get_path_snapshot invocation. Try it Open the live app and choose TRY THE EXAMPLE . Switch between Maya's AI, Hardware, and Learning futures to see different work. Add cards to the plan and watch the evidence coverage change. Open HOW IT WORKS for two judge-ready WebMCP prompts and the visible human-approval boundary. No login or credentials are required. title: RelayPay
pitch: RelayPay uses WebMCP to let an AI agent investigate refund exceptions and prepare recovery actions, while a human approval gate controls consequential execution and verification.
about_excerpt:
RelayPay uses WebMCP to let an AI agent investigate refund exceptions and prepare recovery actions, while a human approval gate controls consequential execution and verification.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 



 
 Inspiration 

 Refunds are simple when everything works. But when a return is verified and the money never arrives, resolving the exception can require checking multiple systems, interpreting evidence, deciding what action is safe, and manually coordinating the recovery. 

 We wanted to explore a different model: what if an AI agent could investigate the exception and prepare the recovery, while the human remained firmly in control of the consequential action? 

 That became RelayPay. 

 What it does 

 RelayPay is a WebMCP-powered refund recovery system where an AI agent can investigate refund exceptions through structured browser tools. 

 The agent can discover and call tools to find an order, inspect return status, check refund status, prepare an escalation, and verify the resulting case. 

 The critical boundary is human approval: the agent can investigate and prepare a proposed recovery, but cannot authorize its own consequential action. The human reviews the exact proposal and explicitly approves it before recovery submission. 

 This makes WebMCP more than a way to expose buttons to an agent—it becomes the interface through which an agent collaborates with a human inside a real application workflow. 

 How we built it 

 RelayPay was built with Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Three.js/React Three Fiber, and browser-native WebMCP. 

 We registered six structured WebMCP tools using document.modelContext.registerTool(): 

 find_order
get_return_status
get_refund_status
prepare_escalation
submit_escalation
verify_case 

 The workflow separates investigation, preparation, consequential execution, and verification. 

 We also built an application-enforced human approval boundary. Approval is tied to the exact proposed action, is single-use, and is consumed when the recovery is successfully submitted. 

 The result is a deterministic demo environment that lets an agent repeatedly reproduce the same recovery scenarios without relying on external merchant or payment APIs. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The biggest challenge was making WebMCP the actual product interface for the agent, rather than adding WebMCP as a thin integration on top of an existing UI. 

 We had to think carefully about tool boundaries, structured inputs, read-only versus consequential operations, and what an agent should be allowed to do autonomously. 

 The hardest design problem was the approval boundary. We wanted the agent to be genuinely useful without allowing it to silently turn its own recommendation into an irreversible action. 

 We also had to make the experience work across WebMCP-capable environments while honestly handling browsers where WebMCP is unavailable. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We're proud that RelayPay demonstrates a complete agent → tools → reasoning → human approval → action → verification loop rather than just a chatbot calling an API. 

 The agent can investigate a real-looking refund exception through multiple WebMCP tools, build a recovery proposal, and reach a clear human decision point. 

 We're especially proud of the separation between preparation and execution. The agent can do the investigative work, but the application—not the agent—enforces the final approval boundary. 

 We also built an execution trace so the interaction is observable rather than hidden behind a black box. 

 What we learned 

 We learned that building an agent-native application requires designing around capabilities and boundaries, not just adding AI to an existing interface. 

 WebMCP made us think of the browser itself as an agent-accessible application surface. Tool descriptions, schemas, permissions, state transitions, and failure cases all become part of the product design. 

 Most importantly, we learned that human-agent collaboration works best when the agent handles the tedious investigation and preparation while the human retains authority over consequential decisions. 

 What's next for RelayPay 

 The next step is connecting RelayPay to real commerce and payment infrastructure so the same workflow can operate on live refund data. 

 We want to add richer evidence collection, policy-aware recovery recommendations, merchant-side integrations, audit trails, and stronger verification. 

 Longer term, RelayPay could evolve from a refund exception tool into an agent-native operations layer for commerce, where humans set the boundaries and agents handle the repetitive work inside them.

title: Airlock
pitch: An analytics workspace where the AI agent does the whole analysis without ever seeing your data. It stays in DuckDB in your tab; WebMCP tools return only aggregates. Raw rows need your approval.
about_excerpt: An analytics workspace where the AI agent does the whole analysis without ever seeing your data. It stays in DuckDB in your tab; WebMCP tools return only aggregates. Raw rows need your approval. Like 1 Comment Story Updates When the agent needs specific rows, you see why, SQL, and the exact preview. You choose what to release - or say no. Nothing auto-approves Airlock: AI analytics in your browser. Data stays in the tab. The counter shows how many values you actually released — starting at zero. One click runs a full gender pay-gap review: charts in the shared notebook, every tool call in the audit log. Aggregates only — no raw rows. The agent tries to pull individual rows. Blocked by default. run_query only returns grouped results — not a setting you forgot to turn on. Turn off raw row requests: the tool is crossed out and gone from the agent's list. Permission is capability control - not a polite error msg Full story: ~7% gap within grade, not ~20% headline. Then a controlled release - only the columns you approved, counted on screen. Inspiration Analysts sit on payroll files, patient extracts, and transaction logs they cannot paste into ChatGPT . The barrier is policy, not preference. Until WebMCP, the browser had no way to offer AI help without an upload. What it does Airlock is a local-first analytics workspace. Your file loads into DuckDB in the tab and never leaves the device . An AI agent works through 14 WebMCP tools — profiling, guarded SQL, charts, findings — and returns aggregates, not rows. When individual values are truly needed, the agent must ask in writing. You see the SQL, the preview, and the cell count before you approve. A header counter tracks every value that crossed the boundary . One click runs a full gender pay-gap demo: Headline gap ~20% Within-grade gap ~7% Cells released: 0 Try it: live demo · source on GitHub Why WebMCP is the only way to build this A remote MCP server cannot read a file that never left the browser. Uploading defeats the purpose. Screen-reading agents see every rendered row — the boundary is gone on contact . WebMCP runs the code that touches the data and the code that filters what the model receives in the same page . execute is the choke point: // Tier 3 gone → tool unregistered, not just refused controller.abort(); // request_raw_rows disappears from getTools() When raw requests are disabled, we abort the tier's AbortController and request_raw_rows vanishes from the agent's tool list — it cannot call a tool it cannot see. How we built it Next.js 16 static export — no backend, no API routes DuckDB-Wasm for in-tab SQL 14 tools in one Zod-backed registry via document.modelContext.registerTool() Tiers map to AbortController lifetimes : page open → dataset loaded → raw requests permitted Every handler returns an envelope — never throws: { "ok": true, "summary": "...", "data": { ... } } { "ok": false, "error": "too_many_rows", "hint": "Use aggregates or request_raw_rows" } Privacy pipeline: SQL guard → aggregate-only run_query → column redaction → k-anonymity → human gate on raw release. Privacy model, honestly We claim: no server, no upload, provable cell count, explicit release approval. We do not claim: protection against a patient adversary reconstructing rows from many narrow aggregates. That limit is stated openly in the app. Challenges we ran into DuckDB-Wasm inside a static export (no Worker at build time) React Strict Mode double-registering WebMCP tools Observable Plot tooltips on a dark theme Making capability withdrawal visible in the UI — red dot, strikethrough — not just in code Accomplishments that we're proud of A complete pay-gap review with the counter at 0 Permission as tool lifetime , not tool logic One registry serving WebMCP agents, the in-page demo, and manual inspection Judges can verify in DevTools → Network: no request carries your data What we learned Tool descriptions are part of the product — agents read failures and hints. The airlock meter turns an abstract privacy promise into something a judge can glance at. Presentation beats feature lists in a hackathon. What's next for Airlock OPFS session persistence, org-side audit export, AST-tightened SQL guard, query-budget accounting against aggregate reconstruction. title: Pinnwall
pitch: A sticky-note board where the agent is a teammate, not a script. It claims notes, moves them and comments back — running in your browser session, so it never sees a credential.
about_excerpt: A sticky-note board where the agent is a teammate, not a script. It claims notes, moves them and comments back — running in your browser session, so it never sees a credential. Like Comment Story Updates The agent flags a note as four tasks in one, you answer on the note, it reports back when done. Claim pills show what the agent is working on right now. Badges show which notes it wrote. Every board merged into one view, with the agent's work visible across all of them. Inspiration Adding MCP to Pinnwall was already on my list. I use it as my own sticky-note board and kept wanting an assistant that could tidy it up, but not enough to build a whole server with its own auth just for that. I hadn't heard of WebMCP before this hackathon. It turned out to be the shape I actually needed, so I finally built it. What it does Pinnwall is a sticky-note board with no database. With WebMCP, an agent works it with you. It has 13 tools: read the board, create and move notes, add columns, switch the board you're looking at. It can also claim a note, so a marker appears before it starts, and comment on one to say what it did or ask you something. You answer on the note. Anything the agent writes gets badged, so you can always tell who did what. Why WebMCP fits this A board is shared state that two people edit. Before, I had two bad options: let an agent click through the UI from screenshots, which is slow and breaks every time I touch the CSS, or stand up an MCP server with its own auth and deploy, just so something could edit a board I'm already signed into. WebMCP skips both. The tools run in the page, on my session. The agent can do what I can do and nothing more, there's no key to leak, and access ends when I close the tab. Concretely: one note on my board said "ship pricing page, update the FAQ, brief support, schedule the newsletter." Splitting that by hand is four notes typed, four drags, then delete the original. Now it's one sentence, and I watch the agent claim it, split it, and tell me what it did. Then I answer it on the note. That last part is the bit I didn't expect to care about — the conversation stays on the work instead of disappearing into a chat window. How I built it Node, Express, vanilla JS. No build step, no new dependencies. All the tools sit in one file. Each is registered with document.modelContext.registerTool and calls the same fetch helper the buttons call, so the agent rides my session cookie and hits the same CSRF check and validation as a click. They take names, not ids. move_note({ note: "brief support", column: "Done" }) finds the note from a piece of its text and tells the agent what it matched if there's more than one. Pinnwall itself predates the hackathon. The agent side is all new. WEBMCP.md in the repo has the split. Challenges I ran into Mirroring my REST API one to one gave me tools the agent used badly. It doesn't have ids and it thinks in names, so half its calls missed. Making every tool resolve by name fixed more than anything I did on the server. The board reloads itself after the agent writes. The first version did that even while I was typing in a note, and wiped what I'd written. Now it waits until I stop. Accomplishments that I'm proud of No new dependencies, no API key, no second service. You sign in normally and the agent can do what you can do. It's also additive. Existing Pinnwall installs run unchanged and old notes work without a migration. What I learned The useful part of WebMCP is the session, not the protocol. Running in the page turns authorisation from the hardest part into a non-problem. And you have to build for two actors from the start. Almost every bug worth fixing came from assuming only one of us was touching the board at a time.
