title: Falsify
pitch: A browser-native research workspace where humans and WebMCP agents test ideas against frozen contracts, shared evidence, and approval-gated decisions.
about_excerpt: A browser-native research workspace where humans and WebMCP agents test ideas against frozen contracts, shared evidence, and approval-gated decisions. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Falsify started from my work on Kaggle hackathons and machine learning competitions. I wanted a system that could analyze a target model, explore several research branches in one session, and keep each branch grounded in its own evidence. The practical goal was to reduce context contamination and hallucination as a long research session accumulated hypotheses, failed attempts, and partial results. A frontier GPT model using Ultra reasoning and subagents can already explore several branches in parallel. That helped with throughput, but it did not solve visibility. When multiple paths were active, I still could not answer simple questions at a glance: Which configuration produced the best result? Which branch failed for a technical reason? Which idea had already been tested? What should run next? Conversation logs were too linear for this job. I added an experiment graph so that model lineage and outcomes would be visible, then introduced tickets as an active reservation queue for research ideas. A person can record a hypothesis before stepping away, while a main orchestrator or a Codex agent connected through WebMCP can read the current progress and understand what the ticket is asking for. The longer-term goal is an overnight research loop in which the agent uses the accumulated evidence to refine or rewrite the next ticket when its assumptions are no longer valid, then continues with the correct experiment instead of blindly following stale instructions. The current browser MVP establishes the state, provenance, and approval rules needed for that workflow. What changed for this submission The earlier project focused on coordinating multi-branch research inside a single session. For the WebMCP Challenge, I built a browser-based research control plane that turns that progress into shared, inspectable state. I added the ticket queue, experiment lineage graph, frozen research contract, deterministic browser runner, evidence comparison views, human approval center, and 12 task-specific WebMCP tools. Human actions and agent actions now operate on the same workspace instead of producing separate conversation histories. What it does Falsify is a browser-based research workspace operated by a human and a WebMCP agent through the same shared state. Every project begins with a research contract that defines: the objective and primary metric the evaluation protocol the experiment budget the minimum effect required to count as an improvement the configuration keys an experiment may change Once the baseline produces valid evidence, the contract freezes. Ideas enter the workspace as tickets. A claimed ticket becomes exactly one experiment node under a frozen parent. Running the node produces evidence, and a decision can then promote it, discard it, or create follow-up tickets. This structure prevents a result from being reinterpreted after the fact. It also preserves the path from an idea to its configuration, run, evidence, and final decision. Technical failure and scientific failure are handled differently. If a run crashes or diverges before producing a valid measurement, the node becomes repairable. It is not labeled as a regression because the hypothesis was never properly tested. A valid but worse measurement, on the other hand, remains part of the scientific record. How I built it This submission is a browser-only MVP. It has no backend, user account, remote runner, or arbitrary code execution. The interface is built with React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, and shadcn/ui. Project state is stored in IndexedDB. Experiment training runs in a Web Worker so that the interface remains responsive. The demonstration uses a deterministic two-moons classification problem and a small multilayer perceptron implemented from scratch. A fixed seed and frozen evaluation contract make the results repeatable during judging. The application registers 12 focused WebMCP tools on document.modelContext. They cover the complete research loop: inspect the project list and create tickets claim a ticket materialize an experiment start or cancel a run inspect evidence compare nodes commit a decision The tools call the same application service used by the React interface. Agent actions therefore appear in the human workspace without maintaining a separate copy of the project. Falsify deliberately exposes no generic shell, file, or delete tool. Mutations are checked against the frozen research contract, project revision, and idempotency key before execution. In Copilot mode, starting a run and committing a decision return an approval request instead of executing immediately. The proposal appears in the Approval Center, where a person can inspect and approve it. Manual mode applies approval gating to every agent mutation. Challenges The first challenge was preserving one consistent state machine across the human interface and WebMCP tools. A command had to obey the same rules regardless of whether it came from a button or an agent call. The second challenge was handling retries and concurrent actions safely. Each mutation includes an idempotency key and expected project revision. Retrying the same request replays its original result, while stale commands are rejected instead of silently overwriting newer work. The third challenge was separating technical failure from scientific evidence. A diverged run must remain repairable, while a valid negative result must remain immutable. Treating both outcomes as a simple failed status would undermine the research record. The final challenge was making the demonstration deterministic without hiding the real workflow. The benchmark is intentionally small, but it still performs actual training in a Web Worker and produces metrics, curves, configuration differences, logs, and a decision boundary. What I learned I learned that an agent tool catalog is more than an API surface. Its names, descriptions, schemas, approval behavior, and output annotations collectively define what the agent believes it is allowed to do. I also learned that sharing storage is the easy part of human-agent collaboration. The harder part is sharing meaning: which contract governed a run, why a node exists, whether a measurement is valid, and who approved the next step. Explicit state transitions, frozen inputs, provenance links, and narrow tools made those boundaries easier for both the human and the agent to understand. What is next The next version will connect the same research model to local repositories and real experiment runners. Planned work includes a local daemon, SQLite and artifact storage, one Git worktree per experiment node, coding-agent adapters, and remote execution. The current browser profile remains intentionally narrow. It demonstrates the complete measure, compare, and decide loop without granting an agent generic access to the user’s machine. title: Runcard
pitch: A GitHub for molecular-dynamics runs: every number traces to a file, and your agent gets seventeen calibrated scientific operations through WebMCP. The agent reasons, Runcard checks, a person approves
about_excerpt: A GitHub for molecular-dynamics runs: every number traces to a file, and your agent gets seventeen calibrated scientific operations through WebMCP. The agent reasons, Runcard checks, a person approves Like Comment Story Updates Main page System 1 System 2 Inspiration I had somehow come across the field of Molecular Dynamics through a summer project, and gained experience with AMBER through building an LLM orchestration engine around it. The biggest thing on my mind was just the lack of guardrails that this software had. It was like working with Assembly. It got me thinking a lot more about the experiences of those working in MD, and how I can build software that lowers the barrier to entry. What it does Sharing a MD simulation with someone usually means just giving your entire directory. I guess it works, but it's very hard to decode, and with hundreds of literal text files as the input, it's just not a very friendly way to share results. Runcard is essentially GitHub for MD simulations. A prepared system is like a repo, a run is like a commit, and users can "fork" runs, adding their own changes to someone else's work. Runcard turns your MD directory into a shareable, validated record, with analysis tools not just invocable by users, but directly invocable by agents through WebMCP. How we built it I was already quite familiar with building AMBER validators, and I used that knowledge to process .in files to ensure that the records were physically sound. That's the "validated record" part of things. I knew along the way that I wanted to do something analogous to Github, which helped with a lot of design work. If a run was a commit, and a rerun was a fork, many more things became clear. Proposals became like pull requests, which had to be approved by the user. Primarily, I had to work on creating functions that converted the raw files into the data presented in the website, and the analysis tools that drove both user/agent interaction. One table drives both users and agent interactions, so both sides are getting the exact same functions. At this point, most of the work was done, the rest just went into presenting it in a way that was intuitive to the user. Challenges we ran into Some of the things we have agents watch out for (like assuming spread as error) were lessons I had learned when generating the bundles in the first place. Some of the runs were with different engines (PMEMD vs Sander), and also had different total times (2 ps vs 30 ps) yet we treated them the same. AMBER is just very tricky to get right, so many of the challenges we had, despite my previous experience, were with honest our results were. Accomplishments that we're proud of To be honest, I'm just proud that I was able to finish this as a final product. Getting to the finish line means a lot to me, since I've never done hackathons all the way through before. On the product side, I was really proud of how the agent performed given these tools. I first asked it to check the math of a calculation with the tools, and it insisted on refusing to give an error score, because only 2 of 3 matched runs exist. Then, I asked it after to consider the system with 310K temperature instead of 300. It not only did that experiment correctly, but noticed that the missing 3rd matched run in the original run was also missing in this 310K run, and automatically proposed a fix. The tools made this possible, and agents kind of did the rest, which was cool to see What we learned I think I've reinforced the idea that the biggest failure modes are silent. Things that are confidently wrong. Both in AI's hallucinating, but also in molecular dynamics where things look ok, but are secretly messed up on the inside. What's next for Runcard I think the obvious answer is to a second person's runs onto the website. If we're really going to be the Github of MD, then we need collaboration and people. I want people to be able to share their results, and iterate on each other's work with much more ease.  SOUND Buoy 

 Human-Anchored Context Governance and Repair for Autonomous Web Agents via WebMCP 

 Live Demo: https://sound-buoy.vercel.app 
 GitHub Repository: https://github.com/elnicoborja/sound-buoy 

 Inspiration 

 Autonomous web agents are becoming active digital workers. They can read a page, navigate an interface, call browser tools, and execute workflows inside web applications. The problem is that most agents still enter complex work environments without enough grounded context. 

 In creative, operational, and commercial work, this creates a recurring failure mode: the agent acts before it understands the world. It guesses priorities, misreads brand identity, ignores human constraints, and turns partial context into confident plans. 

 SOUND Buoy was built for that gap. 

 A buoy marks position, listens to the environment, and gives people a reference point in moving water. SOUND Buoy applies that principle to agent-native web apps. It gives humans a browser-native way to teach an agent the operating reality of a project, review what the agent understood, approve or correct the facts, and only then generate a repair plan. 

 The goal is simple: before an agent acts, it should know where it is, what is true, what is missing, and what a human has actually approved. 

 What It Does 

 SOUND Buoy is a WebMCP-native application for creating, verifying, and exporting actionable operating context. 

 It runs a structured 5-step protocol: 

 
 Intake and source selection 
The user enters raw teaching notes or uploads a Markdown brief that represents the current reality of a project, business, artist, venue, or campaign. 
 Context reflection 
WebMCP tools parse the input against a 9-slot Benchmark Spine covering income streams, products or releases, audience, distribution channels, content assets, evidence, operations, partnerships, and team capacity. 
 Human verification gate 
The application shows candidate facts, gaps, and operating principles. The human must approve, refine, or correct the context before the system can continue. No repair plan can be generated until this approval step is complete. 
 First repair computation 
Once the context is approved, the agent identifies the first useful operational repair. This can be something like creating a world-to-release brief, building an owned-audience bridge, clarifying the next commercial decision, or resolving a documentation gap. 
 Portable agent world export 
The approved truth, repair action, and 90-day milestone roadmap are exported as agent-world.md . This gives downstream agents, collaborators, and future sessions a clean operating file instead of another loose prompt. 
 

 The demo uses independent music as the lead case, with Sonido Vector as the example environment. The same structure also supports seven sector profiles: 

 
 Independent Music 
 Restaurants and Bars 
 Alcohol Brands 
 Live Events and Festivals 
 Digital Media and Publications 
 Agencies and Professional Services 
 Hospitality and Venues 
 

 Each sector uses the same 9-slot topology, but the language adapts to the operating model. For example, music uses releases, fans, and sync. Restaurants use menu moments, guests, and local reach. Agencies use engagements, clients, acquisition, authority, and delivery. 

 How We Built It 

 SOUND Buoy is a lightweight static web application with no server dependency. 

 We registered six browser-level WebMCP tools through navigator.modelContext and document.modelContext : 

 
 get_learning_modules : exposes the active learning modules and sector specifications. 
 get_artist_cases : provides pre-configured benchmark fixtures and domain examples. 
 reflect_candidate_context : turns human notes into a structured 9-slot candidate reflection. 
 approve_or_correct_context : enforces the human verification gate and stores approved facts. 
 generate_first_repair : creates a targeted repair action from approved context only. 
 export_agent_world : compiles the verified truth into a portable agent-world.md export. 
 

 The app uses a dual-mode interaction model. A human can complete the flow manually through the interface, and an autonomous agent can complete the same flow through WebMCP tool calls. Both paths share the same application state, which keeps the experience consistent across human use, browser inspection, and agent execution. 

 We also implemented a deterministic privacy and redaction layer. Before reflection, the app strips script tags, executable payloads, local machine paths, emails, and credential-like strings. The full parsing, verification, repair, and export lifecycle runs client-side in the browser. 

 The visual system uses a compact SOUND OS 3-tone palette: deep canvas, card surface, aqua signal accents, and neon lime approval states. A Dark and Light mode switcher is included. 

 Finally, we added a contract test suite in tests/webmcp-contract.test.js to verify tool schemas, state transitions, approval gating, and export integrity. 

 Challenges We Ran Into 

 The hardest problem was enforcing human approval inside an agentic flow. It is easy to let an agent generate a plan immediately after reading input. It is harder to make the state machine refuse that step until a human has approved or corrected the candidate facts. 

 We also had to balance sector specificity with a shared architecture. Music, hospitality, restaurants, events, media, and agencies use different operating language. We solved that by keeping the same 9-slot spine while allowing each sector to adapt the slot labels and examples. 

 The third challenge was WebMCP discovery and compatibility. We wanted the app to remain useful as a normal web interface while also exposing structured tools for WebMCP inspectors and agent runtimes. That required the human UI and WebMCP tool layer to operate on the same state, not as separate demos. 

 Accomplishments That We Are Proud Of 

 SOUND Buoy is fully client-side. The user can paste or upload sensitive operating context without sending it to an external server. 

 The application enforces true human governance. It separates raw notes, candidate interpretation, approved truth, and generated repair into distinct stages. 

 The export is portable. agent-world.md gives future agents a verified operating file they can reuse instead of starting from an ungrounded prompt. 

 The system is not limited to one demo case. The same 9-slot spine works across seven sectors while preserving sector-specific language. 

 The WebMCP implementation is testable. The contract suite verifies the core tool calls and state transitions. 

 What We Learned 

 Building SOUND Buoy with WebMCP showed us that the next step for web apps is not just better UI for humans. It is better shared workspaces for humans and agents. 

 When an application exposes structured tools, an agent does not have to guess how the app works by scraping the screen. It can use the app through clear capabilities, schemas, and state boundaries. 

 The most important lesson was that agent capability needs context governance. A powerful agent without approved context can move quickly in the wrong direction. A grounded agent with human-approved operating truth can become a reliable collaborator. 

 What Is Next for SOUND Buoy 

 The next version of SOUND Buoy will add live read-only adapters for platforms like Spotify for Artists, Google Analytics 4, Stripe, Humanitix, and CRM systems. The goal is to let users combine raw human notes with verified platform signals. 

 We also want to support multi-agent review inside the approved boundary. For example, a financial agent and a creative director agent could inspect the same agent-world.md and recommend different repairs without overwriting the approved truth. 

 Longer term, SOUND Buoy can become an opt-in benchmarking layer. Creators, venues, publications, and agencies could compare operational health against anonymized sector patterns while keeping their private context under human co

title: Hi AUDIT Triage Room
pitch: Turn security findings into a shared, actionable remediation plan with your browser agent.
about_excerpt: Turn security findings into a shared, actionable remediation plan with your browser agent. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Security review becomes slow when findings live in a dense dashboard while an agent must guess its way through pixels—or when the agent works in a separate chat that the human cannot easily verify. We built Hi AUDIT Triage Room so both can work from the same structured, visible security workspace. What it does Hi AUDIT Triage Room is a shared security-triage workspace for a person and their browser agent. It exposes a fixed synthetic audit scenario through seven imperative WebMCP tools. Together, a user and agent can inspect the workspace, focus the visible findings, review evidence, record status and priority with a rationale, build a phased remediation plan, and verify that the structured result matches the page. The important interaction is not “agent clicks dashboard buttons.” The agent works with security outcomes—scope, findings, decisions, and plan tasks—while every change appears in the same interface the person is reviewing. The user can take over at any point with normal controls, and the shared activity trail makes authorship visible. The public demo contains five clearly labeled synthetic findings and never uploads source code or claims to scan a real repository. Why WebMCP is a good fit Security findings are dense, structured, and consequential. Asking an agent to infer them from pixels is fragile, while hiding the work in a chat makes human review difficult. WebMCP gives the agent narrow, typed capabilities and keeps the human-facing UI as the source of shared context. Read tools let the agent ground itself before acting. Write tools update the same browser-local state as the human controls. A final read-back tool lets the agent verify the plan that is visibly on screen. This creates a legible human-in-the-loop workflow rather than a parallel automation channel. How it was built The challenge experience is a Next.js 16 and React 19 Client Component. At the top-level /webmcp route it feature-detects document.modelContext and registers seven tools: get_audit_workspace set_audit_scope filter_findings get_finding_details triage_finding build_remediation_plan get_remediation_plan Each tool has a narrow JSON Schema plus runtime validation. Read-only tools use readOnlyHint ; responses containing synthetic code evidence also use untrustedContentHint . Registration is cancelled with an AbortController on cleanup or partial failure. The state is stored locally in the browser, and defensive validation safely discards malformed persisted data. Browsers without WebMCP still get the complete human interface. Challenges The hardest part was making one state model safe and understandable for two actors. Tool calls needed to update the UI immediately without stale React closures, while human edits needed to be visible to the next agent call. A ref backs the current state for tool execution, React renders it, and local storage provides deterministic reloads. We also handled development Strict Mode, partial tool-registration failures, runtime input checks, cancellation, responsive layout, reduced motion, and accessible status controls. Accomplishments Seven working WebMCP tools were exercised in ChatGPT's in-app browser. Agent actions and human actions use the same state and activity trail. A complete workflow goes from five findings to focused release blockers, documented triage, and a six-step remediation plan. The experience remains useful in a browser without WebMCP. The demo is deterministic, transparent about synthetic data, and requires no account, secret, or environment variable. What we learned The best site tools model domain outcomes, not UI mechanics. Small schemas and explicit read-back tools make agent behavior easier to guide and verify. We also learned that feature detection and cleanup are part of the experience: the human UI must remain trustworthy even when tool support is absent or registration is interrupted. What's next We plan to connect the same interaction model to authenticated Hi AUDIT scans, add approval gates before high-impact workflow changes, attach ownership and due dates to plan tasks, and export approved plans to engineering trackers. Production connections will retain the product's existing authorization and audit boundaries rather than trusting tool schemas as a security boundary. title: Ombuds
pitch: A form that teaches the agent how to fill it, refuses the answers it cannot accept, corrects the agent when it is wrong, and hands every value to a human before it counts.
about_excerpt: A form that teaches the agent how to fill it, refuses the answers it cannot accept, corrects the agent when it is wrong, and hands every value to a human before it counts. Like Comment Story Updates What it does Ombuds is a work authorization worksheet, rebuilt so that the page is the authority instead of the agent. The worst forms on the web are long conditional government forms. A work authorization application asks you for an eligibility category code, and that one answer silently rewrites which of the next forty questions apply to you. Pick category c(3)(C) and you now owe a CIP code and an employer E-Verify number. Pick c(9) and neither of those exists, and you owe an I-485 receipt number instead. Say you want a Social Security card and both your parents' names become mandatory. None of this is written down anywhere the form can show you. It lives in footnotes and in the head of whoever has filled one out before. Agents are bad at these forms for the same reason people are. An agent reading the screen has no way to know that picking a category changed the rules. A backend MCP server cannot help either, because it has no idea what the person sitting in the browser has already answered. Ombuds moves the rules into the page and hands them to the agent directly. You talk to your agent in plain language about your situation. The page tells the agent exactly which questions apply to you right now, gives it the precise list of values each answer accepts, rejects anything malformed with the actual rule and a valid example so the agent fixes itself, and then holds every single value in a review queue until you personally accept it. Nothing an agent says about your immigration status is true until you agree with it. Three things it deliberately will not do. It will not tick your certification, because only the person filing can attest to their own application, so there is no tool for it at all. It will not give legal consent on your behalf, so the field authorizing disclosure to the Social Security Administration refuses agent writes outright. It will not let you generate your filing packet until every section is valid, your review queue is empty, and you have signed by hand. It is an independent worksheet. It is not affiliated with USCIS, it does not file anything, and everything stays in the browser tab. Inspiration I spent a year doing missionary work in Cambodia and watched people lose months to paperwork written as though the rules were obvious. The rules are never obvious. Putting them in the page, where an agent can be told them directly and a person can still overrule the answer, is a better use of this standard than making a shopping cart marginally faster. How I used WebMCP Eight mechanics. The first five are things WebMCP can do that a backend integration structurally cannot. 1. The tool schemas are generated from live form state. answer-category-questions is one tool with one name. Its schema is assembled from whichever eligibility category you picked. Category c(9) advertises a single field. Category c(3)(C) advertises four completely different ones. Change your category and the tool is unregistered and registered again with an entirely different shape. A server-side tool would have to accept a vague bag of optional strings and hope for the best. This one accepts exactly the four things you actually owe and rejects anything else as FIELD_NOT_APPLICABLE. Every enum is generated the same way from the same lists the HTML renders, so an agent cannot invent a state code or a category code, because the accepted values are sitting in the schema it was handed. 2. One predicate drives both the human UI and the agent's schema. Every conditional field carries a single showWhen function. The renderer uses it to decide whether to draw an input. The WebMCP layer uses the same one to decide whether that field belongs in the tool's schema. The human and the agent are looking at the same form, always, because there is only one description of the form and it cannot drift out of step with itself. 3. Tools appear and disappear so the agent only ever sees a legal move. Sections unlock as their prerequisites become valid, and a section's tool exists only while that section is open. Before Part 1 is valid there is no set-personal-info to call. Answer no to having used other names and add-other-name is not disabled, it is gone. Say your mailing address is where you live and set-physical-address unregisters itself. The agent gets a state machine rather than a flat API, and toolchange tells it when the machine moved. The sidebar shows the live registered set so you can watch tools flash in and out as you answer. 4. Rejections are structured, so the agent corrects itself. The page owns the validation rules, so it can hand back something an agent can act on instead of a red border. Send a bad SEVIS number and you get a machine-readable code, the rule in plain language, where to find the real value on your Form I-20, and a concrete valid example. The agent reads that and fixes its own argument on the next call. Nobody retypes anything. Cross-field conflicts work the same way. Claim category c(3)(C) while declaring H-1B status and you get the specific contradiction with both responsible fields named, because that is the class of error that actually gets real filings bounced back weeks later. 5. Nothing an agent writes is true until a human agrees. State is kept in two layers. Committed values are what the applicant accepted. Pending values are what the agent proposed. Proposals are validated the instant they arrive so the agent gets its feedback immediately without waiting on a human, and they surface in the page as amber diff cards with accept and reject buttons. Only a human click promotes a value. 6. Both halves of the spec, each where it fits. The imperative API carries the conditional sections, because branching logic is exactly what a form cannot express. The category finder at the top of the page is a declarative <form> carrying toolname , tooldescription and toolparamdescription , which a supporting browser turns into a tool with no registerTool call at all, and its submit handler answers the agent through SubmitEvent#respondWith() so the page never navigates away and throws out the conversation. Declarative suits that panel because it is a flat search over a fixed list. One ranked search with synonym expansion backs both paths, so a person typing "spouse of an H-1B worker" and an agent sending the same words get the same answer. Using each API where it fits is the argument the WebMCP explainer itself makes, and building both is what made me believe it. The tag beside the finder reports whether the browser actually synthesized the declarative tool rather than inferring it from a version number, and declarative calls are badged separately in the call log. 7. Tools that cross an origin boundary. The document vault at the bottom of the page is a separate service on its own origin, embedded in an iframe carrying allow="tools" so the permissions policy lets it register tools at all. It registers with exposedTo naming only the form's origin, and the form discovers them with getTools({ fromOrigins: [...] }) and runs them through executeTool . The browser refuses the call unless both halves agree. The point of the split is the trust boundary. The form asks whether a required document exists and when it lapses, and never receives the document. A form that stored your passport scan is a different product with a different risk profile, and only tools that carry an origin can express that difference. The payoff chains both origins: the precheck builds a document checklist here from your eligibility category, then each line is resolved by a tool running over there, coming back as on file, expiring, expired, or missing. My own I-20 line comes back expired, which is the kind of thing you would otherwise learn by mail. Cross-origin exposedTo needs browser support the origin trial does not universally have yet, so the same tools are also reachable over a postMessage bridge with a deliberately identical shape. The calling code does not branch, and the panel reports which transport is actually live rather than claiming the stronger one. Both paths enforce the same origin allowlist, and a probe from a disallowed host origin gets no reply at all. 8. A working answer to an open question in the standard. WebMCP Issue #165 is open on how a tool should prompt the user for explicit authorization mid-execution. No API for it exists yet, so I built one from what the spec already provides, since execute may return a promise and it receives an AbortSignal. request-certification suspends until a person clicks. The page raises the question with the agent's own note attached, cancellation propagates and clears it, and there is no code path by which the agent produces its own approval. An agent may ask for a signature. Only a human can supply one. That replaced an earlier des

title: LaunchPad
pitch: An evidence factory where browser agents research, challenge, and trace one defensible solution while humans retain control of sensitive decisions.
about_excerpt: An evidence factory where browser agents research, challenge, and trace one defensible solution while humans retain control of sensitive decisions. Like Comment Story Updates Short summary LaunchPad turns one messy problem into one evidence-backed solution. A WebMCP-capable browser agent works inside the same live workspace as the human: it reads the current state, researches evidence, closes explicit gaps, tests counterfactual evidence policies, preserves counter-signals, and traces every recommendation component back to its source. Human consent remains mandatory for evidence acceptance, finalization, and private-data export. What it does Most research agents end with a persuasive answer. LaunchPad ends with an auditable decision. A person enters a real product or business problem. LaunchPad plans the research, collects and validates sources, extracts atomic findings, preserves counter-evidence, synthesizes mechanisms, generates candidate solutions, stress-tests them, and returns one recommendation with a concrete validation plan. The result includes the full lineage from each proposed feature to the insight, finding, and source that supports it. The interface is a live production line rather than a chat transcript. The human can see the current stage, the evidence ledger, the selected candidate, the gaps that remain, and every workspace version transition. The agent operates that exact workspace through WebMCP instead of copying context into a separate assistant conversation. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP This workflow depends on state that only the current page truly knows: the active problem brief, research stage, current evidence, privacy scope, policy, selected candidate, stale-version boundary, and consent status. A conventional chatbot must ask the user to paste that context, risks acting on an old snapshot, and cannot prove that its answer matches what the page displays. WebMCP makes the browser page an agent-operable evidence environment: The agent discovers only the tools valid for the current workflow stage. Pure read tools expose live state, gaps, candidate structure, proof traces, and previews without mutating anything. Mutation tools return compact receipts with before/after workspace versions, modified IDs, recovery guidance, and useful next operations. Browser-found evidence enters atomically with provenance, retrieval time, evidence lane, caveat, and public/private scope. Policy comparison answers questions such as “What changes if we exclude community sources or require two independent sources?” without modifying the ledger. Apply and rollback make policy effects visible and reversible. Evidence review, finalization, and private export pause at visible human-consent dialogs bound to exact finding IDs and the current workspace version. A stale agent call fails safely instead of silently overwriting newer human work. The result is not “an AI button.” It is a long-running human-agent collaboration with live shared state, explicit authority boundaries, recoverable operations, and proof that survives the final answer. What people and agents can do together now Before LaunchPad, a researcher could ask an agent to browse, then manually move citations into a document, reconcile contradictions, rerun the analysis under a stricter policy, and hope the final recommendation still matched the evidence. That process loses provenance and makes it hard to tell which decision changed and why. With LaunchPad, the human sets the mission and retains responsibility while the agent performs the high-volume work: Read the exact live state and identify the next evidence gap. Search different evidence lanes and ingest a provenance-rich batch. Preserve negative or contradictory evidence instead of optimizing it away. Compare a stricter policy as a pure preview. Apply or roll back that policy and see the candidate ranking change on the same page. Ask for human approval before committing sensitive judgments. Trace any final feature through component → insight → finding → source. Export a public-safe blueprint that automatically excludes private evidence. Humans supply intent, judgment, and consent. Agents supply breadth, repetition, gap closure, and exact stateful operations. The product makes that division of responsibility visible. How WebMCP is implemented LaunchPad registers a stage-aware catalog through document.modelContext.registerTool . The catalog grows and contracts as the workspace moves through planning, research, evidence review, synthesis, ideation, stress testing, and finalization. The full implementation exposes 22 tools, including: get_foundry_state , get_evidence_gaps , inspect_candidate , and trace_evidence for pure inspection; plan_research , search_sources , ingest_evidence_batch , extract_findings , synthesize_insights , and generate_idea_candidates for the evidence workflow; compare_evidence_policy , apply_evidence_policy , and rollback behavior for reversible counterfactual analysis; review_evidence_with_consent , finalize_blueprint_with_consent , and export_blueprint_with_consent for human-authorized commits; preview_finalization and preview_export so an agent can inspect the consequence before requesting consent. Schemas reject undeclared fields. Pure reads carry read-only hints. Evidence-returning tools mark untrusted content. Registration is asynchronous and abortable, and the UI reports readiness only after every stage-valid tool has registered. Receipts are capped so the agent gets the information needed for its next move without flooding context. The same TypeScript domain service owns page interactions and WebMCP calls, so the browser agent cannot drift into a hidden parallel workflow. State changes use optimistic workspace versions. Connected evidence retains its origin and privacy scope. Public export is generated from the same graph but omits private evidence by construction. Demonstrated WebMCP journey The final public build was exercised inside ChatGPT’s in-app browser against the exact judging URL. The browser discovered the 22-tool stage-aware catalog and completed 26 calls from workspace version 1 to version 19: six evidence lanes searched; nine findings extracted, including a retained caution; human evidence review completed; five insights and three candidates generated; a stricter evidence policy compared, applied, and rolled back; the selected candidate inspected and stress-tested; a four-hop proof path traced; finalization previewed and approved; a public-safe Markdown blueprint exported. The winning candidate in this reproducible mission was Admin Guild , supported by eight findings and one caution, with 100% component coverage. The final reload preserved the finalized workspace, showed the completed run state, and produced zero browser console errors. The exact receipts are recorded in artifacts/demo/webmcp-journey.json . What was added during the submission period LaunchPad is an existing project that was materially rebuilt for the WebMCP Challenge after August 25, 2026. The hackathon work transformed an early agent surface into a WebMCP-native evidence system: expanded the catalog from 17 general tools to 22 stage-aware tools; removed mutation from legacy read behavior and added explicit pure previews; added batch provenance and privacy-aware ingestion; added evidence-gap actions and counter-evidence requirements; added pure policy comparison, non-destructive apply, and rollback; added version-bound consent for review, finalization, and private export; added compact versioned receipts, stale-version recovery, and agent-visible next operations; added an in-page judge mission and WebMCP activity rail; added provider-backed tool-selection evals covering ambiguity, denied consent, stale state, and mid-chain recovery; ran and recorded a 26-call production journey on the final public deployment; added regression coverage for the shared human/WebMCP workflow and finalized UI state. Challenges The hardest problem was not registering many tools; it was designing a trustworthy protocol for a long-running agent workflow. Reads had to be truly pure. Mutations needed version boundaries. Evidence from a browser had to remain untrusted until reviewed. Private evidence could not leak into public export. And the interface had to make all of this understandable to a judge without exposing implementation noise. A second challenge was eval honesty. The configured provider-backed selection harness completed a rich live run in which four cases passed before the provider account began returning HTTP 429. The committed report records the rate limit rather than fabricating a green result. Independent deterministic tests and the complete production browser journey remain green. Accomplishments A complete, coherent product experience rather than a tool-registration demo. 22 stage-aware WebMCP tools sharing one state machine with the visible UI. Human consent and stale-version safety for consequential actions.
video_title: LaunchPad — The Trust Layer for AI Business Decisions | WebMCP
video_transcript_excerpt: Hi, I'm Casey and I built Launchpad because teams are making expensive decisions with a process that is far more fragile than it looks. Imagine your product lead deciding what to build next. You have customer conversations in one place, market research in another, a handful of promising links, conflicting feedback, and an AI summary that sounds convincing. But you can't tell exactly why it made the recommendation. So the real work begins after the answer. Someone has to check the sources, find what's missing, reconcile contradictions, and defend the decision in the next morning. That is the business problem Launchpad solves. Launchpad is a decision intelligence workspace for product, research, and strategy teams. It turns a messy question into one evidence-backed recommendation that the whole team can actually inspect, challenge, and act on. What makes it different is that it doesn't treat AI as a black box that gives you a polished conclusion. The agents works inside the live workspace, finds the gaps in the evidence, gathers support and counter evidence, and shows exactly what changed. If the team decides to trust only recent public sources or raise the standard for corroboration, Launchpad can show how that policy changes the recommendation before anyone commits to it. And when someone asks, "Why are we building this feature?" Launchpad can trace that decision all the way back to the insight, finding, and original source. This is what companies would pay for, not another AI answer, but faster decisions that are still defensible. Less time stitching research together. Less rework when someone challenges the logic. More confidence when a team needs to put real money, engineering time, and reputation behind a choice. WebMCP is what makes that collaboration real. The agent is just the same live browser context the team sees, while people keep control of sensitive evidence, policy changes, and final approval. We start with product and strategy teams, where one wrong bet can cost months. But the bigger opportunity is becoming the trust layer between AI research and real business decisions. Launchpad doesn't just help teams move faster. It helps them know what they can stand behind. Thank you.

title: FinalPick
pitch: FinalPick turns human choices between AI generated text and image option into reusable decision memory, while 6 WebMCP tools help agents prepare reviews without taking final authority away from people
about_excerpt: FinalPick turns human choices between AI generated text and image option into reusable decision memory, while 6 WebMCP tools help agents prepare reviews without taking final authority away from people Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI gives creative teams more options than ever, but the reasoning behind a final choice often disappears in chat, spreadsheets, or handoff notes. The next teammate or model sees the result without knowing the brief, rejected alternatives, or why the decision made sense at that moment. We built FinalPick around a question raised by agentic browsing: how can an agent reduce review work without quietly taking over human judgment? What it does FinalPick is a browser-based decision workspace for reviewing actual text and image candidates. Each round contains one medium, a brief, constraints, and evidence, so options are compared on equal terms. A person selects a candidate, records reasons and an optional note, and saves that context as decision memory. In later rounds, FinalPick requires a current assessment before revealing compatible past decisions as useful, non-binding precedent. Six WebMCP tools let an agent inspect the review and candidates, retrieve precedent, and stage a comparison or follow-up question in the same visible interface. The agent can commit only after a person creates a short-lived, one-time approval in the page. How we built it We built FinalPick as a static top-level web app using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript ES modules, with localStorage for versioned rounds, staged work, and decisions. When a browser exposes document.modelContext.registerTool , the page registers six narrow WebMCP tools; without it, the complete human workflow still works. Tool schemas reject extra fields, read tools are annotated as read-only, and UI actions and tool handlers share the same validated state layer. We used Codex in a recursive improvement loop: define a small slice, implement it, run unit and Playwright browser checks, inspect responsive captures and UX feedback, then use those findings to shape the next slice. This loop expanded the prototype from built-in image examples to user-created text and HTTPS-image rounds while preserving the authority boundary. Challenges we ran into The hardest challenge was making WebMCP essential rather than decorative. A chat recommendation alone would not improve the product, so agent work had to appear visibly in the review and reduce copying between systems. We also had to make chained tool calls reliable by returning the candidate, analysis, decision, and approval identifiers needed by later calls. Human approval introduced edge cases around changed selections, expiration, cancellation, and token reuse. Finally, early screens felt like dense metadata dashboards, so we progressively disclosed evidence, agent staging, and history while keeping the creative artifact and decision controls prominent. Accomplishments that we're proud of The prototype supports complete create, select, save, and reload flows for real text and image candidates. It registers exactly six WebMCP tools in the local integration harness, keeps staged agent work visibly separate from committed decisions, and rejects missing, revoked, expired, or reused approvals. Decision memory preserves the brief, chosen artifact, reasons, note, and later superseded revisions. The current verification suite reports 27 passing unit tests, a successful static build, six registered tools in the browser roundtrip, responsive desktop and mobile captures, and no browser console errors. What we learned Structured tools are most useful when they act on the same state people can see, not when they create a second agent-only workflow. Human control is stronger when enforced by application state—here, an approval that no WebMCP tool can create—rather than by prompt wording. We also learned that memory should provide context, not automatic preference: showing what changed between then and now makes precedent useful without turning it into a hidden scoring model. What's next for FinalPick Next, we want to harden hosted-browser interoperability across supported ChatGPT configurations and test the workflow with more first-time users. Beyond the prototype, we would add collaborative persistence, accounts, richer asset versioning and uploads, and explicit review or dispute states only after designing the necessary permission, privacy, retention, and conflict-resolution rules. title: WebMCP Demo — a live map for thinking with your own agent
pitch: Put down what you want to think through. Your own ChatGPT grows the map with you — and it becomes a plan.
about_excerpt: Put down what you want to think through. Your own ChatGPT grows the map with you — and it becomes a plan. Like Comment Story Updates The live map: your own ChatGPT asks questions, clears "don't know" marks, and turns branches into checkable tasks — via 6 WebMCP tools. What it does Most WebMCP demos let an agent operate a site's transactional surface — fill a form, add to cart. This project inverts that: the page is a blank thinking canvas, and the tools it publishes are generative . You put down one thing you want to figure out ("I want to buy my first home"), and your own ChatGPT — with your context and memory — thinks with you on the map: It starts by asking questions as nodes , not by dumping a plan. You answer by growing branches yourself ; every edit you make on the canvas is delivered to the agent on its next tool call. Mark anything with "Don't know" and your confusion literally becomes the agenda — the agent clears those marks first, with concrete first steps. Steps become checkable task nodes , a Plan view folds the map into goal / premises / next tasks, and checking a task off in either place updates both. The page runs no AI of its own . It publishes six WebMCP tools; the visitor brings the intelligence. Thoughtful use of WebMCP The interesting problems turned out to be protocol-level, and we solved them in ways any WebMCP app can reuse: Read-before-write, enforced server-side. read_map returns a state token; every write requires it. A stale or missing token gets a 409 whose error text steers the agent back to read_map . The guard doubles as optimistic locking between the human and the agent. Human actions as first-class input. Everything the human does on the canvas (add, edit, move, delete, mark, check) is queued and delivered inside the next tool result — with a consuming read reserved for the agent and a non-consuming variant ( ?deliver=0 ) for the page's own refreshes, so the UI can never starve the agent of events. Granularity enforced by schema, not prose. add_nodes accepts at most 3 nodes per call (schema + server both), because a map that fills up in one shot stops feeling like a conversation. A capability split that matches the relationship. Agents can add, annotate, resolve, remove, and bulk-arrange — but the layout engine owns placement, and destructive actions on human-placed nodes are steered to require conversation first. Robust registration in the real world. Tools register before app mount, tolerate late injection of navigator.modelContext / document.modelContext (ChatGPT's browser and Chrome differ), and the footer shows live tool status for devtools-less in-app browsers. Why it matters "I know what I want, but not the way there" is a universal state — buying a home, relocating, incorporating, a first tax return. Chat alone answers and scrolls away; to-do apps assume you already know the steps. A shared, persistent map that your own agent can touch bridges the two: the conversation leaves a structure, and the structure becomes a plan you can execute and check off. Because the page hosts no model and pays no inference cost, this pattern is adoptable by any site: publish tools, let visitors bring their agents. How we built it Go + Postgres single-origin service (API, SSE live updates, static React/TypeScript SPA) on Render. The canvas is Miro-like: pan/zoom, drag, click-to-grow, right-click menu. A height-aware tidy-tree layout engine keeps the map clean after every structural change, verified against real DOM rects. WebMCP tool descriptions live in one file — they were the main behavior-tuning surface, iterated against the real ChatGPT desktop browser. What's next Multiple maps as a shelf, session-to-session continuity ("continue from where the fog cleared last week"), and the same canvas working with other WebMCP-capable agents out of the box. title: WebMCPify
pitch: WebMCPify converts existing Forms on an HTML to be WebMCP ready for Agents to interact with the Website directly, which will substantially reduce efforts for Dev Team
about_excerpt:
WebMCPify converts existing Forms on an HTML to be WebMCP ready for Agents to interact with the Website directly, which will substantially reduce efforts for Dev Team

 Home page of Project 
 
 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 The web has been built primarily for human interaction, while the next generation of applications will increasingly be accessed by AI agents. Today, agents often have to scrape the DOM, interpret screenshots, and simulate clicks and form inputs—making interaction fragile, slow, and highly dependent on page structure. 

 With WebMCP, websites can expose structured, machine-readable tools and page states that AI agents can understand and interact with directly. This inspired us to ask: How can we make the billions of existing websites ready for this agentic web without forcing developers to rebuild them? 

 That led to WebMCPify - a simple bridge that transforms existing HTML forms into WebMCP-ready interfaces. 

 What it does 

 WebMCPify converts existing web forms into WebMCP-ready tools that AI agents can discover and interact with directly. 

 For example, traditional automated form testing typically requires developers to: 

 
 Identify form fields and attributes 
 Write automation scripts to populate and submit the form 
 Execute and maintain those scripts 
 

 With WebMCPify, the existing form can expose a structured tool interface to an AI agent. The agent can understand the available inputs, provide the required values, interact with the form, and execute the desired action - without manually hard-wiring the DOM elements or writing custom interaction scripts. 

 In essence, WebMCPify turns “web pages built for humans” into “web pages ready for AI agents.” 

 How we built it 

 We built WebMCPify as a lightweight transformation layer between existing HTML pages and AI agents. 

 The solution analyzes existing web forms, identifies their structure and input elements, and generates the required WebMCP-compatible tool definitions and interactions. This allows an AI agent to discover what Tools are available, understand the required inputs, and invoke those actions through a structured interface rather than relying on visual or DOM-based guessing. 

 Our approach focuses on bringing WebMCP capabilities to existing websites with minimal or no changes to the underlying application. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The biggest challenge was bridging the gap between unstructured legacy web interfaces and structured agent interactions . 

 Existing forms can have inconsistent HTML structures, different input types, validation mechanisms, dynamic fields, and complex submission workflows. We needed to determine how these elements could be reliably interpreted and represented as tools that an AI agent can understand. 

 Another challenge was ensuring that the generated interface remains aligned with the website's actual behavior, particularly when forms contain client-side validation, dynamic states, or dependencies between fields. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We demonstrated that an existing web form can be transformed into an AI-agent-ready interface without requiring developers to manually identify every form attribute and write custom automation scripts. 

 Our biggest accomplishment is proving the concept of “WebMCP enablement without rebuilding the web.” 

 WebMCPify has the potential to significantly simplify agent-based website testing and, more broadly, enable AI agents to interact with existing web applications through structured contracts rather than fragile screen scraping and DOM automation. 

 What we learned 

 We learned that the biggest opportunity in the agentic web may not be creating new AI-native websites—it may be making the existing web agent-ready. 

 We also learned that structured tool contracts can fundamentally change how agents interact with applications. Instead of asking an AI to figure out how to use a website , we can give it a clear interface describing what the website can do, what inputs it needs, and what state it can produce. 

 This can make agent interactions more reliable, deterministic, maintainable, and scalable. 

 What's next for WebMCPify 

 Our next step is to evolve WebMCPify from a form converter into a broader “Agentification Layer for the Web.” 

 Future capabilities could include: 

 
 Automatic WebMCP discovery across complete websites, not just forms 
 Conversion of buttons, search, navigation, APIs and workflows into agent-accessible tools 
 Support for dynamic and multi-step forms 
 Automatic generation of tool descriptions and schemas 
 AI-powered mapping of complex legacy web applications to WebMCP 
 Integration with AI-powered testing agents for autonomous functional testing 
 A browser extension/developer tool that can WebMCPify a website with one click 
 Enterprise capabilities around security, authorization, governance and observability 
 

 The vision 

 WebMCPify aims to make the existing web ready for the agentic era—turning billions of human-first web pages into structured, discoverable and AI-agent-ready experiences.

title: Capability Navigator - Give browser agents tools, not pixels
pitch: Capability Navigator uses WebMCP to turn vague software needs into typed, evidence-backed decision packets. Browser agents use explicit tools while humans keep the final decision.
about_excerpt: Capability Navigator uses WebMCP to turn vague software needs into typed, evidence-backed decision packets. Browser agents use explicit tools while humans keep the final decision. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most people do not arrive at a software website with a perfect technical specification. They arrive with a problem: I need public data to make sense on mobile. I need a field workflow that still works offline. I need to replace a fragile manual process. A human can spend time translating that need into a vendor's vocabulary. A browser agent has an even stranger problem: it usually has to infer what a website means from pixels, labels, buttons, and page structure. That led to the core idea behind Capability Navigator: Agents shouldn't have to guess what your website means. Give them tools, not pixels. WebMCP made it possible to explore what a more agent-native web could look like—one where a website exposes the small set of actions it genuinely understands while keeping evidence, uncertainty, and final authority visible to the human. What it does Capability Navigator turns a fuzzy software need into an evidence-backed, nonbinding decision packet. The human interface and the browser agent share the same capability model, evidence, constraints, and decision surface . On a WebMCP-enabled browser, the page registers six typed tools: list_capabilities get_capability find_examples draft_scope prepare_decision_packet stage_human_review An agent can discover relevant capabilities, inspect their proof boundaries, find public evidence, draft a bounded scope, prepare a structured recommendation, and finally stage that recommendation directly into the visible page for human review. The last step is important. The goal is not invisible automation. The agent's work converges back into the interface the person is already looking at. Every WebMCP invocation is reflected in the visible Agent Trace , so the user can see what tool was called, what bounded input was used, and whether it succeeded. Five tools are read-only. stage_human_review changes only reversible state in the current browser tab. It cannot contact anyone, submit anything, make a payment, sign something, modify an account, or persist a decision. The human remains the authority boundary. How we built it Capability Navigator uses the WebMCP Imperative API and registers its tools through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . Each tool has a deliberately narrow purpose, explicit JSON Schema, agent-facing parameter descriptions, annotations, bounded outputs, and additional runtime validation. We do not rely on schema validation alone: malformed types, unsupported capability IDs, oversized inputs, and empty selections fail visibly rather than producing a plausible-looking recommendation. The same deterministic JavaScript core powers both the human workflow and the WebMCP tools. There is no separate "agent truth" hidden behind the interface. Natural-language discovery is deterministic and tied directly to the public capability and evidence model. That keeps the demo reproducible and avoids requiring an external AI model or search service just to determine what the website itself knows. The production deployment is also configured specifically for WebMCP's browser requirements, including origin isolation and the tools=(self) permissions policy. The project includes an ordinary-browser fallback, responsive/mobile behavior, accessibility safeguards, deterministic regression tests, a release preflight, and a short judge path printed directly on the product. Challenges The hardest part was not simply registering a tool. It was deciding what authority an agent should actually have . A single giant "do everything" tool would have made the demo easier, but it would also undermine the point of the project. We instead separated discovery, evidence inspection, scope generation, packet preparation, and human handoff into small tools with different authority boundaries. Another challenge was making the agent behavior judgeable. A technically successful WebMCP call hidden in a console is not a good human experience, so we added the visible Agent Trace and made stage_human_review update the same decision surface the human uses. We also had to handle the progressive-enhancement boundary correctly. In a browser without WebMCP, the product still works and truthfully reports that WebMCP is unavailable; it does not pretend that six tools were registered simply because six tools are defined. Finally, we spent substantial time on failure behavior: malformed inputs, unknown IDs, empty selections, output limits, mobile overflow, reduced motion, deployment headers, and distinguishing an actual WebMCP execution from a normal UI interaction. What we learned The biggest lesson is that WebMCP is more interesting than "letting an AI click a website faster." The website itself knows the semantics of its domain. When those semantics become a typed browser contract, an agent can operate with far less guesswork—and the developer can define much clearer limits around what the agent may do. We also learned that human-in-the-loop does not have to mean bolting an approval modal onto the end of autonomous behavior . The human and agent can share state from the beginning: the same evidence, the same constraints, and the same visible output. That feels like a promising direction for the open web. What was built during the challenge Maps + Apps and the public case-study evidence used by Capability Navigator existed before the challenge. The WebMCP-specific product layer was built or meaningfully extended during the challenge period: the typed browser tools and schemas, deterministic capability discovery, evidence-aware lookup, decision-packet generation, visible Agent Trace, shared human/agent review surface, reversible local staging, safety validation, ordinary-browser fallback, judge workflow, testing, and challenge release packaging. What's next Capability Navigator is intentionally narrow today, but the pattern is much larger. A travel site could expose trip-planning primitives. A government portal could expose eligibility and application-preparation tools. A healthcare site could expose carefully bounded navigation tools. A software company could expose capability discovery without giving an agent permission to initiate sales actions. The idea is simple: A website should not have to be only a collection of pixels that an agent learns to operate. It can become a collaborator with an explicit contract. I defined the human/agent workflow, designed the six typed WebMCP tools and their safety boundaries, built the shared capability and evidence model, implemented the visible Agent Trace and Human Review handoff, and coordinated QA, deployment, browser verification, documentation, and the final demo. title: AgentAds
pitch: The web runs on ads — agents don't see ads. AgentAds auctions a sponsored slot in your page's WebMCP tools: one script tag, quality beats money, and the site owner is paid per agent call
about_excerpt: The web runs on ads — agents don't see ads. AgentAds auctions a sponsored slot in your page's WebMCP tools: one script tag, quality beats money, and the site owner is paid per agent call Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration The web pays for itself with advertising — and agents don't see ads. As browsing shifts to agents, every publisher's ad revenue quietly disappears: no banner impressions, no clicks, just crawlers reading content for free. At Oasy we work on exactly this problem — we call it the advertising layer for the AI era. WebMCP made us ask a sharper question: if a page can now offer tools to an agent, then the scarce, valuable surface is no longer the viewport — it's the agent's tool list . Someone will run the auction for that surface. We wanted to prove it can be run honestly: in the open, quality-weighted, disclosed, and additive — instead of as paid steering buried somewhere in a model's context. What it does AgentAds is an ad auction that lives inside a page's WebMCP tools. Our demo site is a fictional editorial publisher. It exposes its articles as regular WebMCP tools ( list_articles , read_article , search_articles ), with a human-visible panel showing the exact tool list an agent sees — one-click try buttons, live call log. Humans and agents literally share the same tools. Then one script tag adds the AgentAds SDK: <script src="/agentads-sdk.js" data-publisher="oasy-demo" defer></script> On page load, the SDK: Detects the page context (an article about a musician → music ). Runs an auction : every advertiser in that category bids per tool call, ranked by $\mathrm{adRank} = \mathrm{rankScore} \times \mathrm{bid}$. The rankScore is computed live from how agents actually behave: $$\mathrm{rankScore} = (1-w)\cdot \mathrm{prior} + w\cdot\left(0.7\cdot\frac{\mathrm{calls}}{\mathrm{impressions}} + 0.3\cdot\frac{\mathrm{conversions}}{\mathrm{calls}}\right),\quad w=\frac{\mathrm{impressions}}{\mathrm{impressions}+20}$$ Registers the winner as one extra, disclosed tool — its description opens with [SPONSORED · advertiser] . Sponsored tools sit next to the site's own tools, never in their place. Nothing is injected into content; the agent decides whether it's worth calling. Pays the publisher per call : the winner pays a quality-weighted second price, $\mathrm{price} = \mathrm{adRank}_2 / \mathrm{rankScore}_1$, capped at its own bid — and 70% of every call goes to the site owner, ticking up live on the page. On our tech article — a deadpan dossier on Atlas-9, the first AI agent with a documented net worth — three advertisers fight for the slot: ClankBank (savings accounts for agents), Captcha & Casualty (liability cover for hallucination claims and prompt-injection incidents), and GPUnow. The insurer bids the most (€0.61) and still loses to the bank, whose rankScore is higher — and the bank then pays only €0.40. The full bidder table, the live telemetry behind each rankScore, the price paid, and the publisher's earnings are all rendered on the page. Nobody has to be tricked: not the user, not the agent, not the site owner. The landing page is an interactive explainer that runs the production auction endpoint, including a "try to buy the slot" slider: crank a weak bidder's bid high enough and it can take the slot — at a punishing second price, which only holds until agents ignoring the tool drag its rankScore back down. How we built it Site : Next.js 15 / React 19 on Vercel. WebMCP layer : a small compat shim supporting both navigator.modelContext and document.modelContext , and both registerTool() and the older provideContext() , via a shared on-page registry — so the site's tools and the SDK's sponsored tools always compose instead of clobbering each other. It also keeps watching for runtimes that inject after page load (extension polyfills, agent browsers) and registers everything the moment one appears. AgentAds SDK : fully standalone vanilla JS, zero dependencies, self-styling widget. Config from the script tag, call/conversion reporting via sendBeacon . Marketplace ( /api/agentads/auction ): a serverless route implementing the quality-weighted generalized second-price auction over a per-category catalog, with rankScores computed per request from live telemetry — impressions the route logs itself, calls from the track endpoint, conversions from attribution pageviews — plus a 10% exploration share that occasionally serves a losing bidder so it can earn the data to climb. A small multi-armed bandit, in production. Measurement : every impression, call, and conversion lands in the same event store; the /stats page shows the raw per-offer telemetry the rankScores are computed from. Challenges we ran into WebMCP is a moving target. The spec migrated between navigator.modelContext and document.modelContext , and implementations disagree on registerTool() vs provideContext() — where provideContext replaces the whole toolset, which is fatal when two independent parties (site + ad SDK) register tools on one page. Our shared-registry convention exists because of this. Runtimes that arrive late. Our first version checked for a WebMCP runtime once at load — and silently offered nothing to runtimes injected afterwards. Now both layers watch for ~30 seconds and flip to live registration the moment a runtime appears. Calibrating disclosure. We started with belt-and-braces marking: sponsored_ name prefixes, UI badges, annotations, disclosure text in every result. Testing in ChatGPT's browser showed that over-marking backfires — agents surfaced the annotations as scary "untrusted content" warnings, and the prefixes bloated every tool list. We landed on stating sponsorship exactly once, in the tool description: the one field agents always read. Making the evals real. A hardcoded "quality score" is theater. Wiring rankScore to actual behavior meant solving cold start (priors that fade with data) and the winner-takes-the-data loop (the exploration share) — the difference between claiming quality-weighting and demonstrating it. Accomplishments that we're proud of A closed live loop : agents reading the site right now feed the rankScores that decide the next auction. A sponsored tool agents ignore genuinely loses its slot on its own. Everything visible : the auction table, each winner's impressions/calls/conversions, the second price paid, the publisher's earnings, and every tool call — human or agent — on the page itself. An answer to the incentive problem: an ad market where every party's payoff increases with the sponsored tool actually being useful . Agents are perfect ad-blockers; attention sold to an optimizer is worth nothing, but being the tool an optimizer chooses is worth everything. It works today in ChatGPT's in-app browser, end to end. What we learned Quality-weighting isn't fairness theater — it's what makes advertising possible in agentic contexts at all. An agent's operator can measure task success and switch away instantly, so a marketplace that lets money outrank quality destroys its own inventory. Second-price mechanics matter for the same reason: the equilibrium is advertisers bidding their true value, and winners being the tools that actually help. And on the human side: the best thing we built for trust wasn't a disclosure banner — it was showing the whole machine running, on the page, to everyone. What's next for AgentAds A machine-readable sponsored convention for WebMCP tools, so agent policies can uniformly accept, weight, or strip sponsored capabilities; cost-per-outcome bidding; real settlement rails; and rolling AgentAds into the Oasy publisher stack — analytics, licensing, and monetization for the half of the web that's already agents. title: Sauna Quote X-Ray
pitch: People and AI turn a sauna quote into an honest shared canvas, exposing hidden costs and the exact questions to ask before signing.
about_excerpt: People and AI turn a sauna quote into an honest shared canvas, exposing hidden costs and the exact questions to ask before signing. Like Comment Story Updates The $11,750 quote exposes missing scope and a sourced $12,250–$18,650 planning range. The buyer and agent start from the same visible quote canvas. The quoted $11,750 can reach $18,650 once hidden scope is made visible. Inspiration A sauna quote can look complete while leaving out the electrical circuit, panel upgrade, foundation, permits, assembly, ventilation, or service responsibility. A buyer sees one confident number. The real landed cost can be thousands higher. We built Sauna Quote X-Ray so the buyer and their AI agent can investigate that gap together before anyone signs. What it does Sauna Quote X-Ray turns a sauna quote into a shared, visible decision canvas. The buyer can see and edit every priced item, scope decision, planning range, risk finding, contractor question, and agent action. In the reviewer-safe demo, a quoted total of $11,750 becomes a sourced projected range of $12,250 to $18,650 after missing electrical and site scope is made explicit. The agent can then create the exact questions the buyer should ask the contractor. Why WebMCP This workflow is a strong fit for WebMCP because the source of truth should remain the website, not disappear into a separate chat transcript. The agent is fast at turning ambiguous scope into structured state. The human knows what the seller promised and must retain authority over every assumption. WebMCP lets both act on the same interface: The agent loads or structures the quote. The human sees every change immediately. Either side can correct a line item or scope status. The agent re-reads the visible state and builds the next questions. Nothing is sent or persisted unless the product explicitly adds such a capability. This demo does not. That shared round trip was difficult before WebMCP. A normal chatbot can produce advice, but it cannot reliably keep its work synchronized with the buyer's live, editable decision surface. How we built it The app is a standalone Next.js 16 and React 19 project deployed on Vercel and presented inside Sauna Guide. It registers eight narrow, page-scoped tools through document.modelContext.registerTool() : load_demo_sauna_quote get_sauna_quote_xray_state set_sauna_project_context upsert_sauna_quote_line_item remove_sauna_quote_line_item set_sauna_quote_scope build_sauna_contractor_questions start_sauna_quote_xray The tools and human controls operate on one React state model. Pure TypeScript summary functions calculate completeness, priced exposure, the projected total, and quote-specific questions. The read tool marks seller and user text with untrustedContentHint: true . JSON schemas reject unknown properties and cap strings, arrays, amounts, and line count. Safety and privacy All demos use synthetic quote data. Working state stays in the current tab. No tool uploads a quote, stores customer data, sends email, contacts a seller, or creates a lead. Every agent mutation is visible in the shared activity log and can be corrected by the human. The app links each planning range and risk finding to buyer-facing Sauna Guide sources. It also labels estimates as planning aids rather than contractor quotes. Challenges we ran into The hard part was not registering a tool. It was designing tool boundaries that are useful without quietly crossing the line from analysis into a real commercial action. We separated reading, editing, scope resolution, question building, and reset behavior so each action is explicit and reviewable. We also had to keep React's visible state and WebMCP execution synchronized without stale closures. A state ref feeds tool execution while normal React state renders the same result to the buyer. Accomplishments that we're proud of Eight working WebMCP tools with narrow schemas and explicit safety annotations One shared canvas where human and agent edits stay synchronized A coherent buyer workflow, not a hidden prompt wrapper Safe synthetic fixtures that judges can use without creating a customer lead Automated unit, type, lint, production-build, and browser journey coverage Production verification in ChatGPT's in-app browser with all eight tools discovered and invoked What we learned WebMCP is most valuable when the website already has meaningful state, domain rules, and human controls. The agent becomes a collaborator inside the product instead of a separate destination. We also learned that reversible actions and visible provenance make agent behavior easier to trust. The activity log is not decoration. It is part of the interaction contract. What's next The next step is optional local document parsing that lets a buyer structure their own quote without uploading it to a server. We would also add side-by-side quote comparison, saved local sessions, and a handoff package the buyer can choose to send only after explicit confirmation. Try it Live WebMCP app: https://sauna.guide/tools/sauna-quote-xray Public MIT repository: https://github.com/Ac0AI/sauna-quote-xray Buyer research and source guides: https://sauna.guide Suggested prompt: Load the backyard quote. Make the missing electrical work explicit, flag anything still unclear, and build the contractor questions. Contact nobody. This project was created after the challenge opened on August 25, 2026. The public Git history shows the implementation, safety hardening, tests, deployment, and submission media created on August 27, 2026.
