title: Cadding
pitch: Cadding makes CAD as easy as describing what you want. Create, edit, and export 3D-printable parts with AI, directly in your browser.
about_excerpt: Cadding makes CAD as easy as describing what you want. Create, edit, and export 3D-printable parts with AI, directly in your browser. Like Comment Story Updates Wheel Iphone Cover WebMCP in action Inspiration Cadding was built to make real CAD work faster and more accessible for people who want to design real, 3D-printable objects without having to master complex traditional CAD software. Our goal is not simply to generate 3D meshes from text. Cadding is a browser-based CAD environment where users can create and modify precise, editable geometry, work with multiple parts, and prepare designs that can actually be manufactured and 3D printed. For the WebMCP Challenge, we wanted to take this one step further: make the same CAD environment accessible to external AI agents such as Codex . What we built For the challenge, we connected Cadding's CAD system to WebMCP and exposed 35 structured CAD tools to external agents. These tools give an agent access to a large part of the real Cadding modelling workflow. An agent can: Inspect the complete live CAD scene and understand existing parts Read exact dimensions, parameters, faces, edges and vertices Create primitives and profile-based geometry using extrusions, revolves, sweeps and lofts Change dimensions, positions, rotations and other editable parameters Add holes, fillets, shells and other features Perform boolean operations between parts Create linear and circular patterns Edit topology Align, assemble and mate multiple components Add mechanical connectors and joints Work directly with the same editable CAD scene that the user sees A typical agent workflow can look like: $$ \texttt{cad.get_scene} \rightarrow \texttt{cad.inspect_part} \rightarrow \texttt{cad.get_faces} \rightarrow \texttt{cad.add_profile_shape} \rightarrow \texttt{cad.edit_part} \rightarrow \texttt{cad.fillet_edges} $$ This is important because the agent is not generating an isolated mesh, and it is not trying to control Cadding by guessing where to click. Through WebMCP, the agent operates the actual modelling system using structured CAD operations. Every operation happens inside the live Cadding project, so the human and the AI agent are working on the same editable model . How we built it One of the most important parts of Cadding is the Cadding API . We originally developed this API to give our own AI agent a simple and reliable way to interact with the CAD editor. For the WebMCP Challenge, we extended that architecture so external agents could use the same modelling capabilities. Instead of building a small set of WebMCP-specific demo commands, we connected WebMCP directly to Cadding's canonical CAD API. The architecture is: $$ \text{External Agent} \rightarrow \text{WebMCP} \rightarrow \text{Cadding API} \rightarrow \text{CAD Engine} \rightarrow \text{Live Editable Scene} $$ This means the WebMCP integration is not a separate prototype sitting next to Cadding. It is an interface into the real CAD system . An external agent can first understand what exists: $$ \texttt{cad.get_scene} + \texttt{cad.inspect_part} + \texttt{cad.get_parameters} $$ and then act on that information using operations such as: $$ \texttt{cad.add_shape}, \quad \texttt{cad.add_hole}, \quad \texttt{cad.boolean_parts}, \quad \texttt{cad.mate_parts} $$ This allows agents to chain multiple operations together to build and modify much more complex objects. Biggest challenge The biggest challenge while building both the Cadding AI agent and the WebMCP integration was making every CAD step extremely easy for an AI model to understand and execute correctly. CAD becomes complex very quickly. An agent needs to reason about dimensions, coordinate systems, part relationships, faces, edges, transformations, feature order, boolean operations, assemblies and the constantly changing state of the model. In simple terms: $$ \text{Reliable AI CAD} \text{Clear Tools} + \text{Precise Geometry Context} + \text{Predictable Execution} $$ Because of this, we spent a significant amount of time improving the Cadding API itself . Our goal was to hide as much unnecessary CAD-engine complexity as possible and turn modelling actions into clear, predictable and structured operations. Instead of expecting an AI model to understand the internal implementation of a CAD engine, we expose actions that map directly to the modelling intent: Create a part Inspect its dimensions Get its faces or edges Add a hole to a specific face Resize an existing body Round selected edges Subtract one body from another Pattern a component Align two parts Mate two faces together We also worked extensively on stable identifiers, constrained parameters, clear tool descriptions, validation and useful execution feedback. This work was critical for making both Cadding's own AI agent and external WebMCP agents more reliable. What we learned One of our biggest learnings was that giving an AI model access to tools is not enough . The way those tools are designed has a huge impact on how capable the agent becomes. We found that: $$ \text{Agent Quality} \propto \text{Quality of the Tool Interface} $$ Complex software like CAD contains a large amount of implicit state and domain knowledge. If the interface presented to the AI is ambiguous, the agent quickly becomes unreliable. By spending months making the Cadding API easier for AI models to reason about, we were able to turn increasingly complex CAD workflows into structured actions that agents can understand and combine. WebMCP allowed us to take that same agent-friendly CAD interface and make it accessible to external agents. The result is a shared CAD workspace where humans and AI agents can work together on the same real, editable and 3D-printable models . title: Sundae Metrics
pitch: A sales dashboard that hands agents 6 WebMCP tools instead of a picture of a chart. Same question, same page: 4m 38s without the tools, 36 seconds with them.
about_excerpt: A sales dashboard that hands agents 6 WebMCP tools instead of a picture of a chart. Same question, same page: 4m 38s without the tools, 36 seconds with them. Like Comment Story Updates An agent just changed the dashboard: the amber WRITE entry in the Agent activity rail, with an Undo on it. Inspiration Ice cream chains are the smallest business that genuinely needs analytics: four shops, six flavors, wildly seasonal, and no data analyst. The products already sold to them - HioPOS, Sipos, GETPOS, Vendty - all ship the same dashboard, and every question that dashboard cannot answer ends the same way: an Excel export. An assistant looking at that screen is in a worse position than the owner. Ask it "how much did North's sales change between February and March?" and, without WebMCP, it has to drive the whole interface: find the store selector in the DOM, synthesize a click, wait for a re-render with no signal that it finished, set the month range through a native picker, read the values back and do the arithmetic itself. It gets there - and I measured that rather than assuming it, which is what the section below is about. What it cannot do is get there cheaply. An interface built for eyes makes an agent pay in clicks, re-renders and round trips for something the page already knows exactly. What it does Sundae Metrics is a sales dashboard for Glace , a fictional chain of 4 artisanal ice cream shops: 12 months x 4 locations x 6 flavors. It is a normal dashboard - KPI cards, a 12-month bar chart, a flavor breakdown, a compare-periods view. The product is the layer underneath. The page registers 6 tools with document.modelContext.registerTool() : Tool What it does readOnlyHint list_stores Lists the locations on this dashboard true get_sales Exact units and revenue for one location in one month true compare_periods Percentage change between two months true get_top_flavors Flavor ranking - best sellers or slow movers true get_summary Revenue across every location over a date range true set_dashboard_view Changes what the user is looking at false The February-to-March question becomes one call: await compare_periods({ store: "north", monthA: "2026-02", monthB: "2026-03" }); // {"revenueChangePct":-17.1,"unitsChangePct":-15.4} And the dataset carries a case the chart actively hides. In January 2026 the North location's pistachio sales collapse from 2,099 units to 554 - down 74%, from the 3rd best seller to the 6th - a supply shortage. But January is also North's highest-revenue month of the year: the other five flavors each rise about 24% and absorb the gap, so the tallest bar on the chart is the one hiding the problem . Nothing on screen shows it. get_top_flavors({store: "north", month: "2026-01", limit: 3, order: "bottom"}) shows it immediately. set_dashboard_view runs the other way. Ask for the South location and the screen changes in front of you: the agent acts on the same interface the human is looking at, not on a copy of the data somewhere else. The measurement The demo video is not a mock-up. Both halves were filmed in the ChatGPT desktop app's built-in browser - same model, same question, same page, changing only ?webmcp=off : Without the tools With the tools Time 4 min 38 s 36 s Work navigated the UI month by month, then asked permission to download the page's data file 5 tool calls Answer pistachio 2,099 -> 554 (-74%) same, "fell from third-best seller to last" Both are right, and that is the honest claim. Without the tools the agent still gets there - the chart prints its values as text, so it reads them. What it cannot do is get there cheaply. It also tried to escape the screen entirely: three minutes in, it asked to download the dashboard's JavaScript data file rather than keep reading the interface. That request was denied on camera, because bypassing the rendered page is precisely what a real app with a backend would not allow. How I built it Vite + React + TypeScript, client-side only, no backend. Plain CSS with custom properties, no Tailwind. The chart is twelve div s with percentage heights, no charting library. Two dev dependencies beyond the template: vitest and webmcp-types . src/lib/queries.ts is the only place in the codebase that computes anything. The dashboard and the tools consume the same pure functions, so a number on the chart and a number returned by a tool cannot drift apart. 39,871 is what get_sales returns, what is printed on the March bar, and what the KPI card shows - one function, three consumers. 56 tests cover that layer, the state and the tool definitions. State is a module-level store exposed through useSyncExternalStore - mutable from outside React, which is exactly what set_dashboard_view needs. The dataset is generated by a seed script with no randomness at all : running it twice produces a byte-identical JSON, and the test file is the only place in the repo where the expected figures are written by hand. If the seed drifts, the tests fail. Accomplishments I'm proud of order: "bottom" is not decoration. The KPI those POS products actually sell to ice cream shops is "best sellers and slow movers", because owners use the second half to decide what to drop from the menu. It costs one parameter, not a seventh tool. No tool carries untrustedContentHint , and that is a decision, not an omission. Every value comes from a committed seed file, so no tool output can carry third-party text an agent might read as instructions. The hint exists for tools that return content someone else wrote; claiming it here would be noise. The Agent activity rail is the security answer, not chrome. How much a site should have to reveal about what an agent did on it is still open in the standard - prompt injection ( webmcp#11 ) and hints for consequential actions ( webmcp#176 ) are both unresolved. This dashboard's response is to make every call visible as it happens: tool name, input, output, elapsed time, output size against Chrome's 1,500-character ceiling, and an Undo on the one call that changed something. Indigo means the agent read; amber means the agent wrote. Nothing an agent does here is invisible. Challenges I ran into Chrome drops a malformed tool without raising anything. Exceed the name limit (30 chars), the tool description limit (500), a parameter description (150) or the output ceiling (1,500) and the tool is simply not registered - no error, no warning. annotations placed as a second argument instead of inside the tool object is ignored the same silent way. The fix was to compare getTools() against the six expected names after registering and log the difference, and to route every execute through one helper that truncates output to 1,500 characters. The question you ask changes whether the agent finds the anomaly. Asked "look at the flavor breakdown and tell me if anything looks off", the tool-driven agent fetched January only and concluded the anomaly was passion fruit - the cheapest flavor per unit. It failed that way twice in a row. With one month of flavor data, 554 units is not remarkable; the agent without tools got it right precisely because navigating the UI forced it through December as well. Asking for the comparison explicitly fixes it without naming pistachio. That is a WebMCP design lesson, not a demo detail: a tool that answers one month invites a one-month answer. The wording that shipped, identical in both halves of the video: "For the North store, what happened to sales in January 2026? Compare the flavor breakdown against December and tell me if anything looks off." Agents are not deterministic. Across five runs of the same question the figures never moved - 15,826 units, $50,800, pistachio 554 against 2,099 - but the conclusion was worded differently every time. The narration was written to whatever the agent actually said, rather than re-asking until a nicer sentence came out. What I learned That the interesting half of WebMCP is not exposing data - it is deciding what a tool is allowed to be . Six tools with one write among them, each one answering a question an owner would actually ask, beats twenty tools that mirror the internal data model. And the write tool is where the standard gets genuinely new: it is the first time an agent and a person can be looking at the same screen, and the agent can change it. What's next for Sundae Metrics Hourly granularity, channel mix (counter / dine-in / delivery), and a real backend behind the query layer - the tool contracts would not change, which is the point. The interesting open question is the trust model: the activity rail is one answer, but the standard has not settled on one yet. title: Gatherwire
pitch: Turn browser-agent actions into visible, source-linked handoffs your team can verify and continue.
about_excerpt: Turn browser-agent actions into visible, source-linked handoffs your team can verify and continue. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration For product and engineering teams using multiple AI assistants, the expensive step is often not generating an answer—it is moving a decision or finding to the next person or agent without losing its source, owner, or next action. Copying a summary into another chat strips away that provenance and makes the handoff hard to verify. Gatherwire explores a simple answer: give a person and a browser agent the same visible workspace, then make a handoff a durable, source-linked product object instead of another disposable chat message. What it does Gatherwire is a public WebMCP collaboration workspace. A person can use it like a compact team room. From that same top-level page, a compatible browser agent discovers seven structured site tools: gatherwire_list_spaces gatherwire_read_messages gatherwire_search_messages gatherwire_list_project_agents gatherwire_publish_handoff gatherwire_post_message gatherwire_create_space The main demo is a five-call mission. The agent lists the spaces, finds a seeded handoff note, reads its source room, finds the available demo project agent, and publishes a handoff to Atlas in the product room using the source message ID as evidence. The result appears immediately in the human interface: a visible capsule with a summary, one next action, the receiving agent, linked evidence, source room, task ID, and correlation ID. A separate receipt panel records the tool call, and clicking the evidence returns to the exact source message. The page marks the mission 5/5 , so evaluators can verify progress without opening a separate transcript. Gatherwire's completed challenge boundary is the handoff layer, not an external agent runtime. Atlas is synthetic and no external agent is started; this keeps discovery, shared state, provenance, and safe write behavior directly testable without implying a production bridge exists. Why WebMCP This experience depends on the page and visitor session the person already has open. A traditional remote API can expose backend functions, but it does not automatically give an agent the exact workspace, on-page progress, or visible receipts that the person sees. WebMCP lets the site declare a narrow capability layer directly: The browser agent does not have to guess where to click or scrape the interface. Human actions and agent calls use the same operations and the same HTTP API. Agent writes refresh the visible product state instead of disappearing into an isolated tool transcript. Inputs, side effects, and boundaries are explicit and inspectable. Without a page-native tool layer, this workflow typically means brittle UI automation or a separately installed integration, plus manual copying between chats. Gatherwire exposes the workflow from the page itself and turns a found message into a traceable collaboration artifact in one bounded flow. How we built it The page registers seven imperative tools with document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . Each definition has a focused description, a bounded JSON Schema, read/write annotations, and JSON-safe output. We intentionally avoided a single all-powerful “operate the workspace” tool. The human UI and WebMCP handlers call the same API. A dependency-free Node.js service serves the application and manages an isolated sample workspace for each visitor. Session IDs are opaque and host-only; unknown caller-supplied IDs are rotated instead of adopted. The handoff endpoint accepts only the synthetic agent returned by the demo. Every evidence ID must exist in the selected source space. Successful writes return stable task and correlation IDs. A caller-supplied request ID makes a retry idempotent; reusing the same ID with different content is rejected. All user-controlled content is length-bounded and rendered as text, never HTML. The live app runs on Google Cloud Compute Engine behind a dedicated Cloudflare Tunnel at gatherwire.vistua.de . The repository includes the complete source, deployment files, MIT license, verification record, and 15 automated tests covering session isolation, evidence validation, idempotency, security headers, tool contracts, and registration. Challenges The hardest question was not how to register a tool. It was how much authority a public demo should honestly give it. A useful handoff needs enough context to be actionable, but an unconstrained “run an agent” endpoint would be unsafe and misleading. We separated discovery, reading, searching, posting, room creation, agent listing, and handoff publication. We allowlisted the destination, required source-local evidence, and kept execution outside the challenge demo. The second challenge was legibility. A successful tool call is not enough if the person cannot tell what happened. That led to the five-step mission, visible receipts, evidence links, stable identifiers, and the handoff capsule itself. Accomplishments Seven native WebMCP tools are discoverable and executable from the live page. The complete mission was run in ChatGPT's in-app browser using native WebMCP. The final handoff was read back from the target room with matching task and correlation IDs. Repeating the same write request returned the existing capsule instead of creating a duplicate. Fifteen automated tests pass with zero failures, errors, or skips. Every visitor gets an isolated workspace; no account or credential is required. No customer data, private repository, production conversation, or external agent participates in the demo. What we learned WebMCP makes tool design part of product design. A good tool is not only callable; it has a truthful name, a narrow contract, understandable side effects, useful output, and visible feedback. We also learned that provenance can be a collaboration primitive. A summary is easy to lose or distrust. A source-linked artifact with evidence and stable IDs can survive the chat that created it and support the next person or agent. Challenge-period work The broader idea of Slack-like collaboration between people and project-bound agents, plus private experiments with backend orchestration, existed before this challenge. Gatherwire itself is a new standalone WebMCP app created during the submission period. The public commit history documents the seven browser-facing contracts, isolated workspace, handoff ledger, visible mission and receipts, validation rules, tests, deployment, and documentation added for the challenge. What's next The next layer is a real, permission-aware project-agent bridge behind the same handoff contract. Organizations could connect their own apps and runtimes while keeping the interaction stable: discover context, select an authorized destination, publish a source-linked task, and follow its status from the shared workspace. The longer-term goal is not another closed chat app. It is a modular context and handoff layer that helps existing web apps become safely usable by people and agents together. title: Agent Market: agents negotiate, you confirm
pitch: A marketplace where your browser's agent haggles a full deal (price, quantity, free add-ons, shipping, coupons) with the store's agent through WebMCP page tools. You confirm every order.
about_excerpt: A marketplace where your browser's agent haggles a full deal (price, quantity, free add-ons, shipping, coupons) with the store's agent through WebMCP page tools. You confirm every order. Like Comment Story Updates negotiation between seller and buyer interface Inspiration People delegate the boring parts of shopping, but the boring part that a plain API integration can never capture is the haggle . A price is one number; a real deal is price times quantity, which freebie the seller throws in, whether shipping is waived, and which coupon stacks on top. We wanted the shopper's browser agent to work that whole space on the site the user is already looking at, and still leave the final yes/no to a human. What it does Agent Market is a multi-vendor storefront with 95k+ real products. Every page registers storefront tools on document.modelContext (WebMCP): search, product details, cart, add-ons, coupons, and a full negotiation set. A buyer's agent opens a negotiation and haggles a multi-dimensional deal against the store's agent over several rounds. When they settle, the page shows a Confirm dialog and nothing is bought until the human confirms the price . The same tools work in a WebMCP browser (ChatGPT's in-app browser, Chrome with the flag) or drive an in-page agent loop that needs no API key from the user. How we built it Frontend: Next.js 15 / React 19 / TypeScript on Vercel. StorefrontTools registers every tool on document.modelContext ; lib/agent-loop.ts is a tool-agnostic agent harness that discovers tools from the registry and runs a hand-rolled chat-completions loop. Backend: Spring Boot (Java) on Render, Azure SQL, Flyway, Hibernate. One mutation path: every state change (buyer, seller, or the server-side auto-negotiator) goes through OffersService.applyTurn , a pure function that is the only code allowed to decide a negotiation transition. It enforces the two hard economic limits (buyer total <= budget, seller net >= floor); which freebie and how much to concede is agent judgment. Human gate: accepting mints an HMAC confirm token; the order is placed only when the human clicks Confirm. Model: Google Gemini through the OpenAI-compatible endpoint, key server-side only. Challenges we ran into Gemini "thinking" models and tool history. Gemini 3.x rejects a multi-turn tool conversation unless each function call's thought_signature is echoed back. The OpenAI-compat shim dropped it, so turn 2 always 400'd. We now capture tool_calls[].extra_content on the way in and replay it on the way out. Small models stall on long tool loops. Asking a fast model to drive search then offer then counter then counter then accept meant it derailed a turn later every time. We collapsed the buyer's negotiation into a single deterministic negotiate tool: the server plays both sides of the haggle, persists every round so the transcript is real, and returns a confirm token. The agent's job is now two calls, and reaching the confirm step no longer depends on the model finishing a loop. Optimistic concurrency vs agent reliability. A strict round guard made the agent stall forever when its round number drifted. We made the guard opt-in for proposals and mandatory only for the binding accept. What we learned WebMCP's value is not "expose an API"; it is that the agent operates the same surface the human sees, so the human can step in on any turn. And the moment a flow depends on an unreliable model completing N steps, move the deterministic part What we learned WebMCP's value is not "expose an API"; it is that the agent operates the same surface the human sees, so the human can step in on any turn. And the moment a flow depends on an unreliable model completing N steps, move the deterministic part to the server and leave the model the judgment call. What's next Seller-side takeover controls, agent-negotiated bundles across multiple sellers, and a browser-vs-browser two-agent mode for a fully agentic negotiation. title: Blnq Studio
pitch: Accessible-by-default web building. Blnq exposes its editor, live preview and WCAG audit to browser agents via WebMCP — so the AI that writes your code also catches its a11y violations.
about_excerpt: Accessible-by-default web building. Blnq exposes its editor, live preview and WCAG audit to browser agents via WebMCP — so the AI that writes your code also catches its a11y violations. Like Comment Story Updates 1 Inspiration I built blnq.studio because front-end work had become a pile of tabs: an editor, a dev server, a browser, DevTools, an accessibility checker, a design spec, and now an AI chat window that can't see any of them. Every one of those handoffs is where quality leaks out — especially accessibility, which is the first thing dropped when you're moving fast and the last thing an AI agent notices, because it can't see what it built. I wanted a single tab where the code, the live preview, the audit and the AI all look at the same thing. WebMCP was the missing piece: it lets the editor tab itself become the tool surface an agent uses, so the loop closes without any extra setup. What it does blnq.studio is a browser-based editor purpose-built for front-end: code, preview, ship — all in one tab. Live multi-file editing — Monaco under the hood, real HTML/CSS/JS files with folders and ES module imports, no build step. The preview updates as you type. Accessibility first — every preview refresh runs the pour engine against WCAG 2.0–2.2 A/AA plus best-practice rules. The A11y panel lists each violation with its impact, a plain-English fix and the exact element. Colour-contrast checks are built into the editor, not bolted on afterwards. Multi-device preview — switch viewports, check every breakpoint, see the FPS overlay, all without leaving the tab. Design systems your AI respects — drop a DESIGN.md at the project root and the editor treats it as the source of truth: colour and font literals that drift from your tokens get flagged, so AI-written CSS stays inside the system instead of inventing new values. Baseline compatibility — a built-in tool tab tells you which features you're using aren't yet widely available across browsers. Collaborate and fork — real-time multi-cursor collaboration over Yjs, forks and merge requests, a community showcase. Ship from the editor — push to GitHub, deploy from the menu, or download the whole project as one self-contained HTML file. AI & MCP, on your terms — AI is optional. When you want it, connect Claude Code (or any MCP client) over the built-in MCP server, use the in-editor chat with your own model, or — new for this challenge — turn on WebMCP and let a browser-native agent drive the tab directly. WebMCP: the editor tab is the tool server Click Start WebMCP and blnq registers 30+ tools with the browser via document.modelContext . No MCP ID, no config file, no separate process. An agent running in the browser can then: Read and edit files by line range or find-and-replace, with undo snapshots and live edits landing in the editor and preview See what it built — blnq_screenshot returns a real PNG, plus element inspection, console errors and viewport switching Audit with blnq_check_preview , which returns JS errors, every WCAG violation with its element HTML and fix hint, and any design-token drift Interact — click, type, press keys, wait for elements — so it can tab through a form or open a modal and re-audit the new state Fix and re-audit until the report is clean The key design decision was that WebMCP isn't a separate integration. blnq has one shared tool registry; the MCP server and the WebMCP endpoint are two thin adapters over it. A tool added to the registry appears in both, and edits behave identically — same validation, same undo, same activity toasts, same prompt history — whichever transport the call came in on. How I built it blnq is an Express + Monaco + Yjs app with a plugin system; the MCP server, AI chat, Baseline and spellcheck tools are all plugins. The accessibility engine runs inside the preview iframe and posts results up to the editor, so the panel a human reads and the result an agent reads come from the same run. WebMCP was around 350 lines: a client module that fetches tool descriptors and calls registerTool() for each (with readOnlyHint annotations and MCP-shaped { content } results including images), and a server endpoint that Zod-validates and runs the shared handler. The endpoint is same-origin only and still requires the tab's random bridge ID; the browser handles user consent on its side. What I learned The accessibility audit turned out to be the most valuable thing blnq can hand an agent. A screenshot tells a model roughly what it built; a WCAG report with the offending element and a fix hint tells it exactly what to change. Structured, model-readable audit output beat any amount of prompt engineering. And WebMCP inverts the usual relationship: the page stops being something an agent scrapes and becomes something it calls . Once you have a decent tool registry, the browser becomes the integration layer for free. What's next Structured JSON from blnq_check_preview so agents can diff violations between audits A blnq_fix_a11y tool that applies remedies for common rule classes automatically Focus-order and keyboard-navigation audits driven by key-press sequences Ship the Chrome origin-trial token on blnq.studio so WebMCP works without flags Share a collaboration session with an agent so humans and AI can work on the same project live Built With ai css framework-free html javascript Try it out blnq.studio Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by David Yarham Like Share this project: Updates David Yarham posted an update — Aug 26, 2026 04:58 PM EDT I dont have a youtube or any video of Blnq, it is a live site and no need Log in or sign up for Devpost to join the conversation. title: Airlock: Agent-Native Data Workspace
pitch: AI analysis for file you can't upload. In-browser DuckDB plus WebMCP tools, every change staged for your approval, with a signed receipt of what the agent saw.
about_excerpt: AI analysis for file you can't upload. In-browser DuckDB plus WebMCP tools, every change staged for your approval, with a signed receipt of what the agent saw. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Every team has a spreadsheet nobody is allowed to paste into ChatGPT: compensation, customer lists, finances under NDA. Yet people paste anyway — roughly 11% of ChatGPT pastes contain confidential information, a fifth of breaches now involve shadow AI, and AI chats have been ruled discoverable in court. We wanted the analysis without the upload: AI help with data that physically cannot leave the room. What it does Airlock is a data workspace in a single browser tab. Your file is read locally and queried with in-browser DuckDB-WASM — nothing uploads, ever. An AI agent works on it through WebMCP tools the page exposes: 8 read tools that run immediately and are logged, and 12 staged actions where every change (filters, derived columns, charts, flags, reports, redaction, export) appears as a visible diff that nothing applies until you press Approve. An activity ledger records every call with exact rows disclosed. A signed attestation receipt — hashes and counts, never values — verifies offline at /verify.html . God mode runs a Qwen model fully on-device via WebGPU for genuine airplane-mode analysis, or bring your own endpoint key, which never leaves tab memory. It also imports PDF, DOCX and images OCR'd on-device into queryable tables. How we built it React 18 + Vite + TypeScript + Tailwind, npm workspaces. The reusable core is packages/webmcp-staged — a zero-dependency propose→review→commit primitive spanning WebMCP, OpenAI tool-calling and plain MCP transports. DuckDB-WASM, pdf.js, Tesseract and the model weights are all self-hosted same-origin; an egress monitor wrapping fetch/XHR/beacon/WebSocket proves zero bytes leave, live, in the top bar. 530+ tests, npm audit clean, Netlify deploy with COOP/COEP, WASM MIME types and origin-trial support. Challenges we ran into Honesty was harder than engineering: "data never leaves the browser" is false the moment a cloud agent reads query results, so cloud mode states plainly that slices travel (and counts them) while the fully-local loop makes the strong claim literally true. Small models were the second fight — 1.5B-parameter callers loop, invert comparisons and stuff GROUP BY into filter boxes — answered with schema-tolerant tools, corrective errors, repeat guards and a fail-fast circuit breaker. Third was host discovery: WebMCP gates on origin isolation and trial enrollment, which took real header and deploy work. Accomplishments that we're proud of A complete loop the camera can verify: offline analysis with Seal at zero, every mutation human-gated, a signed receipt that verifies offline, and an agent surface ChatGPT, a local model, your own endpoint, or the built-in console can all drive unchanged. Plus a reusable MIT primitive any WebMCP app can adopt for the same propose→approve→commit safety. What we learned Agent UX is approval UX — the review queue, not the chat, is where trust happens. A privacy claim the code can't back is worse than no claim at all. And tiny on-device models are usable agents if the tool surface is tight enough to hold them. What's next for Airlock: Agent-Native Data Workspace Depth over breadth: the pay-equity workflow first (EU Pay Transparency deadlines make the receipt a requirement, not a nicety), then adjacent regulated-data reviews. On the tech side: richer provenance-linked reports, local folder and localhost-database sources, and a second independent implementation of the staged-authority protocol so the receipt becomes an interoperable standard, not a single-app artifact. title: Live Canvas
pitch: This demo explores user interfaces that adapt to the humans that browse it, and asks what would the web be if you could B-Y-O-U-I: Bring your own user interface.
about_excerpt: This demo explores user interfaces that adapt to the humans that browse it, and asks what would the web be if you could B-Y-O-U-I: Bring your own user interface. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration For as much as marketers have optimized for conversion, they haven't been able to cut through the number one reason that people leave open carts. they're not ready to buy. It had just happened to me while shopping for a microphone: I started at one site, then realized I needed more information to determine which was going to be the best fit. What if the shopping interface could have met me where I was at--researching the options, ranking the matches, explaining its rationale, and then designing a search result layout to fit its conclusions? That's just one glimpse of how web-interfaces of the future will adapt to their users' needs through a Live Canvas. What it does Each demo walks you through a conventional user interface, and then cordons off a bounded portion of it as WebMCP to redesign (the Live Canvas) The Storefront demo lets the agent curate the search results with a toolbox of approved card presets and badges. This constrained design is a good fit for the untrusted nature of the public internet, keeping users safe from XSS attacks. The Dashbord demo scales the idea up by giving you an entirely blank page. It imagine how the future of CRM / ERP dashboards might function. Prompt the agent to onboard you, collaborate on a vision with the agent as you would with your analytics team, and the end result is an entirely personal dashboard of controls, visualizations and reports. The Distribution demo scales the idea outwards by asking whether you distribute a Live Canvas as part of conventional component libraries. It demonstrates what a future Datatable component could be, with the ability to generate bespoke reports and save them to your browser - all without backend engineering or ai-vendor lock-in. How we built it The architecture north star is "agent composition, application execution". The application exposes its UI primitives through WebMCP. The agent supplies a composition, and then the live canvas renders that composition using application-owned components. This solution prevents data from leaking out of the organization's security boundary, and also prevents token bloat. Challenges we ran into and accomplishments that we're proud of There are two large challenges that required creativity: The largest challenge was discoverability. WebMCP is not bidirectional: an agent can invoke tools, but there's no mechanism for the website to initiate a conversation. The past 30 years of the web have trained users for the affordance of buttons and forms. I built a new set of visible prompts and verbs to communicate to surface the new modality which was an interesting accomplishment, but does highlight an apparent shortcoming in the standard. The second challenge is the built-in approval flow of agentic browsers. ChatGPT would auto-deny requests to access the user's simulated library to make recommendations, e.g. In the short term, this is solved with instructional text to ask for permission in advance. However, what WebMCP needs is a built in consent layer where tools are tied to required consent artifacts. What we learned WebMCP shows great potential to break interfaces out of the "ai chatbot jail". What's next for Live Canvas The most likely next step is to select an existing open-source component library and use it to build the first end-to-end WebMCP UI framework. That would turn the Live Canvas from just a demo pattern into a production-hardened implementation. title: Cobweb - WebMCP enabled Micropython IDE
pitch: Cobweb is a zero-install browser IDE bringing WebMCP to physical hardware: AI agents can probe microcontrollers, edit device files, run MicroPython code live, and debug boards with human approval.
about_excerpt: Cobweb is a zero-install browser IDE bringing WebMCP to physical hardware: AI agents can probe microcontrollers, edit device files, run MicroPython code live, and debug boards with human approval. Like Comment Story Updates 💡 Inspiration Physical computing and IoT have always promised an exciting world of creativity—turning code into blinking LEDs, motor movements, robotics, and environmental sensors. Yet for beginners, educators, and even seasoned makers, the onboarding experience is plagued by toolchain friction: Hunting down and installing OS-specific USB-to-UART drivers (CH340, CP2102, FTDI). Configuring desktop IDEs like Thonny, Arduino IDE, or heavy VS Code toolchains. Juggling serial baud rates, COM port drops, and manual file transfer scripts. With modern browser capabilities like the Web Serial API and File System Access API , we realized that the entire embedded development lifecycle could run 100% inside the browser with zero installation . When WebMCP was introduced as an open standard for agentic web applications, we asked a fundamental question: Why should AI agents only interact with web forms, spreadsheets, and SaaS tools? What if an AI agent had physical hands on hardware? Cobweb was born to bridge this divide—creating a zero-install MicroPython IDE where humans and AI agents collaborate seamlessly to probe, code, execute, and debug physical microcontrollers. ⚡ What it Does Cobweb turns any Chromium browser into a full-featured MicroPython development environment that connects directly to microcontrollers (such as Raspberry Pi Pico, ESP32, or BBC micro:bit) over Web Serial at $115{,}200\text{ baud}$. Key capabilities include: Zero-Install Python IDE : Code editor powered by CodeMirror 6 with syntax highlighting, automatic indenting, and multi-file local storage. Interactive xterm.js REPL : Direct serial connection with live terminal streaming, ANSI color rendering, and raw-paste mode. Device Filesystem Management : Browse, read, write, edit, and delete files stored on the microcontroller's onboard flash memory. Deep WebMCP Integration : Exposes 15+ fine-grained, structured tools to external AI agents via document.modelContext.registerTool . Human-in-the-Loop Safety : Every mutating agent action (flashing files, modifying code, running hardware commands) triggers an interactive approval modal with live side-by-side diff previews before anything touches the physical board. Board Hardware Notes : Persistent scratchpad where the agent and user track pin mappings (e.g., $I^2C$ SDA/SCL pins, SPI buses, ADC channels, and sensor addresses). 🛠️ How We Built It Cobweb is built as a pure client-side Progressive Web App (PWA) with no backend servers or cloud dependencies: ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ External AI Agent │ │ (ChatGPT / Chrome with WebMCP) │ └──────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┘ │ WebMCP JSON-RPC / Tools API ▼ ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Cobweb WebApp │ │ ┌───────────────────────┐ ┌────────────────────────┐ │ │ │ WebMcpBridge.tsx │◄─────►│ Tool Registry │ │ │ │ (use-webmcp-tool) │ │ (15+ Structured Tools) │ │ │ └───────────┬───────────┘ └───────────┬────────────┘ │ │ │ │ │ │ ▼ ▼ │ │ ┌─────────────────────┐ ┌────────────────────────┐ │ │ │ CobwebApproval Modal│ │ ReplInterface (TS) │ │ │ │ (Live Diffs) │ │ (Raw REPL State Mach.) │ │ │ └─────────────────────┘ └────────────┬───────────┘ │ └──────────────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────┘ │ Web Serial API ▼ ┌───────────────────────────┐ │ Physical Board (Pico) │ └───────────────────────────┘ 1. The WebMCP Bridge ( WebMcpBridge.tsx ) We utilized use-webmcp-tool to dynamically expose our tool registry to the browser's model context: useWebMCP({ name: def.name, description: def.description, inputSchema: def.parameters, async execute(args) { if (def.requiresApproval) { const approved = await requestApproval({ id, name: def.name, args }); if (!approved) throw new Error('Tool execution rejected by user.'); } return await tool.call(args, {}); } }); 2. High-Performance Serial Communication ( ReplInterface.ts ) MicroPython communication relies on a custom finite state machine implementing the raw-REPL protocol : Raw Mode Entry : The host sends \x01 ($\text{Ctrl-A}$) to enter raw REPL. Raw-Paste Windowing : To prevent buffer overrun on microcontrollers with constrained RAM ($\approx 264\text{ KB}$ on RP2040), we implement dynamic flow control: $$\text{Chunk Size} \le W_{\text{window}}, \quad \text{replenished by } \text{\textbackslash x01 bytes}$$ Execution & Stream Separation : Code is executed via \x04 ($\text{Ctrl-D}$), returning structured stdout and stderr delimited by end-of-transmission bytes: $$\text{Banner} \longrightarrow \text{OK} \longrightarrow \text{stdout} \longrightarrow \text{\textbackslash x04} \longrightarrow \text{stderr} \longrightarrow \text{\textbackslash x04}$$ Queue Serialisation : An AsyncBlockingQueue<Uint8Array> safely decouples serial reads from async execution promises while mirroring bytes to xterm.js . 🧗 Challenges We Ran Into 1. Single-Channel Serial Contention The Web Serial port is a single, non-multiplexed stream. If a user is typing in the REPL while an AI agent attempts to run get_board_info or read_device_file , raw bytes interleave and corrupt the state. Solution : We built a single-slot promise lock chain for all read/write/eval calls ( send , sendRaw , reset ), ensuring strict atomicity without blocking UI rendering or serial event dispatching. 🏆 Accomplishments That We're Proud Of 100% Client-Side Architecture : Zero backend servers, zero telemetry, zero credential relay. Everything runs directly between the user's browser and their USB port. True Agentic Physical Computing : An AI agent running in ChatGPT or Chrome can inspect the board identity ( os.uname().machine ), write sensor drivers, execute test snippets, and diagnose hardware errors in real time. Rich Human-Agent Co-Pilot Experience : Instead of replacing the human, WebMCP in Cobweb creates a fluid dialogue where the human handles breadboarding and hardware wiring, while the agent handles MicroPython syntax, pin registers, and driver debugging. 📚 What We Learned WebMCP is a Game Changer for Browser Capabilities : Traditional desktop agent tools require complex native MCP servers (stdio/SSE over localhost). WebMCP brings tool calling directly to the browser DOM and Web APIs, making cutting-edge capabilities like Web Serial, Web Bluetooth, and File System Access instantly accessible to AI agents. Structured Tools Beat Vision/DOM Scraping : Prior to WebMCP, agents navigating web IDEs had to guess button positions or scrape xterm canvases. With WebMCP, tool calls are typed, deterministic, and instant. title: Aletheia
pitch: Research and human–AI collaboration made simple.
about_excerpt: Research and human–AI collaboration made simple. Like Comment Story Updates Shared evidence desk with linked sources, focused excerpts, and a separate agent-review workspace. Sources view: five curated excerpts from three linked pages at two institutions. Actual WebMCP calls placed an evidence-backed proposal in visible shared state without accepting it. A bounded request records missing Panamanian and Caribbean perspectives without inventing a citation. Reviewer controls keep evidence inspection, qualifications, source requests, and acceptance visible. Automated QA test of the acceptance control—not presented as a historical human approval. The activity trail distinguishes agent calls, the scripted guided demo, and reviewer actions. Inspiration My inspiration is wanting to teach proper information. For months, I have been gathering information about history and other subjects and turning it into a teaching structure. I wanted a way to work with AI without hiding the sources, intermediate steps, or places where human judgment is still necessary. What it does Aletheia Evidence Desk turns the open webpage into a shared research workspace for a person and an agent. The Panama Canal example brings together a working claim, five curated excerpts from three source pages at two institutions, direct links to the source material, a proposed revision, an evidence-gap request, and an activity record. The agent can read the current workspace, list the checked sources, search the curated evidence, focus excerpts in the visible canvas, select a source, propose a revised claim, leave a review note, and request another source. Those actions stay visible to the person. The reviewer can inspect the evidence and original sources, qualify the draft, ask for more material, leave the proposal unaccepted, or accept it as a draft. Why WebMCP fits this use case This workflow depends on shared page context: which source is selected, which excerpts are focused, what proposal is pending, and what the reviewer has decided. A separate remote research service would not automatically share that live context. WebMCP exposes small, typed, page-native actions so the person and agent can work on the same visible state instead of moving disconnected answers between a chat and a research page. That creates a better experience because the evidence selected by the agent appears immediately in the human interface, every displayed source can be opened at its institutional page, and the activity trail explains what happened. This cooperation between person and agent is the part that was difficult before: the agent can do bounded research work while the person can see, question, and redirect every important step. How we built it We built a standalone React and Vite application in JavaScript. Eight tools are registered through document.modelContext.registerTool and call the same state handlers used by the ordinary interface: get_workspace_state, list_sources, search_evidence, focus_evidence, set_source_focus, propose_claim_revision, leave_review_note, and request_additional_source. JSON schemas constrain the inputs, annotations identify read-only and untrusted content where appropriate, and automated tests cover the tool handlers and review boundary. The application is deployed through GitHub Actions to GitHub Pages. The public repository contains the source code, assets, tests, instructions, and an MIT license. Desk, Sources, and Review are browser-addressable views, and the ordinary interface remains usable when WebMCP is unavailable. Challenges we ran into The main challenge was making agent actions visible without turning the product into a developer console. Working with an AI agent also requires the same kind of communication and checking that any collaboration requires. Model output can be incomplete, incorrect, or poorly timed, so the interface needed to distinguish source evidence, interpretation, and reviewer approval. We also needed to keep the claims honest. The source set supports a limited demonstration, not a complete history of the Panama Canal. The app therefore records missing Panamanian and Caribbean perspectives instead of pretending that the current material is comprehensive. Accomplishments we are proud of We are proud that the finished prototype exposes eight usable WebMCP tools while keeping their effects understandable to a person. The agent proposal remains separate from the working claim, source links open the underlying institutional material, evidence gaps stay visible, and the review can be exported. We are also proud to be participating in the early stages of a more cooperative open web for people and AI. What we learned What we learned during this exercise is how to use AI efficiently through cooperation with human interaction. Professionally, we can use this whenever we need to research and verify our steps using AI and the information currently available on the internet. I use this process for teaching and for developing other historical presentations. The most important lesson is that human interaction remains necessary. AI can accelerate searching, organizing, testing, and drafting, but the person must still inspect sources, recognize missing perspectives, and decide what should become part of the final work. Prototype limits The demonstration searches five prepared excerpts rather than the wider web. It does not automatically verify or attach a new citation. Source requests record evidence gaps without inventing evidence. Local browser storage retains the working example rather than providing a secure shared database. The guided review is explicitly labeled as scripted, and the reviewer controls are a workflow distinction rather than an authentication barrier against general browser automation. What's next for Aletheia We plan to continue developing Aletheia for teaching, historical presentations, and other evidence-heavy work. Future steps include user-supplied source collections, persistent projects, citation-range verification, collaborative review, accessibility testing, and support for additional research domains.
